cards.title: Backends and stateless services
cards.body:
The **frontend** is the part people touch: a web page or a mobile app. It only deals with one person's data. The **backend** runs on servers and answers requests from every user at once, so that's where the hard data problems are.

A backend service is usually application code plus **data infrastructure**: databases, caches, message queues. The code is often **stateless**: once it has answered a request, it forgets it. Anything that has to survive until the next request, like a half-filled form, must live on the client or in that infrastructure.

cards.prompt: A backend service is stateless. A user adds an item to their cart, then opens the cart in a separate request. Where must the cart be kept between the two requests?
choices: On the client, or in a database or cache the service uses
In the service's memory, until the user's session ends
Nowhere: a stateless service can't support a shopping cart
cards.explanation: Stateless means the service forgets each request once it's handled, so anything that must outlast a request lives on the client or in the data infrastructure. Keeping it in memory would make the service stateful. Statelessness doesn't forbid state; it moves it out of the application code.

cards.title: OLTP and OLAP
cards.body:
Picture a food delivery app. When a customer orders, the app looks up a few rows by key and inserts or updates one or two. That's **online transaction processing (OLTP)**: lots of small, fast queries, fixed in the app's code, on the *current* state of the data.

Now a manager asks for the average delivery time per city last quarter. That query scans millions of rows and returns a few totals. That's **analytics (OLAP)**: few, heavy, ad-hoc queries written by analysts, over the *history* of what happened. Its data arrives as bulk imports or a stream of events, not one record at a time.

cards.prompt: How do OLTP and OLAP workloads differ? Compare reads, writes, who writes the queries, and what the data represents.
keyPoints: Reads: OLTP fetches a few records by key; OLAP aggregates over huge numbers of records
Writes: OLTP creates, updates and deletes single records; OLAP takes bulk imports or event streams
Queries: OLTP runs a fixed set built into the app; OLAP runs ad-hoc queries from analysts
Data: OLTP holds the current state; OLAP holds the history of what happened
cards.explanation: OLTP serves users one record at a time; OLAP serves analysts looking at the big picture.

cards.prompt: Before showing an account page, a banking app checks whether the logged-in user may view that account. What kind of workload is this check?
choices: OLAP, because a machine runs it rather than a human analyst
OLAP, because it only reads data
HTAP, because the app both reads and writes
OLTP: a quick lookup of a few records by key, on current data
cards.explanation: It's a point query on current state, the core OLTP pattern. Machines run analytical queries too (fraud detection, for example), so who runs it doesn't decide. OLTP reads as well as writes. HTAP means one system serving both kinds of workload, not an app that reads and writes.

cards.title: Who writes the queries
cards.body:
In an operational system, end users generally don't get to write SQL. The application runs a fixed set of queries that its developers wrote.

Letting users write their own would be risky in two ways. A query could read or change data the user has no right to touch. And one badly written query could keep the database busy and slow it down for everybody else.

Analytical systems work the other way round. Analysts are trusted to explore, so they write whatever SQL they like, or let a dashboard tool generate it.

cards.prompt: Why do operational systems rarely let users run their own SQL queries?
choices: SQL is designed for analytics and handles single-record lookups poorly
Custom queries could reach data the user isn't allowed to see, and expensive ones could slow the database for everyone
Operational databases only hold current state, so ad-hoc questions about history would fail
cards.explanation: Access control and performance are the concerns, so OLTP apps run a fixed set of queries built into the code. SQL handles point lookups and analytics equally well. Missing history limits what you could learn, but it isn't why custom queries are blocked.

cards.title: Data warehouses
cards.body:
Companies used to run reports straight against their operational databases. Most now copy the data into a separate **data warehouse**, for four reasons.

The data is scattered over many operational systems (*data silos*), so one query can't combine it. Schemas and storage layouts that suit OLTP are a poor fit for analytics. Heavy analytical queries would slow the app down for its users. And the operational databases may sit on networks that analysts aren't allowed into.

A warehouse holds a read-only copy of all of it, laid out for analysis, where analysts can run anything without touching production.

cards.prompt: Why do companies run analytics on a separate data warehouse instead of querying their operational databases directly?
keyPoints: The data is spread across many operational systems, so one query can't easily combine it
Schemas and data layouts that suit OLTP suit analytics poorly
Heavy analytical queries would slow the database down for its regular users
Operational systems may sit on networks analysts aren't allowed to reach
cards.explanation: A warehouse is a read-only copy that analysts can query as much as they like without touching production.

cards.title: ETL
cards.body:
Data reaches a warehouse through **ETL**: *extract, transform, load*.

A job first extracts data from the operational databases, either as periodic dumps or as a continuous stream of changes. Then it transforms the data: reshaping it into a schema built for analysis and cleaning up bad values. Finally it loads the result into the warehouse, where analysts can query it.

In **ELT** the last two steps swap: the raw data is loaded first and transformed inside the warehouse. Some sources are SaaS products, like a CRM, that you can only read through the vendor's API.

cards.prompt: Put the steps of loading a data warehouse with ETL in order.
items: Pull data out of the operational databases, as periodic dumps or a stream of changes
Reshape it into an analysis-friendly schema and clean it up
Load it into the warehouse
Analysts query it
cards.explanation: In ELT, transform and load swap places: raw data is loaded first and transformed inside the warehouse.

cards.title: HTAP
cards.body:
**HTAP** (hybrid transactional/analytical processing) databases offer OLTP and analytics in one system, with no ETL in between. They shine when a single application needs both at once: say, a ride app that scans the last hour of trips in an area to set a surge price, then writes the fare for one ride.

They don't make warehouses obsolete. A company has many operational databases, often one per service, and analysts still need one place that brings them together. And many HTAP systems are really an OLTP engine and an analytical engine behind one interface, so the split is still there inside.

cards.prompt: Which workload is the best fit for an HTAP database?
choices: A payment check that scans a customer's recent history, then updates their record, in a single request
A monthly report that combines sales, inventory and HR data from separate systems
A nightly job that trains an image model on millions of photos
A web store's product pages, served by key lookups
cards.explanation: HTAP fits when one application needs large scans and low-latency record updates together, as in fraud detection. Combining many separate systems is a warehouse's job. Training on photos suits a data lake. Plain key lookups are ordinary OLTP.

cards.prompt: Why doesn't HTAP make data warehouses unnecessary?
keyPoints: Companies have many operational databases, often one per service, but analysts need one place that combines them
HTAP suits a single application that needs both large scans and fast record updates
Many HTAP systems are an OLTP engine and an analytical engine behind one interface, so the split still exists
cards.explanation: HTAP blurs the line inside one application; the warehouse still joins data across the whole company.

cards.title: Data lakes
cards.body:
Warehouses suit business analysts, who think in SQL tables. Data scientists often don't. Turning rows into features for a machine learning model takes custom code that's awkward in SQL. Their inputs may be text, images or audio. And they'd rather use dataframe libraries in Python or R than a relational database.

A **data lake** serves them: a central store of *files* in any format, with no schema imposed. It's usually cheaper too, since it can sit on object storage. Lakes often keep data *raw*, as the source produced it, so each consumer can reshape it however it needs.

cards.prompt: What's the key difference between a data lake and a data warehouse?
choices: A lake is the system of record; a warehouse is derived from it
A lake serves business analysts; a warehouse serves data scientists
A lake stores files in any format with no imposed schema; a warehouse stores data in a relational schema
A lake only holds real-time event streams
cards.explanation: A lake accepts anything (records, text, images, sensor readings) as plain files. Both are copies of operational data, so neither is the system of record. The audiences are the other way around: lakes arose for data scientists, warehouses for BI analysts. And a lake holds files of any kind, not only streams.

cards.prompt: Why do data scientists often prefer a data lake to a data warehouse?
keyPoints: Preparing ML features takes custom code that's hard to write in SQL
Their data includes text, images and other unstructured data that doesn't fit tables
They prefer dataframe libraries and general-purpose languages over a relational database
A lake is usually cheaper, since it can sit on object storage

cards.prompt: Why keep data in its raw form in a data lake instead of transforming it once on the way in?
choices: Raw data takes less space than transformed data
Each consumer can shape the raw data into whatever form suits it best
Raw data needs no pipeline to get out of the operational systems
Raw data is faster to query
cards.explanation: One fixed transformation serves one set of needs; raw data lets every consumer do its own. Raw data isn't necessarily smaller or faster to query, and it still has to be copied out of the operational systems by a pipeline.

cards.title: Reverse ETL
cards.body:
Data doesn't only flow from operational systems into analytical ones. Sometimes the results of analysis flow back: this is **reverse ETL**.

Say a music app copies everyone's listening history into its analytical system and trains a model there that predicts which songs you'll like. The trained model is then deployed into an operational service, which uses it to suggest songs to listeners as they use the app.

cards.prompt: Order how an ML recommendation reaches users through reverse ETL.
items: Users' purchases are recorded in operational databases
The data is copied into the analytical system
A recommendation model is trained there
The model is deployed to an operational service
Users see its recommendations
cards.explanation: Reverse ETL closes the loop: results built on the analytics side flow back into the systems users touch.

cards.title: Systems of record, derived data
cards.body:
A **system of record**, or *source of truth*, holds the authoritative copy of some data. New data is written there first, and if any other copy disagrees, the system of record wins by definition.

**Derived data** is computed from another system: a cache, a search index, a materialized view, a trained model. If you lose it, you can rebuild it from the source, and whenever the source changes, some process has to update it. It duplicates information, but it earns its place: it makes reads fast, and it lets you view the same data in different shapes.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between a system of record and derived data?
keyPoints: The system of record holds the authoritative version, and new data is written there first
If the two disagree, the system of record is right by definition
Derived data is computed from another system and can be rebuilt from it if lost
Derived data needs a process that updates it when the source changes
cards.explanation: Caches, indexes, materialized views and trained ML models are all derived data.

cards.prompt: A disk failure destroys a product search index. The products table in the primary database is fine. What now?
choices: The products are gone for good, since the index held them
Restore the index from a backup; it can't be rebuilt
Rebuild the index from the products table
Roll the database back to before the failure
cards.explanation: The index is derived data: everything in it came from the table, so it can be recreated. The products themselves live in the system of record, which is untouched. Nothing is wrong with the database, so there's nothing to roll back.

cards.prompt: Derived data duplicates information that already exists. Why keep it?
choices: It makes reads fast, and lets you look at the same data in different ways
It acts as a backup if the system of record is lost
It makes sure each fact is stored exactly once
cards.explanation: Indexes, caches and views are redundant on purpose, to answer queries the source can't answer quickly. They aren't backups: they may be partial or stale, and they aren't authoritative. Storing each fact once is the system of record's job; derived data does the opposite.

cards.title: A role, not a product
cards.body:
Most databases aren't systems of record or derived stores by nature. Each is a tool, and your architecture gives it the role. The same PostgreSQL might be where a clinic first records its appointments, making it the source of truth, or it might hold a search-friendly copy rebuilt every night from another system.

Being explicit about which data comes from which keeps a complex system understandable. It also tells you what to build: every derived dataset needs a pipeline that carries changes over from its source. Many databases assume they're the only one you use, so you often wire this up yourself.

cards.prompt: Two teams use the same database software. Team A writes orders into its database. Team B copies those orders into its own database to power dashboards. Which one is the system of record?
choices: Both, since they run the same software
Team A's, since that's where orders are first written
Team B's, since that's where people read the data
Neither: only databases built for the purpose can be systems of record
cards.explanation: Being a system of record depends on how a database is used, not on the product. Team A's database gets the data first; Team B's is a derived copy. Reads happen everywhere, so they don't decide it.

cards.prompt: A user changes their display name. Order how the change flows through the system.
items: The backend receives the request
The backend writes the new name to the system of record
A process updates the search index built from that data
A later ETL run copies the change into the data warehouse
cards.explanation: New data lands in the system of record first; every derived system (indexes, caches, the warehouse) catches up from there.

cards.title: Build or buy
cards.body:
For anything an organization needs, it can do it in-house or outsource it. A rule of thumb: keep what gives you an edge in-house, and buy what's routine.

With software there are two questions: who writes it, and who runs it. At one end is software you write and run yourself. In the middle is **self-hosting** off-the-shelf software, like an open-source database, either on your own hardware (*on-premises*) or on a rented cloud VM (*IaaS*). At the far end is a **SaaS** or cloud service: the vendor builds and runs it, and you only touch its API.

cards.prompt: Order these from most done in-house to most outsourced.
items: Software you write and run on your own servers
Open-source software you install on servers you own
Open-source software you install on a cloud VM
A SaaS product you use only through its API
cards.explanation: Two separate choices: who builds the software and who runs it. Down the list, you first outsource the building, then the hardware, then the running.

cards.title: When the cloud saves money
cards.body:
Cloud providers promise to save you time and money. Whether they do depends on your skills and on your load.

If your team already knows how to run a system and the load is steady, buying your own machines is often cheaper. If the system is new to you, a managed service spares you hiring and training people to operate it.

The cloud wins clearly when load **varies** a lot. Hardware sized for the peak sits idle the rest of the time; in the cloud you scale up when you need to and hand resources back afterwards. Large interactive analytics is the classic case.

cards.prompt: A team has years of experience running their database, and its load barely changes through the year. Which option is likely cheapest?
choices: A cloud service, because providers' scale makes them cheaper
A cloud service, because autoscaling saves the most on steady load
Buying their own machines and running it themselves
cards.explanation: With the skills already in-house and predictable load, owning the hardware is often cheaper. The cloud isn't cheaper by default. Autoscaling pays off when load swings, not when it's flat.

cards.prompt: Analysts occasionally run huge interactive queries over a very large dataset. Between queries, the hardware sits idle. What's the most cost-effective setup?
choices: Own servers sized for the largest query
Own servers sized for the average load
Queue the queries and run them one at a time to smooth out the load
Cloud resources scaled up for each query and handed back afterwards
cards.explanation: Spiky load is where the cloud wins: you pay for lots of parallel compute only while it's in use. Servers sized for the peak sit idle most of the time; servers sized for the average make interactive queries slow. Queueing works for scheduled reports, but interactive users are waiting for answers.

cards.title: Giving up control
cards.body:
With a cloud service, you give up control. If a feature is missing, you can only ask the vendor for it. When the service is down, you wait. When it's slow or buggy, you can't read its logs or its OS metrics to find out why.

If the vendor raises prices, changes the product or shuts it down, you have to migrate, because running the old version yourself isn't an option. Without standard APIs, switching is costly: that's **vendor lock-in**. You also have to trust the provider to keep your data safe.

cards.prompt: What do you give up when you use a cloud service instead of running the software yourself?
keyPoints: You can't add missing features or fix bugs yourself; you can only ask the vendor
When the service is down, all you can do is wait
Debugging is hard: you can't see the server's logs or OS metrics
If the vendor raises prices, changes or shuts down the product, you're forced to migrate
cards.explanation: Without a standard API, switching is costly: that's vendor lock-in. Other risks are sanctions cutting you off from a foreign provider, and having to trust the provider with your data's security.

cards.title: Cloud native
cards.body:
Running a database on a cloud VM doesn't make it **cloud native**. A cloud native system is designed for the cloud: rather than relying only on its machines' CPUs, memory and disks, it's built on top of lower-level cloud services.

The main building block is **object storage**, such as Amazon S3. Its API is simpler than a filesystem's: you read and write whole files. In return it spreads the data over many machines for you, so you never run out of disk, and a failed disk loses nothing. Systems built this way tend to recover faster, scale more easily and handle larger datasets.

cards.prompt: What makes a database cloud native, rather than just running in the cloud?
choices: It's built on other cloud services, such as object storage, instead of only its machines' own disks and OS
It runs on VMs rented from a cloud provider
It's offered by a cloud vendor as a managed service
It's deployed with a container orchestrator
cards.explanation: Cloud native systems are designed around lower-level cloud services. Traditional software on a rented VM is still self-hosted. A managed version of traditional software is convenient but not cloud native by design. Deployment tooling doesn't change the architecture.

cards.title: Disks in the cloud
cards.body:
A VM's **local disk** is fast, but cloud native systems treat it as a cache. If the instance fails, or is swapped for a bigger one on another machine, the data on it can no longer be reached.

**Virtual disks** survive that: a separate service pretends to be a block device that can be attached to any instance. But every read or write becomes a network call, which adds overhead and exposes the database to every network glitch.

So cloud native databases use storage services built for the job. Object stores suit large files, so databases pack many small rows into big blocks before storing them.

cards.prompt: Why do cloud native systems treat a VM's local disk as a cache rather than durable storage?
choices: Local disks are much slower than object storage
Cloud providers don't allow writes to local disks
Its contents become unreachable if the instance fails or is swapped for one of a different size
cards.explanation: A VM's local disk lives and dies with that instance. Local disks are actually fast, which is what makes them a good cache. You can write to them; you just can't count on the data staying.

cards.prompt: Why do cloud native databases avoid keeping their data on virtual disks (network-attached block devices), and what do they use instead?
keyPoints: Emulating a block device adds overhead that a system designed for the cloud can avoid
Every disk I/O becomes a network call, so network glitches hit the database directly
They use storage services built for the workload, such as object storage for large blocks

cards.prompt: A new cloud database stores each row as its own object in an object store. What's wrong with this design?
choices: Object stores suit large files, and rows are tiny; cloud databases group many values into big blocks
Object stores lose data when one of their machines fails
Object stores are limited to one machine's disk space
cards.explanation: Object storage is built for files from hundreds of kilobytes to gigabytes, so cloud databases keep small values in a separate service and write large blocks to the object store. Object stores spread data across many machines, so they neither lose it when one fails nor run out of a single disk.

cards.title: Storage apart from compute
cards.body:
On a traditional server, the same machine keeps the data on its disks and processes it with its CPU and memory.

Cloud native systems often **separate storage from compute**. One service, such as an object store, only keeps the data. Separate machines, which can be added or removed on their own, run the queries.

The price is distance: before any data can be processed, it has to travel over the network from where it's stored to where the work happens.

cards.prompt: What does separating storage from compute mean in a cloud native system, and what does it cost?
keyPoints: Data is stored by one service (such as an object store) and processed on separate machines
Data has to travel over the network to wherever it's processed

cards.title: Multitenancy
cards.body:
Cloud native services are often **multitenant**. Instead of giving each customer its own machines, one service handles many customers' data and queries on the same shared hardware.

That uses hardware better and makes the service easier to scale and to run. The risk is interference between customers. Without careful engineering, one customer's sudden heavy load could slow everyone else down, or a bug could expose one customer's data to another.

cards.prompt: Cloud native systems are often multitenant. What's the main risk?
choices: Every customer needs a dedicated machine, which wastes hardware
One customer's activity can hurt performance or security for others on the same hardware
Customers can't scale beyond a single machine
cards.explanation: Sharing hardware between customers improves utilization and makes scaling easier, but it needs careful isolation. A dedicated machine per customer is the opposite of multitenancy. Shared services usually make scaling easier, not harder.

cards.title: Operations in the cloud
cards.body:
The cloud doesn't remove operations work; it changes it. Ops has moved from tending individual machines toward automation, short-lived VMs, frequent releases and learning from incidents, the DevOps and SRE approach.

As a cloud customer you still pick services, connect them and migrate between them. Capacity planning turns into cost planning: you track what you use and what it costs, and you plan around each service's quotas. And you still keep your application and its libraries secure, watch the load, and track down slowdowns and outages.

cards.prompt: Which operations work stays with you even when you use cloud services?
keyPoints: Choosing services, integrating them, and migrating between them
Tracking what you use and spend, and planning around quotas
Keeping your application and its libraries secure
Monitoring load and tracking down slowdowns and outages
cards.explanation: Capacity planning turns into financial planning, and performance tuning into cost tuning. The need for operations doesn't shrink; it shifts.

cards.title: Why go distributed
cards.body:
A **distributed system** is several machines cooperating over a network; each process taking part is a **node**. There are many reasons to build one.

Some apps are distributed by nature, like a chat between two phones. Spare machines give **fault tolerance**: when one fails, another takes over. More machines let you **scale** beyond one, and servers near users worldwide cut **latency**. In the cloud you get **elasticity**, growing and shrinking with demand. Other reasons: matching hardware to each job, laws that keep residents' data inside their country, and running jobs where and when clean power is plentiful.

cards.prompt: Your database runs on one large server with plenty of room to grow, and all its users are in one region. Which reason to add more machines still applies?
choices: Handling more data
Making queries faster
Keeping the service up if that server fails
Making operations simpler
cards.explanation: One machine, however big, is a single point of failure; redundancy needs more machines. With room to grow, scaling out isn't needed yet. Extra nodes don't automatically speed queries up, since network calls add overhead. And distribution makes operations harder, not simpler.

cards.prompt: A health app has patients in several countries. Each country's law requires its residents' medical records to be stored only on servers inside that country. What does this mean for the system?
choices: One server is still enough, as long as the records are encrypted
Every record must be copied to every country, so any server can serve any patient
The data must be split across servers in each of those countries
The rule only matters if the app runs its own hardware rather than a cloud
cards.explanation: Data residency laws pin data to a location, so a service whose users live under several such laws has to spread their data across servers in each country. Encryption doesn't change where data is stored. Copying every record everywhere breaks the same laws. Cloud servers are physical machines in some country too.

cards.title: When a request times out
cards.body:
Every call over a network can fail. The network can lose the message, or the other service can be overloaded or crash, so a request may get no reply at all before it **times out**.

The nasty part is the uncertainty. A timeout doesn't say whether the request was lost on the way, or was handled and only the reply got lost. Retrying is safe only if doing the action twice does no harm. Otherwise a retried payment could charge a customer twice.

cards.prompt: A request to another service times out. Why is just retrying it risky?
keyPoints: You can't tell whether the service received and processed the request
If it did, a retry may perform the action twice
cards.explanation: A network fault, an overload or a crash can all cause a timeout, and from the outside they look the same.

cards.title: One machine is often enough
cards.body:
Distribution has costs. A call to another machine is far slower than a function call inside one process, so shipping data between nodes can eat the gain; it's often faster to send the computation to where the data is. More nodes don't always make a job faster. Debugging is harder too: when a request is slow, you need **observability** tools, such as tracing, to find which service is at fault.

Meanwhile single machines keep getting bigger and faster, and embedded databases like SQLite or DuckDB handle a lot. If one node will do, stay on one node.

cards.prompt: A job spread over a 100-core cluster is beaten by a plain single-threaded program on a laptop. What's the most likely reason?
choices: Network and coordination overhead outweigh the extra cores
The cluster doesn't have enough nodes yet
Single-threaded programs are always faster than parallel ones
cards.explanation: Calls over the network are far slower than calls within a process, and shipping data to where it's processed takes time. Adding nodes adds more of that overhead. Parallelism does help when the work outweighs the overhead, so 'always' is wrong.

cards.prompt: When one machine is enough, why is it often better than a distributed system?
keyPoints: No network failures or timeouts to handle
Calls inside one process are far faster than calls over a network
Problems are easier to track down than across many nodes
Today's hardware and single-node databases can handle many workloads

cards.title: Microservices
cards.body:
In a **microservices** architecture, an application is split into services that each have one job, offer an API that clients call over the network, and belong to one team. Each team can release on its own schedule and change the internals freely as long as the API holds.

Each service usually gets its **own database**. A shared one would make its schema part of every service's API, so it would be hard to change, and one service's heavy queries could slow the others. The cost: keeping data consistent across services becomes the application's job. **Distributed transactions** could help, but they tie services back together, and many databases lack them.

cards.prompt: Why does each microservice usually get its own database instead of sharing one?
keyPoints: A shared database makes its schema part of every service's API, so it becomes hard to change
One service's queries could slow down the others

cards.prompt: Why are distributed transactions rarely used across microservices?
choices: Microservices don't need data to be consistent across services
They only work within a single database
They tie services together, against the goal of keeping them independent, and many databases don't support them
cards.explanation: Consistency across services still matters; without distributed transactions it becomes the application's job. Distributed transactions do span several systems (chapter 8), but they couple the services they touch.

cards.title: The cost of many services
cards.body:
Many small services bring their own complexity. To test one service, you have to run every service it depends on. Each one needs its own release pipeline, scaling, logs, monitoring and on-call alerts. And changing an API is risky: dropping a field can break its clients, often noticed only once the change reaches staging or production.

Microservices mainly solve a *people* problem: they let many teams move without waiting for each other. In a large company that's worth the overhead. A small company with one or two teams usually does better with the simplest design that works.

cards.prompt: What costs come with splitting an application into many services?
keyPoints: Testing one service means running all the services it depends on
Each service needs its own deployment, scaling, logging, monitoring and alerting
Changing an API can break clients, often noticed only late, in staging or production

cards.prompt: A five-person startup with one product team plans to split its app into a dozen microservices. What's the strongest argument against it?
choices: Microservices can't run in the cloud
Microservices mainly let many teams work without coordinating; with one team, they're mostly overhead
Microservices require all services to share one database
cards.explanation: Microservices are a technical fix for a people problem. A small team gains little and pays for testing, deploying and monitoring many services. They run fine in the cloud, and they usually avoid sharing a database.

cards.title: Serverless
cards.body:
**Serverless**, or functions as a service (FaaS), hands even more to the cloud provider. You never start or stop VMs. You upload a function; when a request comes in, the provider finds hardware to run it, and frees that hardware once it's idle. You pay only while your code runs, much as cloud storage bills for space used instead of disks bought upfront.

The catches: providers cap how long a function may run and restrict its runtime, and a first call can be slow while hardware is found (a *cold start*). There are still servers; each call may just land on a different one.

cards.prompt: Order what happens when a serverless function handles a request.
items: A request arrives
The provider assigns hardware to run the function, slowly if it's the first call
The function runs, and you're billed for that time
The provider frees the hardware once it's no longer needed
cards.explanation: You never choose when to start or stop machines. The trade-offs: time limits on each run, restricted runtime environments, and slow first calls.

cards.title: Supercomputers
cards.body:
**High-performance computing** (HPC), or supercomputing, also uses many machines, but with other priorities than the cloud. It runs long scientific batch jobs, such as simulating airflow over a wing, rather than services that must always answer users.

So it handles failure differently. A job saves a **checkpoint** of its state to disk every so often. When a node dies, the whole job stops, the node is fixed, and the job resumes from the last checkpoint. A cloud service can't pause for everyone like that. HPC also assumes trusted users and nodes close together, while the cloud isolates strangers and can span continents.

cards.prompt: Order how a supercomputer typically recovers from a node failure.
items: The job periodically saves a checkpoint of its state to disk
A node fails
The whole job stops
The faulty node is repaired
The job restarts from the last checkpoint
cards.explanation: This suits long batch computations. Online services can't stop everything for one failed node, so they're built to keep serving users through failures.

cards.title: The right to be forgotten
cards.body:
Data systems also answer to the law. Privacy rules such as the EU's **GDPR** give people rights over data about them, including the right to have it **erased**.

That clashes with how many systems are built. Lots of them keep data in **immutable**, append-only logs, so deleting one record in the middle isn't simple. And by then the data has usually been copied into derived datasets: caches, warehouses, even the training data of ML models. Erasing a person means finding every copy. The law states principles, not technologies, so engineers have to work out what compliance means.

cards.prompt: Why is the right to have your data erased hard to implement in data systems?
keyPoints: Many systems are built on immutable, append-only logs, so deleting one record in the middle is hard
Copies of the data spread into derived datasets such as caches, warehouses and ML training data
cards.explanation: The GDPR sets out principles, not technologies, so there's no checklist that makes a system compliant.

cards.title: Data minimization
cards.body:
Keeping data costs more than the storage bill. A leak brings liability and bad press. Processing that breaks the law brings fines. And data that a government can demand may put users at risk, for example when location history reveals something a state has made a crime.

**Data minimization** means not keeping data that isn't worth those risks. It's the opposite of the big data habit of hoarding everything in case it's useful one day, and it matches the GDPR: you may collect personal data only for a stated purpose, never reuse it for another, and keep it no longer than that purpose needs.

cards.prompt: A team keeps every user's IP address history forever because it might be useful for analytics someday. Is that a problem?
choices: No: storage is cheap, so keeping extra data costs almost nothing
Yes: data kept without a specific purpose, or longer than needed, goes against data minimization and the GDPR
No, as long as the data is encrypted
Only if the servers are outside the EU
cards.explanation: The GDPR allows personal data only for a stated purpose, and only for as long as it's needed. The real cost of storing data includes breaches, fines and authorities demanding it, and IP history reveals roughly where people have been. Encryption lowers the breach risk but doesn't make purposeless retention lawful, and the rules don't depend on where the servers are.

cards.title: Functional and nonfunctional requirements
cards.body:
Every app starts with a list of what it must do. A banking app must show your balance, send a transfer and list past payments. Those are **functional requirements**: the screens, the buttons and what each operation does.

Alongside them sit **nonfunctional requirements**, which say how well the app does all that: fast, reliable, secure, within the law and easy to maintain. They often go unwritten because they feel obvious, but they count just as much. An app that crawls or keeps losing your data is as good as useless.

This chapter looks at four of them: performance, reliability, scalability and maintainability.

cards.prompt: A spec for a concert-ticket app lists: buy a ticket, request a refund, view a seat map, pages load in under a second, and card data is stored encrypted. Which items are nonfunctional requirements?
choices: The refund and the seat map, since not every user will need those features
None of them: nonfunctional requirements are the ones left unwritten
The load-time and encryption rules, since they describe qualities, not operations
All five, since each one constrains how the code has to be written
cards.explanation: Functional requirements say what the app does: its screens and operations. Nonfunctional ones say how well it does them: speed, reliability, security, compliance, maintainability. An optional feature is still a feature. Nonfunctional requirements often go unwritten because they seem obvious, but writing one down doesn't change its kind.

cards.title: Feeds computed on read
cards.body:
Picture a photo app where your home feed shows recent photos from everyone you follow. The obvious design keeps users, photos and follows in three tables, and a join query builds your feed on demand: find who you follow, fetch their recent photos, sort them by time.

To show new photos within seconds, each app reruns that query every few seconds: it **polls**. The work multiplies: users online, times polls per second, times accounts each one follows. With 5 million people polling every 10 seconds and following 300 accounts each, that's 150 million lookups a second, mostly finding nothing new. For someone following 20,000 accounts, even one run is slow.

cards.prompt: Why does building each user's feed with a join query, polled every few seconds by every online client, break down at scale?
keyPoints: Every poll reruns the query, even when nothing new was posted
Each run fetches recent posts from every followed account and merges them
Total work is online users times poll rate times accounts followed
For users who follow thousands of accounts, a single run is very slow
cards.explanation: Pushing new posts to online clients and precomputing feeds removes most of that read work.

cards.title: Precomputed feeds
cards.body:
Two changes fix this. The server **pushes** new posts to followers who are online, so nobody polls. And each user's feed is computed ahead of time and kept up to date, so opening it is a quick lookup. A stored query result like that is a **materialized view**.

The work moves to writes. When someone posts, the post is saved, the system finds their followers and adds the post to each stored feed; online apps subscribed to their feed see it at once. One request turning into many downstream ones is **fan-out**: 300 followers, 300 writes. Reads far outnumber posts, so it's still cheaper. In a burst of posts, deliveries can queue: posts arrive late, but feeds still load fast.

cards.prompt: A video site builds each user's subscriptions feed with a query at read time. It switches to storing every feed precomputed, inserting each new upload into the feed of every subscriber. What's the trade-off?
choices: Reads and writes both get cheaper, since the feed query no longer has to run
Uploads get cheaper to process, but every feed read must now merge many lists
Feeds get fresher, but new uploads can no longer be pushed to online clients
Reads become cheap lookups, but each upload now costs one write per subscriber
cards.explanation: The feed is now a materialized view: derived data kept up to date on every write so reads are fast. The work moves to write time rather than disappearing. Merging many lists on read is what the old query did. Precomputed feeds pair well with push: clients just subscribe to what gets added.

cards.prompt: A user publishes a post, and the system delivers it by fan-out into precomputed feeds. Put the steps in order.
items: The post is saved
Then the system looks up everyone who follows the author
A delivery for each follower is queued, and may lag during a traffic spike
The post is inserted into each follower's precomputed feed
Followers who are online get the post through their feed subscription
cards.explanation: Fan-out is how much one request multiplies into downstream ones: with 200 followers, one post means 200 feed writes. Queueing lets a spike delay delivery without slowing feed reads.

cards.title: Accounts at the extremes
cards.body:
Fan-out is cheap for a typical account, but two kinds of user push it to extremes.

Someone who follows tens of thousands of busy accounts gets a flood of writes into their feed. They can't read it all anyway, so it's fine to drop some of those writes and show them a sample.

An account with millions of followers is the opposite problem: each post means millions of feed writes, and dropping any isn't acceptable, since followers expect to see it. One fix is to handle such accounts separately. Their posts are stored once instead of being copied into every feed, and merged into a follower's feed when it's read.

cards.prompt: On a podcast app, each new episode is written into every subscriber's precomputed feed. One host has 40 million subscribers. What's the better way to handle accounts like that?
choices: Write each of their episodes into only a random sample of subscribers' feeds
Store their episodes separately and merge them into each feed when it's read
Have subscribers poll that host's account directly every few seconds instead
Write to all 40 million feeds before telling the host the upload succeeded
cards.explanation: Skipping the huge fan-out and merging at read time keeps both sides affordable. Dropping writes is fine for someone who follows so many accounts they can't read everything, but subscribers of a big account expect every episode. Polling brings back the expensive read-time query. Waiting for 40 million writes would make publishing painfully slow.

cards.title: Response time and throughput
cards.body:
Performance is usually described with two numbers. **Response time** is how long a user waits, from sending a request until the answer arrives. **Throughput** is how many requests, or how much data, the system handles per second; given hardware has a ceiling. Users care most about response time. Throughput decides how many machines you need, and so the cost.

The two are linked. At low load, answers come quickly. As throughput nears the ceiling, response time shoots up because of **queueing**: a new request usually finds the CPU busy with earlier ones and waits its turn, like a coffee line at rush hour. No request needs more work than before; each just waits longer.

cards.prompt: How do response time and throughput differ, and what does each mainly tell you?
keyPoints: Response time is how long a client waits from sending a request to getting the answer
Throughput is how many requests, or how much data, the system handles per second
Response time is what users care about most
Throughput decides how much hardware you need, and so the cost

cards.prompt: Why does a service's response time climb steeply as its throughput nears the maximum, even with unchanged code and hardware?
choices: Requests find the CPU busy more often and must queue, and that wait soars near capacity
Each request's own processing takes longer in proportion to how many are in flight at once
The network slows down as more bytes flow, whatever the server is doing
Under heavy load, the server deliberately slows every request to protect itself
cards.explanation: Near capacity, a new request usually arrives while earlier ones still hold the CPU, so queueing delay comes to dominate. The work per request stays roughly the same, so service time barely moves. Network delay can vary, but it doesn't explain a rise tied to the server's own load. Asking clients to slow down (backpressure) is a defense against overload, not its cause.

cards.title: Retry storms
cards.body:
A service running near its limit can get stuck there. Requests pile up in a queue, responses slow down, and clients give up waiting and resend the same requests. The retries add load, so responses slow further: a **retry storm**. The overload feeds itself, and even after the original traffic drops, the service may stay swamped until it's restarted. That's a **metastable failure**.

Both sides can defend against it. Clients can wait longer between retries, with some randomness (**exponential backoff**), and stop calling a service that recently failed or timed out (a **circuit breaker** or **token bucket**). The server can reject some requests early as it nears overload (**load shedding**), or tell clients to slow down (**backpressure**).

cards.prompt: Order how a retry storm can leave a service stuck in overload.
items: The service runs close to its maximum throughput
A queue builds up and response times climb
Clients hit their timeouts and send the same requests again
The retries push the request rate even higher
Even after the original load falls, the service stays overloaded until it's reset
cards.explanation: This is a metastable failure: the overload sustains itself. Exponential backoff, circuit breakers, load shedding and backpressure help break the loop.

cards.prompt: How can clients and servers stop retries from overloading a service?
keyPoints: Clients wait longer, with random variation, between successive retries (exponential backoff)
Clients pause calls to a service that recently failed or timed out (a circuit breaker or token bucket)
The server rejects some requests early when it nears overload (load shedding)
The server tells clients to slow down (backpressure)

cards.title: Latency and queueing delay
cards.body:
**Response time** is everything the client sees, from sending a request to getting the reply. **Service time** is only the part when the service is actively working on it. Time when a request isn't being worked on is **latency**: **network latency** while it travels between machines, and **queueing delay** while it waits, for example for a free CPU after it arrives.

Queueing explains much of why response times vary. A server works on only a few requests at once. If slow ones fill every slot, quick ones behind them wait, and their clients see long response times despite tiny service times. That's **head-of-line blocking**. The server's own timings miss that wait, so measure response time on the client.

cards.prompt: Order what a client's measured response time is made of, from the moment it sends a request.
items: The request travels across the network to the server
It waits in a queue until a CPU is free
The service actively works on it
The response travels back across the network to the client
cards.explanation: Only the third step is service time. The network trips and the queueing are latency: time the request spends waiting rather than being processed.

cards.prompt: A server has 4 worker threads. Four requests arrive that each need 3 seconds, followed right away by 50 requests that each need 2 ms. What do the 50 quick requests see?
choices: About 2 ms each, since response time matches service time when work is tiny
An error each, because the server refuses requests while all its threads are busy
Waits of seconds: they queue behind the slow ones despite tiny service times
About 2 ms each, as the operating system runs short requests ahead of long ones
cards.explanation: This is head-of-line blocking: a few slow requests occupy the workers and everything behind them queues. Service time stays at 2 ms, but the client sees the wait, which is why response times should be measured on the client side. Servers usually queue requests rather than reject them, and nothing reorders them by size for you.

cards.title: Mean, median and percentiles
cards.body:
Response time is a spread of values, not one number: most requests are quick, a few far slower.

The **mean**, the total of all times divided by the count, helps estimate throughput limits, but it hides how many users actually waited that long, and a few very slow requests can drag it far from the usual experience. **Percentiles** work better. Sort the times from fastest to slowest: the middle one is the **median**, or **p50**. If it's 80 ms, half the requests finish faster and half take longer, so it shows a typical wait. For outliers, look at p95, p99 or p999: a p99 of 2 seconds means 1 request in 100 takes 2 seconds or more.

cards.prompt: Why is the median usually a better measure of a typical response time than the mean?
choices: It splits requests into a faster and a slower half, so it shows a typical wait
The median includes the slow outliers, while the mean leaves them out
The mean can't be computed for response times, only for throughput
The median is the same as the p99, so it also captures the slowest requests
cards.explanation: The median (p50) splits requests in half, so it reflects a typical experience. The mean includes every request, outliers too, so a few slow ones can drag it far from what most users see, and it doesn't say how many actually waited that long. It's still useful, for example to estimate throughput limits. The p99 is a much higher point.

cards.title: Tail latencies
cards.body:
High percentiles are called **tail latencies**, and the users who hit them really notice. Some companies set targets at p999, just 1 request in 1,000, because the slowest requests often come from customers with the most data, like an accountant with thousands of invoices, and those tend to be the most valuable. Going to p9999 rarely pays: delays there come from random events you can't control, so gains cost a lot and help little.

Tails matter most when one page needs many backend calls. Even in parallel, the page waits for the slowest, so rare slowness becomes common: if each of 10 calls is slow 5% of the time, about 40% of pages are slow. That's **tail latency amplification**.

cards.prompt: Why do teams set response time targets at high percentiles like p999, but rarely beyond?
keyPoints: Slow requests directly hurt the experience of the users who get them
The slowest requests often come from customers with the most data, who tend to be the most valuable
Beyond about p999, random events outside your control dominate, so gains cost a lot and help little

cards.prompt: Loading a dashboard calls 20 backend services in parallel. Each is slow on 1% of its calls, independently. Roughly what share of dashboard loads are slow?
choices: About 1%, because the calls run in parallel rather than one after another
Almost none, because all 20 calls would have to be slow at once
Almost all, because each slow call adds its delay to the other calls
About 18%, because one slow call is enough to hold up the whole page
cards.explanation: The page waits for its slowest call, and the chance that all 20 are fast is 0.99^20, about 82%. That's tail latency amplification: rare backend slowness becomes common for users. Running calls in parallel doesn't help, since one slow call is enough. Parallel delays don't add up either; the page simply takes as long as the worst call.

cards.title: SLOs and SLAs
cards.body:
Percentiles are the usual way to state what a service promises. A **service level objective (SLO)** sets targets for its performance and availability. An SLO for a payments API might say: median response under 100 ms, p99 under 500 ms, and at least 99.95% of valid requests answered without an error.

A **service level agreement (SLA)** is a contract that says what happens if the SLO isn't met, such as customers getting money back.

That's the idea, anyway. In practice, picking availability measures that truly reflect what users experience is harder than it looks.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between an SLO and an SLA, and how are percentiles used in them?
keyPoints: An SLO is a target for a service's performance and availability
Targets are often percentiles, such as a median and a p99 bound, plus a minimum share of successful responses
An SLA is a contract saying what happens if the SLO is missed, such as refunds
cards.explanation: In practice, choosing good availability metrics for them is harder than it looks.

cards.title: Combining percentiles
cards.body:
To chart percentiles on a dashboard, you compute them continuously. A common setup keeps the response times of the last few minutes and, once a minute, works out the median and other percentiles over that window.

The simple way is to sort the whole list each time. When that's too costly, estimation libraries approximate percentiles with little CPU and memory, typically by keeping a **histogram**: a count of requests in each range of times.

Never average percentiles, whether over time periods or across machines; the result means nothing. To combine data, add the histograms together and read the percentiles off the total.

cards.prompt: You collect response times on 12 servers and want the p99 for the whole fleet. How should you combine the data?
choices: Average the 12 servers' p99 values, weighting each by its traffic
Take the highest of the 12 p99 values, which equals the fleet's p99
Add the servers' histograms together, then read the p99 off the sum
Take the median of the 12 p99 values, so odd servers don't skew it
cards.explanation: A percentile of combined data can't be rebuilt from per-server percentiles, so averaging them is meaningless, weighted or not. Histograms keep the whole distribution, and they add up. The highest p99 is only an upper bound, and a median of percentiles is no more meaningful than a mean. Percentile-estimation libraries keep such histograms cheap to maintain.

cards.title: Faults and failures
cards.body:
We expect software to do what users want, cope with their mistakes, perform well enough and keep intruders out. Being **reliable** means it keeps doing that when things go wrong.

A **fault** is one part breaking: a disk, a machine, a service you call. A **failure** is the whole system no longer serving users as required, say missing its SLO. They're the same event at different levels: a single-engine plane whose engine quits has failed, but a twin-engine plane flies on with the other, so for it a dead engine is a mere fault.

A system that keeps serving through certain faults is **fault-tolerant**. A part whose fault takes the whole system down is a **single point of failure** (SPOF).

cards.prompt: A storage cluster keeps three copies of every file. One disk dies, and users notice nothing. How is this best described?
choices: A failure of the system, since any component that stops working is a failure
A single point of failure, because a disk broke without any warning
Nothing worth describing, since no data was lost and no user ever noticed
A fault from the cluster's view, not a failure, since the service kept working
cards.explanation: A fault is one part going wrong; a failure is the whole system no longer providing its required service, such as missing its SLO. They're the same thing at different levels: the disk itself failed, but for the cluster it's a tolerated fault. A single point of failure is a part whose fault does bring the system down, which this disk wasn't.

cards.prompt: A web shop runs three app servers behind one load balancer. All three use a single database server. Which components are single points of failure?
choices: The load balancer and the database, since losing either takes the shop down
Each app server, since any requests sent to it would fail if it crashed
None of them, since three app servers share the load between them
Only the database, since a load balancer just forwards traffic
cards.explanation: A single point of failure is a part whose fault escalates into a failure of the whole system. If one app server dies, the load balancer can route around it. But there's only one load balancer and one database, and the shop stops if either does. Forwarding traffic is simple, but the box doing it can still crash.

cards.title: Fault injection
cards.body:
Oddly, a fault-tolerant system can benefit from more faults, as long as you cause them on purpose. **Fault injection** means triggering faults deliberately, for example cutting a random server off the network without warning.

Many serious bugs hide in error handling: code that runs only when something breaks, so it rarely gets exercised. Causing faults regularly keeps the failover machinery tested. You find its bugs at a time you choose, and you gain confidence it will work when a real fault strikes. **Chaos engineering** turns such experiments into a discipline.

cards.prompt: Why would a team deliberately kill random processes in its production system?
choices: It keeps failover code exercised, so error-handling bugs show up while people watch
It reclaims memory from processes that leak, which avoids planned restarts
It cuts the total number of faults by weeding out unreliable hardware early
It measures how long users are willing to wait during short, unplanned outages
cards.explanation: Many serious bugs live in error handling, which rarely runs. Injecting faults keeps that machinery tested and builds confidence it will work in a real outage; chaos engineering makes a discipline of this. Restarting leaky processes treats a symptom. Killing processes reveals nothing about hardware. And in a fault-tolerant system, users shouldn't notice at all.

cards.title: Hardware faults at scale
cards.body:
Hardware breaks more often than you'd think. A few percent of hard drives die each year. SSDs die less often, but they hit errors they can't correct. Power supplies fail, memory gets corrupted, and about one machine in a thousand has a CPU core that now and then computes a wrong answer. A whole datacenter can lose power, or burn down.

On a small system you can mostly shrug and replace parts as they break. At scale, the numbers add up. Run 5,000 servers whose power supplies each have a 1% chance of dying in a year, and you'll replace about 50 a year, roughly one a week. Faults become part of normal operation.

cards.prompt: A storage cluster has 20,000 hard drives, each with about a 2% chance of failing in a year. How should its operators think about disk failures?
choices: As rare emergencies, since each drive almost never fails
As routine: about one a day, so recovery must be part of normal operation
As yearly events, best handled in a scheduled maintenance window
As not worth planning for, since RAID makes single disk failures harmless
cards.explanation: 20,000 times 2% is about 400 a year, slightly more than one a day. At this scale hardware faults are part of normal operation, not exceptions. Waiting for a maintenance window would leave the system running degraded for months. RAID helps within one machine, but correlated faults and whole-machine losses still happen.

cards.title: Redundancy and its limits
cards.body:
The classic answer to flaky hardware is **redundancy** inside each machine: disks in a RAID array, so one dead disk loses no data; dual power supplies; batteries and diesel generators in the datacenter. That can keep a single machine up for years.

Redundancy works best when faults are independent, but in practice they're often correlated, and whole racks or datacenters still go dark. No spare part inside one machine survives that.

So cloud systems care less about each machine. They tolerate the loss of whole machines, racks or zones in software, letting another node take over. Clouds group resources into **availability zones**: things in one zone tend to fail together, so copies go in different zones.

cards.prompt: Why do cloud systems rely less on redundant hardware inside each machine and more on tolerating lost machines in software?
keyPoints: Hardware redundancy works best when faults are independent, but real failures are often correlated
Whole racks or datacenters still go down, and no single machine's redundancy survives that
Software fault tolerance can survive losing entire machines, racks or availability zones
Putting copies in different availability zones avoids resources likely to fail together
cards.explanation: RAID, dual power supplies and backup generators still help; they just can't cover a whole datacenter going dark.

cards.title: Rolling upgrades
cards.body:
A system that survives losing a machine has a bonus: you can take machines down on purpose. A single server needs planned downtime every time it must reboot.

With several nodes that cope with one missing, you upgrade them one at a time instead. Say a five-node database cluster needs a new software version. You take one node out while the others keep serving, upgrade and restart it, and wait until it's healthy and back in service. Then you move on to the next node, and so on. Users never notice. This is a **rolling upgrade**.

cards.prompt: A three-node cluster needs an OS security patch with no downtime. Order the steps of a rolling upgrade.
items: Take one node out of service while the other two keep serving users
Patch that node and restart it
Wait until it's healthy and serving again
Repeat with the next node, until all three are patched
cards.explanation: A single server would need planned downtime to reboot. Being able to lose one node at a time is what makes this possible.

cards.title: Software faults
cards.body:
Hardware faults, though somewhat correlated, are mostly independent. Software faults are often highly correlated: every node runs the same code, so one trigger can crash them all at once, say a date bug that hangs every server on February 29. Such bugs can sleep for years until an unusual situation breaks an assumption that had always held. So software tends to cause far more outages than hardware.

Other typical kinds: a **runaway process** using up shared CPU, memory, disk, bandwidth or threads; a dependency that slows down, stops answering or returns corrupt data; systems that misbehave only together; and **cascading failures**, where one overloaded component overloads the next. Testing, process isolation, crash-and-restart, avoiding retry storms and monitoring all help.

cards.prompt: A database cluster has 60 nodes across three datacenters. Within the same few seconds, every node crashes. What's the most likely cause?
choices: A wave of disk failures, since disks are the least reliable part of a server
A power outage in one of the three datacenters, cutting off its nodes
Random bit flips in memory, caused by cosmic rays striking the servers
A software bug they all hit at once, since every node runs the same code
cards.explanation: Software faults are highly correlated: identical code on every node means one trigger can crash them all together. Hardware faults are mostly independent, so disk or memory errors wouldn't strike 60 nodes in the same few seconds. A power cut in one datacenter couldn't take down the other two.

cards.prompt: What kinds of software faults tend to cause system failures?
keyPoints: A bug that crashes every node at once under a particular condition
A runaway process that exhausts a shared resource such as memory, disk, CPU or threads
A dependency that slows down, stops responding or returns corrupt data
A cascading failure, where one overloaded component overloads the next
cards.explanation: Such bugs often lie dormant until an unusual situation breaks an assumption about the environment that was usually true.

cards.title: Humans and outages
cards.body:
People make mistakes, and those cause more outages than hardware. A study of big online services ranked operators' config changes as the top cause, with hardware involved in only 10 to 25%. Stricter rules won't fix that. What helps is limiting the damage: thorough testing, a fast way to roll back config, gradual rollouts, clear monitoring, and interfaces that make the right action easy.

Blaming whoever slipped is counterproductive. *Human error* is a symptom of how people, tools and priorities fit together, not the root cause. In a **blameless postmortem**, those involved share the full story without fear of punishment, so everyone can learn. Distrust simple answers, from 'be more careful' to 'rewrite it all'.

cards.prompt: At a video platform, most outages last year began with an engineer changing a configuration setting. Which investment most directly limits the damage from such slips?
choices: Redundant disks and power supplies in every server, so machines break less often
Rolling out each change gradually, with a fast way to revert it
A rule that two managers must sign off on every configuration change
Replacing every manual step with automation, so no person touches production
cards.explanation: When people's changes cause most outages, the best defense limits how far a bad change spreads and how long it lasts: a gradual rollout catches it early, and a quick revert undoes it. Hardware redundancy targets a small share of outages. Extra sign-offs are stricter rules, which don't stop slips. Automation can also go wrong, and it leaves the hardest cases to people.

cards.prompt: An engineer's config change took down the checkout service for an hour. What response is most likely to prevent similar outages?
choices: A blameless postmortem that gets the full story and fixes what made the slip easy
Disciplining the engineer, so that everyone takes more care with future changes
Rewriting the deployment tooling from scratch in a safer language
Logging it as human error, since people will always make some mistakes
cards.explanation: Human error is a symptom of how the sociotechnical system works, not the root cause. Without fear of punishment, people share the details others need to learn from, which may reveal neglected areas or misplaced priorities. Blame makes people hide details. A big rewrite is a simplistic fix that ignores what happened. Labeling it human error ends the investigation.

cards.title: How much reliability matters
cards.body:
For many apps, a few hours of downtime is tolerable, but losing or corrupting data for good is a disaster: an invoicing tool may be down for an afternoon, but must never lose a year of invoices. Cut corners, as in a prototype, only knowingly.

Bad software can even ruin lives. From 1999 to 2019, hundreds of people running British Post Office branches were found guilty of theft or fraud after the **Horizon** accounting software showed money missing. Many shortfalls were really bugs, as no software is bug-free, and many convictions were overturned. English law presumed computers work correctly unless shown otherwise, so the accused had to prove the software wrong, with no way to look inside it.

cards.prompt: A small startup hosts people's personal journals, some written over decades. Its budget covers one major reliability investment. Which should come first?
choices: Five-nines uptime, since any minute offline drives users away
Faster saves at p999, since slow requests hit the best users
Making sure stored entries can't be lost or silently corrupted
Running active in two regions so the app never goes down
cards.explanation: For many apps a short outage is tolerable, but losing or corrupting people's data is catastrophic and often can't be undone. Uptime targets and multi-region setups protect availability, which matters less here than durability. Faster tails are nice but don't save anyone's writing. Cutting reliability corners can be a fair trade, as long as it's a conscious one.

cards.prompt: Why is a legal presumption that computers work correctly dangerous, as the Post Office Horizon scandal showed?
keyPoints: Real software has bugs, so its output can be wrong
The presumption leaves people having to prove the computer wrong, which they usually can't
Bugs in Horizon's accounting produced shortfalls that led to hundreds of wrongful convictions
cards.explanation: Unreliable software can wreck lives, not just cost revenue.

cards.title: When to worry about scale
cards.body:
**Scalability** is a system's ability to cope with growing load. For a young product with few users, though, the goal is to stay simple and flexible, so you can change features as you learn what customers want. Building for imagined scale then is premature: at best wasted effort, at worst a rigid design that's hard to change. Real bottlenecks show up as you grow; deal with them then.

Also, 'X scales' or 'Y doesn't scale' means nothing on its own. Scalability is about a particular kind of growth. Ask: if load grows this way, what are our options? How would we add resources? And at the expected rate of growth, when will the current design hit its limits?

cards.prompt: A three-person startup with 300 users wants to design for 100 million users from the start. What's the main risk?
choices: Wasted work on guessed needs, and a rigid design that's hard to change later
None: designing for scale from day one avoids a costly rewrite later on
Their cloud bill, since capacity for 100 million users is paid for from day one
cards.explanation: Early on, the goal is to stay simple and flexible while learning what customers need. Scaling work for hypothetical load is premature at best, and at worst it locks in a design that resists change. Real bottlenecks show up as the product grows, and that's when to tackle them. Designing for scale doesn't mean buying the capacity up front.

cards.prompt: In a design review, someone says 'this database doesn't scale.' What's the most useful response?
choices: Agree, and move to a distributed database before the load starts to grow
Disagree, since any database scales once it's on a big enough machine
Ask what kind of growth they mean, how you'd add resources, and when limits hit
Run one benchmark of its maximum throughput to settle it for good
cards.explanation: Scalability isn't a yes-or-no label on a system; it's about specific kinds of growth and how you'd cope with each. Migrating on a vague worry is premature. A bigger machine has limits, and its cost climbs fast. One benchmark measures one workload today, not how the system copes as the load changes.

cards.title: Describing load
cards.body:
Before asking what happens if load doubles, describe today's load. Often that's a throughput: requests per second, gigabytes of new data per day, orders per hour. Sometimes what matters is the peak of something that varies, such as how many people are online at once.

Other statistics shape how data is accessed: the ratio of reads to writes, the cache **hit rate**, or how many items each user has, like followers. Your bottleneck may be set by the average case, or by a few extreme ones.

Then you can ask two things. With the same resources, how does performance change as load grows? And how much must resources grow to keep performance the same?

cards.prompt: Before asking 'what if our load doubles?', what should you know about the current load?
keyPoints: A throughput measure, such as requests per second or new data per day
Peaks of quantities that vary, such as users online at the same time
Statistics that shape access patterns, such as the read/write ratio, cache hit rate or items per user
Whether the average case or a few extreme cases drive the bottleneck
cards.explanation: Then you can ask how performance changes with fixed resources, or how resources must grow to keep performance fixed.

cards.title: Linear scalability
cards.body:
A system is **scalable** if adding computing resources lets it handle a lot more throughput. The usual goal is to keep performance within the SLA while keeping the bill as low as possible.

If twice the resources handle twice the load at the same performance, that's **linear scalability**, and it's a good result. Now and then you do better than linear, thanks to economies of scale or peaks that even out over more users. Far more often, cost grows faster than load. One reason: as data grows, each request can need more work, so the same small write costs more against a big dataset than a small one.

cards.prompt: What does it mean for a system to be scalable, and what is linear scalability?
keyPoints: Scalable: adding computing resources can raise its maximum throughput significantly
Linear: doubling the resources handles double the load at the same performance
In practice cost usually grows faster than linearly, for example because each write does more work as data grows
cards.explanation: Occasionally it's better than linear, thanks to economies of scale or peak loads that are spread more evenly.

cards.title: Scaling up and out
cards.body:
The simplest way to grow is a bigger machine with more cores, RAM and disk: **vertical scaling**, or *scaling up*. All its threads share one RAM, so it's a **shared-memory** architecture. But twice the resources usually cost well over twice as much, and internal bottlenecks likely stop it handling twice the load.

**Shared-disk** systems use several machines with their own CPUs and RAM, storing data on one disk array over a fast network. Contention and locking limit how far they scale.

**Shared-nothing** systems (*horizontal scaling*) use nodes with their own CPUs, RAM and disks, coordinating over an ordinary network. They can scale linearly, use best-value hardware, resize with load and span datacenters, but need explicit sharding and bring distributed-systems complexity.

cards.prompt: A team plans to move its overloaded database to a machine with twice the cores and RAM. What should they expect?
choices: Twice the capacity at twice the price, since scaling up is linear
Well over twice the price, and probably less than twice the capacity
Twice the capacity, since the new cores are also faster than the old ones
No gain, since one database process can only use a single core
cards.explanation: High-end machines cost disproportionately more, and bottlenecks inside the machine keep it from handling double the load. Individual cores aren't getting much faster; you get more of them. Threads in one process share memory and can use many cores, which is what a shared-memory architecture is.

cards.prompt: What limits each of these architectures: shared-memory, shared-disk, shared-nothing?
keyPoints: Shared-memory (one big machine): cost grows faster than capacity, and internal bottlenecks cap it
Shared-disk (machines sharing a disk array over a fast network): contention and locking overhead
Shared-nothing (independent nodes on an ordinary network): it needs explicit sharding and brings distributed-systems complexity
cards.explanation: In return, shared-nothing can scale linearly, use whatever hardware is cheapest for the job, grow or shrink with load, and spread across regions for fault tolerance.

cards.title: No one-size-fits-all scaling
cards.body:
There's no general-purpose architecture that scales every workload. The right design depends on the shape of the load, not just its volume. Two services may each take 10,000 requests a second, but if one serves a few popular pages from a cache and the other runs heavy searches over terabytes of data, they need very different designs.

Designs also have a range. One that suits today's load rarely copes with ten times as much, so a fast-growing service should expect to rethink its architecture at each tenfold increase. Since needs keep changing too, planning more than about one order of magnitude ahead is rarely worth it.

cards.prompt: Two systems each take in 50 MB per second. A sensor platform receives 50,000 tiny readings per second; a video archive receives one 3 GB recording per minute. What follows?
choices: One architecture fits both, since scaling depends on bytes per second
They probably need very different architectures, despite equal throughput
The video archive is easier, since fewer requests always means less work
cards.explanation: No generic scalable architecture exists; the right design depends on the shape of the load, not just its volume. Many tiny requests stress per-request overhead and concurrency, while huge files stress transfer and storage. Fewer requests isn't automatically easier: each 3 GB upload brings its own problems, such as long transfers that can fail partway.

cards.prompt: How far ahead is it worth designing the architecture of a fast-growing service?
choices: For the most load it could ever see, so it never needs redesigning at all
Only for today's load, since any planning ahead is premature
Two or three orders of magnitude, since redesigns cost too much
About ten times today's load, expecting a rethink at each tenfold jump
cards.explanation: A design that fits one level of load rarely survives ten times as much, and the product's needs keep changing, so planning further than one order of magnitude ahead is mostly guesswork. Planning only for today leaves a fast-growing service no headroom. Designing for the largest imaginable load is premature scaling that makes systems rigid.

cards.title: Principles for scaling
cards.body:
A good general rule is to split a system into parts that can work largely on their own. That's the idea behind microservices, sharding, stream processing and shared-nothing systems. The hard part is deciding what belongs together and what should be kept apart.

Another rule: don't make things more complex than they need to be.
