If one database machine can do the job, it beats a complicated distributed setup. **Autoscaling**, which adds and removes resources as demand changes, is appealing, but if your load is predictable, scaling by hand may bring fewer surprises. A handful of services is easier to run than dozens. Good designs usually mix approaches pragmatically.

cards.prompt: What general principles help a system scale?
keyPoints: Split it into components that can run largely independently of each other
The hard part is deciding what belongs together and what should be apart
Keep it no more complex than needed: one database machine beats a distributed setup if it's enough
With predictable load, manual scaling can bring fewer surprises than autoscaling
cards.explanation: Splitting is the idea behind microservices, sharding, stream processing and shared-nothing systems.

cards.title: The cost of maintenance
cards.body:
Software doesn't wear out like a machine, yet it keeps needing work. Requirements change, the platforms and libraries under it change, and bugs need fixing. Most of a system's cost comes after its first release: keeping it running, investigating failures, porting it, adding features and paying down technical debt.

**Legacy systems** are the hardest. They may rely on technology few engineers still know, and the people who knew why it was built that way have often left. So maintenance is partly a people problem.

Any valuable system will one day be legacy. Three principles ease the pain: **operability**, **simplicity** and **evolvability**.

cards.prompt: Software doesn't wear out. Why does most of its cost still come after it's first built, and why is legacy maintenance especially hard?
keyPoints: Requirements change, the platforms and dependencies under it change, and bugs need fixing
Ongoing work includes keeping it running, investigating failures, paying down tech debt and adding features
Legacy systems may use old technology that few engineers still know
The reasons behind the design leave with the people who made it, so maintenance is partly a people problem

cards.title: Operability
cards.body:
**Operability** means making it easy to keep a system running smoothly. At scale, automation is essential, but it cuts both ways. Rare situations still need a person, and since automation takes the easy cases, the ones left over are the hardest, so more automation needs a more skilled team. A misbehaving automated system is also often harder to debug than a manual one.

A data system helps its operators when it exposes key metrics to monitoring and supports observability; doesn't depend on any single machine, so nodes can be taken down for maintenance; has clear docs and a predictable model ('if I do X, Y happens'); and offers good defaults and self-healing that admins can override.

cards.prompt: Why can heavy automation of operations call for more skilled operators rather than fewer?
choices: Automated systems fail more often than ones run by hand, so there's more to fix
Operators must double-check every automated action by hand before it runs
It doesn't: full automation removes the need for an ops team entirely
Humans are left the rare, hardest cases, and broken automation is hard to debug
cards.explanation: Whatever automation can't handle tends to be the most complex situations, and an automated system that misbehaves is harder to troubleshoot than a manual one. Automation isn't inherently less reliable, and checking everything by hand would defeat its purpose. Edge cases always remain, so some manual intervention is always needed.

cards.prompt: How can a data system make life easier for the team that operates it?
keyPoints: Expose its key metrics to monitoring tools, and support observability
Avoid depending on any one machine, so nodes can be taken down for maintenance
Document it well, with a predictable model of what each action does
Provide good defaults and self-healing, while letting admins override them
cards.explanation: Good operability makes routine tasks easy, so the team can spend its time on higher-value work.

cards.title: Simplicity and abstraction
cards.body:
Large projects tend to grow into a tangle, a **big ball of mud**, that slows everyone down and makes bugs easy to introduce. So **simplicity** is a key goal, though what counts as simple is partly a matter of taste.

One view splits complexity in two. **Essential complexity** comes from the problem itself; **accidental complexity** comes only from the limits of our tools. The line between them shifts as tools improve.

A strong weapon against complexity is **abstraction**: a simple interface hiding lots of detail, the way a file system hides which disk blocks hold your file. One good abstraction serves many applications, and every improvement to it helps all of them.

cards.prompt: A payroll system must apply each country's tax rules. It also has a large module that works around its message queue's lack of ordering. How would the essential/accidental split classify these?
choices: Tax rules are accidental, and the queue workaround is essential since the system can't run without it
Both are essential, since the system needs both to work correctly
Tax rules are essential to the problem; the queue workaround is accidental, caused by a tool's limits
Both are accidental, since better code could make either one simpler
cards.explanation: Essential complexity comes from the problem domain; accidental complexity comes from limits of our tools. The split has a flaw: the boundary moves as tools change, so a queue with ordering guarantees would make the workaround vanish. Needing something to run doesn't make it essential, and cleaner code doesn't remove the complexity of tax law.

cards.prompt: Why are good abstractions one of the best tools for managing complexity?
keyPoints: They hide a lot of implementation detail behind a simple interface
One abstraction can be reused by many applications instead of each rebuilding it
Improvements to the shared component benefit every application that uses it
cards.explanation: SQL, for example, hides storage structures, concurrent clients and crash recovery from whoever writes the query.

cards.title: Evolvability
cards.body:
Requirements never stand still. You learn new facts, users ask for features, priorities shift, platforms get replaced, laws change, and growth forces a new architecture. **Evolvability** is how easily a data system can be changed to keep up. It goes hand in hand with simplicity and good abstractions: loosely coupled, simple systems are easier to change than tightly coupled, complex ones.

A big obstacle is **irreversibility**. Say you move a service to a new message queue. If you can switch back when something goes wrong, the move is low-stakes; if you can't, every mistake sticks. So take irreversible steps with great care, and keep a way back wherever you can.

cards.prompt: A team wants to move every stored record to a new encoding format. Which plan best keeps the system easy to evolve?
choices: Convert all records in place over one weekend, discarding the old copies
Write both formats for a while, so they can fall back if needed
Wait to change the format until the requirements stop changing
Freeze the schema after the switch, so nothing can ever break it again
cards.explanation: Irreversible steps raise the stakes of any change, so keeping a way back makes the switch safer and the system more flexible. Converting in place and discarding the originals removes the escape route. Requirements never stop changing. A frozen schema makes the system harder to change, the opposite of evolvability, which comes from simplicity, good abstractions and loose coupling.

cards.title: Layers of data models
cards.body:
Software usually layers data models, each one built from the one below it.

You start from the part of the world your app is about, say a bakery's customers, cakes and orders, and model it as objects and data structures in your code. To store those, you express them in a general-purpose model: JSON documents, relational tables, or a graph of vertices and edges. The database's engineers decided how that model becomes bytes, in RAM, on disk or sent over a network. Lower still, hardware represents bytes as electrical charge, light or magnetism.

Each layer hides the mess below behind a clean model, so people on different layers can work together.

cards.prompt: Order these layers of data modeling, from the highest level to the lowest.
items: The real world: people, goods, money, events
Objects and data structures in the application's code
A general-purpose model: JSON documents, relational tables or a graph
Bytes in RAM, on disk or sent over the network, laid out by the database engine
Electrical currents, light pulses or magnetic fields in the hardware
cards.explanation: Each layer hides the complexity below it behind a cleaner model, which lets the people working on different layers, like database vendors and app developers, cooperate.

cards.title: Declarative queries
cards.body:
SQL and most query languages here are **declarative**. You describe the result you want, which conditions the data must meet and how to sort, group or total it, but not how to get there. The **query optimizer** picks the indexes, the join method and the order of steps.

In ordinary code you write the algorithm yourself. A declarative query is usually shorter, but the bigger win is that it hides the engine's internals. So the database can get faster between releases, say with a better join algorithm, and your queries gain without any change.

cards.prompt: Your database's next release can run a single query across many CPU cores at once. Which part of your code speeds up without being rewritten?
choices: A loop in your app that fetches rows by key and sums them itself
Both, since the database parallelizes any code that talks to it
A SQL query that states which rows to group and total
Neither: parallel execution only applies to queries rewritten with hints
cards.explanation: A declarative query says what result is wanted, not how to compute it, so the engine is free to choose indexes, join order and parallelism. Your loop is an algorithm the database can't see or change. The database can't parallelize code running in your app, and declarative queries need no rewriting to benefit.

cards.title: Objects, tables and ORMs
cards.body:
In the **relational model**, data lives in tables (*relations*) of rows (*tuples*). App code mostly works with objects, though, and translating between the two takes glue code. That awkward gap is the **impedance mismatch**.

**Object-relational mapping (ORM)** frameworks write most of the glue for you, and some also cache results or manage schema migrations. But they have critics. The gap still leaks, so you end up thinking in objects and tables at once. Analysts read the tables directly, so the schema still needs careful design. Generated schemas can be clumsy or slow, and customizing them can cancel the gain. And ORMs make slow queries easy to write by accident, most famously the N+1 problem.

cards.prompt: What are the common complaints about object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks?
keyPoints: They can't fully hide the gap between objects and tables, so developers still think about both
Analytics teams work with the tables directly, so the relational schema still has to be designed well
Schemas they generate can be awkward or inefficient, and customizing them erodes the benefit
They make it easy to write slow query patterns by accident, such as N+1 queries
cards.explanation: Many ORMs also support only relational OLTP databases, which leaves gaps for teams that also run search engines or graph databases.

cards.title: The N+1 problem
cards.body:
Say a music app lists 30 songs, each with its artist's name. Each song row holds only an artist ID, so the names have to come from the artists table.

In hand-written SQL you'd join the two tables and get songs and names back in a single query. A naive ORM often does something else: one query loads the 30 songs, then reading each song's artist fires off its own lookup. That's 31 queries where one would do, and the count grows with the list. This is the **N+1 problem**.

The fix is to tell the ORM to load the artists together with the songs.

cards.prompt: A page lists 200 invoices along with each customer's name. The database log shows 201 queries for every page load. What's going on?
choices: A missing index on customers forces a separate scan for each invoice
One query loads the invoices, then the ORM fetches each customer on its own
The database executes the invoice-customer join as one query per row
Each cache miss in the ORM's result cache adds an extra query
cards.explanation: This is the N+1 problem: one query for the list, then one lookup per row. Telling the ORM to fetch customers along with the invoices, or writing the join by hand, gets it down to one query. A missing index slows lookups but doesn't add queries, a join runs as one query, and caching removes queries rather than adding them.

cards.title: Documents for one-to-many data
cards.body:
The NoSQL movement of the 2010s made the **document model** popular: each record is a JSON document, often closer to the objects in your code.

Take a hotel listing: one name and address, plus lists of photos, room types and amenities that belong to that hotel alone. Each list is a **one-to-many** relationship, and together they form a tree. Tables split that tree apart, so loading a listing takes several queries or a messy join. A document keeps the tree together, so one lookup fetches it all. That's **locality**.

This suits short lists, really *one-to-few*. If one could grow into the thousands, store those items separately, each pointing to its parent.

cards.prompt: A recipe has one title and author, plus lists of ingredients, steps and photos that belong only to it. Why is it often faster to load as one JSON document than from several tables?
choices: It's all stored together, so one lookup replaces several queries or a multiway join
JSON is a more compact encoding than rows, so less data is read from disk
Document databases enforce a schema, so reads can skip validation
The tables would need a separate join table for each list
cards.explanation: The lists are one-to-many relationships owned by the recipe, forming a tree, and a document keeps that tree in one place: that's locality. JSON isn't necessarily more compact than rows, and most document databases enforce no schema. Each list belongs to one recipe, so plain tables with a foreign key would do; no join tables needed.

cards.prompt: A store keeps each product as a document with all its customer reviews embedded. Some best-sellers now have tens of thousands of reviews. What's the better design?
choices: Keep embedding them: one document always gives the best locality
Compress the embedded reviews so each document stays a manageable size
Store each review separately, with a reference to its product
cards.explanation: Embedding suits one-to-few relationships, like a handful of variants per product. With thousands of related items the document becomes unwieldy, and loading or rewriting it gets ever more expensive. Locality only pays when you need most of a document at once, and compression shrinks the bytes without fixing a list that keeps growing.

cards.title: IDs or plain text
cards.body:
Say a marketplace files every listing under a category. You could store the category's text, or the ID of an entry in a standard list. The list has advantages. Every listing spells the category the same way. Clashing names stay distinct: 'Pool' for swimming gear and 'Pool' for billiards get different IDs. A rename, or a translation, happens in one place and shows up everywhere. And search gets smarter, since the list can record that billiard tables belong under games.

Storing the ID is **normalized**: the human-readable text lives in one place. Copying the text into every record is **denormalized**. An ID means nothing to people, so it never needs to change.

cards.prompt: Why might a profile store a city as an ID from a standard list of places rather than as free text?
keyPoints: Every profile spells and formats the place the same way
Places that share a name can't be confused
The name lives in one place, so a rename or translation changes it everywhere
Search can use facts the list records, such as which wider region the place is in
cards.explanation: Storing the ID makes the data normalized; copying the text into every profile makes it denormalized.

cards.title: Normalization trade-offs
cards.body:
Normalized data keeps one copy of each fact, so a change is one cheap write. The cost lands on reads: showing a record means resolving its IDs, with a **join** in a relational database, or a second query from your code if your document database lacks joins.

Denormalized data flips that. Reads find the values right there, but a change must reach every copy: more code, more writes, more disk. Some process must keep the copies in step, making them a kind of derived data, and if it crashes halfway, copies disagree. Multi-record transactions help, where available.

OLTP and smaller systems usually do best normalized. Analytics, with bulk updates and heavy reads, often prefers denormalized.

cards.prompt: Compare normalized and denormalized data: reads, writes, and keeping it consistent.
keyPoints: Reads: normalized data needs joins or extra lookups; denormalized data has the values right there
Writes: normalized data has one copy to change; denormalized data has many, which also take more disk
Consistency: denormalized copies need a process to keep them in sync, and a crash midway can leave them disagreeing
cards.explanation: That makes denormalized data a kind of derived data; atomic transactions across several records, which not every database offers, help keep the copies in step.

cards.prompt: A podcast app stores the network's name and artwork URL inside every episode record. The network rebrands with new artwork. What's the problem?
choices: None: each episode is self-contained, so nothing else needs changing
None: the copies update themselves, since they came from one network record
The foreign keys from episodes to the network break and must be rebuilt
Every copy of the old URL must be found and updated, or some episodes stay stale
cards.explanation: Copying the network's details into every episode is denormalized, so one change means many writes and a risk of inconsistency. A network record referenced by ID would need a single update. Being self-contained is exactly why every copy must change, copies don't update themselves, and with copied values there are no foreign keys to break.

cards.title: Hydrating IDs
cards.body:
Precomputed results are denormalized, but you needn't copy everything. Say a news app builds each reader's front page in advance. Headlines get edited and comment counts climb all day, so copies would go stale. Instead each entry holds just the article ID, and the app fetches the current headline and count when the page is shown. That's **hydrating** the IDs: a join done in application code. Lookups by ID parallelize well, so this scales.

So decide field by field. Fast-changing data is better fetched by ID at read time; stable data can be copied. Weigh read costs against write costs, counting outliers like an account with millions of followers. Often the best design copies some fields and keeps others normalized.

cards.prompt: A shop precomputes a 'picked for you' list for each user. Product prices and stock levels change many times a day. What should each list entry store?
choices: Only the product ID; price and stock are looked up when the list is shown
The full product details, so showing the list needs no lookups
The full details, plus a nightly job that rewrites every list
Nothing: compute the picks from scratch on every page view
cards.explanation: Storing IDs and resolving them at read time (hydrating them) keeps fast-changing fields fresh without rewriting every list. Full copies would go stale within hours and multiply storage, and a nightly rewrite still shows stale prices all day. Recomputing the picks on each view throws away the expensive work you precomputed.

cards.prompt: How do you decide whether to denormalize a particular piece of data?
keyPoints: Consider how often it changes: fast-changing data is better looked up by ID when read
Weigh the cost of reads against writes, including outliers such as unusually active users
It doesn't have to be all or nothing: denormalize some fields and keep others normalized
cards.explanation: Joins at read time needn't block scaling: looking up records by ID parallelizes well, and its cost doesn't grow with how connected an account is.

cards.title: Many-to-one, many-to-many
cards.body:
Not every relationship is one-to-many. Take a recipe app. Many recipes share one cuisine, and each recipe has only one: that's **many-to-one**. A recipe uses many ingredients, and each ingredient turns up in many recipes: that's **many-to-many**.

Neither fits neatly inside a self-contained document. Embedding full cuisine and ingredient records in every recipe would copy the same data into thousands of documents. So these lean toward normalization: a document keeps what belongs to it alone, like its steps, and refers to shared things by ID. In a relational schema, a many-to-many link becomes a **join table**, where each row pairs one ID with another.

cards.prompt: A travel app stores each trip as a JSON document. Which of these belongs embedded in the trip document?
choices: The hotel, which many travelers' trips also reference
The traveler's day-by-day notes, written for this trip only
The fellow travelers, each of whom joins many trips
The departure airport's details, which many other trips share
cards.explanation: The notes belong to one trip: a one-to-many relationship that forms a tree inside the document. The hotel, airport and companions are each shared by many trips (many-to-one or many-to-many), so they're better stored once and referenced by ID; copies in every trip are hard to keep consistent.

cards.title: Querying both ways
cards.body:
Many-to-many links are often queried from both ends. With actors and films, you want an actor's films and a film's cast.

One way is to keep ID lists on both sides: each actor lists film IDs, and each film lists actor IDs. That's denormalized, since every link is stored twice, and the two copies can drift apart.

The normalized way stores each link once, as a row in a join table, with a **secondary index** on each of its two ID columns. The database can then find the rows quickly from either side. Document databases, and relational ones with JSON support, can likewise index values inside a document's nested lists.

cards.prompt: You need to list the courses a student has taken, and the students who took a course. How does a normalized design make both queries fast?
choices: Store each course's student IDs in the course and each student's course IDs in the student
Embed the full student records inside each course document
Store enrollments once, indexed by student; course lookups scan the table
Store each enrollment once in a join table, indexed on both its student and course columns
cards.explanation: A join table stores each relationship once, and secondary indexes on both ID columns make it fast to query from either side. Keeping ID lists on both sides works, but it's denormalized: the two copies can drift apart. Embedding students duplicates them in every course, and indexing one column leaves the other direction slow.

cards.title: Star schemas
cards.body:
Data warehouses are usually relational, and many arrange their tables as a **star schema**. Picture a cinema chain. At the center is a **fact table** with one row per event, at the finest grain: one ticket sold. That keeps analysis flexible but makes fact tables huge.

Each fact row holds values, like the price paid and the cost, plus foreign keys into **dimension tables** that give the who, what, where and when: which film, which cinema, which customer, which day. Even dates get a dimension, so a day can carry facts like being a holiday. A family buying four tickets at once isn't one row: it's four fact rows that share the customer, cinema and time.

cards.prompt: How is a star schema in a data warehouse laid out?
keyPoints: A central fact table has one row per event, such as a single sale
Fact rows hold values like price and cost, plus foreign keys to dimension tables
Dimension tables give each event's context: which product, store, customer and date (so holidays can be flagged)
cards.explanation: A snowflake schema goes further and splits dimensions into subdimensions: more normalized, but harder for analysts to work with.

cards.prompt: A bookshop customer buys three different books in one order. How does a typical star schema record this?
choices: One fact row for the order, with a list of the book IDs
One fact row for the order, plus an order dimension listing its books
Three fact rows, one per book, that share the customer, shop and date
Three dimension rows, linked to one fact row for the payment
cards.explanation: Facts are usually kept as individual events, here one book bought, so the order becomes three fact rows sharing their customer, shop and date keys. A list of IDs doesn't fit a relational column. Dimensions describe the context of events, such as which book or which shop, not the events themselves, so neither an order dimension nor purchase rows in a dimension fits.

cards.title: Snowflakes and one big table
cards.body:
Two variants of the star schema go in opposite directions. A **snowflake schema** normalizes further, splitting dimensions into subdimensions. Instead of storing each film's studio as text, the film dimension would point to a separate studio table. That's tidier, but analysts face more tables and joins, so plain stars are often preferred.

**One big table (OBT)** denormalizes completely: dimension columns are copied into the fact table, as if every join were done in advance. It takes more storage but can make queries faster.

Copying like this is fine in analytics. The data records past events that won't change, apart from the odd correction, so the copies rarely need updating.

cards.prompt: A warehouse's product dimension stores each product's supplier and country of origin as text. An engineer moves suppliers and countries into their own tables, referenced by key from the product dimension. What's the trade-off?
choices: The fact table shrinks, since sales rows now point straight at suppliers and countries
It becomes one big table: faster queries in exchange for more storage
It's more normalized, but analysts must join more tables, so queries get harder to write
Queries get simpler, since each table now has fewer columns to search
cards.explanation: Splitting dimensions into subdimensions turns a star into a snowflake schema: less duplication, but more tables and joins for analysts, which is why stars are often preferred. The fact table doesn't change; it still references the product dimension. One big table goes the other way, folding dimensions into the fact table, and narrower tables don't make queries simpler.

cards.prompt: One big table (OBT) folds dimension data into the fact table, duplicating it across millions of rows. Why is that acceptable in a warehouse but risky in an OLTP database?
choices: Warehouses enforce consistency automatically across duplicated columns
Historical facts rarely change, so the copies seldom need updating
Warehouses keep data compressed in memory, so duplication costs nothing
OLTP databases can't store wide tables with hundreds of columns
cards.explanation: Analytical data is mostly a log of past events, fixed except for the odd correction, so the update cost and consistency risk of copies barely apply. OBT spends extra storage to skip joins, which can make queries faster. Warehouses don't sync copies by magic, and table width isn't what makes denormalizing OLTP data risky.

cards.title: Where documents fit
cards.body:
Documents suit a tree of one-to-many links that's usually loaded whole. Splitting such a tree across tables, called **shredding**, makes schemas and code clumsy. Relational tables win on joins and on many-to-one or many-to-many links.

A nested item has no identity of its own: you can only point at it by position, like 'the third address of customer 7', which breaks if the list changes. A relational row has its own ID.

User-ordered lists favor documents. If people drag photos around an album, the IDs sit in a JSON array whose order is the album's. Rows have no order, so tables need a trick: a position column renumbered on inserts, a linked list of IDs, or *fractional indexing*.

cards.prompt: A support ticket needs to point at one line item inside a customer's order. Orders are stored as documents. What's the difficulty?
choices: It has no ID of its own, so you refer to it by position: 'item 3 of order 88'
Documents can't contain lists, so line items must be stored elsewhere
Document databases forbid references from one document to another
cards.explanation: Nested items aren't directly addressable, so a reference must name the parent and a position, which breaks if the list changes. In a relational schema each line item is a row with its own ID. Documents hold lists happily and can reference other documents by ID; pointing inside one is the hard part.

cards.prompt: Users drag and drop tracks to reorder a playlist. Why is this easier to model in a document database than a relational one?
choices: Documents keep their fields sorted, so the tracks stay in order on their own
Relational databases can't store any kind of ordering
Relational tables are ordered by insertion, so moving a track means deleting and reinserting rows
The track IDs can sit in a JSON array whose order is the playlist's order
cards.explanation: An array preserves order, so moving a track just rewrites the array. Relational rows have no inherent order, so you need a workaround: an integer position column (renumbering on inserts in the middle), a linked list of IDs, or fractional indexing. That's awkward, not impossible. Documents don't sort anything automatically.

cards.title: Schema-on-read
cards.body:
Most document databases enforce no schema: a document can hold any fields. They're often called **schemaless**, but that's misleading. The code reading the data still expects certain fields, so a schema exists; it's just implicit, and nothing checks it on write. A better name is **schema-on-read**. Relational databases are **schema-on-write**: they check every write against an explicit schema. It's like dynamic versus static type checking, with no clear winner.

Schema-on-read suits mixed data: many kinds of objects, too many for a table each, or a structure set by outside systems that may change it at any time. When all records should look alike, an enforced schema documents that shape and guarantees it.

cards.prompt: Why is calling a document database 'schemaless' misleading?
choices: Code reading the data still assumes a structure; nothing enforces it on write
Document databases check every write against a schema, only a looser one
The schema is kept in a hidden catalog that the database applies on read
Each document must declare its schema in a reserved field
cards.explanation: The schema is implicit and applied by whoever reads the data, hence schema-on-read; relational databases check it on write instead. It's like dynamic versus static type checking. Most document databases enforce nothing on write, keep no hidden catalog and need no schema field; that lack of enforcement is the point.

cards.prompt: When does schema-on-read suit data better than an enforced schema, and when doesn't it?
keyPoints: When there are many kinds of objects and a table for each isn't practical
When the structure is set by outside systems that can change it at any time
When all records should share one structure, an enforced schema documents and checks it
cards.explanation: Schema-on-read has a cost: every piece of code that reads the data must cope with old formats written long ago.

cards.title: Changing the shape of data
cards.body:
Say you stored prices as one text field, like '12.50 EUR', and now want amount and currency apart.

With documents, you just start writing the new fields and make the app handle old documents when it reads them. The catch: every part of the app that reads the data must cope with old formats, maybe years old.

With an enforced schema you run a migration. Adding a column that defaults to NULL is quick in most relational databases, even on huge tables. Filling it with an UPDATE is slow, since every row is rewritten; changing a column's type usually copies the table. Or skip the backfill: add the empty column and fill it in as rows are read.

cards.prompt: A huge relational table stores each customer's full address in one column. You want a separate postcode column. What's the least disruptive way to add it?
choices: Add the column, then run an UPDATE that fills it on every row
Rebuild the table, since adding any column copies it entirely
Add the column as nullable, and fill it in when an old row is read
Move the table into a document database, which needs no migrations
cards.explanation: Adding a nullable column is quick in most relational databases; the slow part is a backfill that rewrites every row. Filling the value in lazily when rows are read, as a document store would, avoids that. A document database doesn't remove the problem: every reader must handle old-format records. Adding a column doesn't copy the table, though changing a column's type usually does.

cards.title: Data locality
cards.body:
A document is usually stored as one continuous string, in JSON or a binary form of it. When you need the whole thing, say to render a page, that's fast: one read, where data spread across tables takes several index lookups and possibly more disk seeks.

The gain only holds when you need most of the document. The database usually loads all of it, even to read one field, and an update usually rewrites all of it. So it pays to keep documents small and not to update them often in tiny ways.

Locality isn't unique to documents. Some relational databases can store a child table's rows inside their parent's, and wide-column stores use column families for the same purpose.

cards.prompt: When does keeping a record as one document stop paying off for performance?
keyPoints: When you usually need only a small part of it: the database typically loads the whole document anyway
When it's updated often in small ways: an update usually rewrites the entire document
So it's best to keep documents small and not update them often in tiny ways
cards.explanation: Locality isn't unique to documents: some relational databases can store a child table's rows inside their parent's, and wide-column stores use column families for the same goal.

cards.title: The models converge
cards.body:
Document databases vary in how you query them. Some only fetch a document by its key, some can also index fields inside documents, and some have rich query languages, such as a pipeline of stages written in JSON that can do roughly what a subset of SQL can.

Over time the two camps have moved closer. Relational databases added JSON column types, operators that query inside JSON, and indexes on values within documents. Document databases added joins, secondary indexes and declarative queries.

That's good news, because each model needs some of the other. Documents often refer to other records, relational-style, and relational schemas have corners where flexibility helps. A hybrid offers both.

cards.prompt: How have relational and document databases converged, and why is that useful?
keyPoints: Relational databases added JSON types, JSON query operators and indexes on values inside documents
Document databases added joins, secondary indexes and declarative ways to query
Document data often needs references to other records, and relational schemas often have parts that need flexibility
cards.explanation: Nesting isn't new to the relational model: Codd's original proposal allowed a value in a row to be a whole nested table.

cards.title: Graphs
cards.body:
When many-to-many links are everywhere and tangled, a **graph** becomes the natural model: **vertices** (also called nodes) joined by **edges**. Scientific papers form one, with each citation an edge between two papers; so do flights, where a route planner searches for the shortest path between airports.

Vertices needn't all be the same kind of thing. One graph can hold people, venues, concerts and photos, with edges for who went to which concert, where it was held, and who appears in which photo. Graphs suit data where anything may link to anything and queries follow chains of links of unknown length. Documents suit the opposite: self-contained trees with few links between them.

cards.prompt: A fraud team links accounts, cards, devices, phone numbers and addresses. Any of them may connect to any other, and investigators follow chains of links. Which data model fits best?
choices: A document model, embedding each account's cards and devices
A star schema, with accounts as the fact table
A DataFrame, pivoted into an account-by-device matrix
A graph, with each entity a vertex and each link an edge
cards.explanation: Many-to-many links everywhere, and queries that hop an unknown number of steps, are where graphs shine. Documents suit trees with few links between records; a device shared by many accounts breaks that. Star schemas serve aggregate analysis of events, and a matrix suits ML input rather than following chains.

cards.title: Property graphs
cards.body:
In a **property graph**, each vertex has a unique ID, a **label** for what kind of thing it is, its outgoing and incoming edges, and key-value **properties**. Each edge has an ID, a *tail* vertex where it starts, a *head* vertex where it ends, a label naming the relationship, and properties of its own.

That's very flexible. Any vertex can connect to any other; no schema limits what links to what. Every vertex knows its incoming and outgoing edges, so you can follow paths forward or backward. Labels let one graph hold many kinds of data cleanly. And as the app grows, new kinds of vertices and edges fit right in.

cards.prompt: What makes the property graph model flexible for data modeling?
keyPoints: Any vertex can connect to any other; no schema limits which kinds of things may be linked
Incoming and outgoing edges can both be found quickly, so paths can be followed forward or backward
Labels on vertices and edges let one graph hold many kinds of data cleanly
New kinds of vertices and edges can be added as the application grows
cards.explanation: Irregular data fits easily, such as regions structured differently in each country, or places known at different levels of detail.

cards.title: Cypher patterns
cards.body:
**Cypher** is a language for querying property graphs. It draws edges as arrows: `(a) -[:KNOWS]-> (b)` is an edge labeled KNOWS with tail a and head b. A MATCH clause finds every part of the graph that fits a pattern like that, binding named vertices to variables; an unnamed `()` matches any vertex.

A pattern can repeat an edge. Writing `*0..` after a label means follow that kind of edge zero or more times, like `*` in a regular expression. So `-[:INSIDE*0..]->` reaches the vertex you started from, plus everything one, two or more INSIDE hops away. That lets a short query handle hierarchies of any depth.

cards.prompt: A Cypher query matches (p) -[:WORKS_AT]-> () -[:PART_OF*0..]-> (:Org {name:'Acme'}). One employee's WORKS_AT edge points straight at the Acme vertex. Is that employee matched?
choices: No: the pattern needs at least one PART_OF edge
Yes: *0.. allows zero PART_OF hops, so Acme itself can be the vertex reached
Only if Acme also has a PART_OF edge pointing to itself
No: the unnamed vertex must be different from the Acme vertex
cards.explanation: *0.. means follow the edge zero or more times, like * in a regular expression, so the target of WORKS_AT can be Acme itself or any unit nested under it. Requiring at least one hop would need a lower bound of 1. No self-loop is needed, and an unnamed vertex can match the same vertex as a named one.

cards.title: Running a graph query
cards.body:
A Cypher query is declarative, so the database chooses how to run it. Say you want everyone who studied at a school anywhere in Scotland.

It could start from every person, check where each one studied, and keep those in Scotland. Or it could work backward. If vertex names are indexed, it first jumps straight to the Scotland vertex. Then it follows incoming INSIDE edges, again and again, to collect every place within Scotland. From each of those places it follows incoming STUDIED_AT edges to reach the people, and returns their names. Which way is faster depends on the data, and the optimizer picks.

cards.prompt: A graph query finds staff who work anywhere inside Germany, and location names are indexed. Order how the database can answer it by working backward from the location.
items: Use the name index to find the Germany vertex
Follow incoming WITHIN edges, again and again, to collect every location inside Germany
From each of those locations, follow incoming WORKS_AT edges to find people
Return each person's name
cards.explanation: The same query could also run forward, scanning every person and checking where they work; a declarative query leaves that choice to the database.

cards.title: Graph queries in SQL
cards.body:
A property graph fits in a relational database as a vertices table and an edges table, with an index on each end of an edge. Querying it with SQL is harder.

Each edge a query follows is one more join with the edges table. Most SQL queries know their joins in advance, but a graph query may follow a chain of any length, such as from a street up through its district and city to its country. SQL expresses that with **recursive common table expressions** (`WITH RECURSIVE`). They work, but they're verbose: a few lines of Cypher can become dozens of lines of SQL, and cycles and the choice between breadth-first and depth-first search add more.

cards.prompt: Graph data can live in relational tables. Why are graph queries over it clumsy in SQL?
keyPoints: Every edge followed is another join with the edges table
A path can have any number of hops, so the number of joins isn't known when you write the query
Variable-length paths need recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE), which are verbose
cards.explanation: Cycles and the choice between breadth-first and depth-first traversal add more to handle; a few lines of Cypher can turn into dozens of SQL.

cards.title: Triple stores
cards.body:
A **triple store** holds much the same information as a property graph, in another shape. Every fact is a triple: *subject*, *predicate*, *object*.

The subject is a vertex. The object decides what the triple means. If it's another vertex, the predicate is an edge between the two: (ana, livesIn, lisbon) links the vertex ana to the vertex lisbon. If it's a plain value, like a number or some text, predicate and object work as a property's key and value: (ana, age, 34) gives the vertex ana an age of 34.

Since edges and properties share one form, a query can match both with the same syntax.

cards.prompt: A triple store holds (sensor9, mountedOn, pole4) and (sensor9, batteryLevel, 82). How do these two triples differ?
choices: Both are edges; a triple store has no notion of properties
The first is a property and the second an edge, since numbers are vertices
The first is an edge between two vertices; the second is a property, since 82 is a value
Both are properties of sensor9, since they share a subject
cards.explanation: A triple's subject is a vertex. When the object is another vertex, the predicate is an edge label; when it's a plain value, predicate and object act as a property's key and value. Triple stores do have properties, written just like edges, which is why SPARQL matches both with the same syntax.

cards.title: RDF and URIs
cards.body:
The **Semantic Web** was an early-2000s plan to publish data across the internet in a standard format machines could read. It never worked out as imagined, but parts live on, such as knowledge graphs, linked-data formats and triple stores.

Its data model, **RDF**, was built for merging data from many sources. So the parts of a triple are often URIs, like `urn:shop:price` rather than plain price. If another publisher means something else by price, their URI differs, and merged data doesn't clash. The URI is just a namespace; it needn't lead to a real page, and you declare the prefix once per file. RDF's query language, **SPARQL**, inspired Cypher's pattern matching.

cards.prompt: Why do RDF triples often use URIs as predicates, such as urn:acme:contains, rather than plain words like contains?
choices: Because RDF requires each predicate's URI to resolve to a page defining it
So data merged from many sources won't clash when two use one word differently
So the database can look predicates up by URI faster than by name
cards.explanation: RDF was designed for exchanging data across the internet, so predicates are namespaced: your 'contains' and a partner's 'contains' stay distinct. The URI needn't resolve to anything; it's only a namespace, usually declared once as a prefix. Lookup speed has nothing to do with it.

cards.title: Datalog
cards.body:
**Datalog** comes from 1980s research, older than SPARQL or Cypher. Its model is relational, not a graph, but it's especially good at recursive queries.

The data is a set of **facts**, each like a row in a table: `city(7, 'Lyon')` says the city table has a row holding 7 and Lyon. You query by writing **rules** that define new virtual tables, like SQL views that aren't stored. A rule has a head left of `:-` and patterns right of it. When values match every pattern on the right, the head, filled with those values, counts as a new fact.

Rules can use other rules and themselves, like functions calling functions. That recursion lets Datalog walk graphs.

cards.prompt: How does Datalog build up a query?
keyPoints: Data is stored as facts, each one like a row in a relational table
Rules define new virtual tables, like views that aren't stored
A rule applies when everything on its right-hand side matches, adding its left-hand side as a derived fact
Rules can use other rules and themselves, so recursion handles graph traversal
cards.explanation: It's like breaking a program into small functions that call each other.

cards.title: Recursive rules
cards.body:
Here's how recursion climbs a hierarchy. Say the facts are: Gion is within Kyoto, and Kyoto is within Japan.

A base rule says every place is within itself, which gives 'Japan is in Japan'. A recursive rule says: if X is within Y, and Y is in some region, then X is in that region too. Combining 'Kyoto is within Japan' with the base result gives 'Kyoto is in Japan'. Applying it again, to 'Gion is within Kyoto', gives 'Gion is in Japan'. Rules keep firing until nothing new appears. Then another rule can join these results with where people live, to find everyone living in Japan.

cards.prompt: Datalog facts say Ribeira is within Porto, and Porto is within Portugal. Order how recursive rules work out who lives in Portugal.
items: A base rule says every place is within itself, so Portugal is within Portugal
A recursive rule combines 'Porto is within Portugal' with that result: Porto is in Portugal
The same rule, applied to 'Ribeira is within Porto', derives that Ribeira is in Portugal
A rule joining people's home locations with these results finds everyone living in Portugal
cards.explanation: Each step needs the fact derived just before it. The system keeps applying rules until no new facts appear.

cards.title: GraphQL
cards.body:
**GraphQL** lets a client app ask a server for a JSON document shaped exactly for its screen. Despite the name, it runs on any kind of database.

Queries come from untrusted devices, so the language is deliberately narrow: nothing that could be expensive, or costly queries could swamp the server. There are no recursive queries and no arbitrary search conditions; clients get only the searches the service's owners chose to offer.

A response mirrors its query, with exactly the requested fields. It's often denormalized: five orders from one store repeat the store's name five times. Returning IDs instead would mean extra requests, so GraphQL accepts the bigger payload to keep UI code simple. The server's own storage can stay normalized.

cards.prompt: A mobile developer wants a GraphQL query that returns every user who signed up in March and lives in Spain. The API offers no such search. What happens?
choices: They can write it anyway, since GraphQL supports arbitrary filters like SQL
They can, but only if the server's data lives in a graph database
They can express it as a recursive query over the users
They can't until the service owners offer it; GraphQL omits arbitrary filters by design
cards.explanation: GraphQL queries come from untrusted clients, so the language rules out anything potentially expensive, including arbitrary search conditions and recursive queries, to avoid accidental denial of service. The server exposes only the fields and joins its schema declares. GraphQL can sit on any kind of database: relational and document as much as graph.

cards.prompt: In a GraphQL response, a commenter's name and avatar are repeated in every comment they wrote. Why does GraphQL accept this duplication?
choices: The server must keep its data denormalized to answer GraphQL queries
GraphQL can't express a reference from one object to another, so it copies
A UI-shaped response is simpler to render, at the cost of a bigger payload
cards.explanation: GraphQL returns exactly the fields requested, nested the way the client asked, trading a bigger response for simpler rendering. Returning IDs instead would force extra requests for anything not already loaded. The server's database can still be normalized and resolve IDs with joins declared in its schema, and a client could request IDs if it wanted them.

cards.title: Event sourcing and CQRS
cards.body:
So far, data has been read in the same shape it was written. Sometimes no single shape serves every way the data is used. Then you can write it in one form and derive others, each tuned for certain reads.

The simplest write format is an **event log**: each change is appended as a self-contained record with a timestamp. Events are **immutable**, never edited or deleted. Whenever one is appended, **materialized views** (also called *projections* or *read models*) update to reflect it.

Using the event log as the source of truth is **event sourcing**. Deriving separate read-optimized representations from the write-optimized one is **CQRS**, command query responsibility segregation. The two often go together.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between event sourcing and CQRS?
keyPoints: Event sourcing: every state change is recorded as an event, and the event log is the source of truth
CQRS: data is written in one form and read from separate representations derived from it and optimized for queries
cards.explanation: They're often used together: the log is the write-optimized form, and materialized views (projections) are the read-optimized ones.

cards.title: Commands and events
cards.body:
Take a gym booking app built this way. A member asks to book a spin class: that request is a **command**. The system first checks it: is a bike free, is the membership active? Only if it passes does it become a fact, appended to the log as an event. The views update from that event, and later reads are served from the views.

Since only valid events reach the log, a view must apply every event; it can't reject one. Name events in the past tense, like 'class booked', because each records something that already happened. If the member cancels later, the booking still happened; the cancellation is a new event.

cards.prompt: Order how a request to borrow a library book is handled in an event-sourced system.
items: A member's request to borrow a book arrives as a command
The command is checked: is a copy available, and does the member have no overdue loans?
Being valid, it becomes a fact, recorded as a new event at the end of the log
Materialized views, like availability and each member's loans, update from the event
Later reads are answered from those views
cards.explanation: Events get past-tense names, like 'book borrowed', because each records something that already happened; returning the book is a separate, later event.

cards.prompt: A service building a view from the event log reads an event saying a table was reserved, but its view shows the restaurant already full. What should it do?
choices: Apply it: the event was validated before logging, so it's a fact
Skip the event, since applying it would make the view inconsistent
Delete the event from the log and notify the user who reserved
Reject it, so the command can be retried against fresh data
cards.explanation: Validation happens when the command is handled; once logged, an event is a fact. A view that disagrees is buggy or behind, and skipping or rejecting events would make views drift from the log and from each other. Events are never deleted: corrections are made by appending new ones.

cards.title: Event logs and fact tables
cards.body:
An event log looks a lot like a star schema's fact table: both record things that happened. Two differences matter.

A fact table's rows all have the same columns. An event log mixes many event types, each with its own properties: a booking carries different details from a refund.

And a fact table is an unordered set, while an event log's order is essential: processing a cancellation before its booking makes no sense. So every view must see the events in exactly the order they sit in the log, which is harder than it sounds in a distributed system.

cards.prompt: An event log and a star schema fact table both record past events. How do they differ?
keyPoints: Fact table rows all have the same columns; an event log mixes many event types with different properties
A fact table is unordered; in an event log order matters, since a refund only makes sense after its payment

cards.title: Benefits of an event log
cards.body:
Events capture intent: 'order canceled' tells a developer why data changed, where a list of row updates across three tables doesn't.

Views are derived from the log reproducibly, so they're disposable. If view code has a bug, fix it and rebuild the view from the log. Want to present data in a new way? Build a new view from the events you already have. New features can add event types or fields, and old events stay untouched. A mistaken event is undone by appending one that reverses it, so fewer actions are irreversible. The log also serves as an audit trail, and being append-only, it can soak up bursts of writes.

cards.prompt: What are the main advantages of event sourcing with CQRS?
keyPoints: Events record intent: why something changed, not just which rows changed
Views can be dropped and rebuilt from the log, so bugs in view code are easy to fix
New views can be built from the existing log later, with old events left unchanged
Mistakes are reversed by appending a correcting event, so fewer actions are irreversible
cards.explanation: The log also serves as an audit trail and, being append-only, absorbs bursts of writes that views catch up on later.

cards.title: Rebuilding a view
cards.body:
A view must come out identical whenever the same code replays the same events in log order. That makes a broken view easy to replace.

First fix the bug in the view's code. Then build a fresh view by replaying the log from its very first event through the fixed code. Meanwhile the old view keeps answering reads. Once the new one has caught up with the latest events, switch reads over to it and delete the old one.

Views can use any database and any data model, denormalized for fast reads. One can even live only in memory, rebuilt from the log on each restart.

cards.prompt: A materialized view shows wrong totals. Order how you fix it in an event-sourced system.
items: Find and fix the bug in the view code
Build a new view by replaying the log from the start through the fixed code
Let the new view catch up with the latest events
Switch reads over to the new view
Delete the old, wrong view
cards.explanation: Building the new view alongside the old one means reads never go without a view. Replay only works if processing is deterministic and sees events in the log's order, and it mustn't repeat side effects such as sending emails.

cards.title: Safe replays
cards.body:
Replaying the log must give the same result every time, and must not disturb the outside world.

Beware of outside information. Say a ride app's view prices each trip by asking another service for the current surge multiplier. Rebuild the view next month and the multipliers differ, so the prices change. Put the value in the event itself, or fetch it from a source that always returns the same answer for the event's timestamp.

Beware of side effects, too. If handling an event charges a card or emails a receipt, a rebuild would do it all over again. Keep such actions out of the code that rebuilds views.

cards.prompt: While processing order events, a view looks up today's sales tax rate from an external service. What's the problem?
choices: None, provided the tax service stays up whenever the view is rebuilt
Replaying later may use a different rate, so the event should carry the rate used
The log refuses events whose processing depends on outside data
Lookups slow the view down, so the rate should be cached in memory
cards.explanation: Views must be reproducible from the log, so processing has to be deterministic, and tax rates change: a rebuild next year would compute different totals. Store the rate in the event, or query a source that returns the rate as of the event's timestamp. Availability and speed aren't the issue, and the log accepts any valid event.

cards.prompt: A team rebuilds a view by replaying three years of signup events. The code that handles each signup also sends the new user a welcome text. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing: the log is immutable, so a replay can't affect anything outside it
Everyone who signed up in those three years gets the welcome text again
The view rejects the old signups, since their texts were already sent
Only users who joined since the last rebuild get a text; older events are skipped
cards.explanation: A rebuild runs the same code over every old event, so any side effect visible outside the system happens again. Sending texts belongs outside the code that maintains views. Immutability protects the log, not the outside world; views must apply every event, never reject one; and a rebuild replays the log from its first event.

cards.title: Erasing personal data
cards.body:
Immutable events clash with privacy laws like the GDPR, which let people demand that their personal data be deleted.

If each user has their own log, you can simply delete that user's whole log. A shared log that mixes many users' events is harder, because you can't edit events in place. One option is to keep personal data outside the events and refer to it. Another is **crypto-shredding**: encrypt each user's personal data with a key of its own, and destroy the key when they ask to be forgotten, leaving their data unreadable. Both make it harder to recompute derived state later.

cards.prompt: Your immutable event log mixes events from many users, and any user may ask to have their personal data erased. Which design handles that?
choices: Edit that user's events in place to blank out their personal details
Start a fresh log without that user's events whenever someone asks
None: an immutable log can't support erasure, so refuse the request
Encrypt personal data with per-user keys; delete a user's key on request
cards.explanation: Deleting a user's key, known as crypto-shredding, makes their data unreadable without touching the log; keeping personal data outside the events is another option. Both make rebuilding derived state harder. Editing events, or copying the log minus one user's events, breaks immutability; deleting a whole log only works when each user has their own. Erasure is a real obligation, so refusing isn't an option.

cards.title: DataFrames
cards.body:
Data scientists often work with **DataFrames**, in R or Python libraries. A DataFrame looks like a database table or a spreadsheet, and it supports relational-style bulk operations: filtering rows, grouping and aggregating, applying a function to every row, and joining two DataFrames on a key, which is called a *merge*.

The workflow is different, though. Instead of one declarative query, you change the DataFrame step by step with a series of commands, wrangling the data until it answers your question. It's usually your own private copy, often on your laptop. And DataFrames offer many operations a relational database doesn't, such as reshaping data into the matrices that ML algorithms expect.

cards.prompt: How does working with a DataFrame differ from working with a relational database?
keyPoints: You change it step by step with a sequence of commands rather than one declarative query
It's usually the data scientist's private copy, often on their own machine
It offers many operations beyond relational ones, like reshaping data into matrices
cards.explanation: It still has relational-style bulk operations: filtering, grouping, aggregating and joining (called merging).

cards.title: From rows to matrices
cards.body:
Many ML algorithms are built on linear algebra, so they want their input as a **matrix** of numbers. DataFrames are a handy bridge.

Say a podcast app has rows of (listener, show, episodes played). A data scientist pulls those rows out of the database into a DataFrame, drops the broken ones, then pivots: one row per listener, one column per show, each cell a count. Most cells are empty, since each listener follows few shows. Such a **sparse** matrix may have thousands of columns, too many for a relational table, but sparse-array libraries handle it easily. Then the model is trained on it.

cards.prompt: A data scientist turns rows of (customer, product, purchase count) into input for a recommendation model. Order the steps.
items: Query the purchase rows out of the database
Load them into a DataFrame and drop malformed rows
Pivot into a matrix with one row per customer and one column per product
Train the model by running linear algebra on the matrix
cards.explanation: Most cells are empty, since each customer buys few products. Sparse arrays store that cheaply, whereas a table with thousands of columns wouldn't suit a relational database.

cards.title: Turning values into numbers
cards.body:
A matrix can hold only numbers, so other values must be converted. Dates, for example, can be scaled to floating-point numbers in a suitable range.

For a column limited to a small fixed set of values, like a pet's species (cat, dog or rabbit), the usual method is **one-hot encoding**. Each possible value gets its own column. In each row, the column for that row's value holds 1 and the others hold 0. It also works for rows with several values: a recipe that's both vegan and spicy gets a 1 in both columns. Numbering the values 1, 2, 3 instead would invent an order that doesn't exist.

cards.prompt: A model's input matrix can hold only numbers, but each order row has a delivery method: standard, express or pickup. What's the usual encoding?
choices: One column per method, holding 1 for the row's method and 0 elsewhere
Number them 1, 2 and 3 and store that in a single column
Drop the column, since matrices can't represent categories
Keep the method's name as a text column beside the numbers
cards.explanation: One-hot encoding gives each possible value its own column, and it extends to rows with several values at once. Numbering the methods 1 to 3 invents an order and distances the model may take seriously. Categories can be encoded, so dropping them wastes information, and a matrix can't hold text.

cards.title: Logs and indexes
cards.body:
Imagine a notes app that saves each change as a new line, key and value, at the end of one file. That's a **log**: an append-only sequence of records. Appending is cheap, whatever the file's size. Reading is the problem: to find a key you scan the whole file for its last line, so lookups slow down in proportion to the data, O(n).

An **index** is an extra structure, derived from the data, that speeds up lookups without changing the contents. But each index takes disk space and must be updated on every write. So you pick indexes yourself, from what you know of your app's queries.

cards.prompt: A prototype key-value store appends every write to the end of one file and finds a key by scanning the file for its last occurrence. The data grows tenfold. What happens to performance?
choices: Writes and reads both slow down about tenfold, since the file is ten times bigger
Writes stay fast, but each lookup takes about ten times longer
Reads stay fast, since the latest value is always near the end of the file
Writes slow down, since the file must be rewritten to keep old values in order
cards.explanation: Appending costs the same however big the file is, so writes stay cheap. A lookup scans the whole file, so its cost grows in step with the data: O(n). Starting from the end would only help keys written recently; old or missing keys still mean reading everything. Nothing is ever rewritten; old values just pile up.

cards.prompt: Indexes speed up reads. Why don't databases index every column by default?
keyPoints: Each index takes up extra disk space
Every write must also update each index, so writes get slower
The people building the app know its query patterns, so they choose the indexes worth the cost
cards.explanation: An index is derived from the data: adding or dropping one changes only performance, never what the database contains.

cards.title: A hash index
cards.body:
Keep the log, but hold a **hash map** in memory from each key to the byte offset of its newest value. A write appends to the file and updates the map; a read jumps straight to the offset.

Four problems remain. Old values are never cleaned up, so the file grows until the disk is full. The map lives only in RAM, so a restart means rebuilding it by scanning the whole log, which is slow. Every key must fit in memory, since hash maps on disk perform badly. And fetching a range, like IDs 500 to 599, takes one lookup per key.

cards.prompt: A store keeps an append-only log plus an in-memory hash map from each key to the byte offset of its latest value. What problems remain?
keyPoints: Overwritten values are never removed, so the log keeps growing until the disk fills up
The hash map is lost on restart and must be rebuilt by scanning the log, so restarts are slow
All keys must fit in memory, since hash maps kept on disk perform poorly
Range queries need a separate lookup for every key in the range

cards.title: SSTables
cards.body:
Most databases prefer files **sorted by key** to hash maps. A **Sorted String Table (SSTable)** holds key-value pairs in key order, each key at most once.

Then you don't need every key in memory. Split the file into small blocks, a few kilobytes each, and keep a **sparse index** listing only each block's first key. To find an unlisted key, take the last listed key below it, jump to that block, and read forward until you reach your key or pass where it would be. Blocks can also be compressed, saving disk space and I/O for a little CPU.

cards.prompt: An SSTable's sparse index lists one block starting at key 'pepper' and the next starting at 'pickle'. You look up 'pesto'. What does the engine do?
choices: Reports that 'pesto' is missing, since it isn't in the index
Scans the block that starts at 'pickle', since its keys are close to 'pesto'
Jumps to the 'pepper' block and scans it until it reaches 'pesto' or a later key
Scans the file from the beginning, since a sparse index can't locate unlisted keys
cards.explanation: The file is sorted, so 'pesto' can only sit between the two indexed keys, and one block of a few kilobytes is all that needs reading. A sparse index holds only the first key of each block, so being absent from the index doesn't mean absent from the file. The 'pickle' block starts after 'pesto', and scanning from the start throws away the benefit of sorting.

cards.title: The memtable
cards.body:
Sorted files are easy to read but hard to write: an out-of-order key can't just be appended, and rewriting the file per insert is far too slow.

So writes land first in the **memtable**, a sorted structure in memory, such as a balanced tree, that takes keys in any order and returns them sorted. Each write is also appended to a log on disk, used only to rebuild the memtable after a crash. Past a few megabytes, the memtable is written out in one go as a new SSTable, the newest **segment**, and its part of the log is discarded. Later, background **compaction** merges segments. This design is the **LSM-tree** (log-structured merge-tree).

cards.prompt: Why does an LSM engine collect incoming writes in a memtable instead of adding them straight to an SSTable on disk?
keyPoints: An SSTable must stay sorted, so keys arriving in random order can't just be appended
Rewriting the sorted file for every insert would make writes far too expensive
A sorted structure in memory, such as a balanced tree, accepts keys in any order and reads them back sorted
Once it reaches a few megabytes, it is written out in one go as a new sorted segment

cards.prompt: Order what happens to a write in an LSM storage engine.
items: The write is appended to a log on disk and inserted into the memtable
The memtable grows past its size threshold
The memtable is written to disk as a new sorted segment, and its part of the log is discarded
Later, a background compaction merges that segment with older ones
cards.explanation: The log is unsorted and exists only to rebuild the memtable after a crash. While a full memtable is being written out, new writes go to a fresh one.

cards.title: Newer data wins
cards.body:
An LSM engine may hold several values for one key, in the memtable and in segments of different ages. Only the newest counts. So a read checks the memtable, then the newest segment, then each older one, stopping at the first hit. If even the oldest segment lacks the key, it doesn't exist.

A delete can't erase anything from a segment. Instead the engine writes a **tombstone**, a marker saying the key is gone. Whenever compaction meets it, older values of that key are discarded. Once the tombstone reaches the oldest segment, nothing older is left, so it's dropped too.

cards.prompt: Order where an LSM engine looks when reading a key, stopping as soon as it finds it.
items: The memtable
The most recent segment on disk
The next-older segment, and so on
The oldest segment; if the key isn't there either, it doesn't exist
cards.explanation: Newer data shadows older data, so the first match is the current value. Reading a missing key, or one not written for a long time, is therefore the slowest case.

cards.prompt: Order what happens when a key is deleted in an LSM engine.
items: An application deletes a key
The engine appends a tombstone for the key instead of removing anything
Compactions discard older values of the key wherever they meet the tombstone
The tombstone reaches the oldest segment and is dropped too
cards.explanation: Until the tombstone has passed through every level, old copies of the data may still be on disk. That's a problem when a deletion must be guaranteed, for example under data protection law.

cards.title: Merging segments
cards.body:
Compaction works like the merge step of mergesort. It reads several sorted segments side by side, keeps copying whichever next key is smallest into a new file, and keeps only the newest value of a key found in several. The output is sorted too, and little memory is needed.

Segments are **immutable**: written in one pass, never changed. During a merge, reads keep using the old segments; when it's done, they switch to the new file and the old ones are deleted. So a crash mid-merge is easy: the inputs are untouched, and the engine throws away the half-written output and starts again.

cards.prompt: An LSM database crashes while merging three segments into one. What does recovery have to do about the merge?
choices: Restore the three input segments from backup, since the merge may have corrupted them
Replay the log to finish writing the half-merged segment
Delete the unfinished output file; the input segments were never modified
Roll each input segment back to its state before the merge began
cards.explanation: Segment files are immutable once written, so a merge only reads its inputs and writes a new file. A crash leaves the inputs intact and a partial output that can be thrown away. The log exists to rebuild the memtable, not to finish merges, and there's nothing to restore or roll back. Immutability also lets reads keep using the inputs until a merge completes.

cards.title: Bloom filters
cards.body:
Checking every segment is slow, worst of all for a missing key. So each segment usually carries a **Bloom filter**, a small bit array that says whether a key might be in it.

Each of the segment's keys is hashed to a few positions, and those bits are set to 1. To test a key, hash it the same way. If any of its bits is 0, the key is certainly absent: skip the segment. If all are 1, it's probably there, but other keys may have set those bits by chance, a **false positive**. So the engine still checks the block, moving on to older segments if the key isn't there.

cards.prompt: During a read, a segment's Bloom filter finds every bit for the key set to 1. What does the engine do next?
choices: Looks in the segment's block for the key, and moves on to older segments if it isn't there
Returns the value from this segment straight away, since the filter has confirmed the key is present
Skips this segment, since only a 0 bit gives the engine a useful answer
cards.explanation: All 1s means the key is probably present: other keys may have set those bits by chance, a false positive. The engine checks the block, and a false positive only costs a little wasted work. A 0 bit does give certainty, but that the key is absent; skipping on all 1s could miss a key that really is there.

cards.title: Compaction strategies
cards.body:
Engines differ in when they compact and which segments they merge.

**Size-tiered** compaction merges newer, smaller SSTables into older, larger ones. Most data goes through just a few big sequential merges, so it sustains very high write throughput. But the oldest SSTables grow huge, and merging them needs lots of spare disk.

**Leveled** compaction keeps SSTables a fixed size, in levels that each hold more than the last, every level after the first split by key range. Compaction proceeds in small steps, so it needs less disk. Reads also check fewer SSTables. Rule of thumb: size-tiered for mostly writes, leveled for mostly reads.

cards.prompt: Compare size-tiered and leveled compaction on write throughput, read cost and disk space.
keyPoints: Writes: size-tiered sustains higher write throughput, because each piece of data goes through only a few big merges
Reads: leveled needs to check fewer SSTables per lookup
Disk space: leveled uses less; size-tiered needs a lot of temporary space to merge its huge older SSTables
cards.explanation: Leveled keeps SSTables a fixed size, in levels that grow larger, each split by key range. It suits read-heavy workloads; size-tiered suits mostly writes.

cards.title: Embedded databases
cards.body:
Most databases run as a server you query over the network. An **embedded** database is a library inside your application's process: you call it with ordinary functions, and it reads and writes files on the local disk. SQLite is the best-known example.

Phone apps use them everywhere. On a backend they fit when the data is small enough for one machine and there aren't many concurrent transactions. If the data splits into parts that are never queried together, each part can even get its own instance: a note-taking service could keep each user's notes in a separate SQLite file.

cards.prompt: A survey app hosts thousands of small customers. No query ever combines two customers' data, and each customer has light traffic. Which storage design fits?
choices: One shared database server, since embedded databases are meant for phones, not backends
A separate embedded database per customer, running inside the application process
One embedded database for everyone, since embedded engines handle heavy concurrency best
cards.explanation: Embedded engines run as a library inside the application, called through ordinary functions rather than over a network. On a backend they fit small data with few concurrent transactions, and fully separate tenants can each get their own instance. They aren't limited to mobile apps, and they suit low concurrency, not high.

cards.title: B-trees
cards.body:
The **B-tree** is the most widely used index, standard in almost every relational database. Like an SSTable it keeps keys sorted, so lookups and range queries are efficient. Otherwise it's very different.

LSM segments are files of varying size, megabytes or more, never changed once written. A B-tree splits the database into fixed-size **pages** of a few KiB and overwrites them **in place**. Pages refer to each other by page number. A **root** page holds boundary keys with a child reference for each range; you follow references down to a **leaf** page with the keys. With several hundred children per page, the **branching factor**, three or four levels hold most databases.

cards.prompt: How does the way a B-tree lays out data on disk differ from an LSM engine's segments?
keyPoints: B-trees use small fixed-size pages of a few KiB; LSM segments are variable-size files of megabytes or more
B-tree pages are overwritten in place; segments are written once and never modified
Pages refer to each other by page number, forming a tree from a root page down to leaf pages
With a branching factor of several hundred, three or four levels hold most databases
cards.explanation: Both keep keys sorted, so both support efficient lookups and range queries.

cards.title: Splitting pages
cards.body:
To change a value, a B-tree finds the leaf page with the key and overwrites it with the new version. To add a key, it walks down from the root to the leaf whose range covers it.

If that leaf has no room, it **splits**: its keys are divided between two pages, each half full, and the new key goes into whichever covers it. The parent gets a reference to the extra page, with a boundary key between them. If the parent is full too, it splits as well, possibly all the way up; splitting the root adds a new root above it. That keeps the tree balanced.

cards.prompt: Order what happens when you insert a key into a B-tree and its target page is full.
items: From the root, follow page references down to the leaf page whose range covers the key
Find that the page has no room for the new key
