Split it into two half-full pages, putting the new key in whichever covers it
Add a reference to the new page, with its boundary key, to the parent
If the parent overflows too, split it as well, possibly up to a new root
cards.explanation: Splits keep the tree balanced, so its depth grows only logarithmically with the number of keys.

cards.title: Crash safety in B-trees
cards.body:
Overwriting pages is risky. A split rewrites several pages, and if the power fails partway, the tree is left inconsistent, perhaps with an **orphan page** that no parent points to. Hardware may even leave one page half-written, a *torn page*.

So most B-trees keep a **write-ahead log (WAL)**: an append-only file where each change is recorded and flushed to disk before any page is touched. After a crash, replaying it restores a consistent tree. It also lets changed pages wait in memory.

Some engines use **copy-on-write** instead: the changed page goes to a new place, along with new copies of its parent pages pointing to it.

cards.prompt: A B-tree page split has to rewrite three pages, and the power fails after only two have been written. With no write-ahead log, what can result?
choices: Nothing serious: the split is atomic, so the tree stays at its old version
Only the newest key is lost; the rest of the tree is intact and consistent
A tree that is unbalanced but still correct, fixed by the next split
A corrupted tree, such as a page that no parent refers to
cards.explanation: Overwriting several pages isn't atomic, so a crash partway leaves pages that disagree, like an orphan page, and hardware may even leave a page half-written (a torn page). A write-ahead log fixes this: each change is appended and flushed before pages are touched, so recovery can replay it into a consistent tree. That also lets modified pages wait in memory.

cards.prompt: Some B-trees use copy-on-write instead of a write-ahead log. How do they change a page?
choices: They copy the old page to a backup area, then overwrite it in place
They copy the whole tree to a new file and swap the files when done
They write the modified page to a new location and leave all its parent pages as they are
They write the page to a new location, plus new copies of its parents pointing at it
cards.explanation: Nothing is overwritten: the changed page and its chain of parents are written elsewhere, so the old version stays intact until the new one is complete. Backing up and then overwriting is still an in-place update. Copying the whole tree would be far too costly. If the parents weren't updated, nothing would point at the new page. Old versions also help with concurrency control.

cards.title: LSM-trees or B-trees
cards.body:
Rule of thumb: LSM-trees suit write-heavy work, B-trees are faster for reads. But results depend a lot on workload details, so benchmark with yours. And it isn't all or nothing: some engines mix both, such as several B-trees merged LSM-style.

A B-tree lookup reads one page per level, so reads are fast and predictable. An LSM lookup may check several SSTables, though Bloom filters cut disk reads. Ranges are simple on a B-tree: walk one sorted structure. On LSM, each segment holds part of the range, so all are scanned and the results merged. Bloom filters can't help, since you'd hash every possible key in the range.

cards.prompt: A team must choose between an LSM-based and a B-tree-based engine for a new service. What's the soundest approach?
choices: Pick the B-tree, since LSM-trees are slower for every kind of read
Expect LSM to favor writes and B-trees reads, then benchmark both on their own workload
Pick the LSM-tree, since its sequential writes make it the faster engine for reads and writes alike
Treat it as all or nothing, since no engine combines ideas from both
cards.explanation: The rule of thumb is that LSM-trees suit write-heavy loads and B-trees give faster, more predictable reads, but results depend heavily on workload details. Both can read well: Bloom filters cut an LSM engine's disk reads. Fast writes don't make reads fast. And some engines blend the two, for example several B-trees merged LSM-style.

cards.prompt: On an LSM engine, why is a range query more expensive than a lookup of one key?
choices: SSTables aren't kept in key order, so a range query must scan every key in every segment
Each segment's slice of the range must be scanned and merged, and Bloom filters can't help
It must wait for compaction to merge all the segments into one before it can begin scanning
Range queries have to go through the memtable, which is unsorted
cards.explanation: Each segment is sorted, so each can scan its slice of the range, but the slices must be combined. Bloom filters test single keys, and hashing every possible key in a range is impractical. Queries don't wait for compaction, and the memtable is sorted too. A B-tree handles ranges more simply by walking one sorted structure.

cards.title: Write stalls
cards.body:
An LSM engine can only accept writes as fast as it can push full memtables to disk. Under a heavy, sustained stream of writes, that flushing can fall behind, often because compaction is busy with the disk and can't keep up.

If the memtable fills before the previous one has been written out, there's nowhere to put new data. Many engines then apply **backpressure**: they pause all reads and writes until the flush catches up. Clients see sudden **latency spikes**, even though nothing is broken.

cards.prompt: During a sustained burst of writes, an LSM database briefly stops answering both reads and writes. What's the likely cause?
choices: The memtable filled faster than compaction let it be flushed, so the engine paused requests
Its Bloom filters are being rebuilt for all the new keys and can't be checked in the meantime
A page split is propagating all the way up to the root, locking the tree
Tombstones from the burst are blocking reads of the keys they mark
cards.explanation: When writes arrive faster than data can reach disk, often because compaction can't keep up, the memtable fills. Engines then apply backpressure, suspending requests until it's flushed, which shows up as latency spikes. Bloom filters are built once when a segment is written, page splits belong to B-trees, and tombstones don't block reads.

cards.title: Sequential and random writes
cards.body:
Disks handle a few large writes in a row (**sequential writes**) faster than many small writes in scattered places (**random writes**).

When an app updates keys all over the key space, a B-tree overwrites pages that could sit anywhere on disk: random writes. An LSM engine writes whole segment files at once, when flushing or compacting, each far bigger than a page: sequential writes. That's a big reason LSM engines usually take more writes per second on the same hardware.

The gap is widest on spinning hard drives, where each random write waits for the head to move. On SSDs it's smaller, but real.

cards.prompt: A fleet of sensors sends readings whose keys are spread randomly across the key space, at a high rate. On the same disk, why would an LSM engine usually sustain more writes per second than a B-tree?
choices: The LSM engine writes each value to disk only once, while the B-tree writes it twice
The B-tree rebalances the whole tree after each insert, rewriting every level of pages
The LSM engine keeps its keys in a hash map, so it never has to keep them sorted
The LSM engine writes large segment files in one go; the B-tree overwrites pages all over the disk
cards.explanation: Disks take a few big sequential writes faster than many small scattered ones, and that's the pattern each engine produces. An LSM engine actually writes each value several times: to its log, at flush and in compactions. A B-tree splits a page only when it's full. And LSM segments are sorted files, not hash maps.

cards.title: Why SSDs prefer sequential writes
cards.body:
SSDs have no moving parts, yet they also write sequentially faster. Flash memory is written one small **page** at a time, a few KiB, but erased only in whole **blocks** of hundreds of KiB.

Before erasing a block, the drive's controller copies any pages still holding valid data elsewhere: the SSD's **garbage collection**. Big sequential writes tend to fill a block with one file, so once it's deleted the block is erased with nothing to copy. Random writes leave blocks mixing valid and stale pages, so garbage collection copies more, takes bandwidth from the application, and wears the flash out sooner.

cards.prompt: SSDs have no moving parts. Why do they still write sequentially faster than randomly?
keyPoints: Flash is written a small page at a time but can only be erased a large block at a time
The controller has to move a block's still-valid pages elsewhere before it can erase it (garbage collection)
Random writes leave blocks mixing valid and stale pages, so garbage collection does more work and takes bandwidth from the application
The extra copying also wears the drive out faster
cards.explanation: With sequential writes a whole block tends to belong to one file, so it can be erased in one go once that file is deleted. On spinning disks the gap is much bigger, because each random write waits for the head to move.

cards.title: Write amplification
cards.body:
One write from your app becomes several on disk. **Write amplification** is the bytes written to disk divided by what a bare append-only log would write.

An LSM engine writes a value to its log, again at flush, and again in each compaction that includes it. A B-tree writes each change at least twice, to the WAL and to the page, and may rewrite a whole page for a few changed bytes so it can recover after a crash. LSM usually comes out lower.

When disk bandwidth is the limit, more amplification means fewer writes per second. A fresh LSM database has no compaction competing for the disk yet, so run benchmarks long enough.

cards.prompt: Where does write amplification come from in LSM-trees and in B-trees?
keyPoints: LSM: each value is written to the log, again when the memtable is flushed, and again in every compaction that includes it
B-tree: each change is written at least twice, to the write-ahead log and to the page
B-tree: a whole page is sometimes written even when only a few bytes changed, so it can be recovered after a crash
cards.explanation: It's the bytes written to disk divided by the bytes a plain append-only log would write; for typical workloads LSM-trees come out lower, since they skip full-page writes and compress their files.

cards.prompt: A team runs a ten-minute write benchmark on a freshly created LSM database and gets great numbers. Why might production be slower?
choices: The benchmark's writes all stayed in the memtable, so it never measured disk writes
Production will have more Bloom filters to update on every write
Once data accumulates, compaction starts sharing disk bandwidth with new writes
cards.explanation: An empty LSM-tree has nothing to compact, so all disk bandwidth goes to new writes. As the database grows, compaction rewrites data in the background, and that write amplification eats into throughput, so benchmarks must run long enough to show it. A memtable is flushed every few megabytes, and Bloom filters are built per segment, not updated per write.

cards.title: Disk space
cards.body:
A B-tree can become **fragmented**. After many deletes, its file holds lots of unused pages. New data can reuse them, but since they sit mid-file, the space can't easily go back to the operating system; a background job such as PostgreSQL's *vacuum* must move pages around.

LSM compaction keeps rewriting files, so there are no half-empty pages, and SSTable blocks compress better, often giving smaller files. But overwritten and deleted values use space until compaction clears them: little with leveled compaction, much more with size-tiered.

Immutable files have a bonus: to snapshot the database, write out the memtable, then note which segments exist and keep them, with no copying.

cards.prompt: How do B-trees and LSM-trees differ in how they use disk space?
keyPoints: B-trees fragment: pages freed by deletes can be reused, but sit mid-file and can't easily go back to the OS without a vacuum-style process
LSM compaction keeps rewriting files, so there are no half-empty pages, and blocks compress better
In LSM, overwritten and deleted values take space until compaction removes them: little with leveled, much more with size-tiered
cards.explanation: Immutable segments also make snapshots cheap: record which files exist and keep them, with no copying, which a B-tree that overwrites pages can't do as easily.

cards.title: Secondary indexes
cards.body:
So far each key has pointed to one record, like a **primary key**, which identifies exactly one row. Often you also want to search by another column, say all orders from one customer. That needs a **secondary index**.

It's built like a key-value index, with one twist: its keys can repeat, since many rows can share a value. There are two fixes. Either each entry's value is a list of matching row IDs, like a search engine's postings list, or each entry is made unique by tacking the row's ID onto the indexed value.

cards.prompt: Unlike a primary key, a secondary index's values may repeat across many rows. What are the two ways to handle that?
keyPoints: Store a list of matching row IDs as each entry's value, like a postings list
Make each entry unique by appending the row ID to the indexed value
cards.explanation: Either way, both B-trees and log-structured engines can store the index.

cards.title: What an index stores
cards.body:
An index entry has a key, which you search by, and a value. The value can take three forms.

A **clustered index** stores the whole row inside the index. Otherwise the value is a reference: either the row's primary key, or its place in a **heap file**, which keeps rows in no particular order. If a heap row grows and must move, every index has to point to its new spot, or a forwarding pointer is left behind.

In between is a **covering index**: it copies a few columns next to the reference, so some queries need only the index. That duplicated data costs disk space and slows writes.

cards.prompt: What can an index store alongside each key? Describe the options and the cost of the in-between one.
keyPoints: The whole row, which makes it a clustered index
A reference to the row: its primary key, or its location in an unordered heap file
Copies of some columns plus a reference (a covering index), so some queries can be answered from the index alone
Covering indexes take extra disk space and slow down writes, because data is duplicated
cards.explanation: When a row in a heap file grows and has to move, every index must be updated to its new spot, or a forwarding pointer left behind.

cards.title: In-memory databases
cards.body:
Disk structures exist because disks are durable and cheap per gigabyte. As RAM gets cheaper, many datasets fit wholly in memory, hence **in-memory databases**.

Some are pure caches that accept losing data on restart. Others are durable: they use battery-backed RAM, append a log of changes to disk, save periodic snapshots, or replicate to other machines, and reload from those on restart. Reads are still served entirely from RAM.

Their speed isn't really from avoiding disk reads: with enough RAM, the OS caches a disk-based database's blocks anyway. It comes from skipping the work of encoding data structures into an on-disk layout.

cards.prompt: How can an in-memory database survive a restart without losing data?
keyPoints: Special hardware such as battery-backed RAM
Appending a log of changes to disk
Writing periodic snapshots to disk
Replicating its state to other machines it can reload from
cards.explanation: It still counts as in-memory because every read is served from RAM; the disk is only an append-only record for recovery. Pure caches skip all this and accept losing data on restart.

cards.prompt: A disk-based database has enough RAM to cache its whole dataset. Why can an in-memory database still be faster?
choices: The disk-based one still has to read every query's data from disk
In-memory databases skip durability, so they never write to disk
It skips encoding its data structures into a format that can go to disk
In-memory databases keep data compressed, so more of it fits in the CPU cache
cards.explanation: With enough memory, the OS caches disk blocks anyway, so a disk-based engine may rarely touch the disk. The real saving is not having to turn in-memory structures into an on-disk layout. Many in-memory databases do write to disk, through logs, snapshots or replicas, for durability. Compression isn't what sets them apart.

cards.title: Warehouse building blocks
cards.body:
Cloud data warehouses keep data in object storage, apart from the machines that run queries. Open-source warehouses on data lakes went further, splitting one system into four parts.

A **query engine** parses SQL, plans it and runs it, usually in parallel across many machines. A **storage format** decides how a table's rows become bytes in files, typically on object storage. Those files are immutable, so a **table format** tracks which files make up a table, plus its schema; that adds inserts, deletes, *time travel* to past versions, even transactions. A **data catalog** tracks which tables a database contains, and creates, renames and drops them.

cards.prompt: Open-source warehouses on data lakes have split into separate components. What does each do: query engine, storage format, table format, data catalog?
keyPoints: Query engine: parses SQL, plans it, and runs it, usually in parallel across machines
Storage format: encodes a table's rows as bytes in files, often on object storage
Table format: tracks which files make up a table and its schema, adding inserts, deletes and features like time travel
Data catalog: tracks which tables a database contains, and handles creating, renaming and dropping them
cards.explanation: Cloud warehouses keep data in object storage apart from compute, and splitting the components also lets other tools read the same files and catalog.

cards.prompt: A data lake holds immutable columnar files on object storage. The team now needs row deletes and to see the table as it stood last Tuesday. What should they add?
choices: A data catalog, which keeps track of every version of each file
A new storage format that supports editing files in place
A faster query engine that can filter out deleted rows
A table format, tracking which files form the table over time
cards.explanation: A table format sits on top of immutable files and records which files form the table, which enables deletes, time travel and even transactions. A catalog tracks which tables exist, not their files. Columnar files are written once by design. A query engine runs queries; it doesn't decide what the table contains.

cards.title: Column-oriented storage
cards.body:
Analytics tables are often very wide. A fact table may have over a hundred columns, yet a typical query uses only a handful, over millions of rows.

Most OLTP databases are **row-oriented**: each row's values sit together on disk. For such a query they load every matching row in full and discard most of it. A **column-oriented** store keeps each column's values together, so a query reads only the columns it uses. All columns keep rows in one shared order: the 7th value of each column belongs to row 7.

cards.prompt: A fact table has 150 columns, and a typical analytics query uses four of them across billions of rows. Why does column-oriented storage speed this up?
choices: Each column is stored separately, so it reads only the four it needs
It keeps a separate index on every column, so filters never need to scan
It stores each row as one compact record, so whole rows load from disk faster
It caches each query's results, so repeated queries are free
cards.explanation: A row store has to load every matching row in full, all 150 values, even when an index says which rows match. A column store reads just the needed columns. It doesn't need an index per column, keeping whole rows together is the row-oriented layout, and caching results is a materialized view, not column storage.

cards.title: Bitmap encoding
cards.body:
Columns repeat a lot: millions of rows may share a few thousand distinct values. A column with n distinct values can become n **bitmaps**, one per value, with a bit per row that's 1 when the row has that value. Most bits are 0, so bitmaps are often **run-length encoded**, storing just the length of each run of 0s or 1s.

Filters become bitwise operations. To accept any of several values in one column, OR their bitmaps. To require conditions on two columns, AND them. That works across columns because they all keep rows in one shared order, so bit k always means row k.

cards.prompt: A column store keeps a bitmap for each distinct value of each column. How does it find rows where region is 'north' or 'east', and channel is 'online'?
choices: AND the 'north' and 'east' bitmaps, then OR the result with the 'online' bitmap
Decode the bitmaps back into rows and filter each row one at a time
Bitmaps from different columns can't be combined, so it scans the channel column
OR the 'north' and 'east' bitmaps, then AND the result with the 'online' bitmap
cards.explanation: Either region qualifies, so those bitmaps are ORed; the channel must also match, so its bitmap is ANDed. This works across columns because every column lists rows in the same order, so bit k always means row k. Bitwise operations are far faster than decoding rows, and sparse bitmaps are usually run-length encoded to stay small.

cards.title: Wide-column is not columnar
cards.body:
Don't confuse column-oriented storage with **wide-column** databases, also called column-family databases. That name describes a data model: each row may hold thousands of columns, and different rows can have different ones.

On disk, though, a wide-column database keeps all of a row's values together. So despite the name, it's row-oriented. Column orientation is about layout: one column's values, for many rows, stored side by side.

cards.prompt: Is a wide-column (column-family) database a kind of column-oriented store?
choices: Yes: both store each column's values together, just under different names
Yes: allowing thousands of columns per row requires column-oriented storage
No: it stores all of a row's values together, so it's row-oriented
cards.explanation: The name describes the data model: rows can have thousands of columns, and rows needn't share the same ones. On disk, each row's values sit together. Column-oriented storage is about layout: one column's values for many rows stored together. Having many columns doesn't require that layout.

cards.title: Sort order in column stores
cards.body:
A column store can keep rows in a chosen order, which acts like an index. Whole rows are sorted, then stored by column; sorting each column on its own would scramble which values belong to which row.

Pick sort keys from common queries. If most queries look at one region, sort by region first so they read only its rows. A second key orders ties: region, then product, groups each product's rows within a region.

Sorting also aids compression. The first key forms long runs of one value; with few distinct values, run-length encoding can shrink it to kilobytes even over billions of rows. Second and third keys have shorter runs; later columns look random and gain little.

cards.prompt: Most queries on a sales table look at the last few days and then group by store. How should the column store sort the rows?
choices: By date first, then by store
By store first, then by date
Sort each column independently, so every column gets long runs of repeated values
By transaction ID, so rows spread evenly across blocks
cards.explanation: Sorting by date lets a query read only the recent rows, and store as the second key groups each store's sales within a day. Store first would scatter recent sales across the whole table. Sorting columns separately breaks the link between the kth entries of each column, so rows could no longer be put back together. A transaction ID helps none of these queries.

cards.prompt: How does sort order affect compression in a column store?
keyPoints: After sorting, the first sort key forms long runs of repeated values, especially if it has few distinct values
Run-length encoding can shrink such a column to a few kilobytes, even with billions of rows
The second and third sort keys have shorter runs and compress less well
Columns further down are in effectively random order and gain little

cards.title: Writing to a column store
cards.body:
Sorted, compressed columns make reads fast but single-row writes painful: inserting one row mid-table means rewriting every compressed column from that point on. Writing many rows at once spreads that cost, and warehouses mostly load data in bulk anyway.

So column stores borrow the LSM idea. New writes first go to a sorted, row-oriented store in memory. Once enough pile up, they're merged with the column files on disk and written out as new files in bulk; old files never change. Queries look at both the files on disk and the in-memory writes, so changes show up right away.

cards.prompt: Why are single-row inserts awkward for a sorted column store, and how do warehouses handle writes instead?
keyPoints: Inserting a row mid-table would mean rewriting every compressed column from that point onward
Writing many rows at once spreads that rewriting cost over the whole batch
New writes first go to a sorted, row-oriented store in memory, then are merged into new column files in bulk
Queries combine the files on disk with the recent writes in memory, so changes show up right away
cards.explanation: Old files are never changed and new ones are written in one go, which makes object storage a good fit.

cards.title: Compiled and vectorized queries
cards.body:
When a query scans millions of rows, CPU time matters. A naive engine interprets the query plan afresh for every row, checking which comparison to do next, and that's too slow. Two faster approaches exist, and both are used.

**Query compilation** generates code for the specific query, compiles it to machine code, much like a JIT compiler, and runs it over the rows one at a time.

**Vectorized processing** stays interpreted, but hands whole batches of a column's values to a fixed set of built-in operators. An equality operator, say, takes a column and a value and returns a bitmap of matching rows; another operator ANDs two bitmaps.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between query compilation and vectorized processing?
choices: Compilation generates machine code for each query; vectorization runs built-in operators over batches of column values
Vectorization generates machine code for each query; compilation runs built-in operators over batches of column values
Compilation suits OLTP queries; vectorization suits analytics
Vectorization compares embedding vectors; compilation runs plain SQL
cards.explanation: A compiled query loops over rows with code made for that query, often built with a compiler like LLVM, much as a JIT does. Vectorization stays interpreted but hands whole batches of values to a fixed set of operators. Both serve analytics. The 'vector' in vectorized processing is a batch of values, not an embedding.

cards.title: Working with the CPU
cards.body:
Compiled and vectorized engines look very different inside, but both get their speed from the way modern CPUs work.

They read memory sequentially rather than jumping around, which cuts cache misses. They do most work in tight inner loops with few instructions and no function calls, which keeps the CPU's pipeline full and avoids branch mispredictions. They use parallelism: several threads, and SIMD instructions that apply one operation to many values at once. And they work on compressed data directly, skipping the cost of decoding it, allocating memory and copying.

cards.prompt: Compiled and vectorized query engines both get their speed from how modern CPUs work. What do they exploit?
keyPoints: Sequential memory access, which reduces cache misses
Tight inner loops with few instructions and no function calls, which keep the pipeline busy and avoid branch mispredictions
Parallelism, from multiple threads and SIMD instructions
Working on compressed data directly, which saves decoding, allocation and copying
cards.explanation: The naive alternative, interpreting the query plan afresh for each row, is too slow when queries scan millions of rows.

cards.title: Materialized views and cubes
cards.body:
A **virtual view** is just a saved query: each read runs the query underneath. A **materialized view** stores the query's actual results on disk. It must be updated when the data changes, which adds work to writes, but repeated reads get cheap.

A **data cube** is a materialized view of aggregates: a grid with one axis per dimension, say month and region, where each cell holds a total such as signups for that pair. Totals along any axis come out instantly. The catch: a cube only answers questions about its own dimensions. Anything else needs the raw data, so warehouses keep it.

cards.prompt: A dashboard runs the same costly aggregation hundreds of times a day, and the underlying data changes only a little. What helps most?
choices: A virtual view, since it stores the query's results so later reads can reuse them
A materialized view, which stores the results and is updated when the data changes
A virtual view, since it stays up to date with the data automatically and at no cost
cards.explanation: A materialized view is a real copy of the query's results, so repeated reads skip the heavy work; the cost moves to writes, which must keep it up to date. A virtual view stores nothing: the engine expands it into its query on every read, so it saves typing, not computation.

cards.prompt: A data cube sums revenue by date, store and product category. An analyst asks what share of revenue comes from orders over 50 euros. What then?
choices: Sum the cube's cells along the store dimension to get the share
The cube answers it instantly, since every possible aggregate is already precomputed
Add up only the cells whose revenue total is over 50 euros
Query the raw data, since order value isn't one of the cube's dimensions
cards.explanation: A cube only precomputes aggregates along the dimensions it was built with, so questions about other attributes need the underlying facts. That's why warehouses keep as much raw data as they can and use cubes only to speed up certain queries. A cell's total sums many orders, so it says nothing about individual order values.

cards.title: Multidimensional indexes
cards.body:
A **concatenated index** joins several columns into one key in a fixed order, like a music index sorted by artist, then album. It finds all of one artist's songs, or one album by one artist, but it's no help for an album title alone.

That hurts with ranges on two columns at once, like every shop inside a rectangle on a map. Sorted by latitude first, the index narrows the latitude range but leaves longitudes scattered within it. **Multidimensional indexes**, such as R-trees, group nearby points in the same subtree, so both ranges narrow together. They aren't only for maps: any pair of ranged columns can use one.

cards.prompt: A housing site filters listings by a price range and a floor-area range at the same time. Why is a concatenated index on (price, area) a poor fit?
choices: It narrows by price only; every listing in that price range must then be checked for area
Concatenated indexes only support exact matches, not ranges
It narrows by area only, since the last column in the key is used first
It works well; a multidimensional index would only help with latitude and longitude coordinates
cards.explanation: Entries are sorted by price and only then by area, so a price range maps to one stretch of the index, but the areas within it are scattered. A multidimensional index, such as an R-tree, narrows both ranges at once. Concatenated indexes do handle ranges on their first column, and multidimensional indexes aren't only for geography.

cards.title: Inverted indexes
cards.body:
**Full-text search** finds documents by words appearing anywhere in them. Think of each possible word, or **term**, as a dimension: a document has a 1 on it if it contains the word, 0 if not. Asking for two words means asking for a 1 on both.

The usual structure is an **inverted index**: a map from each term to its **postings list**, the IDs of documents containing it. With sequential IDs, a postings list can be a bitmap, bit n set when document n has the term. Documents with both terms are then one bitwise AND away, fast even on run-length encoded bitmaps.

cards.prompt: A search index stores each term's postings list as a bitmap over document IDs. What's the fast way to find documents containing both 'kayak' and 'rental'?
choices: Look up 'kayak rental' as one term, since multiword queries are indexed as phrases
OR the two bitmaps, since either term makes a document relevant
Read the 'kayak' postings, then scan each of those documents' text for 'rental'
AND the two bitmaps, which works even while they are run-length encoded
cards.explanation: Each term is like a dimension a document has or lacks, so 'both' means the bit is set in both bitmaps: a bitwise AND, the same trick a warehouse uses to combine two column filters. OR would return documents with either term. Scanning text throws away the index, and terms are indexed one by one, not as phrases.

cards.title: Substrings and typos
cards.body:
A word index only matches whole words. To find any fragment of text, index **n-grams** instead: every substring of n characters. The 3-grams, or *trigrams*, of 'river' are 'riv', 'ive' and 'ver'. An inverted index over all trigrams can find any substring of three or more characters, and even run regular expressions. The downside is size: such an index is large.

Typos need something else. Engines can find words within a given **edit distance**, the number of letters added, removed or replaced; 'card' is one edit from 'cart'. Neither trick understands meaning, though. Both match spelling.

cards.prompt: Engineers want to search logs for arbitrary fragments such as 'eout=3', which don't line up with whole words. Which index fits, and what's the catch?
choices: A word-level inverted index; the catch is that it needs a hand-made list of synonyms
An inverted index of all three-character substrings; the catch is its large size
A vector index; the catch is that its results are only approximate
A B-tree on the whole message; the catch is slower writes
cards.explanation: A trigram index can find any substring of three or more characters, and even supports regular expressions, but indexing every trigram makes it large. Word indexes only match whole terms. Vector indexes find similar meaning, not exact fragments. A B-tree on the message can match prefixes, not text in the middle.

cards.title: Semantic search
cards.body:
Sometimes a query and the right document share no words: someone types 'my phone won't charge' and wants the page 'battery troubleshooting'. **Semantic search** matches meaning, not spelling.

An **embedding model** turns a text into a **vector embedding**, often over a thousand numbers marking a point in space. Similar meanings land close together, measured by *cosine similarity*, the angle between vectors, or *Euclidean distance*, the straight-line gap.

Ahead of time, every document is embedded and stored in a **vector index**. A query is embedded the same way, with context such as the user's location, and the index finds the nearest stored vectors; their documents are the results.

cards.prompt: In a recipe app, a user searches 'quick weeknight dinner' and should find a recipe titled 'Twenty-minute pasta', which shares no words with the query. What makes that possible?
choices: Fuzzy matching that tolerates query words within a small edit distance
A trigram index that matches the substrings the texts share
Vector embeddings that put texts with similar meanings near each other
An inverted index that ANDs together the bitmaps of the query's words
cards.explanation: An embedding model turns each text into a vector, and texts with related meanings land near each other, so the search returns the documents whose vectors are nearest the query's. Edit distance catches typos, trigrams catch shared fragments, and an inverted index needs the query's words to appear in the document. None of them see meaning.

cards.prompt: Order how a semantic search engine answers a query.
items: Documents are turned into embeddings and stored in a vector index ahead of time
A user submits a query
The embedding model turns the query, plus context such as location, into a vector
The vector index finds the stored vectors closest to it
The matching documents are returned
cards.explanation: Closeness is measured with a distance function, such as cosine similarity (the angle between vectors) or Euclidean distance (the straight-line gap).

cards.title: Vector indexes
cards.body:
R-trees break down with that many dimensions, so vector indexes work differently.

A **flat index** compares the query with every stored vector: exact, but slow. An **IVF** (inverted file) index groups vectors into partitions and checks only some; it's faster but approximate, as a close vector may sit in a skipped partition. Checking more partitions is more accurate but slower.

**HNSW** stacks proximity graphs in layers, few nodes on top and more below. A search finds the closest node in the top layer, drops to that node one layer down, follows denser edges toward closer nodes, and repeats to the bottom, returning the closest node found. It's approximate too.

cards.prompt: Compare flat, IVF and HNSW vector indexes.
keyPoints: Flat: compares the query with every stored vector; exact but slow
IVF: groups vectors into partitions and checks only some of them; faster but approximate, and checking more partitions trades speed for accuracy
HNSW: a stack of proximity graphs, sparse at the top and denser lower down; also approximate
cards.explanation: IVF can miss a close match that fell into a partition it didn't check. R-trees, which work for maps, break down with as many dimensions as embeddings have.

cards.prompt: Order how a query finds its nearest vector in an HNSW index.
items: Find the closest node in the top layer, which has only a few nodes
Move to that same node in the layer below
Follow that layer's denser edges toward nodes closer to the query
Repeat layer by layer until the bottom layer, and return the closest node found
cards.explanation: Sparse upper layers make big jumps cheap; dense lower ones refine the answer. The result is approximate: the true nearest vector can be missed.

cards.title: Rolling upgrades
cards.body:
Apps keep changing, and new features often need new fields or new kinds of records. But the code that reads and writes them can't switch over everywhere at once.

On servers you usually do a **rolling upgrade**: move a few nodes to the new version, check that they behave, then carry on. The service never goes down, so you can ship small releases often instead of big ones rarely. And a bad release shows up on a few nodes first, where you can roll it back before most users are hit.

Phone apps are worse: users update whenever they like.

cards.prompt: What makes rolling upgrades worth the trouble of running old and new code side by side?
keyPoints: No downtime: the service keeps running while the new version goes out
Releases can be small and frequent rather than big and rare
A bad release shows up on a few nodes and can be rolled back before most users see it
cards.explanation: The price is that data must stay readable across versions in both directions; client apps add to the mix, since users update whenever they choose.

cards.title: Backward and forward compatibility
cards.body:
During a rollout, old and new code run side by side, and so does data in old and new formats. **Backward compatibility** means newer code can read what older code wrote. **Forward compatibility** means older code can read what newer code wrote.

Backward is usually easy: the new code's author knows the old format and can handle it. Forward is harder, since code already deployed must cope with additions it has never seen.

For an API call, ask of each message who writes it and who reads it. If an old client calls a new server, requests need backward compatibility and responses forward.

cards.prompt: A new version of a mobile app ships while the server it talks to is still on the previous version. Which compatibility does this need?
choices: Requests must be backward compatible and responses forward compatible
Requests and responses must both be backward compatible
Requests must be forward compatible and responses backward compatible
Requests and responses must both be forward compatible
cards.explanation: The old server decodes requests written by newer code, so old reads new: forward compatibility. The new app decodes responses written by older code, so new reads old: backward compatibility. The first choice is the opposite case, an old client calling a new server. Requests and responses travel in opposite directions, so they never need the same kind.

cards.prompt: Why is forward compatibility usually harder to achieve than backward compatibility?
choices: Forward compatibility needs a schema, but backward compatibility can work without one
Old code must cope with additions it has never seen, while new code's authors know the old format
It requires old code to predict exactly which fields future versions are going to add
cards.explanation: Whoever writes the new code knows exactly what older data looks like and can even keep the old parsing code around. Old code was written before the change, so it must be built to skip whatever it doesn't recognize; it doesn't have to predict what's coming. Neither direction requires a schema.

cards.title: Keeping unknown fields
cards.body:
Forward compatibility hides a trap. Say a recipe app adds a `spiceLevel` field, and an upgraded server saves a recipe with it. Then a server still on the old version loads that recipe, fixes a typo in its title, and saves it back.

If the old code decoded the recipe into an object that has room only for the fields it knows, `spiceLevel` was dropped the moment it was read. Saving writes the recipe without it. Nobody meant to delete anything, yet the value is gone.

So old code should hold on to fields it doesn't understand and write them back untouched.

cards.prompt: A new app version adds a loyaltyTier field to customer records. Order how an old version that's still running can wipe it out.
items: New code saves a customer record that includes loyaltyTier
Old code loads the record into an object with no place for loyaltyTier
Old code changes the customer's email address
Old code saves the object back, and loyaltyTier is gone
cards.explanation: To avoid this, old code must hold on to fields it doesn't understand and write them back untouched.

cards.title: Encoding and decoding
cards.body:
Inside a running program, data lives in objects, lists, hash tables and trees, linked by pointers and laid out for the CPU.

To save it on disk or ship it across a network, it must be flattened into a self-contained sequence of bytes. A pointer is a memory address inside your process; to any other process it's meaningless. Turning in-memory data into bytes is **encoding**, also called *serialization* or *marshaling*. The reverse is **decoding**, or *parsing*. This course says encoding, since serialization means something else for transactions.

A few *zero-copy* formats skip the step by using one layout for both.

cards.prompt: Why can't a program write its in-memory data structures straight to disk or the network, without encoding them?
choices: Operating systems don't allow raw memory to be written to files or sockets
Encoding exists only to shrink the data; the raw structures would work fine, just larger
They're full of pointers to memory addresses, which mean nothing to any other process
cards.explanation: In-memory structures are laid out for the CPU and linked by pointers, so they have to be turned into a self-contained sequence of bytes. Writing raw memory is possible; a reader just couldn't make sense of it. Encoding is about portability, not size. Zero-copy formats are the exception: one layout is designed to work both in memory and on disk.

cards.title: Built-in language formats
cards.body:
Many languages can encode objects for you: Java has `Serializable`, Ruby has `Marshal`. Convenient, but the problems run deep.

The bytes are tied to that language. Other languages struggle to read them, so you're stuck with it, and sharing data with other organizations gets hard. To restore objects, the decoder must be able to create instances of any class, so attackers who can feed you bytes may get to run their own code on your servers. Compatibility between versions is usually an afterthought, and so is efficiency: encoding can be slow and the output bloated.

Keep them for data that only lives a moment.

cards.prompt: Why is it usually a bad idea to store or send data in your language's built-in format, such as Python's pickle?
keyPoints: Other languages struggle to read it, which ties you to one language and makes it hard to integrate with other organizations
Decoding can create objects of arbitrary classes, so bytes from an attacker may lead to remote code execution
Forward and backward compatibility are often an afterthought
Encoding and decoding are often slow, and the output bulky
cards.explanation: Such formats are fine only for data that lives very briefly.

cards.title: Numbers in text formats
cards.body:
When data has to cross languages, the obvious picks are text formats every language supports: **JSON**, **XML** and **CSV**, which only handles flat tables.

All three are vague about numbers. XML and CSV can't tell a number from a string of digits without an outside schema. JSON does separate numbers from strings, but not integers from decimals, and it sets no precision.

That hurts with big integers. JavaScript parses every JSON number as a double, and a double can't hold every integer above 2^53 exactly, so a large ID can come out rounded. A common fix is to also send such numbers as strings.

cards.prompt: A server sends 64-bit invoice IDs as JSON numbers. In the JavaScript front end, some large IDs come out with the wrong final digits. Why?
choices: JavaScript reads JSON numbers as doubles, which can't hold every integer above 2^53 exactly
JSON caps numbers at 32 bits, so IDs above that limit overflow and wrap around
JSON doesn't distinguish numbers from digit strings, so the IDs are parsed as text and corrupted
cards.explanation: JSON separates numbers from strings but doesn't say whether a number is an integer or a float, or how precise it is. JavaScript parses all of them as doubles, so large integers get rounded. JSON sets no 32-bit limit, and mixing up numbers with digit strings is a problem of XML and CSV, not JSON. A common fix is to send the ID as a string too.

cards.title: Why text formats survive
cards.body:
Text formats have more rough edges. XML is wordy and complex. JSON and XML have no type for raw bytes, so binary data gets converted to Base64 text, which is clumsy and about a third bigger. CSV has no schema, so the app decides what each column means, and a value containing a comma or line break trips up sloppy parsers.

They stay popular anyway, above all between organizations. Nearly every language and tool handles them, and people can read them. And getting two organizations to agree on any format is so hard that elegance and efficiency hardly matter.

cards.prompt: Why do JSON, XML and CSV stay popular for exchanging data between organizations, despite their flaws?
keyPoints: Almost every language and tool can read and write them
Being text, they're fairly easy for people to read
Getting organizations to agree on a format is the hard part, so efficiency and elegance matter much less

cards.title: JSON Schema
cards.body:
**JSON Schema** describes what a JSON document should contain, in API specifications, schema registries and database validators. Beyond basic types such as string, integer and array, it adds **validation** rules on values: a percentage between 0 and 100, a username matching a pattern.

By default its content model is *open*: `additionalProperties` is true, so a document may carry fields the schema never mentions, of any type. Set it to false for a *closed* model that allows only the listed fields. So a typical JSON Schema says what isn't allowed rather than what is.

All this power makes schemas unwieldy and hard to evolve.

cards.prompt: A JSON Schema defines the fields sku and price and leaves additionalProperties at its default. A document arrives with an extra field, color. What happens?
choices: Validation fails, since the schema lists only sku and price
It passes, but the validator strips color from the document
It passes only if color is a string, the default type for extra fields
It passes: by default, undefined fields are allowed with any type
cards.explanation: additionalProperties defaults to true, an open content model, so a JSON Schema mostly says what isn't allowed: bad values in the fields it defines. Rejecting unknown fields takes a closed model, with additionalProperties set to false. Validators accept or reject documents rather than editing them, and extra fields aren't held to any type.

cards.title: Binary JSON
cards.body:
Text takes space, so dozens of binary encodings of JSON exist, such as **MessagePack**, CBOR and BSON. Some add types JSON lacks, like separate integers and floats, or raw bytes. They save space and can parse faster, yet none comes close to plain JSON's popularity.

They keep JSON's schemaless model, so every encoded record still spells out every field name. Numbers and lengths shrink into compact binary, but the names stay. The saving is modest, around a fifth, and you can no longer read the data by eye. Formats that use a schema can roughly halve the size.

cards.prompt: Why do binary encodings of JSON, such as MessagePack, end up only a little smaller than the text version?
choices: They still write numbers as decimal text, the same as JSON
Without a schema, each record must still carry all of its field names
Their type and length prefixes take more space than the quotes and brackets they replace
cards.explanation: Binary JSON keeps JSON's schemaless data model, so the name of every field is spelled out in every record. Numbers are stored in binary, and the short type and length prefixes take less room than JSON's punctuation, so those aren't the issue. Formats that use a schema can leave field names out and roughly halve the size.

cards.title: Protocol Buffers
cards.body:
**Protocol Buffers** (protobuf) is a binary format that requires a schema. You write it in an *interface definition language* (IDL), giving each field a name, a type and a **tag number**, like `string city = 4`. A code generator turns it into classes, in many languages, that encode and decode records. The schema lists fields and types; it can't restrict values.

In the bytes, each field appears as its tag, a type annotation and, if needed, a length. Field names never appear: the tag alone says which field a value belongs to. Small numbers take fewer bytes, and unset fields are left out.

cards.prompt: In Protocol Buffers, why can you rename a field freely but never change its tag number?
choices: Renames are applied to stored data automatically; tag changes need a manual migration
Tags set each field's position in the data, so changing one would shift all the others
Stored data names fields only by tag, so old records break if a tag changes
cards.explanation: The tag is what identifies a field in the encoded bytes; the name exists only in the schema and the generated code. Nothing rewrites stored data on a rename: the data simply never mentioned the name. Fields aren't positional either: each value carries its own tag, and unset fields are left out.

cards.title: Evolving a protobuf schema
cards.body:
A tag is a field's identity for good.

To add a field, give it a brand-new tag. Old code meeting an unknown tag skips it, using the type annotation to know how many bytes to jump, and can keep those bytes to write back. New code reading old data without the field uses a default, like 0 or an empty string.

When you remove a field, never reuse its tag: old data may still hold values under it. Mark it *reserved*. Changing a type is risky too: if the new type holds bigger numbers, new code reads old values fine, but old code truncates new values too big for it.

cards.prompt: How does Protocol Buffers keep old and new code compatible when a field is added?
keyPoints: The new field gets a tag number that has never been used
Old code skips a tag it doesn't know, using the type annotation to tell how many bytes to skip
Old code can keep the unknown field and write it back unchanged
New code reading old data fills in the type's default, such as 0 or an empty string
cards.explanation: The first three give forward compatibility; the last gives backward compatibility.

cards.prompt: A team removes the field with tag 5 from a protobuf schema. A year later, someone adds a new field and gives it tag 5. What's the risk?
choices: Old records still hold values under tag 5, which new code reads as the new field
None: removing the field from the schema erased its values from stored data
None, as long as the new field uses the same datatype as the field it replaces
cards.explanation: A tag is a field's identity in the data, and old records keep it long after the schema changes. Reusing it makes new code misread stale values that meant something else. Changing a schema never rewrites stored bytes, and a matching type only hides the mix-up. Mark retired tags as reserved so nobody reuses them.

cards.prompt: A storage service widens its protobuf fileSize field from int32 to int64 to record files over 2 GB. While old and new servers run side by side, which reads can return wrong sizes?
choices: New servers reading sizes that old servers wrote, since those lack the upper 32 bits
None: protobuf rejects any change of datatype, so the new schema won't even compile
Old servers reading large sizes that new servers wrote, which they cut down to 32 bits
Every read, until all stored records have been rewritten in the 64-bit format
cards.explanation: Old code still decodes the field into a 32-bit variable, so a 64-bit value too big to fit gets truncated. New code reading old values just fills the missing high bits with zeros. Protobuf does allow some type changes, and old records needn't be rewritten: the risk is only when old code reads new data.

cards.title: Avro
cards.body:
**Avro** is another binary format driven by a schema. Like protobuf's, its schema lists only fields and types, but it has no tag numbers.

An encoded record is just its values, one after another. A string is a length followed by bytes, but nothing marks it as a string or says which field it is. That makes Avro the most compact format here.

A decoder walks the schema's fields in their listed order, taking each one's type from the schema. So the bytes only make sense with exactly the schema that wrote them, the *writer's schema*.

cards.prompt: Avro-encoded data has no field tags and no type markers, just values one after another. How does a reader decode it?
choices: It walks the fields in the writer's schema order, using that schema for each type
It relies on its own reader's schema alone, so the writer's version doesn't matter
It infers each value's type from the bytes themselves, as a JSON parser does
It matches values to fields by names stored once at the start of each record
cards.explanation: Nothing in the bytes says where a field starts or what type it has, so they decode correctly only with the exact schema the writer used. The reader's schema matters afterwards, when Avro maps the writer's fields onto it, but it can't decode the bytes alone. A string's bytes look like any other data, and records carry no names.

cards.title: Writer's and reader's schemas
cards.body:
Avro works with two schemas. The **writer's schema** is the version the encoding app knows, often built into it. The **reader's schema** is what the decoding app's code expects. They don't have to match.

To decode, the reader needs the writer's exact schema. Avro then translates each record into the reader's schema. Fields are matched by **name**, so their order in the two schemas doesn't matter. A field the writer had but the reader doesn't know is ignored. A field the reader expects but the writer never had gets the default value from the reader's schema.

cards.prompt: When the writer's and reader's schemas differ, how does Avro resolve the differences?
keyPoints: Fields are matched by name, so their order in the two schemas can differ
A field the writer has but the reader lacks is ignored
A field the reader expects but the writer lacks gets the default from the reader's schema

cards.title: Avro's evolution rules
cards.body:
In Avro, forward compatibility means the writer's schema may be newer than the reader's; backward means it may be older.

Only add or remove a field that has a **default**. Add one without a default, and a new reader has nothing to fill in for old records: backward compatibility breaks. Remove one without a default, and old readers still expect it in new records: forward compatibility breaks.

Renames work through **aliases**: the reader's schema can list a field's old names and match them in older data. Old readers don't know the new name, so a rename works one way only. So does adding an option to a union type.

cards.prompt: To keep compatibility, why must an Avro field you add or remove have a default value?
keyPoints: Adding a field with no default breaks backward compatibility: a new reader has nothing to fill in for old records
Removing a field with no default breaks forward compatibility: an old reader still expects it in new records
cards.explanation: In Avro terms, backward means the writer's schema is older than the reader's, and forward means it's newer.

cards.prompt: A team renames an Avro field from zip to postcode, and their new reader's schema lists zip as an alias. What works now?
choices: Both directions work, since the alias links the old and new names either way
Old readers can read new data, but new readers can't make sense of old data
New readers can read old data; old readers can't find the renamed field in new data
Neither: once data exists, an Avro field can never be renamed
cards.explanation: The alias lives only in the new reader's schema, so a new reader can match zip in old data: backward compatible. Old readers have no alias and look for zip, which new data doesn't contain, so the change isn't forward compatible. Adding a new option to a union type works the same way. Renaming is possible; it just works in one direction.

cards.title: Finding the writer's schema
cards.body:
An Avro reader needs the writer's schema, but attaching it to every record would often take more room than the data.

A big file of records sharing one schema stores it once, at the start; Avro's *object container files* do this. Two processes on a connection agree on a version when they connect.

In a database, records written years apart use different schemas. So each record begins with a schema **version number**, and every version is kept in a list. To read, you take the number from the record, look up that writer's schema, decode the rest with it, then map the result onto your own schema.

cards.prompt: How does an Avro reader learn the writer's schema? Cover a big file of records, a database, and a network connection.
keyPoints: File: all records share one schema, stored once at the start of the file
Database: each record begins with a schema version number, looked up in a stored list of schemas
Network connection: the two sides agree on a schema version when the connection is set up
cards.explanation: Attaching the full schema to every record would usually cost more than the data itself.

cards.prompt: Order how a reader decodes an Avro record from a database that tags each record with a schema version.
items: Fetch the encoded record
Read the version number at its start
Look up the writer's schema for that version
Decode the rest of the record with the writer's schema
Map the decoded fields onto the reader's schema
cards.explanation: The version can be a simple counter or a hash of the schema.

cards.title: Generated schemas
cards.body:
Avro's lack of tag numbers pays off when a program, not a person, writes the schema.

Say a tool exports a spreadsheet every week, turning each column into a field named after its header. When someone adds or deletes a column, the tool just generates a fresh schema. Readers match fields by name, so an older reader's schema still lines up with the new writer's.

With protobuf, each column would need a tag number. Someone would have to keep a column-to-tag mapping by hand and never reuse a retired tag. That can be automated, but carefully; protobuf simply wasn't built for it.

cards.prompt: A nightly job dumps each table of a relational database to binary files, generating the schema from the current columns on every run. Why does Avro fit this better than Protocol Buffers?
choices: Avro stores the full schema in every record, so readers always see the current columns
Avro matches fields by name, so a regenerated schema needs no hand-assigned tag numbers
Avro schemas can carry over the tables' constraints, such as value ranges and foreign keys
cards.explanation: Column names become field names, so when columns come and go the job just generates a fresh schema, and readers match fields by name. With Protocol Buffers, someone would have to map columns to tags by hand and never reuse an old one. Avro writes the schema once per file, not per record, and its schemas hold only fields and types.

cards.title: Why use a schema
cards.body:
Protobuf and Avro schemas are much simpler than JSON Schema: they list fields and types, with no rules on values such as ranges or patterns. That makes them easy to implement, so many languages support them.

Compared with schemaless JSON, they're more compact, since field names stay out of the data. The schema is documentation that can't go stale, because nothing decodes without it. Keeping every past schema lets you check a change for compatibility before you deploy it. And in statically typed languages, code generated from the schema gets checked at compile time.

The price: nobody can read the data until it's decoded.

cards.prompt: What can a JSON Schema express that a Protocol Buffers or Avro schema can't?
choices: The datatype of each field, such as a string or a 64-bit integer
That a field holds a list of values rather than one
A record type nested inside another record
Constraints on values, such as a minimum or a required pattern
cards.explanation: JSON Schema layers validation rules on top of types: ranges, patterns, conditional logic and more. Protocol Buffers and Avro schemas list only fields and their types, which keeps them simple to implement and widely supported across languages. All three can describe field types, lists and nested records.

cards.prompt: Why use a binary format with a schema, such as Protocol Buffers or Avro, instead of schemaless JSON?
keyPoints: It's more compact, since field names stay out of the data
The schema doubles as documentation that can't go stale, because decoding needs it
A store of past schemas lets you check a change's compatibility before deploying it
Code generated from the schema gives compile-time type checks in statically typed languages
cards.explanation: The cost: a person can't read the data until it's decoded.

cards.title: Dataflow through databases
cards.body:
Compatibility is always between two processes: one encodes data, the other decodes it. With a database, whoever writes a value encodes it, and whoever reads it decodes.

If one app uses the database alone, storing a value is like leaving a note for your future self. The reader is a later version of the writer, so you need backward compatibility.

Usually, though, many processes share a database: different services, or several copies of one. During a rolling upgrade some run new code and some old, so a value saved by an upgraded instance may next be read by an old one. So forward compatibility matters too.

cards.prompt: Why does data in a database usually need both backward and forward compatibility?
keyPoints: Backward: later versions of the code must read what earlier versions wrote
Forward: during a rolling upgrade, instances still on old code read values that upgraded ones wrote
cards.explanation: Storing data is like leaving a note for your future self, but when many processes share a database, the past can read it as well.

cards.title: Data outlives code
cards.body:
A database can hold a value written a second ago next to one written years ago. New code can replace every server in minutes, but stored data keeps its original encoding until something rewrites it: **data outlives code**.

Rewriting everything into a new schema is possible but expensive on big datasets, so databases avoid it or do it lazily. Adding a column with a null default usually leaves existing rows alone: reading an old row just returns null for the missing column. LSM-tree engines move rows to the latest format during compaction. Bigger changes, like turning one value into a list, still need a real rewrite.

cards.prompt: A team replaces every server with the new version within ten minutes and concludes that old-format data is no longer a concern. Why are they wrong?
choices: Data written long ago keeps its original encoding until something rewrites it
Rolling upgrades always leave some servers running the old version indefinitely
Deploying new code makes the database convert old records, which can take hours
cards.explanation: Code can be swapped out in minutes, but a database may hold values written moments ago next to values from years ago, each in the format of its day: data outlives code. Deploying code doesn't touch stored data, and nothing forces servers to stay on the old version. The old data is the problem.

cards.prompt: Adding a nullable column to a table with a billion rows completes almost instantly. How?
choices: Null values take no space, so writing them into every row costs nothing
Old rows are rewritten one by one the next time each is read
The new column goes in a separate table that's joined on every query
Old rows stay as they are; reads fill in null for the missing column
cards.explanation: Rewriting a huge dataset is expensive, so databases avoid or defer it while making every row look like it has the current schema. LSM-tree engines, for instance, move data to the latest format during compaction. Writing a billion nulls would still mean a billion row writes, and reads don't rewrite rows. Bigger changes, such as turning a field into a list, do force a rewrite.

cards.title: Snapshots
cards.body:
Now and then you may copy a whole database, for a backup or to load into a data warehouse. The source may hold records in many schema versions, but the copy needn't: every record is being rewritten anyway, so encode them all in the latest schema.

A dump is written once and never changed afterwards, which suits Avro's object container files. It's also a good moment to switch to a column-oriented format such as Parquet, which analytics tools read efficiently.

cards.prompt: You export a nightly snapshot of a database whose records were written under five schema versions, for loading into a warehouse. How should the snapshot be encoded?
choices: All records in the latest schema, since every record is being copied anyway
Each record in the schema it was first written with, to keep its history
All records in the oldest schema, so that every reader version can decode them
cards.explanation: The whole dataset is being rewritten, so it may as well come out consistent. A dump is written once and never changed, which suits Avro's container files or a column-oriented format like Parquet. Keeping five encodings makes every reader handle all of them, and the oldest schema would lack the newest fields.

cards.title: Services
cards.body:
Processes can also talk over a network. Usually **servers** expose an API and **clients** send it requests; that API is a **service**.

Like a database, a service lets clients store and query data. But a database runs any query its language allows, while a service accepts only the inputs and outputs its business logic defines. That **encapsulation** lets it control exactly what each client may do.

It also frees the team that owns it. As long as the API stays compatible, they can release on their own schedule and change anything behind it, even move its data or rebuild it entirely.

cards.prompt: Why do services expose an application-specific API instead of letting clients query their data directly, as a database would?
keyPoints: The API accepts only the inputs and outputs the service's business logic defines
So the service controls exactly what each client may do
While the API stays compatible, the owning team can change anything behind it, even move its data or rebuild the system
cards.explanation: Old and new versions of clients and servers will run at the same time, so the API's encoding has to work across versions.

cards.title: Web services and IDLs
cards.body:
A service reached over HTTP is a **web service**, whether its caller is a phone app, another service in the same company, or another company's backend. The most popular style, **REST**, leans on HTTP itself: URLs name resources, and HTTP's features handle caching, authentication and content types.

Clients must know the endpoints and data formats, so teams often describe them in an IDL: **OpenAPI** for JSON services, protobuf for gRPC. From one definition, tools generate documentation and client libraries in many languages, and check whether a change keeps the API compatible. Frameworks then handle routing and metrics, leaving developers the business logic.

cards.prompt: What does describing a service's API in an IDL, such as OpenAPI, give its developers and clients?
keyPoints: One definition documents the endpoints and data models for anyone calling the service
Client libraries in many languages can be generated from it
Tools can check whether a change to the API stays compatible
cards.explanation: Some frameworks generate the definition from the server code; others start from the definition and generate the server's skeleton.

cards.title: Remote calls aren't local calls
cards.body:
**RPC**, the remote procedure call, dates from the 1970s: make a request to a remote service look like calling a local function. That illusion, *location transparency*, is flawed.

A local call succeeds or fails depending on things you control. A network request can be lost, or reach a slow or dead machine, for reasons you don't. It can time out, leaving you unsure whether it ran, and a retry may repeat the action unless it's idempotent. Its latency is far higher and swings wildly. And its arguments must be encoded into bytes, not passed as pointers, and translated between languages whose types differ.

cards.prompt: Why is it a mistake to make a call to a remote service look just like a local function call?
keyPoints: The request or response can be lost, or the remote machine can be slow or down, for reasons outside your control
A timeout leaves you not knowing whether the request was processed, so a retry may repeat the action
Latency is much higher than a local call's and varies wildly
Arguments must be encoded into bytes and translated between languages, rather than passed as references
cards.explanation: Part of REST's appeal is that it treats moving state over a network as something different from calling a function.

cards.title: Finding a service
cards.body:
A client has to find the service it calls: that's **service discovery**. A fixed IP address breaks when the server moves. Usually many instances run, and a **load balancer** spreads requests among them.

DNS can spread load too, by listing several addresses under one name. But DNS was built for records that rarely change, and answers get cached, so when instances come and go fast, clients get stale addresses.

A **discovery registry** keeps a live list instead. Each instance registers its host, port and metadata when it starts, then sends heartbeats. Clients ask the registry for current endpoints and connect to one directly.

cards.prompt: Instances of a service start and stop every few minutes, and clients find them through a domain name that lists several IP addresses. Clients keep connecting to addresses where nothing is running. Why?
choices: A domain name can only map to one address at a time, so most of the lookups go to the wrong one
DNS changes spread slowly and are cached, so clients see addresses of instances that are gone
DNS drops an instance only after it misses several heartbeats, which takes too long
cards.explanation: DNS was built for records that change rarely, and answers are cached along the way. A service discovery registry suits fast-changing instances better: each instance registers itself and sends heartbeats. DNS does support several addresses per name, which is how it spreads load, and heartbeats belong to discovery systems, not DNS.

cards.prompt: Order how a client reaches a new service instance through a service discovery system.
items: The new instance starts up
It registers its host, port and metadata with the registry
A client asks the registry for the available endpoints
The client picks one and connects to it directly
cards.explanation: The instance keeps sending heartbeats so the registry knows it's alive. Unlike a load balancer, the registry isn't in the path of each request.

cards.title: Service meshes
cards.body:
A **service mesh** combines load balancing and service discovery. Every client and every server gets its own local load balancer, a library in the process or a *sidecar* process beside it. A client talks only to its local proxy, which talks to the server's proxy, which hands the request to the server.

Since all traffic flows through the proxies, they can encrypt it, so the apps never touch TLS certificates. They also see every call: who calls whom, what fails, how much load. It's complex, so it suits busy, fast-changing setups such as Kubernetes; simple deployments do fine with a software load balancer.

cards.prompt: A company wants every call between its 40 internal services encrypted with TLS, plus a live view of which services call which, without changing each service's code. What fits best?
choices: A service mesh, with a local proxy beside each client and each server
DNS records that list several addresses for each service
A service discovery registry that every client queries before it connects
cards.explanation: In a mesh, each application talks only to a local proxy, so the proxies can encrypt the traffic between them and observe every call. DNS and discovery registries only tell clients where to connect; the connection itself is direct, so each service would still handle TLS on its own and nothing would watch the calls.

cards.title: Evolving service APIs
cards.body:
Services exist so teams can deploy independently, so clients and servers run mixed versions. Usually you can assume servers upgrade first and clients later. Then requests need only backward compatibility, and responses only forward. gRPC follows protobuf's rules. In JSON REST APIs, adding an optional request parameter or a new response field is usually safe.

Public APIs are harder: clients in other organizations can't be forced to upgrade, so old ones may call for years, perhaps forever. A breaking change usually means running several API versions side by side, picked by a number in the URL, an HTTP header, or a per-client setting on the server.

cards.prompt: For dataflow through services, what simplifying assumption can you usually make about compatibility?
choices: Clients and servers are upgraded together, so no compatibility is needed
Clients upgrade before servers, so requests need forward and responses backward compatibility
Services store no data, so only backward compatibility matters
Servers upgrade before clients, so requests need backward and responses forward compatibility
cards.explanation: If every server is updated before any client, new servers read old requests (backward) and old clients read new responses (forward). Services exist so teams can deploy independently, so nothing upgrades in lockstep. Clients usually update last, since they often belong to other teams or to users. Stored data isn't the point: requests and responses cross versions on their own.

cards.prompt: Which change to a JSON REST API is usually safe for existing clients?
choices: Making an optional request parameter required
Renaming a field in the response
Adding a new field to a response object
Changing a response field from a number to a string
cards.explanation: Old clients reading a response with an extra field can simply ignore it, which is forward compatibility on responses. Adding an optional request parameter is safe for the reverse reason. Requiring a parameter breaks old clients that don't send it, and renames or type changes break any client that reads the field.

cards.prompt: Why do public APIs often have to stay compatible for years, and what happens when a breaking change is unavoidable?
keyPoints: The provider can't force clients in other organizations to upgrade
So old clients may keep calling for a very long time, perhaps forever
A breaking change usually means running several API versions side by side
cards.explanation: There's no standard way to pick a version: a number in the URL, an HTTP Accept header, or a per-client setting stored on the server are all common.

cards.title: Durable execution
cards.body:
Say a checkout **workflow** has three *tasks*: check stock, charge the card, book a courier, each a call to a different service. If a machine dies after the charge but before the booking, the customer has paid for nothing. And no database transaction can span separate services, some run by other companies.

**Durable execution** frameworks solve this. While a task runs, they record each call it makes, with its result, in a durable log. If the task fails, they rerun it from the start, but a call already in the log isn't repeated: its logged result is returned. Past the end of the log, calls are made for real.

cards.prompt: Order how a durable execution framework recovers a workflow task that crashed partway through.
items: While the task runs, each completed call and its result is written to a durable log
The machine running the task crashes
The framework runs the task again from the start
Calls already in the log aren't made again; their logged results are returned instead
Calls past the end of the log are made for real
cards.explanation: This gives a multi-service workflow exactly-once behavior without a shared transaction, as long as the external services it calls are idempotent and given unique IDs.

cards.title: Replays must match
cards.body:
