Replay only works if the code makes the same calls, in the same order, as the first run. Insert a new call into a workflow while runs are in progress, and a replay may get the result meant for a different call. So don't edit a live workflow; deploy the change as a new version. Runs under way keep the old code, and only new runs get the new one.

For the same reason, workflow code must be **deterministic**. A replay that reads the clock or draws a random number may take a different branch than the first run. Frameworks offer deterministic versions of these functions.

cards.prompt: A developer swaps the order of two service calls in a durable workflow while thousands of runs are still in progress. Why is that risky?
choices: It isn't risky: logged results are matched to calls by name, so order doesn't matter
It's only risky for new runs, which will now make the calls in a different order
It isn't risky: the durable log stores the code itself, so replays run the old version
In-progress runs replay against the logged call order and may break; ship it as a new version
cards.explanation: The framework logs calls in order and expects a replay to repeat them in that order, so a reordered replay can be handed the wrong results. Deploy the change as a separate version: existing runs keep the old code, and only new runs get the new one. The log holds calls and results, not code. New runs start with an empty log, so they're the safe ones.

cards.prompt: Why must code in a durable workflow avoid reading the system clock or a random number generator directly?
choices: Those calls are too slow to fit inside a workflow step's time limit
A replay must make the same decisions as the first run, or it won't match the log
Timestamps and random numbers can't be encoded into the durable log, so they'd be lost
cards.explanation: Replay re-runs the code and expects it to make the same calls as before; a different timestamp or random value can send it down another branch. Frameworks offer deterministic replacements, and some tools check code for nondeterminism. Reading a clock is fast, and there's nothing hard about encoding a number.

cards.title: Idempotent external calls
cards.body:
Durable execution doesn't make the outside world exactly-once. A call is skipped on replay only if its result reached the log. If an email service sent a receipt but the machine died before the result was logged, the replay sends that email again.

So the services a workflow calls must offer an **idempotent** API, where repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once. The usual way is a unique ID with each request, which lets the service spot repeats and ignore them. Developers have to remember to send it.

cards.prompt: A durable workflow books a hotel room through a partner's API. The worker crashes right after the partner confirms, before the result reaches the log. What stops the replay from booking a second room?
choices: Nothing needs to: the framework never repeats a call that has already been started
A unique ID sent with the request, which the partner's API uses to ignore repeats
Keeping the workflow code deterministic, so the replay takes exactly the same path
A database transaction that rolls back the first booking when the worker crashes
cards.explanation: A call whose result never reached the log looks unmade, so the replay sends it again; only an idempotent API, keyed by a unique ID, turns the repeat into a no-op. The framework skips only logged calls. Determinism keeps the workflow's own choices stable but can't stop a repeated call, and no database transaction spans another company's service.

cards.title: Message brokers
cards.body:
In an **event-driven** architecture, processes send each other *events*, or *messages*. Unlike an RPC caller, the sender usually moves on without waiting for anyone to handle it. And messages don't go straight to the recipient but through a **message broker**, which holds them for a while.

The broker buffers messages when the recipient is down or overloaded, and redelivers them to a consumer that crashed, so nothing is lost. Senders need no service discovery, since they only talk to the broker. One message can reach several recipients, and the sender needn't know who they are.

cards.prompt: What does sending messages through a broker give you, compared with calling the recipient directly?
keyPoints: It buffers messages while the recipient is down or overloaded
It redelivers messages to a consumer that crashed, so they aren't lost
Senders need no service discovery, since they never connect to the recipient
One message can reach several recipients, and the sender needn't know who they are
cards.explanation: The sender usually moves on without waiting for processing; if it needs a reply, that comes back on a separate channel.

cards.title: Queues and topics
cards.body:
Brokers mostly offer two patterns. A **queue** hands each message to one of its consumers, so several consumers share the work. A **topic** delivers each message to every subscriber.

A broker doesn't care what's inside a message: it's bytes plus some metadata. Teams often use protobuf, Avro or JSON, with a schema registry beside the broker that stores schema versions and checks them for compatibility. Many brokers delete messages once consumed, though some can keep them forever.

A consumer that decodes messages and republishes them elsewhere is like old code rewriting a database record: it must keep fields it doesn't know, or they vanish downstream.

cards.prompt: Twenty workers share a backlog of video-transcoding jobs, and each job should be done by just one of them. How should the jobs be sent?
choices: Published to a topic all the workers subscribe to, so every worker sees every job
Published to a topic; the broker deletes each job as soon as any subscriber has read it
Put on a named queue the workers consume from, which hands each job to one of them
cards.explanation: A queue gives each message to a single consumer, which is what splitting work needs. A topic delivers each message to every subscriber, so twenty workers would transcode every video twenty times. Topic delivery doesn't stop at the first reader; reaching all subscribers is the whole point.

cards.prompt: A service reads events from one topic, adds a field, and republishes them to another. The upstream producer has started including a field this service's code doesn't know. What should the service do with it?
choices: Drop it, since downstream consumers may not know it either
Keep it and pass it through unchanged
Reject those events until the service is upgraded
Ask the schema registry to remove the field from the topic's schema
cards.explanation: A consumer that decodes events and re-encodes them can silently erase data it doesn't understand, just like old code writing a database record back. Downstream consumers that do know the field would lose it. Rejecting the events gives up forward compatibility, and a schema registry stores and checks schema versions; it doesn't strip fields from messages.

cards.title: Actors
cards.body:
The **actor model** handles concurrency without you managing threads and locks. Each actor, often standing for one user or entity, keeps private state no other actor can touch, and talks to others only through asynchronous messages, which may get lost. It handles one message at a time, so it needs no locks.

*Distributed* actor frameworks spread actors over many nodes. Sending to a remote actor looks the same as sending to a local one; the framework encodes the message and ships it. Here location transparency works better than in RPC, because actor code already expects lost messages. Rolling upgrades still need compatible encodings, since old and new nodes message each other.

cards.prompt: How does the actor model avoid the race conditions and locking problems of threads?
keyPoints: Each actor's state is private; no other actor can touch it
Actors interact only by sending each other asynchronous messages
An actor handles one message at a time, so it needs no locks
cards.explanation: Distributed actor frameworks still need compatible encodings for rolling upgrades, since nodes on old and new versions message each other.

cards.prompt: Why does location transparency work better in distributed actor frameworks than in RPC?
choices: Actor frameworks bring network latency down to that of in-process calls
Actor messages are synchronous, so failures surface straight away
The framework guarantees that every message is delivered to its actor exactly once
The actor model already assumes messages can be lost, even within one process
cards.explanation: Actor code is written to cope with lost messages anyway, so sending them over the network changes less than turning a function call into a network request does. Latency still goes up across machines. Actor messages are asynchronous, and delivery isn't guaranteed at all, let alone exactly once.

cards.title: Why replicate
cards.body:
**Replication** means storing a copy of one dataset on several machines connected by a network. Picture a photo app with users on three continents. A copy near each group of users makes the app feel quick. If one machine dies, the others keep serving and no photos are lost. Several copies can share read traffic that one machine couldn't handle. And a copy on the phone itself lets the app keep working without a signal.

Copying data that never changes is trivial: you do it once. All the difficulty is in passing along *changes*, and databases do that in one of three ways: **single-leader**, **multi-leader** or **leaderless** replication.

cards.prompt: Why replicate a database onto several machines? Name what the extra copies can buy you.
keyPoints: Copies placed near users cut the time it takes to reach the data
When machines fail, the system keeps running and the data survives
Spreading reads across replicas handles more read traffic than one machine can
An app can keep working while it's cut off from the network
cards.explanation: Copying data that never changes is easy; the hard part of replication is keeping changes in step across the copies.

cards.title: Replicas are not backups
cards.body:
Replication doesn't replace backups. A replica copies every change within moments, mistakes included. If a bad update sets every price in your shop to zero, that update reaches every replica too, and the old prices are gone everywhere at once.

A **backup** is an older snapshot you can go back to. So you need both, and they often work together: a backup can seed a new replica, and an archived replication log can be part of a backup. Old snapshots are often kept in an object store, which is cheap for data that's rarely read.

cards.prompt: A buggy script deletes a month of invoices. The database has two followers in other zones. What gets the invoices back?
choices: Failing over to a follower, since each follower keeps its own independent copy
Nothing: once the deletes have replicated, the rows are gone for good
Restoring from a backup taken before the script ran
Having the followers resync, which brings back rows the leader is missing
cards.explanation: Replication passes the deletes to every follower within moments, so they lose the invoices too. A backup is an older snapshot you can go back to, which is why you need both. A resync copies the leader's current state, deletions included. And the rows aren't gone for good as long as a backup exists.

cards.title: Leaders and followers
cards.body:
The most common setup is **leader-based** replication. One replica, the **leader**, takes every write. It saves each change to its own storage, then sends it to the other replicas, the **followers**, through a **replication log**. Each follower applies the changes in exactly the order the leader did, so all copies end up the same.

Reads can go to the leader or to any follower. Writes can't: to clients, followers are read-only. If the database is split into shards, each shard has its own leader. Many relational databases offer this out of the box.

cards.prompt: A database has one leader and two followers. A network fault cuts an app server off from the leader, but it can still reach both followers. What can the app server do?
choices: Write to a follower, which passes the change on to the leader once the link is back
Write to a follower only if it's synchronous, since that one already holds every change
Read from the followers but not write, since only the leader accepts writes
Nothing at all, since a follower can't answer a read without checking with the leader
cards.explanation: In leader-based replication every write goes through the leader, and followers only apply its stream of changes, so to clients they're read-only. They keep answering reads, which may be slightly stale. Being synchronous doesn't let a follower take writes. Replicas that accept writes and pass them on later are how multi-leader replication works.

cards.title: Synchronous or asynchronous
cards.body:
A **synchronous** follower must confirm each write before the leader reports success. It's always current, so losing the leader loses nothing. But if it stops answering, no write can finish. With every follower synchronous, any one outage would halt all writes. So databases usually make one follower synchronous and the rest **asynchronous**, making another one synchronous if it fails; some wait for a majority instead.

The leader never waits for asynchronous followers. A fully asynchronous setup keeps taking writes even when every follower is down or far behind. The cost: if the leader dies for good, confirmed writes it hadn't sent yet are lost. It's still common, especially with many or distant followers.

cards.prompt: Why do databases that support synchronous replication usually make just one follower synchronous, not all of them?
choices: Synchronous followers can't serve reads, so making all of them synchronous would waste them
If every follower were synchronous, any one of them going down would halt all writes
A leader can only wait on one follower at a time, so a second would be ignored
cards.explanation: The leader waits for every synchronous follower, so with all of them synchronous one outage blocks every write, and the more followers there are, the likelier one is down. A single synchronous follower still keeps each write on two nodes. Synchronous followers can serve reads, and a leader can wait on several, as majority quorums do.

cards.prompt: What do you gain and what do you risk by making leader-based replication fully asynchronous?
keyPoints: Gain: the leader keeps accepting writes even if every follower is down or far behind
Risk: if the leader dies for good, writes it confirmed but hadn't yet passed on are lost
cards.explanation: Despite the weaker durability, it's widely used, especially with many followers or followers spread across regions.

cards.title: Adding a follower
cards.body:
Sometimes you need a new follower, to add capacity or replace a dead node. Copying the leader's files while writes keep coming would capture different parts at different moments, a mess. Locking the database for the copy would mean downtime.

Instead, take a consistent **snapshot** of the leader without locking it, the same feature backups rely on, and copy it to the new node. The snapshot records the precise point in the leader's log that it matches. The follower asks for every change after that point, works through the backlog until it has **caught up**, then follows live changes. Snapshots plus an archived log in an object store double as backups.

cards.prompt: A new follower is seeded from a snapshot of the leader. Why must the snapshot record the precise point in the leader's replication log that it matches?
choices: So the follower can ask for exactly the changes made after it, missing none and repeating none
So the leader can pause writes at that position until the snapshot files have been copied over
So the follower can tell which rows in the snapshot are already stale and drop them
cards.explanation: The position marks the moment the snapshot shows, so the follower requests everything after it, works through that backlog, then follows live. Snapshots are taken without locking, so writes never pause. No row in the snapshot needs dropping: it's consistent as of its position, and later changes come from the log.

cards.title: Databases on object storage
cards.body:
More databases now keep live data in object stores like S3. It's cheap, the store replicates it across zones, and its conditional writes, a compare-and-set, can drive transactions and leader election.

The costs: requests are far slower than a local disk, and per-request fees push you to batch, adding delay. Objects usually can't be edited in place, so changing part of a big one means rewriting it. Mounting a bucket as a filesystem through FUSE often lacks features like random writes.

So some systems keep only cold data there; others keep the main data there but the write-ahead log on fast storage. **Zero-disk** systems keep everything there, using disks only as cache.

cards.prompt: A team moves its database onto object storage, and commits get much slower than on local disk. Which design keeps the object store as the main tier but fixes commit latency?
choices: Store every change as its own small object the moment it commits
Append each commit to the end of one large object in the store
Mount the bucket through FUSE so the database sees an ordinary disk
Keep the write-ahead log on a separate low-latency store
cards.explanation: Some systems write only the WAL to fast storage and send the rest to the object store in batches. Tiny objects per change still pay full latency, plus a fee per call. Objects are often immutable, so appending means rewriting. A FUSE mount hides the object store but not its latency, and often lacks random writes.

cards.title: Follower recovery
cards.body:
A follower records on its own disk every change it receives from the leader. After a crash or a network cut, that record shows the last transaction it applied. It asks the leader for everything since, applies it, and resumes streaming.

That's simple, but it can be heavy. After a long outage or under many writes, the backlog is big, and catching up loads both the follower and the leader that sends it.

The leader may delete log entries once every follower has them. If one stays away too long, the leader must choose: keep the log and risk filling its disk, or delete it, and then the follower must be rebuilt from a backup.

cards.prompt: How does a follower catch up after it crashes or loses its connection, and what can make that hard?
keyPoints: Its own log tells it the last transaction it applied before the fault
It asks the leader for every change since then, applies them, and resumes streaming
After a long outage or under heavy writes, the backlog puts high load on both follower and leader
If the leader has already deleted the log it needs, the follower must be rebuilt from a backup
cards.explanation: The leader has to choose between keeping its log for an absent follower, risking a full disk, and deleting it.

cards.title: Failover
cards.body:
If the leader fails, a follower must take over: **failover**. An admin can do it by hand, or the system does it in three steps. It decides the leader is dead, usually because it stayed silent past a timeout. It picks a new leader, ideally the follower with the newest changes, to lose the least. Then clients are pointed at the new leader, and the old one, if it comes back, must step down.

Setting the timeout is hard. Too long, and recovery is slow. Too short, and a leader that's merely slow, from a load spike or a network hiccup, gets replaced, adding strain when the system can least afford it.

cards.prompt: A database declares its leader dead after two seconds without a reply. During a traffic spike, the leader's responses slow past that limit. What's the likely result?
choices: Nothing, since only a crashed leader triggers failover, not a slow one
A quicker recovery than a longer timeout would give, with no downside
Writes pause until an administrator confirms that the leader is down
A needless failover that adds load just when the system is struggling
cards.explanation: A timeout can't tell a slow node from a dead one, so a short one fails over on load spikes and network glitches, making a strained system worse. A long timeout costs slower recovery instead. Automatic failover doesn't wait for a human; some teams choose manual failover for these very reasons.

cards.title: When failover goes wrong
cards.body:
With asynchronous replication, the new leader may lack the old leader's last writes. When the old leader rejoins, those writes are usually discarded, so writes that clients saw confirmed are gone. That's worse if other systems already used them: a new leader might reissue an order number that a shipping service had already tied to a different order.

A fault can also leave two nodes each sure it's the leader: **split brain**. If both take writes and nothing resolves the conflicts, data is lost or corrupted. Some systems shut one node down when they spot two leaders, but a careless design can stop both, and by the time it acts, the damage may be done.

cards.prompt: With asynchronous replication, order how a write the client saw confirmed can be lost in a failover.
items: The leader applies the write and confirms it to the client
The leader crashes before sending the write to any follower
A follower is promoted and starts taking new writes
The old leader comes back as a follower, and its unreplicated write is thrown away
cards.explanation: Discarding the old leader's extra writes is the usual fix. It's worse if other systems already used that data, for example an ID that the lagging new leader then hands out again.

cards.prompt: After a network fault, two nodes both believe they're the leader and both accept writes. A safety catch shuts one down when it spots two leaders. Why isn't that enough?
choices: It is enough, because the two leaders' writes are merged once the fault clears
It is enough, since split brain only loses data if it outlasts the failover timeout
A careless design can stop both nodes, and data may be corrupt before it acts
cards.explanation: Two leaders accepting writes with no way to resolve conflicts will lose or corrupt data, and detection can come too late. Poorly built shutdown mechanisms have taken down both nodes. A single-leader database has no process for merging the two histories, and harm starts with the first conflicting write, not after some timeout.

cards.title: Statement-based replication
cards.body:
The simplest replication log is the write statements themselves: the leader sends each SQL write to the followers, and they run it as if a client had.

It breaks in subtle ways. A call like NOW() or RAND() gives a different result on each replica. Statements that use an autoincrementing column, or that depend on existing rows like an UPDATE with a WHERE clause, must run in exactly the same order everywhere, which limits concurrent transactions. Triggers and stored procedures can cause different side effects on each node.

The leader can patch some of this, say by logging the value NOW() actually returned. But determinism is hard to guarantee, so most databases prefer other methods.

cards.prompt: A leader replicates by sending each SQL statement to its followers to run. One statement gives each new raffle ticket a random prize code. What happens?
choices: Every replica gets the same code, since they all run the same statement
Each replica draws its own random code, so the copies disagree
The followers refuse the statement, since only a leader may call random functions
The codes match as long as followers run statements in the leader's order
cards.explanation: Nondeterministic calls like RAND or NOW produce a different value on each replica, unless the leader logs the value it actually got. Running statements in the same order fixes order-dependent ones, such as autoincrement or UPDATE with a WHERE clause, but not randomness. Followers don't refuse; they quietly diverge.

cards.title: Shipping the write-ahead log
cards.body:
A storage engine's write-ahead log already records every change, so the leader can just send it to followers, which rebuild identical files from it, indexes included.

The catch: it's very low-level, saying which bytes changed in which disk blocks. That ties replication to the storage format, so if a new version changes the format, leader and followers usually can't run different versions.

That matters for upgrades. If a follower may run a newer version than its leader, you can upgrade with no downtime: upgrade the followers, fail over to one of them, then upgrade the old leader, now a follower. When versions can't mix, as is usual with WAL shipping, upgrades need downtime.

cards.prompt: Why does write-ahead log shipping usually stop the leader and its followers from running different database versions?
choices: The log holds SQL statements, and a different version might parse them in a different way
The log leaves out index changes, which each version rebuilds in its own way
The log records which bytes changed in which disk blocks, tying it to one storage format
The log is too large to send over the network while the versions differ
cards.explanation: A WAL describes changes at the level of disk blocks, so only a node with the same on-disk layout can apply it; upgrades then often need downtime. Shipping SQL is statement-based replication, a different method. The WAL holds everything needed to restore both indexes and table data. Its size has nothing to do with versions.

cards.prompt: Order a zero-downtime upgrade of a database that uses leader-based replication.
items: Check that the replication log lets a newer follower apply an older leader's changes
Upgrade the followers to the new version
Fail over so that an upgraded follower becomes the leader
Upgrade the old leader, which now runs as a follower
cards.explanation: This works with a logical log, which is independent of the storage format. With WAL shipping the versions usually can't mix, so upgrades need downtime.

cards.title: Logical logs
cards.body:
A **logical log** decouples replication from the storage engine by describing changes row by row. An insert logs every column's new value. A delete logs just enough to identify the row: normally its primary key, or, with no key, every column's old value. An update logs what identifies the row plus every column's new value, or at least each changed one. A transaction adds a commit record after its rows.

Since the format doesn't depend on the engine, it's easier to keep backward compatible, so leader and followers can run different versions. Outside tools can read it too, to feed a warehouse or a cache: **change data capture**.

cards.prompt: In a row-based logical log, what is recorded for an inserted row, a deleted row and an updated row?
keyPoints: Inserted: the new values of every column
Deleted: enough to identify the row, usually its primary key, or all its old values if there's no key
Updated: enough to identify the row, plus the new value of every column, or at least of those that changed
cards.explanation: A transaction yields one record per row plus a commit record, and since the format doesn't depend on the storage engine, outside systems can read it too (change data capture).

cards.title: Replication lag
cards.body:
Most online services read far more than they write. With a leader, you can serve reads from many followers and add more as traffic grows. That only works with asynchronous replication: if all were synchronous, any one failure would block writes, and the more nodes, the likelier one is down.

The price is stale reads from followers that are behind. Stop writing for a while and they catch up: that's **eventual consistency**, and asynchronous relational databases behave this way too. But *eventually* sets no limit. The delay, the **replication lag**, is usually under a second; under heavy load or network trouble it can stretch to seconds or minutes.

cards.prompt: What does eventual consistency promise about followers, and what does it leave open?
keyPoints: If writes stop for a while, the followers catch up and match the leader
Nothing limits how far behind a follower can fall in the meantime
Lag is usually under a second, but under heavy load or network trouble it can reach seconds or minutes
cards.explanation: Asynchronously replicated relational databases behave this way too; it isn't only a NoSQL property.

cards.title: Reading your own writes
cards.body:
You post a review, reload the page, and it's missing: the reload hit a follower that hadn't got it yet. It looks lost. **Read-your-writes** consistency, also called read-after-write, rules this out: you always see your own updates, though others' may still lag.

One way: read whatever the user might have changed from the leader, and the rest from followers. That works when it's easy to tell, like a profile only its owner edits. If users can edit almost anything, nearly every read would hit the leader. Use time instead: for a minute after a user's last write, send all their reads to the leader. Or skip any follower over a minute behind.

cards.prompt: On a team task board, any member can edit almost any item. Users must always see their own edits, but most reads should stay on followers. Which approach fits?
choices: Send reads of a user's own profile to the leader, and all other reads to followers
Pin each user to one follower, picked by hashing their user ID
For a minute after a user's last write, send that user's reads to the leader
Have the client resolve stale reads with last write wins
cards.explanation: Tracking each user's last write and using the leader only briefly afterwards keeps most reads on followers. Reading owner-only data from the leader works for profiles, but here almost everything is editable by anyone. A fixed follower stops time going backward but may still lack the write. Last write wins settles conflicts; it can't make a stale replica fresh.

cards.title: Tracking the last write
cards.body:
A client can also remember when it last wrote. Any replica serving that user's reads must have applied writes up to that point; if it hasn't, another replica answers, or the read waits. The mark can be a **logical timestamp**, such as a position in the replication log, which avoids relying on clocks being in sync.

Several devices complicate this. Your laptop doesn't know what your phone just wrote, so the last-write marks have to be stored centrally. And the two may reach the service over different networks and land in different regions. If some reads must come from the leader, first make sure every device of that user reaches one region.

cards.prompt: How can a client's last-write timestamp give read-your-writes, and what gets harder when the user has several devices?
keyPoints: The replica serving the user's reads must have applied writes up to that timestamp; otherwise another replica is used, or the read waits
A logical timestamp, like a log position, avoids relying on synchronized clocks
One device can't see the other's timestamp, so it must be stored centrally
Devices may reach different regions, so reads that need the leader may first need routing to one region
cards.explanation: Read-your-writes promises nothing about other users' updates, only the user's own.

cards.title: Monotonic reads
cards.body:
Picture refreshing a scoreboard twice. The first request hits a follower that's nearly current and shows a new goal. The second hits one that's further behind, and the goal is gone. Time seems to run backward.

**Monotonic reads** rule that out. They're weaker than strong consistency but stronger than eventual consistency: you may see old data, but once you've seen newer data, you never see older data again. One way is to send each user's reads to the same replica every time, chosen for example by hashing their user ID rather than at random. If that replica fails, the user is moved to another.

cards.prompt: A shopper sees a new listing, refreshes, and it's gone; each request went to a random follower. Which change prevents this?
choices: Always route the shopper's reads to one replica, chosen by hashing their user ID
Send the shopper's reads to the leader for a minute after they last wrote something
Store each seller's listings together on one shard so they replicate in order
cards.explanation: This breaks monotonic reads: the second read hit a follower further behind. Sticking to one replica means you never step back in time, though you must reroute if it fails. The shopper wrote nothing, so read-your-writes rules don't apply. Same-shard placement fixes causally related writes appearing out of order, a different anomaly.

cards.title: Consistent prefix reads
cards.body:
Lag can also scramble cause and effect. Maya posts a recipe, and Leo replies 'Made it, delicious!' If his reply sits on a shard that replicates faster than the one holding her post, you may see praise for a recipe that isn't there yet.

**Consistent prefix reads** promise that writes made in some order are seen in that order. A database that applies all writes in one sequence gets this for free. Sharded databases often don't: each shard replicates on its own, with no global order, so you can see one shard's newer state beside another's older one. One fix is to write causally related data to the same shard, though that isn't always efficient.

cards.prompt: In a sharded shop database, 'order placed' goes to one shard and 'order shipped' to another. A dashboard shows the shipment before the order exists. Which fix addresses this?
choices: Send each dashboard user's reads to the same replica every time
Write causally related events like these to the same shard
Read from the leader for a minute after the user's own writes
cards.explanation: This breaks consistent prefix reads. Shards replicate independently, with no global order, so a reader can see one shard's newer state beside another's older one. Keeping causally linked writes on one shard keeps them in order, though that isn't always efficient. Sticking to one replica or reading your own writes doesn't order writes across shards.

cards.title: When lag matters
cards.body:
Ask how your app behaves if lag grows to minutes or hours. If that's fine, good. If not, you need a stronger guarantee, and pretending asynchronous replication is synchronous will bite later.

You can work around lag in application code, as with the tricks above, but that's tricky and error-prone. The simplest choice is a database with strong consistency, called **linearizability**, and ACID transactions: then you can mostly treat it as a single node. NoSQL once claimed that couldn't scale; newer distributed databases now offer both. Weaker replication still has its place: it copes better with network interruptions and has less overhead than a transactional system.

cards.prompt: Why is a strongly consistent database often the simplest answer to replication lag, and why might an app pick weaker guarantees anyway?
keyPoints: With linearizability and ACID transactions, the app can mostly treat the database as one node
Working around lag in app code is tricky and error-prone
Weaker replication copes better with network interruptions
It also costs less overhead than a transactional system
cards.explanation: Either way, ask how the app behaves if lag stretches to minutes or hours; pretending asynchronous replication is synchronous causes trouble later.

cards.title: A leader in each region
cards.body:
**Multi-leader** replication lets several nodes accept writes and pass changes to each other. It rarely pays off inside one region, a cluster of nearby datacenters, but across regions you can run a leader in each.

Compare one leader for all regions. Every write travels to its region; per-region leaders take writes locally and copy them later. If its region fails, a follower elsewhere must be promoted; per-region leaders carry on. If the link between regions falters, remote writes wait on it; local leaders don't.

Consistency suffers. A single leader can give strong guarantees and enforce rules like 'at most three books on loan'. Separate leaders can each accept a loan that's fine alone but breaks the rule with another.

cards.prompt: With replicas in several regions, compare single-leader and multi-leader on write latency, a regional outage, an unreliable link between regions, and consistency.
keyPoints: Latency: single-leader sends every write to the leader's region; multi-leader handles it locally and replicates later
Regional outage: single-leader fails over to a follower elsewhere; multi-leader regions keep running on their own
Unreliable link: single-leader writes from other regions must wait on it; multi-leader leaders carry on independently
Consistency: single-leader can give strong guarantees; multi-leader can't enforce constraints like uniqueness across leaders
cards.explanation: Within a single region, multi-leader rarely justifies its added complexity.

cards.prompt: A concert ticketing site runs a leader in each of three regions, with asynchronous replication between them. Which guarantee can't it give?
choices: That buyers in every region get fast, local writes
That sales keep going when the link between two regions drops
That every region eventually receives the other regions' sales
That no seat is ever sold twice
cards.explanation: Two leaders can each sell the same seat; each sale is fine alone, and the clash only appears when the two are combined. Constraints like this need a single leader. Local writes, surviving a broken link and eventually passing every sale to every region are exactly what multi-leader replication offers.

cards.title: Replication topologies
cards.body:
With more than two leaders, you choose how writes travel. In **all-to-all**, every leader sends to every other. In a **circle**, each forwards to the next; in a **star**, one root forwards to the rest. In those two, a write passes through several nodes, tagged with each one's ID so none handles it twice. But one failed node can cut others off until someone reroutes.

All-to-all avoids that, but some links are faster, so a write can overtake one it depends on: a node may see an edit to a row before the row exists. Timestamps can't fix the order, since clocks aren't reliably in sync. **Version vectors** can, yet many systems lack them.

cards.prompt: In an all-to-all multi-leader setup, a user creates a playlist on leader 1, and a friend then adds a song to it on leader 3. Leader 2 gets the song first. Why won't wall-clock timestamps reliably fix the order?
choices: Clocks on different nodes aren't in sync closely enough to order the two writes
The two writes are concurrent, so there's no true order to recover
Inserts always replicate faster, so leader 2 would get the playlist first anyway
cards.explanation: The song depends on the playlist, so every node must apply the creation first, but skewed clocks can stamp the dependent write earlier; version vectors capture the dependency instead. The writes aren't concurrent, since the friend saw the playlist. Links differ in speed, which is how one message overtakes another. Circular and star topologies have their own weakness: one failed node can cut off the rest.

cards.title: Every device a leader
cards.body:
A workout log on your phone and laptop must work offline. So each device keeps a replica that accepts writes and syncs when it can: multi-leader replication where every device is a region and lag can last days. Live collaborative editors work the same way even without offline support: each open tab applies your edits at once and sends them out in the background.

A library that captures, syncs and merges these changes is a **sync engine**. An app that lets you keep editing offline is **offline-first**. It's also **local-first** if it would keep working even if its maker shut down every server, for example by syncing over an open protocol that several providers offer.

cards.prompt: A shared whiteboard app doesn't work offline, but each open browser tab shows a user's strokes at once and sends them to others in the background. Why is this multi-leader replication?
choices: It isn't: without offline editing, the server is the only leader
The server keeps several replicas of each board in different zones
Each user's strokes are stored on a different shard of the database
Each tab is a replica that takes writes without waiting for the server
cards.explanation: Applying edits locally and replicating them later means many replicas accept writes at once; offline support would only make the lag longer. How the server stores boards, replicated across zones or sharded, isn't what makes it multi-leader.

cards.prompt: A notes app keeps a full copy on each device, works offline, and syncs only through its vendor's closed server. How should it be classified?
choices: Local-first, since all of the data lives on the user's own devices
Offline-first, but not local-first: it depends on the vendor's servers
Plain client-server, not multi-leader, since all sync goes through one server
cards.explanation: Offline-first means you can keep editing while disconnected. Local-first also requires the app to keep working if its developer shuts down every online service, for example through an open sync protocol with several providers. Data on the device isn't enough by itself. A central sync server doesn't change the fact that every device accepts writes.

cards.title: Sync engines
cards.body:
Most web apps keep little on the client and call a server for each read and write. With a sync engine, the data lives on the device and syncing runs in the background. The UI reacts at once, since it reads and writes local data. Offline needs no special mode: it's just a very long network delay. Local reads and writes almost never fail, so there's far less error handling than with service calls. And with a reactive UI, showing others' edits live is easy.

The catch: everything the user may need is downloaded ahead of time. That suits a user's own files, not a streaming service's whole music library.

cards.prompt: What does a sync engine give a frontend app, and when is it a poor fit?
keyPoints: The UI responds instantly, since it reads and writes local data
Offline use needs no separate mode; it's just a very long network delay
Local reads and writes almost never fail, so there's much less error handling than with service calls
All the data the user may need must be downloaded first, so it suits a user's own data, not a huge shared catalog
cards.explanation: Combined with a reactive UI, it also makes showing other people's edits in real time straightforward.

cards.title: Concurrent writes
cards.body:
Two family members rename a shared shopping list on different devices, one to 'Weekly', the other to 'Party'. Each device accepts its own change. When they sync, the replicas disagree: a **write conflict**. A single leader never faces this, but any multi-leader system can.

Two writes are **concurrent** when neither writer knew about the other's write. It doesn't matter whether they happened at the same instant. What counts is whether one write was made with the other already in effect. Writes far apart in time are still concurrent if the second writer hadn't yet seen the first.

cards.prompt: Two rangers edit the same trail description while offline, one in the morning and the other that evening. Their devices sync the next day. Are the edits concurrent?
choices: No: they were hours apart, so the evening edit is simply the newer one
Only if the two devices' clocks disagree about which edit came first
Yes: neither ranger knew about the other's edit when making their own
No: edits only count as concurrent if they reach the server together
cards.explanation: Concurrency is about awareness, not timing: two writes are concurrent if neither was made with the other already in effect. Hours apart and offline, they still conflict. Clocks can't settle what each writer knew, and arrival time at the server is irrelevant.

cards.title: Avoiding conflicts
cards.body:
The easiest conflict is one that never happens. If every write to a given record goes through the same leader, that record can't conflict, even in a multi-leader system. Say users only edit their own data: give each user a home region and always use its leader. For that user, it's effectively single-leader. Offline devices can't do this, but servers sometimes can.

It fails once a record's leader has to change, say because a region is down or a user has moved. Writes made during the switch can reach two leaders and conflict. A similar trick works for new IDs: one leader hands out only odd numbers, the other only even ones.

cards.prompt: A multi-leader app avoids conflicts by sending each user's writes to the leader in their home region. When does this break down?
choices: When users read data that belongs to other users
When a user's home region changes while they're still writing
When there are more than two regions, each one with its own leader
When replication between the regions is asynchronous
cards.explanation: With one home region per user, each user effectively has a single leader. Moving a user after a region outage or a relocation opens a window where writes reach two leaders. Reads don't conflict, the number of regions doesn't matter, and asynchronous replication is the normal case the scheme is built for.

cards.title: Last write wins
cards.body:
The simplest fix for a conflict: stamp each write with a time, keep the highest, and silently drop the rest, though each was acknowledged. That's **last write wins (LWW)**. Replicas converge, but data is lost.

The name misleads. Among concurrent writes none is truly last, so the winner is effectively random. LWW is safe when lost updates don't matter, say when each record is inserted once under a unique key and never changed.

Wall-clock timestamps add a trap. If a node's clock runs fast, a write you make later can carry a lower timestamp than the value it replaces, and lose. A logical clock fixes that, but not the data loss.

cards.prompt: What does last write wins really do with concurrent writes, when is it safe, and what goes wrong with wall-clock timestamps?
keyPoints: It keeps the write with the highest timestamp and silently drops the rest, though each was acknowledged
For concurrent writes no write is truly last, so the winner is effectively random
It's safe when lost updates don't matter, e.g. records inserted once under unique keys and never changed
A node with a fast clock can make a later write lose, because the later one carries a lower timestamp
cards.explanation: A logical clock removes the clock problem but not the data loss.

cards.title: Keeping siblings
cards.body:
Instead of picking a winner, a database can keep all concurrent values, called **siblings**. A read returns them all; your code or the user merges them and writes the result back, like a merge conflict in version control.

It has costs. A field that held one value now holds a set, usually of one, which is clumsy in code. Asking users to merge needs a screen for it, and they may not get the question. Naive automatic merges surprise: a set union keeps any item in any sibling, so a guest removed from one copy of a party list returns. And nodes resolving one conflict at once can conflict again, or merge in different orders.

cards.prompt: Instead of picking a winner, a database can keep all concurrent values as siblings for the app to resolve. What problems does this bring?
keyPoints: Each value becomes a set that usually has one item, which is awkward for app code
Asking users to merge means building a resolution UI, and users may not understand what they're asked
Naive automatic merges can surprise: a set union brings deleted items back
Nodes resolving the same conflict at once can create a new conflict, or merge in different orders

cards.prompt: A packing-list app keeps siblings and merges them by set union. Offline, you remove 'tent' on your phone and 'stove' on your laptop. What happens to those items after syncing?
choices: Both 'tent' and 'stove' are back on the list
Neither item, since both removals are kept
Just one of the removals, picked by timestamp
Nothing yet: sync halts until you choose a version
cards.explanation: Each sibling still contains the item the other device removed, so the union brings both back. A merge that records deletions, as CRDTs do, would remove both. Picking one by timestamp is last write wins, a different strategy. Siblings exist precisely so replication never halts waiting for a person.

cards.title: Merging automatically
cards.body:
For many apps the best answer is an algorithm that merges concurrent writes on its own. Replicas that have seen the same writes then hold the same state, whatever order the writes came in: **strong eventual consistency**.

A good merge keeps every write's intent. For text, keep each side's insertions and deletions. For a list or set, track deletions too, so removed items stay removed. For a counter, add up each side's increments and decrements, so nothing is counted twice or dropped. Some rules can't survive: if a team may have at most ten members and two admins concurrently add people past that cap, the only fix is removing some.

cards.prompt: A museum's visitor counter shows 40 on two replicas. While they're cut off from each other, one records 3 new visitors and the other records 2. Which merge gives every replica the right total once they reconnect?
choices: Keep the count from whichever replica wrote last, by timestamp
Keep the larger of the two counts, giving 43
Add up the increments each replica made since 40, giving 45
Add the two replicas' counts together, giving 85
cards.explanation: A counter merge tracks how much each replica added and sums those changes, so every replica that has seen both reaches 45, with no visitor lost or counted twice. Last write wins keeps one side's count and drops the other's visitors. The larger count also drops 2. Adding the raw counts counts the starting 40 twice.

cards.title: OT and CRDTs
cards.body:
Two families of algorithms do these merges. **Operational transformation (OT)** records each edit by position. Say two replicas hold 'cat'. One inserts 'r' at index 2, giving 'cart'; the other inserts 's' at index 3, giving 'cats'. Applied unchanged, the 's' would land inside 'cart'. So OT adjusts each incoming edit for concurrent edits already applied: the 'r' went in earlier in the text, so the 's' moves to index 4, giving 'carts'.

Most **CRDTs** (conflict-free replicated datatypes) need no shifting. Each character gets a permanent unique ID, and an insert names the ID it goes after; ties are broken by comparing IDs. OT is common in collaborative text editors, CRDTs in some databases, and sync engines use both.

cards.prompt: Two replicas start with the text 'pin'. One inserts 's' at index 0, making 'spin'; the other inserts 'e' at index 3, making 'pine'. With operational transformation, where does the first replica put the 'e'?
choices: At index 3, as the operation says, giving 'spien'
After the character whose unique ID the operation names, with no index at all
Nowhere: the two inserts clash, and one of them is dropped
At index 4, shifted past the earlier insertion, giving 'spine'
cards.explanation: OT adjusts the index of each incoming operation for concurrent ones already applied: the 's' at the front pushes everything one place right. Using index 3 unchanged garbles the text. Referring to character IDs is how most CRDTs avoid transforming at all. Both inserts are kept; nothing is dropped.

cards.title: Conflicts across records
cards.body:
Some conflicts are obvious: two writes set the same field of the same record to different values. Others hide across records.

Take a gym where members book rowing machines by the hour, one row per booking. Two members on different leaders each check that machine 4 is free at 7am, see no booking, and insert one. Neither insert touches an existing record, so nothing collides at the record level; the clash only shows when you look at both bookings together. Checking first didn't help, since neither booking had replicated when the other was checked. There's no quick fix, and later chapters return to it.

cards.prompt: A clinic's booking system adds one record per appointment, and a vet can see only one patient per slot. On two leaders, receptionists book the same vet and slot seconds apart, each after checking it was free. Why is this conflict harder to catch than two edits to one field?
choices: The writes aren't concurrent, since each receptionist checked the slot first
They insert two different records, so no single record shows the clash
It isn't harder: the second insert fails with a duplicate-key error
Last write wins merges the two records into a single booking
cards.explanation: The rule spans records, so neither insert collides with an existing value; the clash only shows when bookings are viewed together. Each check saw the slot free because the other booking hadn't replicated yet, which is what makes them concurrent. Each leader checks only its own data, so nothing rejects the second booking, and last write wins only applies to writes on the same key.

cards.title: Leaderless replication
cards.body:
In **leaderless** replication, any replica accepts writes. The client, or a coordinator acting for it, sends each write to all replicas at once; it's done when enough confirm. A replica that was down misses it, so reads go to several replicas too, and the value with the highest version number wins.

A stale replica catches up three ways. With **read repair**, a client that got an old version writes the newer one back, so only data that's read gets fixed. With **hinted handoff**, another replica holds the missed writes as hints and passes them on when the node returns. And **anti-entropy** compares replicas in the background and copies what's missing, in no set order, often late.

cards.prompt: After a node misses writes, how do read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy each bring it up to date?
keyPoints: Read repair: a client reading several replicas writes the newer value back to a stale one, so it only fixes data that's read
Hinted handoff: another replica keeps the missed writes as hints and passes them on when the node returns
Anti-entropy: a background process compares replicas and copies missing data, in no set order and often with a delay

cards.title: Quorums
cards.body:
Say each key lives on n replicas. A write succeeds once w confirm it, and a read waits for r replies. If **w + r > n**, the replicas written and those read must share at least one, so a read sees the latest successful write. These are **quorum** reads and writes. Majorities, like 3 of 5 for both, are common, but any overlapping pair works.

Requests still go to all n replicas at once; w and r only set how many replies to wait for. Too few reachable, and the operation fails. With w + r no more than n you wait for fewer: faster and more tolerant of outages, but reads may miss the newest value.

cards.prompt: Order how a client reads a key in a leaderless database with read repair.
items: Send the read to all n replicas at once
Wait until r of them have answered
Take the value with the highest version number
Write that value back to any replica that returned an older one
cards.explanation: The highest version wins even if only one replica returned it. Read repair works best for values that are read often.

cards.prompt: A leaderless store keeps n = 5 replicas of each key. Which setting ensures every read overlaps the latest successful write?
cards.explanation: Overlap needs w + r > n, here at least 6, so the 2 nodes written and the 4 read must share one. Neither count has to be a majority. The other options add up to 5 or less, so a read can miss every node holding the new value.

cards.prompt: Why might you choose w and r so that w + r is no more than n?
choices: Requests are then sent to fewer replicas, which cuts network traffic and load
Lower latency and higher availability, at the cost of more stale reads
Reads stay fresh anyway, as long as w and r are both majorities
Concurrent writes to the same key can then no longer conflict
cards.explanation: Waiting for fewer replies is faster, and the system keeps working until fewer than w or r replicas are reachable, but a read may miss the node with the latest value. Requests still go to all n replicas; w and r only set how many replies to wait for. Two majorities would add up to more than n. Conflicts are unaffected.

cards.title: Where quorums fall short
cards.body:
Even with w + r > n, a read can be stale. If a node holding a new value fails and is restored from a replica with an old one, fewer than w nodes may hold it. While data moves between nodes, they can disagree on which n replicas own a key, so read and write sets stop overlapping. A write that reached fewer than w replicas is reported as failed but isn't undone where it landed, so later reads may return it. And with wall-clock last write wins, a node with a fast clock can make a newer write vanish.

Reads racing a write add surprises too. Treat w and r as odds, not guarantees.

cards.prompt: Even with w + r > n, how can a quorum read return a stale value or one from a failed write?
keyPoints: A node holding the new value fails and is restored from a stale replica, so fewer than w nodes have it
During rebalancing, nodes can disagree on which n replicas hold a key, so quorums stop overlapping
A write that reached fewer than w replicas is reported as failed but not undone, so later reads may see it
With wall-clock LWW, a write can be silently dropped if a node with a faster clock wrote the same key
cards.explanation: Concurrent reads and writes add more surprises; treat w and r as tuning the odds of staleness, not as guarantees.

cards.title: Measuring lag
cards.body:
Even if your app tolerates stale reads, you should watch how far replication is behind, and get an alert when it slips, since that points to a network problem or an overloaded node.

With a leader, that's easy. Every node applies writes in the same order, so each one's progress is a log position, and a follower's lag is the leader's position minus its own. Leaderless replicas apply writes in no fixed order, so there's no single position to compare. The number of hints waiting for handoff is one signal, but it's hard to read. Eventual consistency is vague by design, yet operations still need a number for *eventually*.

cards.prompt: Why is replication lag easy to measure with a leader but hard in a leaderless system?
keyPoints: With a leader, every node applies writes in the same order, so each has a position in the log
A follower's lag is the leader's position minus its own
Leaderless replicas apply writes in no fixed order, so there's no single position to compare
cards.explanation: The number of stored hints is one signal, but it's hard to interpret; even when stale reads are tolerable, you need to know how long 'eventually' really is.

cards.title: Leaderless under pressure
cards.body:
A leader-based system is only as quick as its leader: if it slows, every user feels it, and failover means waiting. Leaderless systems shrug this off. Requests already go to several replicas, so the client takes the quickest replies: **request hedging**. A node that's slow but not dead barely matters, and there's no failover to get wrong.

They have weak spots too. Hinted handoff adds load when nodes are already strained. Bigger quorums mean more replies to wait on, so a slow node more likely holds you up. And if a network break leaves too few of a key's replicas reachable, a **sloppy quorum** lets any reachable node take the write: it won't fail, but later reads may miss it.

cards.prompt: One node's disk becomes very slow, but the node never crashes. Why does this hurt a leaderless database less than a single-leader one whose leader is that node?
choices: It detects slow disks sooner, so it fails over faster than a leader-based one
It waits for every replica, so one slow node barely moves the average
Requests already go to several replicas, so the quicker replies win
It keeps all its data in memory, so disk speed doesn't affect requests
cards.explanation: A leaderless system handles normal and degraded operation the same way: it sends requests in parallel and uses the fastest answers, which is called request hedging. A leader-based one must decide whether the slowness warrants a failover, which can itself cause trouble. Leaderless systems have no failover, and they wait for only w or r replies, not all.

cards.prompt: A network break leaves a client able to reach only nodes that aren't among a key's usual replicas. With a sloppy quorum enabled, what happens to its write?
choices: Reachable nodes accept it, and later quorum reads are sure to see it
It's rejected, since no quorum of the key's usual replicas is reachable
It waits on the client until the key's usual replicas are reachable again
Reachable nodes accept it, but later reads may not see it
cards.explanation: A sloppy quorum lets any reachable node take the write so it doesn't fail, but those nodes aren't the ones a normal read asks, so nothing guarantees the value is seen. Rejection is what a strict quorum would do. The client doesn't hold on to the write; the nodes do.

cards.title: Leaderless across regions
cards.body:
Leaderless replication also suits several regions, since it already expects concurrent writes, network breaks and latency spikes. In one design, a client writes to a coordinator in its own region, which sends the write to every local replica and to one replica in each other region to pass on there. The long hop happens once per region.

You then pick how many replies count. A quorum across all regions, or one in each, reads fresher but waits on distant replicas. A quorum in your own region only is fast, but reads may miss writes for a while. Other databases keep each cluster in one region and sync between them in the background, like multi-leader.

cards.prompt: A leaderless database spans three regions. A client asks for a quorum only among the replicas in its own region. What's the trade-off?
choices: No waiting on slow replies from other regions, but more stale reads
Writes then never leave the client's region, so losing that region loses them
Reads become fully up to date, but every write gets slower
It's faster with no downside, since other regions catch up instantly
cards.explanation: The write is still sent to every region, but success waits only on local replicas. That saves the cross-region round-trip, yet a read elsewhere may not see the write yet. A quorum across all regions, or one in each region, is slower but fresher. Remote replicas get the write eventually, not instantly.

cards.title: Happens-before
cards.body:
How can a database tell an overwrite from a conflict? Through the **happens-before** relation. Operation A happens before B if B knew about A, depended on it or built on it. Say you open a document and then save an edit: your save happened after the version you opened.

If neither of two operations happens before the other, they're **concurrent**. So any two writes are in one of three cases: A before B, B before A, or concurrent. A later write simply replaces an earlier one; concurrent writes are a conflict to resolve. Clock time doesn't decide it: writes far apart are concurrent if, say, the network kept each writer from learning of the other.

cards.prompt: Client A writes a key; client B reads A's value and then writes a change based on it. Client C writes the same key without reading anything first. Which is right?
choices: B happened after A, and C is concurrent with both
All three are concurrent, since they come from different clients
Their order is whatever their timestamps say it is
C happened after both, since a write with no prior read overwrites all
cards.explanation: B built on A's value, so A happened before B. C knew about neither, so it's concurrent with both, whatever the clock says. Separate clients aren't automatically concurrent; what counts is whether one knew of the other, which timestamps can't show. A write with no prior read overwrites nothing; it becomes a sibling.

cards.title: Version numbers
cards.body:
Here's how one server can track happens-before for a key. It keeps a version number per key, raising it on each write and storing it with the value. A read returns every value not yet overwritten, the siblings, plus the latest version. To write, a client must read first, then send the version it saw with a value that merges all the siblings it got.

The server drops every value at that version or below, since the client merged them, and keeps any with a higher version: those were written concurrently and stay as siblings. A write with no version is concurrent with everything and replaces nothing. The server never looks inside values.

cards.prompt: For one key, a server holds two siblings, at versions 5 and 7. A client writes a merged value, sending version 5 from its earlier read. What does the server keep?
choices: Only the new value, since each write replaces whatever was there
All three values, since a server never discards siblings
Only the version 7 value, since the write was based on old data
The new value and the version 7 sibling
cards.explanation: The write was based on version 5, so it replaces values at version 5 or below, which the client merged in. It knew nothing of version 7, so that value is concurrent and stays as a sibling. Superseded values are dropped, so siblings don't pile up forever, and a write isn't rejected just because newer values exist.

cards.title: Version vectors
cards.body:
With several replicas accepting writes at once, one counter per key can't capture who has seen what. So each replica keeps its own counter for each key, raising it on every write it handles, and also tracks the counters it has seen from other replicas. Together they form a **version vector**.

It's used like the single counter: the vector goes to the client with each read and comes back with the next write. That lets the database tell an overwrite from a concurrent write, even if you read from one replica and write to another; at worst you get siblings, and nothing is lost as long as they're merged correctly. It's sometimes called a vector clock, though the two differ.

cards.prompt: Why do leaderless databases need version vectors rather than one version number per key, and how are they used?
keyPoints: With several replicas accepting writes at once, one counter per key can't capture who saw what
Each replica keeps its own counter per key, plus the counters it has seen from the others
The vector goes to the client with each read and comes back with the next write
It lets the database tell an overwrite from a concurrent write, even when you read from one replica and write to another
cards.explanation: Version vectors are sometimes called vector clocks, but the two differ; version vectors are the right tool for comparing replica states.

cards.title: Shards and replicas
cards.body:
When one machine isn't enough, a database can spread its data over many in two ways. **Replication** keeps copies of the same data on several nodes. **Sharding** cuts the data into pieces called **shards** (many systems say *partitions*) and puts different pieces on different nodes. Every record lives in one shard and only one, so a shard behaves like a small database of its own.

The two usually go together: every shard is replicated to a few nodes for fault tolerance. With single-leader replication, the leader is chosen per shard, so one node can lead some of the shards it stores and follow for the rest, while each shard still has a single leader.

cards.prompt: A database is sharded, and each shard is replicated with a single leader. What role does a typical node play?
choices: It's the leader for every shard it stores, since sharding removes the need for followers
It leads some of its shards and follows others, while each shard has exactly one leader
It's either a leader for all of its shards or a follower for all of them
It stores a piece of every shard, so each record is spread over several nodes
cards.explanation: Leadership is assigned per shard, so one node can lead some shards and follow others; nothing ties it to one role for all of them. Sharding and replication work together: every record lives in a single shard, and that whole shard is copied to several nodes for fault tolerance rather than cut up further.

cards.title: When to shard
cards.body:
Sharding exists for **scalability**. It's one of the main ways to **scale out**: rather than buying a bigger machine, you add more machines, and each one works on its fair share of the shards in parallel.

But check what has actually outgrown one node. If the dataset no longer fits, or one node can't keep up with the writes, sharding helps. If only *reads* are the problem, you may not need it: followers that each hold a full copy can share the reads between them.

Replication is worth having at any scale, if only for fault tolerance. Sharding is a heavy tool that mostly earns its keep at large scale.

cards.prompt: A recipe site's database fits on one machine and handles its writes easily, but page views have grown tenfold and reads are slow. What's the most fitting fix?
choices: Shard the data, since sharding is the main tool for spreading any kind of load
Shard by a hash of the recipe ID, so reads land evenly on every node
Add read-only followers and spread reads across them, without sharding
cards.explanation: Sharding pays off when the data volume or the write throughput outgrows one node. When only reads are the bottleneck, replication is enough: each follower holds a full copy and takes a share of the reads. Sharding would add partition keys, cross-shard queries and distributed transactions to solve a problem replicas already handle.

cards.title: The cost of sharding
cards.body:
One machine can do a lot these days. If yours can hold the data and absorb the writes, it's usually wiser not to shard, because sharding brings complexity.

First you choose a **partition key**: records with the same key land in the same shard. A lookup that knows the key goes straight to one shard; one that doesn't has to search them all. And once chosen, the scheme is hard to change.

Key-value data shards easily. Relational data is harder, since secondary indexes and joins may need records that sit on different shards. And a write that updates records on several shards needs a **distributed transaction**, which is far slower than a local one and can become a bottleneck.

cards.prompt: Why is it often better not to shard when one machine can handle the data and the writes?
keyPoints: You must choose a partition key, and a query that can't use it has to search every shard
The sharding scheme is hard to change once it's in place
Secondary indexes and joins get harder when related records sit on different shards
A write that touches several shards needs a distributed transaction, which is slow and can become a bottleneck
cards.explanation: Replication is useful at any scale; sharding is a heavyweight tool that mostly pays off at large scale.

cards.title: Sharding by tenant
cards.body:
Many SaaS products are **multitenant**: each customer, or *tenant*, may have many users, but its data is kept apart from every other tenant's. Think of a project tracker where each company sees only its own boards.

Such products often shard by tenant, with a shard per tenant or small tenants packed together. That isolates tenants. A heavy report run by one tenant is less likely to slow tenants on other shards. An access-control bug is less likely to leak data between tenants stored apart. A **cell-based architecture** goes further, splitting services as well as storage into independent cells, so a fault in one cell spares the others. And one tenant can be restored from backup without touching the rest.

cards.prompt: A SaaS product gives each customer its own shard. How does that help with performance, security, outages and recovery?
keyPoints: Performance: one tenant's expensive work is less likely to slow down tenants on other shards
Security: an access-control bug is less likely to expose one tenant's data to another
Outages: in a cell-based design, where each cell has its own services and storage, a fault stays within one cell's tenants
Recovery: one tenant can be restored from backup without touching anyone else
cards.explanation: It also makes it simple to export or delete one person's data for privacy laws, and to keep a tenant's shard in the region its data must stay in.

cards.title: Privacy, residency and rollouts
cards.body:
Separate shards help with the law too. Privacy laws such as the GDPR let people ask for a copy of their data or for its deletion; if each person's data has its own shard, that's a simple export or delete of one shard. And if a tenant's data must stay in a certain country, a region-aware database can place that tenant's shard there.

Schema changes get safer as well. Instead of migrating every tenant at once, you migrate a few, watch for trouble, and carry on only if all goes well. The catch is that a change rolled out shard by shard is hard to make transactional.

cards.prompt: An invoicing SaaS keeps each customer in its own shard and needs to change its schema. Why might it migrate one tenant at a time?
choices: A faulty migration shows up on a few tenants before it reaches everyone
Tenant-by-tenant migration makes the change atomic across all customers
Migrating shards separately removes the need to take backups first
Databases can only apply a schema change to one shard at a time
cards.explanation: A gradual rollout limits the damage: problems surface on the first few tenants and can be fixed before the rest. The catch is that a staged rollout is hard to make transactional, so it's far from atomic. Backups are still wise, and nothing stops a database from changing many shards at once.

cards.title: Limits of tenant sharding
cards.body:
Sharding by tenant assumes each tenant fits on one node. If one customer outgrows a machine, you have to shard inside that tenant as well, and you're back to sharding for scale.

At the other end, a dedicated shard for each of thousands of tiny tenants wastes resources on overhead. Packing several small tenants into one shard fixes that, but then a tenant that grows has to be moved to another shard somehow.

And any feature that looks across tenants, such as a report comparing customers, now needs joins across shards.

cards.prompt: What makes sharding by tenant hard?
keyPoints: A tenant too big for one node must be sharded internally, which brings back sharding for scale
A shard per small tenant costs too much overhead, but grouping tenants means moving them as they grow
Features that combine data across tenants need joins across shards

cards.title: Skew and hot spots
cards.body:
Sharding aims to spread data and queries evenly. If every node gets a fair share, 5 nodes can in theory store 5 times the data and serve 5 times the reads and writes of one.

When some shards hold more data or get more requests than others, the sharding is **skewed**, and much of the gain is gone. A shard with far more than its share of load is a **hot spot**, the bottleneck while other nodes idle. At worst, nearly all traffic lands on one node and the rest add nothing. One key with unusual load is a **hot key**.

So the rule mapping partition keys to shards must spread load evenly, and allow rebalancing when it doesn't.

cards.prompt: What is skew in a sharded database, and why does it undermine sharding?
keyPoints: Some shards hold more data or get more queries than others
The busiest shard, a hot spot, becomes the bottleneck while other nodes sit underused
In the extreme, nearly all load lands on one node and the extra nodes add almost nothing
cards.explanation: With no skew, N nodes would give about N times the capacity of one. A single key with unusually high load is called a hot key.

cards.title: Sharding by key range
cards.body:
One way to shard is to give each shard a continuous **range of keys**, from some minimum to some maximum. Picture exam papers filed by student surname: one box holds names from Aa to Ch, the next from Ci to Fe, and so on. To find a paper, you pick the box whose range covers the name.

The ranges shouldn't be equal slices of the alphabet, though. Lots of surnames start with S and few with Q, so equal slices would leave some boxes overflowing and others nearly empty. To keep shards even, the boundaries have to follow the actual data. An administrator can set them by hand, or the database can choose them itself.

cards.prompt: A land registry shards parcels by postal code, giving each shard an equal-width block of codes. Some shards end up many times bigger than others. What's the fix?
choices: Use more, narrower equal-width blocks so the sizes even out
Add replicas to the biggest shards so that they can hold more parcels
Replace the numeric postal codes with alphabetic district names
Choose shard boundaries that follow where the parcels actually are
cards.explanation: Keys are rarely spread evenly over their range: dense cities use many codes, rural areas few. Range boundaries have to adapt to the data, whether an admin sets them or the database does. Narrower equal blocks stay just as lopsided, replicas copy a shard rather than shrink it, and district names would cluster too.

cards.title: Range scans and hot ranges
cards.body:
Inside a key-range shard, keys are kept in sorted order, for instance in a B-tree or in SSTables. That makes **range scans** cheap: all keys between two values sit next to each other, so a single scan fetches them.

The flip side is that writes to neighbouring keys all land in the same shard. Say a website logs every page view with its timestamp as the key. Each shard then covers a span of time, and every new view belongs to the latest span. That one shard takes all the writes, while the shards holding older data sit idle.

cards.prompt: A card-payments service shards transactions by key range, with the payment time as the key. Adding nodes hasn't raised its write throughput. Why?
choices: Key-range shards are tied to the node they were created on and can't move
Every new payment has a recent timestamp, so all writes hit one shard
Timestamps hash poorly, so the shards end up very unequal in size
Each insert has to rewrite its whole shard to keep keys sorted
cards.explanation: With time as the key, each shard covers a span of time, and all current writes fall into the newest one while the rest sit idle. Range shards can move between nodes, but that doesn't spread one range's writes. Key-range sharding involves no hashing, and sorted structures such as B-trees don't rewrite a shard per insert.

cards.title: Putting another field first
cards.body:
The usual cure for a hot time range is to put something else before the timestamp in the key. In the page view log, the key could be the page ID followed by the time. Keys now sort by page first and by time second, so as long as many pages get visits at once, new writes spread over many shards.
