Range scans still work for one page: its views over a week are still next to each other. What you lose is the cheap scan across everything. Views of *all* pages in the last hour now take a separate range query for every page.

cards.prompt: A payments table is range-sharded on a timestamp key. To spread writes, the key becomes merchant ID followed by timestamp. Which query gets more expensive?
choices: One merchant's payments for last month
One payment, looked up by its merchant ID and timestamp
Every merchant's payments from the last ten minutes
The latest payment made to one merchant
cards.explanation: Keys are now sorted by merchant first, so a time window across all merchants is scattered and needs a separate range query per merchant. One merchant's payments are still contiguous, so last month or the latest one is a single range scan. A full key still points to exactly one shard.

cards.title: Splitting key ranges
cards.body:
An empty database has no data to set range boundaries by. Some let you **pre-split** it anyway, which works only if you can predict how keys will spread.

From then on, shards follow the data. A shard that passes a size limit, or in some systems stays too busy with writes, is **split** into shards that each own a continuous slice of its range, and these can live on different nodes. After big deletions, small neighbouring shards can be **merged**, much like pages in a B-tree.

A split is costly: it rewrites all the shard's data, like a compaction. And the shard that needs one is often the busiest, so the extra work can tip it over.

cards.prompt: How does a key-range sharded database adjust its shards as data grows and shrinks?
keyPoints: A shard that passes a size limit, or in some systems takes too many writes, is split into contiguous subranges
The resulting shards can be spread over different nodes
After large deletions, small adjacent shards can be merged
An empty database can be pre-split, but only if you can guess how the keys will be distributed
cards.explanation: The shard count thus follows the data volume, much like pages splitting and merging in a B-tree.

cards.prompt: A key-range shard is overloaded with writes, so the database splits it. Why can the split make things worse for a while?
choices: Splitting rewrites all the shard's data, adding work to an overloaded shard
During a split, the whole cluster stops accepting any writes until it's done
The two halves lose their sort order until a compaction rebuilds it
A split shard must stay on its original node, so the load can't move
cards.explanation: A split is costly, much like compaction in a log-structured engine: every record is rewritten. The shard that needs it is usually the busiest, so the extra work lands where there's least room for it. Other shards keep working, each half keeps its keys sorted, and moving halves to other nodes is the whole point.

cards.title: Sharding by hash
cards.body:
If you don't need neighbouring keys to stay together, as with user IDs, you can **hash** the partition key first and map the hash to a shard.

A good hash turns lopsided input into evenly spread output: even keys that differ by one character get hashes far apart. It must also be **deterministic**: a key always gets the same hash, on every machine and in every process, or a read could look in a different shard than the write used. It doesn't need to be cryptographic. But take care with the hash functions built into programming languages: some give the same key a different hash in each process, which makes them useless for sharding.

cards.prompt: A team maps keys to shards with their language's built-in string hash, which is seeded randomly in each process. What goes wrong?
choices: It isn't cryptographically strong, so keys spread unevenly across shards
Similar keys get similar hashes, so neighbouring keys crowd onto one shard
Built-in hashes are too slow to run on every single request
The same key can map to different shards in different processes
cards.explanation: Every process must send a given key to the same shard, so the hash has to give the same output for the same input everywhere. A per-process seed breaks that, and reads can miss earlier writes. Sharding doesn't need cryptographic strength, even simple hashes scatter similar inputs, and speed isn't the problem.

cards.title: The trouble with mod N
cards.body:
Once a key is hashed, the obvious way to pick its node is the remainder after dividing by the number of nodes N: `hash(key) % N`.

It breaks down when N changes. A key stays where it is only if its hash leaves the same remainder for the old N and for the new one, and most hashes don't. Going from 4 nodes to 5, a key keeps its node only when its hash mod 20 is 0, 1, 2 or 3: that's 4 hashes in every 20, so about 80% of the data moves. Ideally only a fifth would move, just enough to fill the new node.

cards.prompt: Keys are placed on nodes by hash(key) mod N. The cluster grows from 3 nodes to 4. Roughly what share of the keys has to move?
choices: About 25%
About 50%
About 75%
All of them
cards.explanation: A key stays put only when its hash mod 3 equals its hash mod 4, which holds for 3 out of every 12 hash values, so about 75% move. Ideally only a quarter would move, just enough to fill the new node. Not every key moves, because a few keep the same remainder.

cards.title: A fixed number of shards
cards.body:
A popular fix is to create far more shards than nodes from day one, and give each node many of them. Say a cluster of 8 nodes starts with 400 shards, 50 per node. A key goes to shard `hash(key) % 400`, and the system separately tracks which node holds which shard.

When a node joins, it takes over some whole shards from the others until all have a fair share again; when one leaves, its shards are handed out. Keys never change shard and the count stays put: only the mapping of shards to nodes changes. The move takes time, so reads and writes keep using the old mapping until the copy is done.

cards.prompt: A database has 10 nodes and 1,000 shards; a key's shard is hash(key) mod 1,000. What changes when an 11th node joins?
choices: Only which nodes hold some shards; every key stays in its shard
Keys are rehashed modulo 11, so most of them move
Every shard is split, and the new node gets a piece of each
The shard count grows to 1,100 so that each node keeps 100 shards
cards.explanation: The key-to-shard mapping never changes; the new node takes over some whole shards from the others, which is cheaper than splitting them. Rehashing by node count is exactly the mod N problem this scheme avoids. The shard count stays at 1,000, so each node ends up with about 91.

cards.title: Choosing the shard count
cards.body:
With a fixed count, pick a number with many divisors, so it splits evenly across many cluster sizes and not only powers of 2. You can also give stronger machines more shards, so they carry more of the load.

This works well if you can guess early how many shards you'll ever need. You can never have more nodes than shards, and changing the count means **resharding**: splitting and rewriting every shard, using lots of spare disk, and in some systems blocking writes meanwhile. Since each shard holds a fixed fraction of the data, shards grow with the dataset until moving them or recovering a node gets slow. Starting with many tiny shards instead costs overhead.

cards.prompt: What are the drawbacks of fixing the number of shards when a database is created?
keyPoints: You can never have more nodes than shards
Changing the count means resharding: splitting and rewriting every shard, sometimes with writes blocked
Each shard holds a fixed fraction of the data, so shards grow with the dataset and get slow to move or recover
Starting with many tiny shards to leave room for growth adds overhead
cards.explanation: It works well when you can estimate early on how many shards you'll ever need.

cards.prompt: A team choosing a fixed number of shards picks 720 rather than 512. What's the advantage?
choices: Hashes spread more evenly modulo a number that isn't a power of 2
It divides evenly among many cluster sizes, such as 5, 6, 9 or 10 nodes
More shards always perform better, whatever the size of the data
The cluster can then grow for years without ever moving a shard
cards.explanation: A count with many factors can be shared out equally among many node counts, not just powers of 2; you can also give more shards to more powerful machines. A good hash spreads evenly over either count. Shards that are too small add overhead, and adding nodes still means moving whole shards.

cards.title: Sharding by hash range
cards.body:
Key ranges let the shard count grow with the data, but neighbouring keys can create hot spots. **Hash-range sharding** combines both ideas: each shard owns a continuous range of *hash values* rather than of keys. With hashes from 0 to 999, one shard might own 0 to 249, the next 250 to 499, and so on. Even consecutive keys, like sequential order numbers, get scattered.

As with key ranges, a shard that gets too big or too busy can be split, so the count adapts to the data. The price: keys that were neighbours now sit on different shards, so a range query over the partition key has to ask every shard.

cards.prompt: Compared with key-range sharding, what does hash-range sharding give up?
choices: The ability to split a shard that grows too big or too busy
Protection against hot spots from writes to consecutive keys
A way to find a key's shard without asking every node
Efficient range queries over the partition key
cards.explanation: Hashing scatters neighbouring keys across all shards, so a range of partition keys means querying every shard. Hash ranges can still be split as they grow, so the shard count adapts. Hashing actually removes the hot spot that consecutive keys cause, and a key's hash still points to one shard.

cards.title: Partition key and sort key
cards.body:
You can still get some range queries by using a key made of two or more parts and hashing only the first. Say a fitness app stores workouts under (user ID, start time) and shards on the user ID alone. All of one user's workouts share a partition key, so they sit in one shard, sorted by start time, and any date range for that user is a single scan.

Data warehouses use the same idea under other names. A **partition key** decides which partition a record goes to, and **cluster columns** decide how records are sorted inside it. Clustering speeds up range scans, and it also helps compression and filtering.

cards.prompt: A messaging app stores messages under the key (conversation ID, sent time), with hash-range sharding on the conversation ID alone. Which query can one shard answer with a single range scan?
choices: All messages sent in any conversation during the last minute
All conversations whose IDs fall between 5,000 and 6,000
One conversation's messages from last Tuesday
The newest message in each of one user's conversations
cards.explanation: Records that share a partition key live in the same shard, sorted by the rest of the key, so a time range within one conversation is one scan. A time window across all conversations, or the latest message in many of them, touches many shards. A range of conversation IDs is scattered by the hash.

cards.prompt: In a data warehouse that supports partitioning and clustering, what does each control, and why cluster?
keyPoints: The partition key decides which partition a record lands in
Cluster columns decide the sort order of records inside a partition
Clustering speeds up range scans and also helps compression and filtering
cards.explanation: It's the same idea as a compound key in a sharded database: the first part picks the shard, the rest sets the order.

cards.title: Consistent hashing
cards.body:
Some databases cut the hash space into many ranges with **random** boundaries and give each node several. Random ranges come out unequal, but a node holding many of them ends up with roughly a fair total. A node that joins takes slices of a few ranges from the others, just enough for its share.

This is a form of **consistent hashing**: any scheme that gives each shard about the same number of keys and, when shards are added or removed, moves as few keys as it can. *Consistent* here means a key tends to stay put; it's unrelated to replica or ACID consistency. Some variants instead hand a new node single keys from all the others.

cards.prompt: Some databases cut the hash space into many ranges with random boundaries and give each node several of them. Why several per node?
choices: Random ranges vary in size, but with several per node the differences even out
Random boundaries guarantee that every range ends up the same size
Each key falls into several ranges, so it gets stored on several different nodes
Range queries over the partition key then stay within one node
cards.explanation: With random boundaries some ranges end up larger than others, but a node holding many of them gets roughly a fair total. When a node joins, it takes slices of a few existing ranges, so no more data moves than needed. Each key still falls in exactly one range; replication is separate, and hashing still scatters key ranges.

cards.prompt: What two properties define a consistent hashing algorithm, and what does 'consistent' mean here?
keyPoints: Each shard ends up with roughly the same number of keys
Adding or removing shards relocates as few keys as possible
'Consistent' means a key tends to stay in its shard; it's unrelated to replica consistency or ACID consistency
cards.explanation: In some variants, such as rendezvous and jump consistent hashing, a new node takes single keys from across all the other nodes instead of slices of a few ranges.

cards.title: Hot keys
cards.body:
Hashing spreads *keys* evenly, not *load*. If one key gets a flood of reads or writes, every one of those requests goes to the single shard that owns it, whatever hash you use and however many shards you have. Think of a sports app the moment a final ends: everyone opens the same match page, stored under one match ID.

Some schemes can at least isolate the problem. When shards are defined by ranges of keys or of hashes, a hot key can be given a shard of its own, even a dedicated machine, so it stops slowing down its neighbours. A few cloud databases detect and handle hot shards automatically.

cards.prompt: A crowdfunding site hashes campaign IDs to shards, so keys are spread evenly. When one campaign goes viral, its shard is swamped. Why didn't hashing prevent this?
choices: The hash function was too weak; a cryptographic hash would spread the campaign out
Hashing balances keys, but every request for that campaign still targets one key
There were too few shards; adding more would split the campaign's traffic
cards.explanation: Hashing spreads keys, but load comes per key: one hugely popular key sends all its traffic to whichever shard owns it. No hash function or shard count can split a single key. A range-based scheme can at least give that key a shard, or a machine, of its own; otherwise the application has to split it.

cards.prompt: A social app shards posts by ranges of hashed post ID. One post by a famous singer gets so much traffic that its shard slows down every other post stored there. What can the database do without changing the app?
choices: Rehash every key with a new function, so the post lands on a quieter shard
Add more shards, so that the post's requests are divided among them
Give that post's key a shard of its own, on a dedicated node if needed
Add followers to the shard, so that they can share the post's writes
cards.explanation: With range-based shards, over keys or hashes, one hot key can be carved into a shard by itself and even given its own machine, so its load stops hurting its neighbours. Rehashing only moves the hot key, and its load, to another shard. No number of shards can divide one key. Followers can share reads, but a single leader still takes every write.

cards.title: Splitting a hot key
cards.body:
When the database can't relieve a hot key, the application can. Add a random digit to the key on every write, and the writes for one hot key spread over 10 keys, which can sit on different shards.

Picture a view counter on a breaking news story: each view increments one of `story42:0` to `story42:9`.

Reads pay for it. To show the total, a reader must fetch all 10 keys and add them up. And each of those shards still sees every read of the counter, so the read load isn't reduced at all; only the writes are spread.

cards.prompt: A live-voting app stores each poll's tally under one key. During a TV show, one poll gets thousands of votes a second, so the team adds a random two-digit suffix to spread its writes over 100 keys. What does this cost?
choices: Every vote now needs a distributed transaction that spans all 100 keys at once
Reads get cheaper, but every single write now costs more
The poll's data has to be copied to every shard in the cluster
Reads must fetch and combine all 100 keys, and read load isn't reduced
cards.explanation: Only the writes are split: each vote lands on one of 100 keys at random. Getting the total means reading all 100 and adding them up, so reads do more work while each shard sees the same read traffic as before. No transaction or full copy is needed, and reads get dearer, not cheaper.

cards.title: Tracking split keys
cards.body:
Splitting keys this way takes bookkeeping. It only pays off for the handful of keys that are hot for writes; on every other key, the extra reads are pure overhead. So you need a record of which keys are split, and a process for turning an ordinary key into a split one.

Heat also moves around. A post that goes viral may be swamped for two days and then go quiet, so the set of hot keys keeps changing. And the trick only spreads *writes*: a key that's hot for reads needs a different remedy.

cards.prompt: What makes splitting hot keys with random suffixes hard to manage?
keyPoints: It's worth it only for the few write-hot keys; for the rest it just adds read work
You must track which keys are split, and have a process for converting a key
Keys heat up and cool down over time, so the set of hot keys keeps changing
It only spreads writes, so keys that are hot for reads need a different strategy

cards.title: Automatic rebalancing
cards.body:
Who decides when to split shards and move them between nodes? Some databases do it all by themselves, some leave it to an administrator, and some propose a new assignment that an admin has to approve.

Full automation saves routine operations work, and it lets a system **autoscale**, adding or removing shards within minutes as load rises and falls.

But rebalancing is expensive: it moves lots of data over the network and reroutes requests. Done carelessly, it can overload nodes or the network and slow down everything else. And the system must keep accepting writes meanwhile; near its write limit, splitting may never catch up with the incoming writes.

cards.prompt: What are the benefits and the risks of fully automatic rebalancing?
keyPoints: Benefit: less routine operational work, and the system can autoscale as load changes
Risk: moving lots of data and rerouting requests can overload nodes and the network, slowing other requests
Risk: when writes are already close to the system's limit, splitting shards may fall behind the incoming writes
cards.explanation: Some systems take a middle path: they propose a new shard assignment but wait for an administrator to approve it.

cards.title: A human in the loop
cards.body:
Automatic rebalancing turns dangerous when paired with automatic failure detection. Picture one node that's overloaded and answers slowly. The others decide it's dead and move its shards elsewhere. Copying that data loads up the remaining nodes and the network, so they slow down too, get declared dead in their turn, and the trouble spreads: a **cascading failure**.

So it can pay to keep a person in charge of rebalancing. It's slower, but it avoids surprises. It also lets you rebalance *before* a surge you can see coming, such as launch day for a new game console, rather than in the middle of it.

cards.prompt: A cluster combines automatic rebalancing with automatic failure detection. Order how this can turn into a cascading failure.
items: A node becomes overloaded and slow to respond
The other nodes conclude that it has failed
The cluster moves the slow node's shards to other nodes
The data transfer piles extra load onto those nodes and the network
More nodes slow down and are wrongly declared dead in turn
cards.explanation: Letting an operator approve each rebalancing is slower, but it prevents surprises like this.

cards.prompt: A streaming service expects a huge traffic spike on Friday night, when a hit series releases its final episode. What's the safest way to handle rebalancing?
choices: Rely on automatic rebalancing alone; it reacts within minutes at little cost
Wait for slow nodes to be detected as failed, so their load moves automatically
Switch to a different sharding scheme on the night to absorb the surge
Have an operator rebalance ahead of time, before the spike arrives
cards.explanation: Known events are where manual, preemptive rebalancing shines: shards move while the cluster is calm. Rebalancing during a surge is expensive and may not keep up with the writes. Relying on failure detection can trigger a cascade, and changing the sharding scheme is a major, risky job rather than a quick fix.

cards.title: Request routing
cards.body:
To read or write a key, a client must reach the right node. This **request routing** resembles service discovery, with one big difference: any instance of a stateless service can answer any request, but only a node holding a key's shard can serve that key. So routing must know which shard a key is in and which node has that shard.

There are three common setups. Clients contact any node, which serves the request if it holds the shard and otherwise forwards it and relays the reply. Or a **routing tier**, a shard-aware load balancer that serves nothing itself, forwards every request. Or clients know the assignment and connect straight to the right node.

cards.prompt: Request routing in a sharded database resembles service discovery for stateless services. What's the main difference?
choices: Any instance can serve a stateless request; a key's request needs a node holding its shard
Database routing needs only the key-to-shard mapping, not where each shard lives
Service discovery needs a coordination service, while database routing never does
A database request can go to any node, but a service request must reach its owner
cards.explanation: A load balancer can hand a stateless request to any instance, but a database request needs a node holding the right shard, so routing must know which shard holds a key and which node holds that shard. Coordination services are in fact common for tracking shard assignments. And it's stateless services, not databases, that accept requests anywhere.

cards.prompt: What are the three ways a request can reach the node that owns its key's shard?
keyPoints: Send it to any node, which handles it if it owns the shard and forwards it otherwise
Send it to a shard-aware routing tier that only forwards requests and handles none itself
Make the client aware of the shard assignment so it connects straight to the right node
cards.explanation: Clients still need IP addresses for the routing tier or the nodes; these change slowly, so DNS is usually enough.

cards.title: Who tracks the shards
cards.body:
Whichever setup you pick, some hard questions remain. Who decides which shard lives on which node? A single coordinator is simplest, but it has to survive its own node failing. And if the role can fail over, you must never end up with two coordinators handing out conflicting assignments, which is called **split brain**.

Next, the router, whether it's a node, a tier or the client, has to learn about every change in the assignment. And while a shard is being handed from one node to another, some requests are still on their way to the old node, and something has to deal with them.

cards.prompt: Whichever component does the routing, what problems does every request-routing scheme have to solve?
keyPoints: Deciding who assigns shards to nodes, and keeping that coordinator fault tolerant without two of them making conflicting assignments (split brain)
Telling the router when shard assignments change
Handling requests still in flight to the old node while a shard is being handed over
cards.explanation: Many systems delegate this to a consensus-based coordination service, such as ZooKeeper, which stays fault tolerant and prevents split brain.

cards.title: Coordination services and gossip
cards.body:
Many databases give this job to a dedicated **coordination service**, like ZooKeeper or etcd, which uses consensus to stay fault tolerant and avoid split brain. Each node registers with it, and it keeps the authoritative map of shards to nodes. Routers subscribe to that map, and the service tells them whenever it changes. A shard's owner changes in the map only once its data has reached the new node.

Some leaderless databases skip consensus and spread cluster changes by **gossip** from node to node. That's weaker: parts of the cluster can disagree for a while about who owns a shard. These databases promise only weak consistency anyway, so they can live with it.

cards.prompt: A cluster with a fixed number of shards tracks shard ownership in a coordination service. Order what happens when a new node is added.
items: The new node registers with the coordination service
Some shards are chosen to move to it from the existing nodes
Those shards' data is copied to the new node over the network
The coordination service records the new node as the owner of those shards
The routing tier is notified and sends requests for those shards to the new node
cards.explanation: During the copy, reads and writes still use the old assignment. Keys never change shard; only the mapping of shards to nodes changes.

cards.prompt: Instead of a consensus-based coordination service, a leaderless database spreads cluster changes by gossip between nodes. What's the trade-off?
choices: Gossip is consensus under another name, so it rules out split brain
Every change goes through a central gossip server, a single point of failure
Nodes may disagree for a while on who owns a shard; weak guarantees tolerate it
Gossip can't handle nodes joining, so the cluster size stays fixed
cards.explanation: Gossip has no consensus behind it, so different parts of the cluster can hold different assignments for the same shard, a form of split brain. Leaderless databases already make weak consistency promises, so they can live with it. Gossip is peer-to-peer with no central server, and it spreads news of nodes joining or leaving.

cards.title: Building your own index
cards.body:
So far every lookup knew its partition key. A **secondary index** lets you search by something else, like every order from one customer. It usually doesn't point to one record; it finds all records with a given value. Relational and document databases usually have them, but they don't map neatly onto shards.

Many key-value stores have none. You could build one yourself, storing a map from each value to the IDs that have it. But then only your own code keeps that index in line with the data. Two writes at once can race and leave them disagreeing, and a crash halfway can save a record without its index entry, or the reverse.

cards.prompt: On a key-value store with no secondary indexes, why is it risky to maintain your own value-to-ID index in application code?
keyPoints: Nothing but your own code keeps the index in step with the data
Concurrent writes can race and leave the index and the data disagreeing
A failure partway through can save the record but not its index entry, or the reverse
cards.explanation: Multi-object transactions (chapter 8) are the usual cure.

cards.title: Local secondary indexes
cards.body:
With a **local** index, each shard indexes only its own records. Say a music app shards songs by song ID and indexes them by artist: each shard keeps, per artist, the IDs of its own songs by that artist, a list called a **postings list**. A write touches only one shard.

Reads are another story. If you know the partition key, or want just a few matches, one shard will do. To get *every* match, you must ask all shards and merge the answers. That's costly, and waiting on many shards makes a slow straggler more likely (tail latency amplification). Adding shards adds storage, not query throughput, since every shard still handles every query.

cards.prompt: An online bookstore shards books by book ID and keeps a local secondary index on genre in each shard. To list every mystery novel, which shards must it query?
choices: Only the shard whose index owns the term 'mystery'
All of them, with the results merged afterwards
Any one shard, since every shard indexes the whole catalog
Only the shard holding the lowest-numbered mystery novel
cards.explanation: A local index covers only the books in its own shard, and mysteries can sit in any shard, so a complete list needs every shard, merged. If a few matches would do, one shard might be enough. Owning a term is how a global index works, no local index covers the whole catalog, and IDs say nothing about genre.

cards.prompt: An app's main query filters on a local secondary index. To raise query throughput, the team doubles the number of shards. What happens to throughput?
choices: It hardly improves, since every shard still has to process every query
It roughly doubles, since each shard now holds half as much data
It doubles, provided the shards are queried in parallel
It rises, and tail latency falls as each shard gets faster
cards.explanation: Each query fans out to all shards, so every new shard also has to handle every query: more shards add storage, not query capacity. Querying in parallel helps latency, not throughput. More shards per query actually make tail latency worse, because the slowest of many responses decides when the query finishes.

cards.title: Global secondary indexes
cards.body:
A **global** index covers the records in every shard. It can't sit on one node, which would become the bottleneck, so it's sharded too, but by the indexed value, the *term*, rather than by the record's key. Terms can be assigned to index shards by range or by hash.

Back in the music app, the postings list for one artist now lives in a single index shard and holds that artist's song IDs from every data shard. A query on one artist reads just that index shard. But the list holds only IDs, so fetching the songs themselves still means visiting each data shard that holds one of them.

cards.prompt: A food-delivery app shards orders by order ID and keeps a global secondary index on city, sharded by city name. What does a query for all orders in Lyon read?
choices: Every data shard, since orders are sharded by ID rather than by city
One index shard, which stores complete copies of the Lyon orders
One index shard for Lyon's order IDs, then the shards holding those orders
Every index shard for Lyon's IDs, then the data shards holding them
cards.explanation: A global index uses the term as its partition key, so all of Lyon's IDs sit in one index shard. That postings list holds IDs, not orders, and the orders are spread by ID, so fetching them still touches many data shards. Scanning every data shard is what a local index would need.

cards.title: Combining conditions
cards.body:
Queries with several conditions are harder on a global index. Ask for songs that are by one artist and also in one genre, and the two terms probably live on different index shards. To find records matching both, the database has to read both postings lists, bring them together in one place, and keep only the IDs found in both, before it can fetch the records.

With short lists that's quick. With long ones, shipping them across the network just to intersect them can be slow.

cards.prompt: A rental site has global secondary indexes on its listings. Order how it answers a query for listings that are both pet-friendly and in Porto.
items: Work out which index shard owns each of the two terms
Read each term's postings list from its index shard
Send both lists to one place and intersect them
Fetch the matching listings from the shards that hold those IDs
cards.explanation: The intersection is cheap for short postings lists but slow when long lists have to cross the network.

cards.title: Writing to a global index
cards.body:
Global indexes make writes harder. A record has many terms, each possibly on a different index shard, so one write can touch several shards. One way to keep them all in step with the data is a distributed transaction.

Some databases update global indexes **asynchronously** instead. Writes stay fast, but for a moment after a write, a query on the index may not see it yet, much like reading from a lagging replica.

So global indexes pay off when reads far outnumber writes and postings lists are short. When writes dominate, local indexes, which touch one shard per write, usually fit better.

cards.prompt: A marketplace updates its global secondary index on category asynchronously. A seller moves an item into 'Vintage', and a buyer browsing 'Vintage' a moment later doesn't see it. Why?
choices: Global indexes are rebuilt only by a nightly batch job
The buyer's query hit a shard whose local index lacks the item
The write failed partway, and the seller must retry it
The 'Vintage' index shard hasn't applied the change yet
cards.explanation: A record's index entries live on whichever shards own its terms, so one write can touch several shards. Applying those updates asynchronously avoids a distributed transaction, but index reads can lag behind, much like replication lag. No nightly rebuild is involved, the index is global rather than local, and the write itself succeeded.

cards.prompt: When is a global secondary index a better choice than local ones?
choices: Writes far outnumber reads, and each record has many indexed fields
Reads far outnumber writes, and each term's list of matching IDs is short
Most queries combine several conditions with long lists of matches
Queries usually come with the partition key of the records they want
cards.explanation: Global indexes make single-term reads cheap but writes costly, so they suit read-heavy workloads with short postings lists. Heavy writes that touch many index shards favour local indexes. Intersecting long lists across the network is slow. And if the partition key is known, a local index needs only one shard anyway.

cards.title: What a transaction is
cards.body:
Plenty can go wrong around a database. The database or the app can crash halfway through a series of writes, the network can drop out, and clients writing at once can trample each other's changes.

A **transaction** groups reads and writes into one unit. Either all of it succeeds, a **commit**, or it fails, an **abort** (or *rollback*), leaving nothing half-done. So the app needn't handle each kind of fault: it treats them all as an abort and retries. The database also handles races between clients, as far as its isolation level promises.

Transactions do scale, as newer distributed databases show, but an app touching only single records may not need them.

cards.prompt: What do transactions let an application stop worrying about, and what does it do instead?
keyPoints: Partial failure: a crash or network cut partway through a group of writes leaves no half-done changes behind
Concurrency: the database deals with races between clients, as far as its isolation level promises
Instead of handling each kind of fault, the application treats them all as an abort and retries
cards.explanation: The NoSQL-era belief that transactions can't scale was disproved by systems that combine sharding with consensus, but transactions are still a trade-off, and an app that only reads and writes single records may not need them.

cards.title: Atomicity
cards.body:
Transactions are usually described with **ACID**: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. The label is so loose that two 'ACID' databases can promise quite different things, so it has become mostly marketing.

In multithreaded code, atomic means nobody can see an operation half-done. ACID **atomicity** means something else: it isn't about concurrency at all, but about faults. Say a transaction has made some of its writes when something breaks: a process crashes, a connection drops, a constraint is violated. The database aborts the transaction and discards every write it made so far. Since nothing changed, you can retry without doing anything twice. *Abortability* would have been a better name.

cards.prompt: A transaction makes three writes. After the second, the disk fills up and the transaction can't commit. What does ACID atomicity guarantee?
choices: Other clients never see the first two writes while the transaction is still running
The database keeps the first two writes and finishes the third once space is freed
The first two writes are discarded, so the client can safely retry
The first two writes stay, and the client is told which ones so it can undo them
cards.explanation: Atomicity in ACID really means abortability: on a fault, every write the transaction made is thrown away, so a retry can't apply anything twice. Hiding in-progress writes from others is isolation, not atomicity. Finishing the transaction later, or leaving the cleanup to the client, is the partial failure that atomicity exists to prevent.

cards.title: Consistency
cards.body:
The word *consistency* has at least five meanings in data systems. In ACID, it means your data obeys certain **invariants**, rules that must always hold: in a library app, no book is ever on loan to two people at once. If every transaction starts from valid data and leaves it valid, the rules always hold, even if one breaks briefly in the middle of a transaction.

The database can only enforce rules you declare as **constraints**: foreign keys, uniqueness, check constraints, and sometimes triggers. Any other rule is the application's job. So the C in ACID depends on how the app uses the database, not on the database alone.

cards.prompt: A league app requires every team to have 11 to 25 players, but the rule lives only in application code. A bug lets a transaction commit a team with 30 players. What does this say about the C in ACID?
choices: The database broke its consistency guarantee, since ACID promises the data always stays valid
Atomicity failed: the transaction should have been rolled back once the rule was broken
Isolation failed: a concurrent transaction must have added players at the same moment
It's up to the app: the database only enforces invariants declared as constraints
cards.explanation: ACID consistency means your invariants hold, but the database can only check rules it knows about, such as uniqueness, foreign-key or check constraints. An undeclared rule is up to the application, so the C depends on how the app uses the database. The transaction committed in full, so atomicity held, and one buggy transaction needs no concurrency to break the rule.

cards.title: Isolation
cards.body:
Two friends add a song to a shared playlist at the same moment. Each app reads the list, appends its song and writes the list back. Both writes succeed, yet one song is missing: the second was built on the old list. That's a **race condition**.

ACID **isolation** means concurrent transactions can't step on each other. If one transaction makes several writes, another sees all of them or none, never a subset. Textbooks define the ideal as **serializability**: the outcome is the same as if the transactions had run one after another.

That ideal costs performance, so many databases use weaker levels that let some races through.

cards.prompt: A forum stores each thread's reply count in the thread row, next to the reply rows. While a transaction is adding a reply and bumping the count, a reader sees the new reply but the old count. Which guarantee would have prevented this?
choices: Atomicity, since the count update hadn't happened yet
Durability, since the new count wasn't on disk yet
Isolation: the reader should see both writes or neither
Consistency, since the count no longer matched the replies
cards.explanation: The reader saw another transaction halfway through, a dirty read, which isolation rules out. Atomicity is about undoing writes when a transaction fails, and nothing failed. Durability is about committed data surviving crashes. The count does break an invariant, but the database can't enforce a denormalized count; isolation is what hides the gap from readers.

cards.title: Durability
cards.body:
**Durability** promises that committed data won't be forgotten, even if hardware fails or the database crashes.

On one node, that means the data has reached nonvolatile storage such as an SSD: databases call `fsync` to push buffered writes out to disk, and keep a write-ahead log to recover from a crash mid-write. With replication, it means the data has reached a set number of nodes. Either way, the commit is reported only after those writes finish.

Neither is perfect. A *correlated fault*, one cause that hits every node together, like a software update that crashes every node or a cooling failure in the one data center, wipes out whatever was only in memory. So combine disks, replicas and backups.

cards.prompt: What does durability mean in a single-node database, and in a replicated one?
keyPoints: Single node: committed data has reached nonvolatile storage, using fsync, with a write-ahead log to recover from a crash mid-write
Replicated: committed data has reached a set number of nodes
Either way, the database reports a commit only after those writes have finished
cards.explanation: No durability is perfect: if every disk and every backup is destroyed together, nothing can bring the data back.

cards.prompt: A database keeps three replicas in memory in one data center, confirms a commit only once all three have the write, and never writes to disk. Which event can still lose committed data?
choices: None, since every commit is confirmed by all three replicas first
A power cut, or a bug that brings down all nodes on the same input
One replica crashing, since its share of the data lives only there
cards.explanation: A correlated fault takes out every replica at once, and anything held only in memory goes with them, which is why replicated databases still write to disk. Three confirmations don't help against a shared cause. Each replica holds a full copy, so losing one is exactly what the other two are for. No single technique is enough; disks, replication and backups work best together.

cards.title: Multi-object transactions
cards.body:
Atomicity and isolation matter most when a transaction writes several objects. Relational databases group them by connection: everything between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` belongs together. Many nonrelational stores can't group writes, and even a *multi-put* of several keys can end up applied to only some of them.

Yet many apps need multi-object transactions, whatever the data model. Records that point to each other, through foreign keys or graph edges, must stay valid when written together. Denormalized copies spread over several documents must change in one go, or they drift apart. And secondary indexes are separate objects updated on each write, so without isolation a record may show up in one index but not another.

cards.prompt: Why do many applications need transactions that span several objects, even with a document or key-value model?
keyPoints: Records that refer to each other, such as foreign keys or graph edges, must stay valid when they're written together
Denormalized copies spread over several documents must change together or they drift apart
Secondary indexes are separate objects updated on every write, so without isolation a record can show up in one index but not another
cards.explanation: A multi-key API isn't enough by itself: a multi-put can apply to some keys and not others, leaving a partial update.

cards.title: Retrying aborted transactions
cards.body:
An ACID database would rather abort a transaction than leave it half-done, precisely so that you can retry. Sadly, many ORMs never retry: the error just reaches the user.

Retrying has pitfalls. If the commit worked but its acknowledgment got lost, the client sees a timeout, and a retry applies the transaction twice unless the app deduplicates. If the abort came from overload or contention, retries add load: cap them and use exponential backoff. Retry only transient errors, such as a deadlock or a failover; a permanent one, like a constraint violation, just fails again. And side effects outside the database, like sending an email, happen again on every attempt.

cards.prompt: Retrying an aborted transaction is the standard way to handle errors. When is a retry harmful or useless?
keyPoints: If the commit succeeded but the acknowledgment was lost, a retry applies it twice unless the app deduplicates
If the abort came from overload or contention, retries add load; limit them and back off exponentially
After a permanent error such as a constraint violation, a retry fails the same way
Side effects outside the database, like sending an email, happen again on each attempt
cards.explanation: Many ORMs don't retry at all and pass the error up to the user, which throws away the main benefit of rolling back.

cards.title: Weak isolation
cards.body:
Concurrency bugs only appear when the timing is unlucky, so tests rarely catch them. In a big codebase, you can't even tell what else touches the same data.

Serializable isolation would hide them all, but it costs performance, so most databases default to **weak isolation levels** that stop some races and not others. That's why 'just use an ACID database' misses the point: popular relational databases are ACID and still run a weak level by default.

Don't count on bad timing staying rare, either. An attacker can fire a burst of simultaneous requests at your API precisely to trigger a race. These bugs must be ruled out by design, not left to luck.

cards.prompt: A wallet service runs on a popular relational database and assumes that, being ACID, it's safe from race conditions. An attacker fires hundreds of simultaneous withdrawals and takes out more than the balance. How is that possible?
choices: ACID covers only crashes and hardware faults; concurrency is always left to the app
Being ACID doesn't set the isolation level, and common defaults allow such races
The withdrawals must have bypassed transactions, since every ACID transaction is serializable
cards.explanation: Many relational databases default to a weak level such as read committed, which lets some races through, so 'use an ACID database' misses the point. Isolation is part of ACID, so concurrency isn't purely the app's problem, but serializability usually isn't the default. Attackers can trigger rare timing bugs on purpose, so these bugs must be prevented, not just made unlikely.

cards.title: Read committed
cards.body:
The most basic isolation level, **read committed**, makes two promises.

No **dirty reads**: you see only committed data, and a transaction's writes appear all at once. Otherwise a reader could catch a multi-row update halfway and act on it, or see a write that's later rolled back, data that never officially existed. Anything that read it would have to abort too: *cascading aborts*.

No **dirty writes**: you never overwrite another transaction's uncommitted value; the second writer waits, usually on a row lock held until the first commits or aborts. Otherwise two renames could interleave, leaving a team called Red with a chat channel called Blue. The weaker **read uncommitted** keeps only this promise.

cards.prompt: Why is it worth preventing dirty reads?
keyPoints: A reader could see some of a multi-row update but not the rest, and act on that half-updated state
A reader could see writes that are later rolled back, data that never officially existed
Anything that read uncommitted data would have to abort too, causing cascading aborts
cards.explanation: Most databases avoid dirty reads without read locks: they keep the old committed value and hand it to readers until the writer commits.

cards.prompt: Two fans buy the last ticket at the same moment. Each purchase sets the buyer on the ticket row, then sets the buyer on that ticket's invoice row. If dirty writes are allowed, what can go wrong?
choices: The ticket row names one fan while the invoice names the other
Both purchases abort, because each read the other's uncommitted data
Both fans own the ticket, since each transaction keeps its own copy of the row
Nothing: the later transaction overwrites both of the earlier one's writes
cards.explanation: With interleaved writes, one fan can win the ticket row and the other the invoice row, mixing two transactions. Nothing makes the same transaction win both. Read committed prevents this by making the second writer wait until the first commits or aborts, usually with row locks. Reading uncommitted data is a different anomaly, and a row has one current value, not one per transaction.

cards.title: Read skew
cards.body:
Read committed still lets you see the database at two moments at once. A library moves a rare book from its north branch to its south one. You check the south catalog just before the move commits and the north catalog just after: the book is in neither. Each value was committed when you read it, so read committed allows this. It's **read skew**, a kind of *nonrepeatable read*.

Usually a reload fixes it. Not for a backup that copies a big database over hours: its parts come from different moments, and a restore makes the mismatch permanent. Analytical queries and integrity checks that scan lots of data get nonsense the same way.

cards.prompt: A backup copies a large database over three hours under read-committed isolation. It copies table A early and table B late, and meanwhile a transaction moves stock from A to B and commits. What's wrong with the backup?
choices: Nothing: every value it copied had been committed when it was read
It contains a dirty read of the transfer's uncommitted writes
The moved stock appears in both tables, and a restore would make that permanent
The transfer's write to table B was lost, because the backup was holding a lock on it
cards.explanation: This is read skew: each value was committed when read, but the two tables reflect different moments, so the stock shows up twice. After a restore, the error is permanent. Read committed allows this, which is why backups and long analytical queries use snapshot isolation. The backup read only committed data, and read committed usually takes no read locks that could block the transfer.

cards.title: Snapshot isolation
cards.body:
**Snapshot isolation** prevents read skew. Each transaction sees the database as of its own start: everything committed by then, nothing after.

It's built with **multiversion concurrency control** (MVCC). Read committed usually avoids dirty reads without read locks: while a write is in progress, readers get the row's old committed value. MVCC generalizes that by keeping several committed versions of each row, since transactions that began at different times need different views.

The payoff: reads take no locks, so a reader never waits for a writer, nor a writer for a reader. Writers still lock rows against each other, so a second write to a row waits until the first transaction ends.

cards.prompt: Under snapshot isolation, a long report reads a table while T1 updates one of its rows, not yet committed. T2 then tries to update the same row. Who waits?
choices: T1, which waits for the report to finish because the report has read the row
The report, which waits for T1 so it doesn't read an uncommitted value
Nobody: T2's update replaces T1's uncommitted value right away
Only T2, which waits for T1 to commit or abort; the report never waits
cards.explanation: In MVCC-based snapshot isolation, readers and writers don't block each other: the report keeps reading old versions from its snapshot. Writers do still block other writers with write locks, so T2 waits for T1. Replacing T1's uncommitted value would be a dirty write, which snapshot isolation prevents.

cards.title: Visibility rules
cards.body:
In an MVCC database, each transaction gets a unique, ever-increasing **transaction ID**, and each row version records which transaction created it and which, if any, deleted it. A delete only marks the version; an update becomes a delete plus an insert.

When a transaction reads, it ignores three kinds of writes: those by transactions still running when it started, even if they commit later; those by transactions with higher IDs, which started after it; and those by aborted transactions. Everything else is visible. Put another way, a version is visible if its creator had committed before the reader began, and its deleter, if any, hadn't.

cards.prompt: In an MVCC database, which writes does a transaction ignore when it reads?
keyPoints: Writes by transactions that were still in progress when it started, even if they commit later
Writes by transactions that started after it, which have higher transaction IDs
Writes by aborted transactions
cards.explanation: An update marks the old row version as deleted and inserts a new one, both tagged with the writer's transaction ID, so the same rules handle updates and deletes.

cards.title: What 'repeatable read' means
cards.body:
The SQL standard's isolation levels date from the 1970s, before snapshot isolation was invented, so it never mentions it. Instead it defines **repeatable read**, which looks a bit similar, and defines it vaguely.

So vendors use the names as they please. PostgreSQL calls its snapshot isolation repeatable read, which lets it claim it follows the standard. Oracle calls its snapshot isolation serializable. In MySQL, repeatable read is a weaker MVCC variant, and in Db2 it means full serializability.

In practice nobody can say what repeatable read guarantees. Judge a level by which anomalies it prevents, never by its name.

cards.prompt: Two databases both offer an isolation level called 'repeatable read'. What can you safely assume?
choices: They behave the same, since the level is defined by the SQL standard
Both provide snapshot isolation, since that's what the name means
Both are serializable, since repeated reads must return the same values
Little: products use the name for snapshot isolation, weaker variants and serializability
cards.explanation: The SQL standard predates snapshot isolation and defines repeatable read vaguely, so vendors attach the name to different guarantees. One system's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, another's is weaker, and a third uses the name for serializability. Check which anomalies a level actually prevents rather than trusting its name.

cards.title: Lost updates
cards.body:
Concurrent writers bring their own trouble, the best known being the **lost update**. It strikes when an app runs a *read-modify-write cycle*: read a value, change it in code, write it back. If two transactions do that at once, the second write is built on the old value and wipes out the first. Read committed doesn't help, since the second write comes after the first commits.

The best fix, when it fits, is an **atomic write operation** that lets the database make the change, as in `UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1`. It applies such updates one at a time, with an exclusive lock or a single thread.

cards.prompt: A loyalty app awards points by reading a member's balance, adding to it in code, and writing the total back. When two purchases land at once, one award sometimes vanishes. What's the simplest fix?
choices: Switch to read committed, so one write can't overwrite another
Switch to read uncommitted, so each purchase sees the other's change sooner
Resolve concurrent writes afterwards by keeping the last one written
Have the database do the arithmetic: SET points = points + 50
cards.explanation: Reading, adding in code and writing back is a read-modify-write cycle, and two of them at once can lose an update. An atomic update lets the database apply each increment in turn. Read committed doesn't help, since the second write comes after the first commits. Read uncommitted only shrinks the window, and keeping the last write is what discards an award.

cards.title: Locks and automatic detection
cards.body:
When a change needs logic no atomic operation can express, such as checking a new price against a supplier's contract, lock the rows yourself. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks every row the query returns, so a competing read-modify-write on them waits until you finish. But it's easy to forget a lock somewhere, and locking several rows risks a **deadlock**: the database aborts one transaction, which you retry.

Alternatively, let the cycles run in parallel and have the database detect a lost update and abort the transaction, for you to retry. Snapshot isolation makes this cheap, and since your code needn't do anything, nothing can be forgotten. Not every implementation does it, though, so check yours.

cards.prompt: When do you need explicit locks such as SELECT FOR UPDATE to prevent lost updates, and what are the risks?
keyPoints: When the update depends on logic in application code that no single atomic database operation can express
Locking the rows you read makes concurrent read-modify-write cycles on them take turns
It's easy to forget a lock somewhere and bring the race back
Locking several objects risks deadlock; the database aborts one transaction, which must be retried

cards.prompt: A team keeps causing lost updates by forgetting to lock rows before read-modify-write cycles. Which database feature would catch these mistakes automatically?
choices: Snapshot isolation that detects lost updates and aborts the transaction
Read committed, which makes the second writer wait for the first
Last-write-wins conflict resolution, which keeps the newest value
Read uncommitted, which shows each write to others immediately
cards.explanation: Some snapshot isolation implementations notice when a transaction would overwrite a value changed since its snapshot and abort it, so the app only has to retry; not all of them do, so check yours. Read committed makes writers wait but then lets the second overwrite the first. Last write wins discards updates by design, and read uncommitted only narrows the window.

cards.title: Lost updates across replicas
cards.body:
Stores without transactions sometimes offer a **conditional write**, or *compare-and-set*: change a value only if it still equals what you read, and retry if not.

Locks and compare-and-set both assume a single current copy of each value. Multi-leader and leaderless databases accept writes on several replicas at once and sync them later, so there's no such copy. Instead, they keep the conflicting versions, called *siblings*, and merge them afterwards.

Merging avoids lost updates if the operations **commute**, giving the same result in any order, like adding to a tally or to a set. That's the idea behind CRDTs. Last write wins, the default in many of these databases, simply drops updates.

cards.prompt: A leaderless database resolves conflicts with last write wins. Two clients increment the same view counter at the same time on different replicas. What prevents the lost increment?
choices: A compare-and-set on the counter, which fails if the value has changed
A lock on the counter, taken before each increment
A counter type whose increments commute, merged across replicas
Nothing is needed: last write wins already keeps the newest value
cards.explanation: With several replicas accepting writes and replicating asynchronously, there's no single up-to-date copy for a lock or compare-and-set to check against. Increments commute, so a CRDT counter can merge both, in any order, on every replica. Last write wins keeps one of the two values and drops the other increment.

cards.title: Write skew
cards.body:
A chess club needs at least one keyholder at every evening session. Mia and Theo, both keyholders, ask for the same night off at the same moment. Each request checks that two keyholders are scheduled, sees two, and removes its own person. Both commit, and nobody can open the door.

This is **write skew**. The two wrote different rows, so nothing was overwritten: no dirty write, no lost update. Yet it's a race, since run one after the other, the second request would have been refused. Two transactions read the same data, then each updates something based on it. When both change one object, the result is a dirty write or a lost update, depending on timing.

cards.prompt: Two linked accounts, each holding 100, may go negative as long as their combined balance stays at least zero. Under snapshot isolation, two transactions each check the total (200), then withdraw 150 from different accounts. Which anomaly is this?
choices: Write skew: each decision rested on a total the other changed
A lost update, since one withdrawal overwrote the other
A dirty write, since both wrote before either committed
Read skew, since the two transactions saw different totals
cards.explanation: The transactions wrote different rows, so nothing was overwritten, which rules out a lost update or a dirty write. Each read a consistent snapshot showing 200, so it isn't read skew either. Both acted on a premise the other made false, leaving the total at minus 100: write skew. Run one after the other, the second would have been refused.

cards.title: Preventing write skew
cards.body:
Your lost-update defenses mostly fail here. Atomic single-object operations don't help, because several objects are involved. The automatic lost-update detection of snapshot isolation doesn't catch write skew either. A constraint would need to span several rows, and most databases don't support that, though triggers or materialized views can sometimes stand in.

What's left is **serializable isolation**, the only level that prevents write skew automatically. Failing that, explicitly lock the rows the decision depends on. In the chess club, the check would read the scheduled keyholders with `FOR UPDATE`, so the second request waits until the first commits, then sees just one keyholder left and refuses.

cards.prompt: Why don't the usual defenses against lost updates stop write skew, and what does?
keyPoints: Atomic single-object operations don't help, since several objects are involved
Snapshot isolation's automatic lost-update detection doesn't catch write skew
Constraints spanning several rows are rarely supported, though triggers or materialized views can sometimes stand in
What works: serializable isolation, or else explicitly locking the rows the decision depends on

cards.prompt: Order these anomalies by the weakest isolation level that prevents each one, from the weakest level to the strongest.
items: Dirty writes
Dirty reads
Read skew
Write skew
cards.explanation: Read uncommitted already blocks dirty writes, read committed adds dirty reads, snapshot isolation adds read skew, and only serializable isolation stops write skew. Lost updates are left out because snapshot isolation implementations differ on them.

cards.title: Phantoms
cards.body:
Write-skew bugs share a shape. A query checks a requirement by finding rows that match a condition. The app decides what to do from the result. Then it writes, and the write changes which rows match, so the decision's premise is now false.

In the chess club, the check returned the very rows that got changed, so `FOR UPDATE` could lock them. But often the check looks for the *absence* of rows, like no account using this email, and the write adds one. If nothing matched, there's nothing to lock. A write that changes another transaction's search result is a **phantom**.

cards.prompt: What pattern do write-skew bugs have in common?
keyPoints: A query checks a requirement by looking for rows matching some condition
The application decides whether to go ahead based on that result
It writes, and the write changes which rows match the condition, so the premise of the decision no longer holds
cards.explanation: The steps can come in another order, such as writing first and then running the check before deciding whether to commit.

cards.prompt: A clinic books surgeons by checking that no appointment overlaps the requested time, then inserting one. The check uses SELECT FOR UPDATE, yet two overlapping bookings still get through. Why?
choices: The check found no rows, so FOR UPDATE had nothing to lock
FOR UPDATE releases its locks as soon as the SELECT returns
The two inserts overwrote the same row, which is a dirty write
cards.explanation: The check looks for the absence of rows, and rows that don't exist yet can't be locked. Each transaction inserts a row matching the other's search: a phantom, causing write skew. FOR UPDATE locks last until the transaction ends, and the inserts create separate rows. A plain uniqueness rule could use a unique constraint, but overlapping time ranges need serializable isolation or materialized conflicts.

cards.title: Materializing conflicts
cards.body:
If phantoms leave nothing to lock, create something to lock. Say a club rents tennis courts by the hour. Fill a table, ahead of time, with a row for every court and hour over the coming months. A booking transaction first locks the rows for its court and hours with `FOR UPDATE`, then checks for overlapping bookings and inserts its own. A rival booking for an overlapping hour waits on those rows, and runs its check after the first commits.

The extra table holds no booking data; it exists only to be locked. This is **materializing conflicts**. It's fiddly and error-prone, and leaks concurrency control into your data model: a last resort.

cards.prompt: A makerspace books laser cutters in 30-minute slots and materializes conflicts to stop double bookings. Order the steps.
items: Ahead of time, create a row for every cutter and 30-minute slot for the coming months
A booking transaction locks the slot rows it needs with SELECT FOR UPDATE
Holding those locks, it checks the bookings table for overlaps
It inserts the booking and commits, releasing the locks
A competing booking that was waiting on the same slot rows runs its check and sees the new booking
cards.explanation: The slot table holds no booking data; it exists only to be locked. Letting concurrency control leak into the data model is ugly and error-prone, so this is a last resort when serializable isolation isn't available.

cards.title: Actual serial execution
cards.body:
Serializability can be built three ways: truly serial execution, two-phase locking, or optimistic methods.

The first is the simplest: run every transaction on one thread, one after another, and there's no concurrency left to control. For decades that seemed far too slow. Two things changed in the 2000s. RAM got cheap enough to hold the whole active dataset, so transactions stopped waiting for disk. And designers saw that OLTP transactions are short, with few reads and writes, while long analytical queries only read, so they can run on a snapshot outside the serial loop.

It skips locking overhead, but throughput is capped at one CPU core.

cards.prompt: Running transactions one at a time on a single thread was long considered too slow. What changed in the 2000s to make it viable?
keyPoints: RAM got cheap enough to keep the whole active dataset in memory, so transactions don't wait for disk
OLTP transactions turned out to be short, with only a few reads and writes
Long analytical queries are read-only, so they can run on a snapshot outside the serial loop
cards.explanation: Serial execution is serializable by definition and skips the cost of locking, but its throughput is capped at one CPU core.

cards.title: Stored procedures
cards.body:
Most transactions are *interactive*: the app sends a statement, waits for the result to cross the network, then sends the next. Even with no human in the loop, those round trips add up.

Running one transaction at a time, the database would sit idle through every round trip. So serial systems accept only single statements or **stored procedures**: the whole transaction's code, handed over in advance. With the data in memory, it runs without waiting on network or disk.

Stored procedures got a bad name from clunky vendor languages and code that's hard to test and deploy; modern systems use general-purpose languages.

cards.prompt: Why do databases that run transactions one at a time on a single thread not allow interactive transactions, where the app sends one statement per network round trip?
choices: The thread would sit idle waiting for the app's next statement, stalling everyone else
Interactive transactions need locks, and single-threaded databases have no lock manager
The statements of different transactions would interleave and cause race conditions
Each statement would have to be read from disk, since only stored procedures stay in memory
cards.explanation: Serial execution only works if each transaction is quick, and network round trips make it slow while blocking everyone else. So these systems take single statements, or stored procedures submitted up front that run in memory without waiting on the network or disk. Running one transaction at a time is exactly what rules out interleaving, and the data stays in memory either way.

cards.title: Limits of serial execution
cards.body:
One thread handles only as many writes as one CPU core can. To go further, shard the data so that each transaction stays inside one shard. Each shard then gets its own thread, and throughput grows with the number of cores.

A transaction that spans shards must run in lockstep on all of them. That's far slower, and more machines don't speed it up.

So serial execution fits when every transaction is small and fast, since one slow one stalls everything queued behind it; when the active data fits in memory, since a trip to disk blocks the thread; and when writes fit on one core or shard cleanly.

cards.prompt: Which workload is the best fit for serial transaction execution?
choices: Short transactions on in-memory data, each touching a single shard
Long read-write transactions that work through large parts of the data
Data far larger than memory, with transactions often reaching rarely used rows on disk
Heavy write traffic in which most transactions touch several shards
cards.explanation: Serial execution needs small, fast transactions on data in memory, and work that stays within one shard so each shard's thread runs on its own. One long transaction or one disk read stalls everything queued behind it. Cross-shard transactions must run in lockstep across shards, which is far slower and doesn't improve by adding machines.

cards.title: Two-phase locking
cards.body:
For about 30 years, the standard route to serializability was **two-phase locking** (2PL), which has nothing to do with two-phase commit.

Every object has a lock with two modes. To read, a transaction takes it in *shared* mode; many readers can share it, but not while someone holds it exclusively. To write, it needs *exclusive* mode, which waits until no other transaction holds the lock at all. A transaction that read an object and now writes it upgrades its lock. Locks are kept until commit or abort: gathered while the transaction runs, all released at the end, hence two phases.

So writers block readers too, unlike snapshot isolation. Deadlocks are detected and one transaction aborted.

cards.prompt: How does two-phase locking (2PL) use shared and exclusive locks?
keyPoints: To read an object, take a shared lock; many transactions can share it, but not while someone holds it exclusively
To write, take an exclusive lock, which waits until no other transaction holds any lock on the object
A transaction that read an object can upgrade its shared lock to exclusive to write it
Locks are held until commit or abort: acquired while running, all released at the end
cards.explanation: Don't confuse it with two-phase commit (2PC): 2PL provides serializable isolation, while 2PC provides atomic commit across nodes.

cards.title: The cost of 2PL
cards.body:
2PL stops every race, lost updates and write skew included, but it's slow. Locks have overhead, and worse, transactions spend much of their time waiting, since anything that might race has to take turns.

Take a job that reads an entire table, such as an integrity check. It needs a shared lock on the whole table, which it can't get while any transaction holds an exclusive lock there; once it has it, nobody can write to the table until the job commits. For a big table, writes stop for a long time.

One slow transaction can stall everything, so latency is erratic at high percentiles. Deadlocks are more frequent too, and each wastes work.

cards.prompt: Under two-phase locking, a backup reads an entire table while other transactions want to write to it. Order what happens.
items: The backup waits for transactions that have already written to the table to finish
It gets a shared lock on the whole table
It reads the table, while every new write to the table waits
It commits and releases its lock
The waiting writes go ahead
cards.explanation: For a large table, the database is effectively closed to writes for the whole read. Snapshot isolation avoids this, since readers and writers don't block each other.

cards.title: Predicate locks
cards.body:
To be serializable, 2PL must also stop phantoms, so it has to lock rows that don't exist yet. A **predicate lock** belongs to a search condition rather than a row, say 'concerts in Berlin in May'.

A transaction running a query takes a shared predicate lock on its condition, after waiting for any exclusive lock on a matching row. A transaction about to insert, update or delete a row checks both the row's old value and its new value against existing predicate locks. If either matches a lock held by another transaction, it waits until that one ends.

Since a condition also covers rows added later, this prevents phantoms and write skew.

cards.prompt: Under 2PL with predicate locks, transaction T has searched for tents priced under 100 dollars and hasn't committed yet. Which write by another transaction must wait for T to finish?
choices: Inserting a backpack priced at 80 dollars
Inserting a tent priced at 150 dollars
Repricing a 150-dollar tent to 90 dollars
None, since predicate locks cover only rows that existed when T searched
cards.explanation: A write must wait if either its old or its new value matches another transaction's predicate lock, and the repriced tent's new value falls inside T's condition. The backpack is the wrong category, and a 150-dollar tent is outside the price range. Predicate locks do cover rows that don't exist yet: that's how they stop phantoms.

cards.title: Index-range locks
cards.body:
Checking each write against many predicate locks is slow. So most 2PL databases use **index-range locks** (also called *next-key locks*), a coarser approximation.

The trick is that locking more than you need is safe: any write that matches the exact condition also matches a broader one. For 'concerts in Berlin in May', the database might lock every Berlin concert through an index on city, or every concert in May through an index on date. It puts a shared lock on that index entry or range, and any write that touches it hits the lock and waits.

You get some needless waiting, but much less overhead. With no suitable index, the database locks the whole table.

cards.prompt: A transaction searched for tents under 100 dollars, and the database locked the index range for category 'tent' rather than the exact condition. Another transaction now inserts a 400-dollar tent. What happens?
choices: It goes ahead, since its price doesn't match the search
It waits, since the lock covers every tent at any price
It goes ahead, since index-range locks protect only existing rows
The searching transaction is aborted, since its result is now stale
cards.explanation: An index-range lock covers a wider set than the exact condition, which is safe because any write matching the condition also falls in the range. The cost is some needless waiting, as here, but it's far cheaper than checking many precise predicate locks. With no usable index, the database falls back to locking the whole table.

cards.title: Optimistic concurrency control
cards.body:
2PL is **pessimistic**: if anything might go wrong, wait until it's safe, like a mutex in threaded code. Serial execution is the extreme, one lock on the whole database, made bearable by keeping transactions short.

**Serializable snapshot isolation** (SSI) is **optimistic**. Transactions go ahead without waiting; at commit, the database looks for any violation of isolation, and if it finds one, the transaction aborts and must retry.

Optimism pays off with spare capacity and little contention. When many transactions fight over the same objects, most abort, and near full capacity the retries add yet more load, so it can do worse than locking. Commutative operations help, like increments nobody reads back.

cards.prompt: During a flash sale, thousands of transactions update the stock row of one product under serializable snapshot isolation (SSI), and the system is near its capacity. What's the likely result?
choices: Smooth throughput, since optimistic methods never make transactions wait
Many aborts and retries, which add load and can do worse than locking
Long stalls, since SSI makes reads wait until writers on the row finish
Oversold stock, since SSI checks reads but not writes
cards.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions run and aborts those that conflicted when they try to commit. Under heavy contention most of them conflict, and the retries pile onto a system already near its limit. Under SSI reads never wait for writers, and it's fully serializable, so it won't oversell. Where they fit, commutative operations such as increments that aren't read back avoid the conflicts.

cards.title: Outdated premises
cards.body:
SSI is snapshot isolation plus a detector for write skew, which happens when a transaction acts on a *premise*, a query result that's no longer true when it commits. The database can't see how your code used a result, so any change to it counts as a possible conflict.

One way a premise goes stale: when you read, MVCC hid a write by a transaction that hadn't committed yet. SSI notes each write it hides from you, and at your commit checks whether any has committed since. If so, you're aborted.

Why not abort at the read? You might never write, and a read-only transaction can't cause write skew. And the writer might still abort.

cards.prompt: In SSI, why isn't a transaction aborted the moment it reads a value that another, uncommitted transaction has overwritten?
choices: Aborting at read time would need read locks, and SSI is built to avoid locking
The reader may never write, and the writer may still abort, so the read may cause no conflict
Stale reads are harmless under snapshot isolation, so SSI only checks the writes
The database learns about a stale read only when the writer finally commits
cards.explanation: A read-only transaction can't cause write skew, and at read time the database doesn't know whether writes will follow.
