The other transaction might abort, or still be uncommitted when the reader commits. Waiting avoids needless aborts and keeps long read-only queries cheap. The stale read is noted when it happens; it only matters at commit, and it isn't harmless if the reader goes on to write.

cards.title: Tripwires on reads
cards.body:
A premise also goes stale when another transaction writes data after you've read it.

SSI keeps track of what each transaction reads, for example by noting on an index entry which transactions searched it, or per table if there's no index. A transaction that writes looks up who recently read the affected data and flags them. Unlike a lock, this is a tripwire: nobody waits, and the readers only learn their read may be outdated.

The check comes at commit. If a write that conflicts with your reads has already committed, you're aborted. If its transaction hasn't committed yet, you commit, and it faces the same check at its own commit.

cards.prompt: How does serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) detect that a transaction's decision may rest on an outdated premise?
keyPoints: It notes when a read ignored another transaction's uncommitted write under MVCC rules, and at commit checks whether that write has since committed
It records what each transaction read, for example on index entries, so a later write to that data flags the readers
These records are tripwires, not locks: nothing waits
At commit, a transaction is aborted if a write conflicting with its reads has already committed
cards.explanation: The database can't know how the app used a query result, so it assumes any change to that result may invalidate the transaction's writes.

cards.prompt: Under SSI, transactions A and B each read team 7's purchases to check its budget, then each insert a new purchase for team 7. Order what happens.
items: Both read team 7's purchases, and the database records the reads on the index entry for team 7
Both insert a purchase; each write finds the other's recorded read and flags it as possibly stale, without blocking
A commits first and succeeds, since B hasn't committed yet
B tries to commit, finds that a write conflicting with its read has committed, and is aborted
The application retries B, which now sees A's purchase
cards.explanation: The first to commit wins. Plain snapshot isolation would have let both commit, a write skew that could take the team over budget.

cards.title: SSI in practice
cards.body:
Compared with 2PL, SSI's big win is that nobody waits for locks. Readers and writers don't block each other, so latency is far more predictable, and read-only queries run on a snapshot with no locks at all. Compared with serial execution, it isn't held to one CPU core: conflict checks can be spread over many machines, and transactions can span shards and stay serializable.

The price is aborts. Tracking reads finely means fewer needless aborts but more bookkeeping. A transaction that reads and writes over a long period will likely hit a conflict, so read-write transactions must stay short; long read-only ones are fine.

cards.prompt: An app needs serializable transactions. Its writes exceed what one CPU core can handle and often span shards, and long read-only reports run all day. Which approach fits best?
choices: Serial execution, since skipping locks avoids their overhead
Two-phase locking, since it has been the standard for decades
Snapshot isolation, since reports read from a consistent snapshot
Serializable snapshot isolation, which doesn't block and runs across shards
cards.explanation: SSI doesn't make readers and writers wait for each other, so reports run on a snapshot without locks, and conflict checks can be spread across machines and shards. Serial execution is capped at one core per shard and cross-shard work is slow. Under 2PL, a long report blocks writers. Plain snapshot isolation is fast but allows write skew, so it isn't serializable.

cards.title: Atomic commit
cards.body:
On one node, the storage engine makes commit atomic. It writes the transaction's data durably to its log, then appends a **commit record**; the transaction is committed the instant that record is fully on disk. After a crash, recovery keeps each transaction whose commit record made it and rolls back the rest.

A **distributed transaction** spans several nodes, such as shards. Sending each one a commit isn't enough: one may hit a constraint violation, a request may get lost, a node may crash first. Then some commit and some abort, and a commit can't be undone, since others may already have read its data. All must commit or all abort: the **atomic commitment** problem.

cards.prompt: On a single node, what makes a transaction's commit atomic?
keyPoints: The transaction's writes go durably to the log first, then a commit record is appended
The transaction is committed at the instant the commit record is fully on disk
After a crash, recovery keeps transactions whose commit record is on disk and rolls back the rest
cards.explanation: One disk controller on one node makes the decision; a transaction spread over several nodes has no such single device.

cards.prompt: A transaction writes to two shards, and the client sends a commit to each. Shard 1 commits; shard 2 finds a constraint violation and aborts. Why can't shard 1 simply undo its commit?
choices: Undoing a commit needs a write-ahead log, which shards don't keep
It can: shards routinely roll back commits when another shard fails
It shouldn't: shard 2 will retry its commit until it succeeds
Other transactions may already have read its data and acted on it
cards.explanation: Once committed, data is visible to others under read committed or stronger isolation, so they may have built on it, and retracting it would mean undoing them too. Nodes must all commit or all abort: the atomic commitment problem. A constraint violation fails the same way on every retry, and taking back committed data breaks the very promise a commit makes.

cards.title: Two-phase commit
cards.body:
**Two-phase commit** (2PC) solves atomic commitment with a new component, the **coordinator** or transaction manager, often a library inside the app.

The app gets a global transaction ID from the coordinator, then reads and writes on each database node, the *participants*, in ordinary local transactions tagged with that ID. When the app wants to commit, phase 1 begins: the coordinator asks every participant to *prepare*. A participant answers yes only once it's sure it can commit: its data is stored durably and its constraints pass. If all say yes, the coordinator logs its decision to commit on its own disk, then, in phase 2, tells every participant to commit, retrying until each has it. Any no means abort for all.

cards.prompt: Order the steps of a successful two-phase commit.
items: The application reads and writes on each participant, in local transactions tagged with one global transaction ID
The coordinator asks every participant to prepare
Each participant makes sure it can commit, with the data on disk and constraints checked, and votes yes
The coordinator records its decision to commit in its own log on disk
The coordinator sends commit to every participant, retrying until each one gets it
cards.explanation: Logging the decision is the commit point. A yes vote gives up the right to abort, and a logged decision can't be reversed: those two promises make 2PC atomic.

cards.title: Points of no return
cards.body:
Why does 2PC work when a plain commit sent to each node doesn't? Its messages can get lost just the same. The difference is two promises.

Before voting yes, a participant writes everything the transaction needs to disk and checks for conflicts and constraint violations. From then on, a crash or a power cut is no excuse to back out. By voting yes, it gives up the right to abort, without committing yet.

Once the coordinator logs its decision, the **commit point**, that decision is final. A participant that crashed in the meantime commits when it recovers, because it promised. A single node bundles both promises into one step: writing its commit record.

cards.prompt: In two-phase commit, a participant has voted yes. Before the commit request arrives, its disk fills up. What happens?
choices: It aborts and tells the coordinator, which then aborts the transaction everywhere
It changes its vote to no, and the coordinator starts the vote over
It still commits: before voting yes, it had already written all it needs to disk
It commits the writes that fit and reports the rest as failed
cards.explanation: Voting yes is a promise: the participant has already written the transaction's data durably and checked constraints, so a crash, power cut or full disk can't stop it from committing later. It gives up the right to abort without committing yet. Taking back the vote, or committing part of the transaction, would break the atomicity 2PC exists to provide.

cards.title: Coordinator failure
cards.body:
If the coordinator dies before sending any prepare request, a participant can just abort. Once it has voted yes, though, it can't decide alone: the coordinator may already have told others to commit, or to abort, so guessing after a timeout risks a mismatch either way. Asking the other participants isn't part of 2PC. The transaction is **in doubt**, and the participant can only wait, keeping its locks.

That's why the coordinator logs its decision before sending it. On restart, it reads its log and settles each in-doubt transaction, aborting any without a commit record. So 2PC can block. Three-phase commit avoids that, but stays atomic only if network delays are bounded, which real networks can't promise.

cards.prompt: In two-phase commit, a participant voted yes, and then the coordinator crashed before sending its decision. What should the participant do?
choices: Abort after a timeout, since no decision ever arrived
Commit after a timeout, since it already voted yes
Wait for the coordinator to recover, holding its locks
Ask the other participants how they voted and follow the majority
cards.explanation: After voting yes, the participant is in doubt: the coordinator may already have told others to commit, or to abort, so deciding alone risks a mismatch either way, and polling peers isn't part of 2PC. It blocks until the restarted coordinator reads its decision from its log. Three-phase commit avoids blocking, but stays atomic only if network delays are bounded, which real networks don't guarantee.

cards.title: Exactly once with 2PC
cards.body:
Distributed transactions come in two kinds: *database-internal* ones, among nodes all running the same database software, and *heterogeneous* ones, spanning different technologies such as two vendors' databases plus a message broker.

Heterogeneous transactions enable neat tricks. A consumer can commit a message's acknowledgment together with its database writes: if either fails, both abort, and the broker redelivers the message. However many attempts it takes, the effects land once. That's **exactly-once** processing.

The catch: it covers only systems that take part in the same atomic commit protocol. If handling a message also posts to a chat webhook that knows nothing of 2PC, a failed attempt has still posted, and the retry posts again.

cards.prompt: A consumer handles each queue message in one distributed transaction that commits the database writes and the message acknowledgment together. It also sends the customer an SMS. If processing fails and is retried, what can still happen twice?
choices: The database writes, since each retry commits them again
Nothing: the distributed transaction makes everything exactly once
The acknowledgment, since the broker redelivers on every retry
The SMS, since the SMS service isn't part of the atomic commit
cards.explanation: Exactly-once here means a failed attempt leaves no trace, and that only covers systems taking part in the same atomic commit protocol. The database writes and the acknowledgment are rolled back together on abort, so a retry starts clean. The SMS gateway isn't a participant, so an attempt that sends the SMS and then aborts sends it again on retry.

cards.title: XA transactions
cards.body:
**XA** is the standard for 2PC across different technologies, such as databases and message brokers. It isn't a network protocol, just a C API. The app talks to each participant through its usual driver, and an XA-aware driver lets the coordinator call back into it to prepare, commit or abort.

The coordinator is usually a library inside the app's own process, with its log on that server's local disk. If the app server dies, the coordinator dies too, and prepared participants are left in doubt. The databases can't contact the coordinator themselves. Only once the server restarts can the library read its log and tell each participant, through the drivers, how to finish.

cards.prompt: An application uses XA, with the coordinator as a library inside the application server. The server dies after the participants have voted yes. Order what happens next.
items: The participants stay in doubt, holding their locks
The application server is restarted
The coordinator library reads its log from the server's local disk
It tells each participant, through the database drivers, whether to commit or abort
The participants apply the decision and release their locks
cards.explanation: The databases can't contact the coordinator themselves, since all communication goes through the client library. If the log is lost, an administrator has to resolve the transactions by hand.

cards.title: Stuck in doubt
cards.body:
An in-doubt transaction still holds its locks: exclusive ones on rows it wrote, and under 2PL shared ones on rows it read. It can't release them before learning the outcome. If the coordinator needs half an hour to come back, anything touching those rows waits half an hour, and big parts of the app can stall.

Sometimes the coordinator can't decide at all, say because a bug corrupted its log. Restarting the databases won't help: correct 2PC keeps the locks across restarts, or atomicity could break. An administrator must check each participant and, if any has committed or aborted, apply that outcome to the rest. *Heuristic decisions* let a participant choose alone, but likely break atomicity: emergencies only.

cards.prompt: Why is a transaction stuck in doubt under 2PC so harmful, and how is it resolved if the coordinator can't decide?
keyPoints: It keeps holding its row locks, so other transactions that touch those rows are blocked
The locks survive database restarts, since dropping them could break atomicity
An administrator checks each participant and, if any has committed or aborted, applies the same outcome to the rest
Heuristic decisions let a participant decide alone, but they likely break atomicity and are only for emergencies
cards.explanation: Until it's resolved, large parts of an application can be unavailable.

cards.title: Fixing distributed transactions
cards.body:
Under XA, a lone coordinator can take everything down, and its log on the app server's disk is as critical as the databases. Even a replicated coordinator can reach participants only through the app and its drivers, so the app stays a single point of failure. And as a lowest common denominator, XA can't detect deadlocks across systems or work with SSI.

Distributed databases run 2PC among their own shards without these flaws. The coordinator is replicated, usually with consensus, so it fails over by itself, and it talks to shards directly. Shards are replicated too, so one fault rarely forces an abort. And commit is tied to distributed concurrency control that detects deadlocks and keeps reads consistent.

cards.prompt: What are the main problems with XA transactions across different systems?
keyPoints: The coordinator usually runs inside the application server, a single point of failure whose local log is as critical as the databases
Coordinator and participants talk only through the application and its drivers, so even a replicated coordinator leaves the application as a single point of failure
As a lowest common denominator, it can't detect deadlocks across systems or work with SSI

cards.prompt: Distributed databases also use 2PC across their shards. How do they avoid XA's problems?
keyPoints: The coordinator is replicated, usually with consensus, and fails over automatically
The coordinator talks to the shards directly, not through application code
Shards are replicated, so a fault in one shard rarely forces an abort
Atomic commit is paired with distributed concurrency control, so deadlocks are detected and reads are consistent across shards
cards.explanation: Since every node runs the same software, they aren't stuck with a lowest-common-denominator protocol.

cards.title: Exactly once without 2PC
cards.body:
Exactly-once processing doesn't need 2PC. Give each message a unique ID, and keep a table of processed IDs in your database.

To handle a message, open a database transaction and look up its ID. If it's there, the work is already done: acknowledge the message and drop it. If not, insert the ID and make the message's writes in that same transaction, then commit. Acknowledge to the broker only after the commit. Once the broker has the acknowledgment it won't redeliver, so a later, separate transaction can delete the ID.

A crash before the commit means a clean retry; after it, the retry finds the ID. Recording it makes processing **idempotent**.

cards.prompt: To process each message from a broker exactly once using only database transactions, order the steps.
items: Begin a database transaction and check whether the message's ID is already in the processed table
If it isn't, insert the ID and make the message's writes in the same transaction
Commit the database transaction
Acknowledge the message to the broker
Delete the message ID in a separate transaction
cards.explanation: A crash before the commit leads to a clean retry; a crash after it leads to a retry that finds the ID and drops the message. Recording the ID makes processing idempotent, and a uniqueness constraint on it stops two concurrent attempts.

cards.title: Partial failures
cards.body:
On one computer, software mostly either works or it doesn't. That's by design: the same instruction always gives the same result, and when hardware breaks, the machine crashes outright rather than quietly returning wrong answers.

Spread work over a network and that's gone. One part can be broken while the rest works: a **partial failure**. It's also **nondeterministic**: a call that worked a minute ago may fail now, and you may not even know whether it took effect.

Coping with this pays off. A system that tolerates broken nodes keeps serving while some are down, and lets you upgrade nodes one at a time, a *rolling upgrade*, with no downtime.

cards.prompt: A checkout service calls a payment service and a stock service. Payment replies 'charged'; the stock call hangs, then fails with a timeout. What is the situation?
choices: A total failure: the request failed, so neither service changed anything
A bug in the checkout service, since correct code would give the same result every time
A partial failure: one part worked, and the stock update may or may not have happened
A network partition, which proves the stock service never received the call
cards.explanation: Some parts of a distributed system can fail while others work, and the outcome is nondeterministic: the stock service may or may not have applied the update. The charge clearly went through, so it isn't a total failure. The uncertainty comes from the network, not from a bug. And a timeout can't prove that the call never arrived.

cards.prompt: Partial failures make distributed systems hard to work with. Why is tolerating them worth the effort?
keyPoints: The system as a whole keeps running while some of its nodes are broken
Nodes can be upgraded and rebooted one at a time with no downtime
cards.explanation: That's how you build a system more reliable than any of the machines it runs on.

cards.title: When no reply comes
cards.body:
Nodes in a typical distributed system share no memory or disks; the network is their only link. And datacenter networks, like the internet, are **asynchronous**: a packet may arrive quickly, late, or never.

Say a booking app asks a seat service to hold a seat and hears nothing. The request may have been dropped, or sit in a queue. The service may have crashed, or be frozen in a garbage collection pause and answer later. Or it held the seat, and the reply was lost or is still on its way. The sender can't tell which.

A **timeout** only means you stop waiting. A delayed request may still arrive afterwards.

cards.prompt: A node sends a request to a peer and hears nothing back. What might have happened?
keyPoints: The request was lost, or is still sitting in a queue somewhere
The remote node crashed, or has stalled (in a GC pause, say) and will answer later
The node handled the request, but its response was lost or is still on its way
cards.explanation: You can't tell these apart, and a timeout only means you stopped waiting: a queued request may still be delivered afterwards.

cards.title: How TCP delivers data
cards.body:
Packets hold a few kilobytes at most, so most apps use **TCP**. It splits a long message into packets and rebuilds it at the far end, resends lost packets, reorders late ones, and catches some corruption with a checksum. It also paces itself so it doesn't swamp the network or the receiver: *congestion control*. QUIC and other newer protocols work much the same.

Writing to a socket sends nothing yet; the bytes wait in an OS buffer. When congestion control sees room, it hands a packet to the network card. Switches and routers carry it across. The receiving OS stores the data, sends an acknowledgment back, and only then tells the application.

cards.prompt: Order what happens when an application sends data over an open TCP connection.
items: The application writes to a socket, and the data waits in an OS buffer
Congestion control finds spare capacity and passes a packet to the network interface
The packet travels through switches and routers to the receiving machine
The receiving OS buffers the data and sends an acknowledgment back
The receiving OS tells the application that data has arrived
cards.explanation: The acknowledgment goes out before the application even knows about the data, so it can't confirm the request was handled.

cards.title: Where TCP's promise ends
cards.body:
TCP can't make the network reliable. When no acknowledgment comes back in time, it can't know whether the packet was lost or only the acknowledgment. It resends, but if a cable is cut, resending won't help; after a while it gives up and returns an error.

Its duplicate detection works within one connection. If your app reconnects and sends the request again, the server may get it twice.

And an acknowledgment only proves that the remote OS got the bytes. The application could crash before acting on them. To know that a request really succeeded, you need a reply from the application itself.

cards.prompt: TCP retransmits lost packets and drops duplicates. Why doesn't that make the network reliable for an application?
keyPoints: When no acknowledgment comes, TCP can't tell whether the packet or the acknowledgment went missing
Resending can't get through a dead link; eventually TCP gives up and reports an error
Deduplication only works within one connection, so reconnecting and resending can repeat a request
cards.explanation: An acknowledgment only shows that the remote kernel got the data; to know a request succeeded, you need a reply from the application itself.

cards.title: Network faults are normal
cards.body:
Network faults are common even in one company's datacenter: one study counted about a dozen a month, and human misconfiguration is a leading cause. A link can work in one direction only, and messages can be held up for minutes.

When one part of a network can't reach another, that's a **network partition**. If nobody planned for it, software may do anything: stay stuck after the network heals, or even lose data.

You needn't keep working through every fault; showing an error until the network returns can be fine. But you must know how your system reacts, test it by causing faults on purpose, and make sure it recovers.

cards.prompt: Handling network faults doesn't have to mean tolerating them. What does it require?
keyPoints: Showing users an error while the network is having trouble can be an acceptable response
You must know, and test, how the software reacts when the network fails, for example by injecting faults
The system must recover once the network is back
cards.explanation: Untested error handling can do arbitrary damage: a cluster can stay deadlocked after the network heals, or even lose data.

cards.title: Spotting a dead node
cards.body:
Load balancers must stop sending traffic to dead nodes, and replicated databases must replace a dead leader. Sometimes you get a fast hint that a node is down.

If the machine is reachable but nothing listens on the port, because the process crashed, its OS refuses the connection at once. If the OS still runs, a script there can announce the crash. In your own datacenter, switches can report a dead link. A router sure that an address is unreachable may say so, but it can't see every failure either.

Don't count on any of these. Usually you hear nothing, retry a few times, and give up after a timeout.

cards.prompt: In which case can a client learn that a node is down without waiting for a timeout?
choices: The machine has lost power, and its OS sends a last error packet to its peers
The node is stuck in a long GC pause and replies that it's busy
The network cable is cut, and the router always reports the address as unreachable
The machine is up but the server process crashed, so the OS refuses connections
cards.explanation: If the machine is reachable but nothing listens on the port, its OS rejects the TCP connection at once. A powered-off machine sends nothing. A paused process can't reply at all. A router may report an address as unreachable, but only when it's sure, and it can't detect every failure. In general, expect silence and fall back on timeouts.

cards.title: Declaring a node dead
cards.body:
How long should you wait before declaring a node dead? A long timeout leaves users waiting, or seeing errors, until it's replaced. A short one spots failures sooner but also accuses nodes that were only briefly slow.

A wrong verdict costs. Declaring a node dead doesn't stop it. If it was merely slow, halfway through a job like charging a card, it carries on while its replacement does the job again.

Its load also moves to other nodes. If it was slow because the system was overloaded, that load can push others over too, until nodes keep declaring each other dead: a *cascading failure*.

cards.prompt: A worker is halfway through emailing a batch of invoices when it stalls for a few seconds. The supervisor's timeout fires, and it gives the batch to another worker. What's the risk?
choices: Some customers get the same invoice twice, since the first worker resumes and carries on
The batch is lost, since the first worker's progress disappears when it's declared dead
Nothing, since a worker that's declared dead is stopped before it can send any more
The second worker sends nothing, since the first already marked the batch as in progress
cards.explanation: Declaring a node dead doesn't stop it: if it was only slow, it continues where it left off while its replacement repeats the work. Nothing is lost, since the batch was handed over, and nothing halts the stalled worker. The new worker was told to send the batch, so it does.

cards.title: Where packets wait
cards.body:
Network delays vary for the same reason commutes do: queues. A request can wait at several points.

When many machines send to one destination at once, the switch lines their packets up for the single outgoing link. If that queue fills, packets are dropped and must be resent, though nothing is broken. At the receiver, if every core or worker thread is busy, the OS holds the request until one is free. On a virtual machine, the hypervisor buffers incoming data while the VM is paused so another VM can use the CPU. Even at the sender, TCP's congestion control may hold data back before it leaves.

cards.prompt: Network delays vary mostly because of queueing. Where can a request wait on its way to a busy server?
keyPoints: In a switch, when many senders target the same link; if that queue fills, the packet is dropped
In the receiving OS, until a CPU core or application thread is free
In the hypervisor, while the VM is paused so another VM can run
At the sender, where TCP's congestion control holds data back
cards.explanation: Queues build up fast when a system nears full capacity, and on a shared cloud a noisy neighbor can fill them for you.

cards.title: TCP or UDP
cards.body:
**UDP** neither resends lost packets nor does flow control. That removes some causes of variable delay, though its packets still wait in switch queues and for the CPU.

It fits data that's worthless once late. In a fast online game, each client sends its position many times a second. If one update goes missing, resending it is pointless: by the time it arrived, a newer position would be on its way. The game just uses the next one.

With TCP, the lost packet would be resent, and everything behind it would wait. When freshness matters more than completeness, the app copes with gaps itself.

cards.prompt: A team builds a live voice chat. A lost audio packet resent by TCP would arrive too late to be played. What should they do?
choices: Use TCP, so that every audio sample is eventually played in full
Use UDP, and play a moment of silence for each lost packet
Use UDP, since it avoids switch queues and scheduling delays entirely
Use TCP with a bigger send buffer, so lost packets are recovered in time
cards.explanation: When late data is worthless, UDP skips retransmission and flow control, removing some causes of delay, and the app just fills the gap; people ask each other to repeat. UDP packets still wait in switch queues and for the CPU, though. Playing every sample means stalling the call, and a bigger buffer only adds delay.

cards.title: Choosing a timeout
cards.body:
If every packet were sure to arrive within time d, and a healthy server always answered within r, 2d + r would be a perfect timeout. Real networks and servers promise neither: delays have no upper bound. Being fast most of the time isn't enough, since a tight timeout fires on every brief spike.

Delays swing most near full capacity, and in a cloud a *noisy neighbor* sharing your links and CPUs can slow you down anytime.

So there's no right value. Measure round trips over a long period and many machines, then pick a trade-off. Better, let the system track response time spread (*jitter*) and adjust the timeout itself, as the Phi Accrual failure detector does.

cards.prompt: How should a system on a shared network choose its timeout for declaring a peer dead?
choices: Measure round trips over a long period and many machines, or adapt it to the observed spread
Set it just above the median round-trip time, so that failures are caught as fast as possible
Use twice the network's maximum packet delay plus the server's maximum handling time
Use the cloud provider's recommended value, since datacenter networks have a standard delay profile
cards.explanation: There's no correct value, so pick one by experiment, or use a failure detector that adjusts to measured jitter. Being fast most of the time isn't enough: a timeout near the median fires on every brief spike. The 2d + r formula needs bounded delays, which shared networks don't have. Other tenants' traffic makes delays vary in ways no standard figure captures.

cards.title: Circuits versus packets
cards.body:
A classic phone call gets a **circuit**: a fixed share of bandwidth reserved on every hop for the whole call. Nothing queues, so delay is **bounded**, but the share sits idle when unused.

The internet and datacenters use **packet switching** because data traffic is bursty. A download has no natural rate; it should just finish fast. On a circuit you'd have to guess one: too low wastes capacity, too high and the circuit can't be set up. TCP just uses whatever is free.

So variable delay is a trade-off, not a law of nature. Static reservations buy guarantees, but idle hardware costs more. Dynamic sharing keeps links and CPUs busy and cheap, at the price of queueing.

cards.prompt: A phone circuit gives a call a bounded delay. Why do the internet and datacenter networks rely on packet switching instead?
keyPoints: A circuit reserves fixed bandwidth on every hop, so nothing queues, but the reservation sits idle when unused
Most data traffic is bursty: a web page or file has no fixed rate and should just finish fast
With a circuit you'd have to guess a rate: too low wastes capacity, too high and it can't be set up
TCP adapts its sending rate to whatever capacity is free
cards.explanation: The price of packet switching is queueing, and with it unbounded delay.

cards.prompt: Is variable network delay an unavoidable property of computer networks?
choices: Yes: any network with more than one switch has to queue its packets
No: it was a flaw in early Ethernet, and newer transport protocols such as QUIC have fixed it
No: it's the price of sharing capacity dynamically, which uses hardware better and costs less
Yes: only faster links could remove it, and they're limited by the speed of light
cards.explanation: Static reservation, as with phone circuits or dedicated hardware, can bound delays, but it leaves capacity idle and costs more. Dynamic sharing keeps links busy at the price of queueing. A circuit crosses many switches without queueing. Newer protocols like QUIC share TCP's limits. Faster links don't stop senders from competing for them.

cards.title: Two kinds of clocks
cards.body:
Apps use time two ways: timing how long something took, and naming a moment. Computers have a clock for each.

A **time-of-day clock** gives the calendar date and time. NTP keeps machines roughly in line, so their readings can be compared. But it can jump: if it runs too far ahead, NTP may set it back, and leap seconds cause jumps too. UTC at least has no daylight saving shifts.

A **monotonic clock** is a stopwatch. It only moves forward, so the gap between two readings is elapsed time. Its value alone is arbitrary, like time since boot, so comparing two machines' values is meaningless. NTP may *slew* it, nudging its speed, but never makes it jump.

cards.prompt: A service logs each request's latency as the difference between two time-of-day clock readings. A few entries come out negative. What's the most likely cause?
choices: NTP slewed the monotonic clock, which made it run backward for a moment
Daylight saving time ended, which shifts the clock even when it's set to UTC
NTP reset the time-of-day clock backward between the two readings
The two readings came from different CPUs, whose clocks always disagree
cards.explanation: A time-of-day clock running well ahead of its NTP server can be stepped back, which makes it unfit for measuring durations; a monotonic clock is the right tool. The service isn't using a monotonic clock, and slewing only changes its rate. UTC has no daylight saving time. The OS hides most differences between CPU timers.

cards.prompt: Compare time-of-day and monotonic clocks: what each is for, whether it can jump, and whether readings from two machines can be compared.
keyPoints: Purpose: time-of-day gives a calendar date and time; monotonic measures elapsed time, like a stopwatch
Jumps: time-of-day can jump back or forward when reset; monotonic only moves forward
Across machines: time-of-day readings roughly agree thanks to NTP; a monotonic value is arbitrary, so comparing two is meaningless
cards.explanation: NTP can still speed a monotonic clock up or slow it down slightly (slewing), but never makes it jump.

cards.title: Why clocks drift
cards.body:
Computers keep time with a quartz crystal, and quartz **drifts**: it runs fast or slow, partly with temperature. Google allows for up to 200 parts per million, most of a second per hour, so error grows between syncs.

**NTP** corrects the clock by asking time servers, but it has weak spots. A firewall can silently block it while drift piles up. It's only as accurate as the network delay allows: tens of milliseconds at best over the internet, and congestion makes it worse or makes the client give up. Some servers report the wrong time outright. And a clock found far off may be reset with a jump.

cards.prompt: A server runs NTP. Why might its time-of-day clock still be far from the true time?
keyPoints: Its quartz drifts, faster or slower with temperature, and the error grows between syncs
A firewall can quietly block NTP, letting drift pile up for a long time
NTP is only as accurate as the network delay allows; congestion adds error or makes the client give up
The NTP server itself may be misconfigured and report the wrong time
cards.explanation: Leap seconds, VM pauses and user-set device clocks add more trouble, so software that relies on synced clocks should monitor every node's offset and remove nodes that drift too far.

cards.title: Clocks fail quietly
cards.body:
More traps await. A **leap second** makes a minute 59 or 61 seconds long, and has crashed large systems; some time servers smear it over a day instead. On a VM, the clock seems to leap forward after each pause. Devices you don't control, like phones, can have clocks set to anything, sometimes to cheat in a game.

Worse, a wrong clock rarely breaks anything visibly. A dead network card gets noticed at once; a drifting clock leaves everything looking fine while code that trusts it silently loses data. So if your software relies on synced clocks, monitor each node's offset and remove any node that strays too far.

cards.prompt: A database relies on synchronized clocks, and no one monitors clock offsets. A firewall change has blocked one node's NTP traffic for weeks. What's the most likely symptom?
choices: The node crashes once its clock drifts past a safety limit
Everything looks normal, while some data is quietly lost
The node's monotonic clock stops, so its timeouts never fire
NTP steps the clock back to the right time once the drift reaches a second
cards.explanation: A drifting clock doesn't stop anything from running, so the fault goes unnoticed while decisions based on its wrong timestamps quietly drop data; that's why offsets need monitoring. Nothing crashes at a drift limit. A monotonic clock keeps counting without NTP. And with NTP blocked, nothing is left to correct the clock.

cards.title: Ordering writes by timestamp
cards.body:
With multi-leader or leaderless replication, several nodes can accept writes to the same key, and replicas must agree on which value to keep. **Last write wins** (LWW) keeps the write with the highest timestamp and discards the rest. Each timestamp comes from the time-of-day clock of the node that took the write.

This fails even with well-synced clocks. Suppose a client reads a value, then overwrites it on another node. If that node's clock is behind by more than the time between the two writes, the overwrite gets the smaller timestamp. LWW then keeps the older value everywhere and silently drops the newer one.

cards.prompt: A shared shopping list uses multi-leader replication with last write wins. Ana adds 'milk' on one node; Ben sees it and, 2 ms after her write, changes it to 'oat milk' on another node whose clock is 5 ms behind. Which value survives?
choices: 'oat milk', because LWW keeps the write that really happened later
'milk', because Ben's later edit got an earlier timestamp and was discarded
Both, because LWW sees that the two writes were concurrent and keeps each of them
'milk', because LWW keeps whichever write reaches each replica first
cards.explanation: LWW compares timestamps from each node's clock, so a clock a few milliseconds slow makes a causally later write look older, and it's dropped without any error. LWW doesn't know the real order; it trusts the clocks. It can't tell causal writes from concurrent ones, so it never keeps both. Arrival order doesn't matter, only the timestamp.

cards.title: Where last write wins fails
cards.body:
Lost overwrites can be stopped by giving each new value a higher timestamp than the one it replaces, even if that's ahead of the writer's clock. That costs an extra read, so some databases skip it and use the client's clock. Then three problems appear.

A writer whose clock lags can't overwrite a value set from a faster clock until the gap has passed; its writes vanish with no error. LWW can't tell writes made one after another from truly concurrent ones; that takes causality tracking such as **version vectors**. And two writes can get the same timestamp, needing a tiebreaker, like a random number, which can also break causality.

cards.prompt: What goes wrong when a database resolves conflicts by last write wins, using the clients' clocks?
keyPoints: A writer whose clock lags can't overwrite values from a faster clock until the skew has passed, so its writes vanish without an error
It can't tell writes made in quick succession from truly concurrent ones; that takes something like version vectors
Two writes can get the same timestamp, and the tiebreaker this needs can also break causality
cards.explanation: Making every overwrite carry a higher timestamp than the value it replaces fixes the first problem, at the cost of an extra read.

cards.title: Logical clocks
cards.body:
Could better NTP fix ordering? Not really. Clock error would have to be well below the network delay between nodes, but NTP's own accuracy is limited by that delay. Even with good sync, a message can seem to arrive, by the receiver's clock, before it was sent.

**Logical clocks** sidestep this. Instead of reading quartz, they count events with counters, and record only which event came before which, not what time it was. Clocks that measure real time, like the two kinds above, are **physical clocks**. For putting events in order, a logical clock is the safer tool.

cards.prompt: Two services stamp their events with NTP-synced time-of-day clocks, and an audit tool sorts the events by timestamp. Sometimes a reply sorts before the request it answers. What's the best fix?
choices: Sync with NTP more often, so the clock error drops below the network delay
Order events with a logical clock, which counts events instead of measuring time
Stamp events with monotonic clocks, which never go backward
Record timestamps with microsecond precision, so that events close together are told apart
cards.explanation: A logical clock tracks only which event came before which, and that's all the tool needs. NTP's own accuracy is limited by network round trips, so clock error can't fall well below network delay. Monotonic readings mean nothing across machines. Precision isn't accuracy: digits finer than the clock's error are noise.

cards.title: A reading is a range
cards.body:
A clock may show microseconds, but that's precision, not accuracy. After drift and an NTP sync over the internet, the real error is more like tens of milliseconds, so the fine digits are noise.

Treat a reading as a range: the true time lies between an earliest and a latest value. The width adds up drift since the last sync, the time server's own error and the round trip to it. Most clock APIs hide this, so you can't tell a millisecond of error from an hour. A few, like Google's TrueTime, return the range.

The rule: if two ranges don't overlap, the earlier came first. If they overlap, the order is unknown.

cards.prompt: A clock API returns the time as an [earliest, latest] range. Transaction A got [100, 106] and transaction B got [104, 112], in milliseconds. Which happened first?
choices: A, because its earliest bound is lower than B's
A, because its whole range both starts and ends sooner than B's
Can't tell: the ranges overlap, so either could be first
cards.explanation: Each event's true time lies somewhere in its range, so A could have been at 105 and B at 104. Only ranges that don't overlap give a certain order. Comparing bounds treats a reading as a point, which it isn't. The width comes from drift since the last sync, the time server's own error, and the round trip to it.

cards.title: Clocks as transaction IDs
cards.body:
Snapshot isolation needs transaction IDs that follow causality: a transaction that reads or overwrites another's write needs the higher ID, or snapshots come out inconsistent. One machine can use a counter. Across many shards, a shared counter needs coordination and becomes a bottleneck with many small transactions.

Clock timestamps rise on their own, with no coordination; clock error is the risk, and ranges handle it. Before committing, a transaction waits as long as its clock's range is wide. Anything that later reads its writes then gets a range that can't overlap. Google's Spanner works this way, using GPS receivers and atomic clocks only to keep ranges, and so waits, short.

cards.prompt: Why would a database spread over many shards use synchronized clock timestamps as transaction IDs for snapshot isolation?
keyPoints: Snapshots need IDs that reflect causality: a transaction that reads or overwrites another's write must get a higher ID
A single counter shared by all shards needs coordination and becomes a bottleneck with many small transactions
Clock timestamps rise on their own, so later transactions get higher IDs with no coordination
cards.explanation: The catch is clock error, which is only manageable if the clock reports its uncertainty.

cards.prompt: Order how a database like Spanner uses clock uncertainty to commit a read/write transaction safely.
items: The transaction is ready to commit and reads the clock's [earliest, latest] range
It waits for as long as that range is wide
It commits, and its writes become visible
Any transaction that later reads those writes gets a range that can't overlap the first
cards.explanation: GPS receivers and atomic clocks aren't essential: they just keep the range narrow, so the wait stays short.

cards.title: Leases and paused threads
cards.body:
A **lease** is a lock that expires. Say only a shard's leader may accept writes. The leader holds a lease and renews it before it runs out; if the leader dies, renewals stop, and another node takes over once it expires.

Picture the leader's loop: check that the lease has a few seconds left, then handle a request. If the expiry was set by another machine's clock, skew breaks the check; a monotonic clock fixes that. The deeper flaw is the gap between check and action. If the thread freezes in between for longer than the margin, it acts on an expired lease, and nothing tells it.

cards.prompt: A job dispatcher may send out jobs only while it holds a lease. Before each dispatch it checks that the lease has at least 10 seconds left. How could it still dispatch after another node has taken over?
choices: Its thread pauses for over 10 seconds after the check, and it doesn't notice
Renewing the lease takes a network round trip, and dispatches sent meanwhile aren't covered
It can't, as long as the check uses a monotonic clock rather than the time-of-day clock
The lock service may grant the lease to two nodes if their requests arrive together
cards.explanation: A GC pause, VM suspension or page fault can stop a thread at any line for any length of time, and nothing tells it afterwards. A monotonic clock fixes a separate problem, comparing against an expiry set by another machine's clock, but not pauses. Renewal happens while the lease is still valid. A lease service grants one holder at a time.

cards.title: Why a thread freezes
cards.body:
Can a thread really freeze for seconds? Yes. A garbage collector may stop every thread at once. A VM can be suspended, paused while it moves live to another host, or kept waiting while other VMs use the CPU. A laptop sleeps when its lid closes. A stop signal, like Ctrl-Z, halts a process until it's resumed.

Disk I/O can stall a thread even where the code never mentions files, as in a page fault when memory was swapped out. Busy CPUs and lock contention add waits.

Mutexes don't work across nodes, which share no memory. So every node must assume it may be paused at any line, and declared dead meanwhile.

cards.prompt: Why might a running thread be stopped for seconds or longer without noticing?
keyPoints: A stop-the-world garbage collection
Its VM is suspended, live-migrated, or kept waiting while other VMs use the CPU
It waits on slow disk I/O, including page faults when memory has been swapped out
The process gets a stop signal, or the device goes to sleep, as when a laptop lid is closed
cards.explanation: Mutexes and other single-machine tools don't help across nodes, which share no memory, so every node must assume it can be paused at any point.

cards.title: Hard real-time
cards.body:
Pauses can be removed, at a price. Software running a pacemaker or a train's brakes is **hard real-time**: it must respond by a deadline, every time, or the system has failed.

That takes the whole stack: a real-time OS that guarantees each process CPU time at set intervals, libraries with documented worst-case running times, little or no dynamic memory allocation, and huge amounts of testing. Few languages and tools qualify, so it's very costly. And real-time means predictable, not fast; throughput is often lower.

For most server-side data systems that isn't worth it, so they live with pauses and unsteady clocks.

cards.prompt: Why don't most server-side data systems offer hard real-time response guarantees?
choices: Real-time systems give up correctness for speed, which data systems can't accept
It's possible, but every layer of the stack must be built and tested for it, at great cost
Servers already meet hard deadlines, so the only remaining delays are caused by the network
Real-time guarantees need faster processors than general-purpose servers can offer
cards.explanation: Hard real-time needs a real-time OS, libraries with known worst-case timings, restricted memory allocation and huge amounts of testing, which limits the tools and costs a lot. Real-time means predictable, not fast, and often lowers throughput; correctness isn't traded away. Server processes pause for many reasons besides the network.

cards.title: Living with garbage collection
cards.body:
A well-tuned modern collector usually pauses for a few milliseconds, and you can shrink the damage further. You can skip garbage collection: Swift counts references, and Rust tracks lifetimes in the compiler. Or, in a collected language, reuse objects from pools or keep data outside the heap.

You can also treat a pause as a short planned outage. If the runtime warns that a node will soon need to collect, clients send new requests elsewhere; the node finishes what it has, collects with nothing in flight, then rejoins. A variant collects only short-lived objects, which is quick, and restarts each process in turn before long-lived ones need a full collection.

cards.prompt: Besides tuning the collector, how can a service reduce the impact of garbage collection pauses?
keyPoints: Use a language without a garbage collector, managing memory by reference counting or compiler-tracked lifetimes
Reuse objects from pools, or keep data outside the heap
Collect only short-lived objects, and restart processes in turn before long-lived ones need a full collection
cards.explanation: None of these removes pauses entirely; they make them shorter or rarer.

cards.prompt: Order how a cluster can hide one node's garbage collection pause from clients.
items: The runtime warns that the node will soon need to collect
Clients route new requests away from that node
The node finishes the requests it already has
It collects garbage with no requests in flight
It starts taking requests again
cards.explanation: Treating the pause as a brief planned outage cuts high-percentile response times.

cards.title: The majority decides
cards.body:
A node knows the world only through messages, so it can be wrong even about itself. A node whose outgoing messages get dropped works fine, but no one hears it, so the others declare it dead. A node that froze for a minute resumes unaware, while the rest have replaced it.

So no single node has the final word. Decisions, including who's dead, are made by a **quorum**: a vote among nodes. A node the quorum declares dead must step down, however healthy it feels.

Usually the quorum is a **majority**, more than half. Three nodes can then lose one, five can lose two, and since only one majority can exist, two groups can't make conflicting decisions.

cards.prompt: A coordinator node freezes for a minute. When it resumes, it learns that a majority of the cluster declared it dead and chose a replacement. What should it do?
choices: Keep coordinating, since it knows it's healthy and the others were mistaken
Declare the others dead, since it hasn't heard from them for a minute
Run its own health check, and carry on as coordinator if it passes
Step down and accept the decision, even though it feels fine
cards.explanation: A node can't trust its own view of the situation: to itself, hardly any time passed. Decisions, including who is dead, are made by a quorum, and a single node must abide by them. Its own health check says nothing about what the others saw. Declaring them dead would be the same mistake in reverse.

cards.prompt: A five-node cluster decides by majority vote. A network fault splits it into a group of three and a group of two. What happens?
choices: Only the group of three can make decisions; the two can't reach a majority
Both groups keep deciding, and their results are merged when the network heals
Neither group can decide until the network heals, since a vote needs all five
Whichever group holds the current leader keeps deciding, even with only two nodes
cards.explanation: A majority is three of five, and any two majorities share a node, so conflicting decisions are impossible; that also lets five nodes survive two faults. Merging later would mean reconciling two conflicting histories. Requiring all five would halt on any single fault. A leader without a majority behind it can't act safely.

cards.title: Zombie leaseholders
cards.body:
Leases ensure there's only one of something: one leader per shard, one writer per file, one worker per input. Two holders at once would just waste work in the last case but could corrupt data in the others.

And it happens. A client pauses, its lease expires and moves on, and it wakes up still writing. Or a client sends a write and crashes, and the write lingers in the network until the lease has moved on. A former holder that hasn't noticed is a **zombie**.

Shutting zombies down, by cutting them off or powering off the machine, falls short. It can't recall a write already sent, nodes may shut each other down, and the damage may already be done.

cards.prompt: Why is shutting down a suspected zombie leaseholder not a reliable way to protect storage?
keyPoints: It can't stop a write the zombie already sent that's still delayed in the network
Nodes may end up shutting each other down
By the time the zombie is detected and stopped, it may already have corrupted data

cards.title: Fencing tokens
cards.body:
A sturdier fix puts the check in storage. Whenever the lock service grants a lease, it also issues a **fencing token**: a number higher than any before. Clients attach their token to every write. Storage remembers the highest token it has accepted and rejects any write with a lower one.

A zombie's token is older, so smaller. Once the new holder has written, storage turns the zombie away, so a new holder should write as soon as it gets the lease. The check happens on arrival, so delayed writes are stopped too.

Storage that can't check tokens can use a *conditional write*: it fails if anyone else wrote since you last read.

cards.prompt: A client holding a lease sends a write to storage, then crashes. The write is held up in the network for a minute; meanwhile the lease expires, and another client takes it and writes before the old write finally arrives. What prevents corruption?
choices: Powering off the crashed client's machine, so it can't send anything more
The lock service revoking the expired lease, which cancels the client's pending writes
TCP dropping the packet, since the client's connection closed when it crashed
Storage rejecting any write whose fencing token is lower than one it has already seen
cards.explanation: Only the storage service can check, when a write arrives, whether it comes from an outdated leaseholder. The write was already in flight, so shutting down its sender is too late. The lock service can't recall messages in the network. And a delayed packet can still be delivered after its sender has crashed.

cards.prompt: How do fencing tokens stop a former leaseholder from doing damage?
keyPoints: Each time the lock service grants a lease, it hands out a number higher than any before
The client includes its current token with every write to storage
Storage rejects a write whose token is lower than one it has already accepted
cards.explanation: Storage without token checks can get the same effect from a conditional write that fails if another client wrote since this one last read.

cards.prompt: Order how a fencing token stops a client that paused while holding a lease.
items: Client A gets the lease with token 12
A pauses, and its lease expires
Client B gets the lease with token 13
B writes to storage, which records token 13
A resumes and sends a write with token 12, which storage rejects
cards.explanation: The new holder writes right away: until storage has seen token 13, a write carrying 12 would still be accepted.

cards.title: Fencing across replicas
cards.body:
With one store that supports conditional writes, you may not need a separate lock service at all. Tokens earn their keep when one holder writes to several services or replicas, since every one of them can then refuse the old holder.

Say three replicas each keep whichever write carries the highest timestamp, and every client sends its writes to all three itself. Make the writer's fencing token the most significant part of every timestamp it creates. Then anything the new holder writes outranks anything from the zombie, even if written later. If a zombie's write lands on a replica the new holder missed, quorum reads still prefer the new holder's value, and read repair replaces the stale one.

cards.prompt: A leaderless key-value store resolves conflicts by last write wins, and clients write to each replica directly. How can fencing tokens protect it from a zombie leaseholder?
choices: Have each replica keep the write with the lowest token, since that holder got the lease first
Put the token in the most significant digits of each write's timestamp
Have the new leaseholder delete the zombie's writes from every replica
Drop the tokens, since LWW timestamps already put the writes in order
cards.explanation: Then any timestamp from the new holder beats any from the old one, even if the zombie writes later. Its write may land on a replica the new holder missed, but quorum reads prefer the larger timestamp and read repair overwrites it. Keeping the lowest token favors the zombie. Deleting can't catch writes that arrive afterward. Plain clock timestamps let the zombie's later write win.

cards.title: Byzantine faults
cards.body:
So far we've assumed nodes are unreliable but **honest**: slow, silent or out of date, yet truthful as far as they know. A zombie is honest; it just hasn't heard the news, so fencing stops it. A node set on cheating could simply invent a higher token.

A node that breaks the protocol's rules, sending corrupted, made-up or contradictory messages, has a **Byzantine fault**. Think of a replica telling one peer it saved a record and another that it didn't.

The name comes from the *Byzantine Generals Problem*: generals must agree on a plan by messenger while unknown traitors among them spread lies. Agreeing when some may lie is far harder than when they can only fail.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a Byzantine fault?
choices: A node that crashes and never comes back
A node whose replies arrive a minute late because of a GC pause
A node that keeps writing because it hasn't noticed its lease expired
A node that votes for two different candidates in the same election
cards.explanation: A Byzantine node sends arbitrary or contradictory messages, breaking the protocol's rules. Crashes, delays and stale state are faults of an honest node: it's gone, slow or behind, but what it says is true as far as it knows. Fencing tokens can stop a stale leaseholder; a node set on lying could just fake its token.

cards.title: When lies must be tolerated
cards.body:
A **Byzantine fault-tolerant** system keeps working even when some nodes lie. A few settings need that. In aircraft and spacecraft, radiation can flip bits in memory, and failure is catastrophic. And parties who don't trust each other, agreeing with no central authority as in blockchains and peer-to-peer networks, might cheat.

A company's own datacenter usually skips it. The company controls every node, and the protocols are costly. Most need over two-thirds of nodes behaving, yet all nodes run the same code, so one bug or exploit hits all of them; firewalls, encryption and access control are the real defense.

Web clients can't be trusted either, but there the server is the authority and validates every input.

cards.prompt: When is Byzantine fault tolerance worth its cost, and why do most datacenter systems skip it?
keyPoints: Worth it: aerospace, where radiation can corrupt memory and a failure is catastrophic
Worth it: parties that don't trust each other and have no central authority, as with blockchains or peer-to-peer networks
Skipped: one organization controls all the nodes, and the protocols are expensive
Skipped: every node runs the same software, so a bug or exploit hits them all at once
cards.explanation: Most such protocols need over two-thirds of nodes behaving correctly, so a flaw shared by every node defeats them; authentication, encryption and firewalls remain the defense against attackers.

cards.prompt: A multiplayer browser game must stop players from submitting impossible moves. What's the usual approach?
choices: Run a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol among the players' browsers
Trust the moves, since the browsers are running the game's own code
Encrypt connections with TLS, so clients can't send invalid moves
Validate every move on the server, which decides what's allowed
cards.explanation: Clients under users' control can send anything, so the server acts as the authority and checks their input. Byzantine protocols suit peer-to-peer settings that lack such an authority. Users can modify or replace the code their browser runs. TLS stops tampering in transit, not a client lying about its own moves.

cards.title: Guarding against weak lies
cards.body:
Even honest nodes sometimes send nonsense, through hardware faults, bugs or misconfiguration. Cheap checks catch much of it, though not a determined attacker.

Packets can be corrupted in ways that slip past TCP's and UDP's simple checksums, so add a checksum to your own protocol, or use TLS. Validate input: escape it, check numbers fall in a sensible range, and cap string lengths so one request can't exhaust memory. Internal services behind a firewall can be less strict, but their parsers still need basic checks. And compare several sources: NTP set up with multiple servers can spot one reporting a wrong time and ignore it as an outlier.

cards.prompt: Short of full Byzantine fault tolerance, what cheap checks guard against 'weak lying' caused by bugs, hardware faults and misconfiguration?
keyPoints: Checksums in the application protocol, or TLS, catch corrupted packets that get past TCP's checks
Inputs are sanitized and checked for sensible ranges and sizes, even in internal services
NTP clients use several servers, so one that reports a wrong time is outvoted as an outlier
cards.explanation: These wouldn't stop a determined attacker, but they're simple, practical gains in reliability.

cards.title: System models
cards.body:
To reason about distributed algorithms, you write down what they assume: a **system model**. An algorithm can then be proved correct within it.

For timing, the **synchronous** model assumes delays, pauses and clock error stay under known bounds, which real systems violate. The **partially synchronous** model assumes they usually do but sometimes exceed them by any amount. The **asynchronous** model allows no timing assumptions, not even a clock, so no timeouts.

For nodes, in **crash-stop** a failed node never returns. In **crash-recovery** it may come back later, disk intact but memory lost. A **Byzantine** node can do anything. Partially synchronous with crash-recovery is generally the most useful fit for real systems.

cards.prompt: Which system model is generally the most useful for reasoning about real datacenter systems?
choices: Synchronous timing with crash-stop nodes
Asynchronous timing with Byzantine, arbitrarily faulty nodes
Partially synchronous timing with crash-recovery nodes
Partially synchronous timing with crash-stop nodes
cards.explanation: Real systems mostly stay within timing bounds but sometimes blow past them, and crashed nodes often return with their disks intact but memory lost. The synchronous model assumes bounds that real delays break. The asynchronous model forbids even timeouts, and Byzantine faults are rare within one organization. Crash-stop ignores nodes that restart.

cards.title: Limping nodes
cards.body:
Nodes don't only crash; they can slow down. A driver bug can cut a network card to a sliver of its speed, a process short on memory can spend most of its time collecting garbage, and heat, loose connectors or firmware bugs can make hardware erratic.

Such a **limping node**, or *gray failure*, may still answer health checks promptly while being far too slow for real work. That makes it harder to handle than a node that cleanly died: failure detection sees it as alive, so it stays in service and drags down every request it gets. Similarly, a process can lose one part, like a background thread, while the rest carries on.

cards.prompt: A storage node answers health checks instantly, but its worn-out SSD makes real reads take 30 seconds. Why is this harder to handle than a crash?
choices: It's a Byzantine fault, so only a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol can catch it
It looks alive to failure detection, yet it's too slow to do useful work
It isn't harder: its health checks will soon time out, and it will be removed
It's a crash-recovery fault, so its data on disk may be lost when it restarts
cards.explanation: A limping node, or gray failure, passes the checks that would catch a dead one while dragging down every request it serves. It isn't Byzantine: the node is honest, just slow. Its health checks keep passing, so nothing removes it automatically. And it hasn't crashed, so crash-recovery assumptions don't come into it.

cards.title: Safety and liveness
cards.body:
An algorithm's correctness is written as properties. For a ticket booking service, say: no seat is ever sold twice, and every booking request eventually gets an answer.

The first is a **safety** property: nothing bad happens. If it's broken, you can name the moment, and the damage can't be undone. The second is a **liveness** property: something good eventually happens. It may not hold yet at a given moment, but it still can later. 'Eventually' is a giveaway; eventual consistency is a liveness property too.

Safety must hold in every situation the model allows, even if every node crashes. Liveness may come with conditions, like a majority of nodes being up and the network recovering.

cards.prompt: How do safety and liveness properties differ?
keyPoints: A safety violation happens at a specific moment, and the damage can't be undone
A liveness property may not hold yet, but can still be satisfied later
Safety must hold in every situation the model allows; liveness may come with conditions, such as a majority of nodes being up
cards.explanation: A hint: liveness properties often contain the word 'eventually', and eventual consistency is one of them.

cards.title: Models meet reality
cards.body:
A system model simplifies, and reality breaks it. Crash-recovery algorithms assume what's on disk survives a crash. But disks get corrupted, an operator's mistake can wipe one, and a buggy controller can hide drives that are attached just fine.

Quorum algorithms depend on each node remembering what it said it stored. A node that forgets, then carries on as usual, silently breaks their guarantees. A model allowing such losses would be harder to reason about.

So real code still needs a path for 'impossible' cases, even if it just stops and calls a human. Models stay worth it: they boil reality down to faults you can reason about.

cards.prompt: A replicated store uses quorum reads and writes. After a reboot, a firmware bug makes one node see an empty disk, and it rejoins as if nothing had happened. What's the danger?
choices: Little: crash-recovery algorithms already assume that a node's disk can be lost
Only slower reads, since the other nodes will refill it before it votes
None: quorum reads use checksums to spot the empty node and exclude it
It may count toward quorums for data it no longer has, breaking correctness
cards.explanation: Quorum algorithms rely on each node remembering what it claimed to store, and an amnesiac node breaks that silently. Crash-recovery assumes the opposite: stable storage survives. Nothing refills or excludes it first, since it doesn't know it lost data. Real code still needs handling for 'impossible' cases, even if that's just stopping and calling a human.

cards.title: Model checking
cards.body:
How do you know an algorithm keeps its properties? A mathematical proof catches design flaws that might hide for years, though it says nothing about whether the code matches, so add testing too.

A **model checker** sits in between. You describe the algorithm in a specification language such as TLA+, and the tool tries every sequence of events it can, checking your invariants in each state. Real state spaces are usually infinite, so you shrink the model or cap the run, say at a handful of messages, and bugs that need longer runs go unseen. And it checks the spec, not your code, so the two can drift apart.

cards.prompt: A model checker explores a protocol's TLA+ specification and finds no violations. What could still be wrong?
choices: Nothing: the checker has proved the invariants for every possible state
Only performance, since the checker has confirmed that the running code is correct
Bugs that need longer runs than were checked, or code that doesn't match the spec
Only the spec's syntax, since the checker runs the code generated from it
cards.explanation: Real state spaces are usually infinite, so a checker explores a reduced model or bounded runs, and bugs needing longer executions slip through. It checks a model, not your code, and the two can drift apart. Covering every state takes a formal proof. TLA+ doesn't generate the implementation.

cards.title: Fault injection
cards.body:
**Fault injection** tests the real thing. You run your system somewhere like production, or in production itself (*chaos engineering*), and deliberately break things: crash machines, kill or pause processes, unmount disks, cut network links with firewall rules. Then you check that it still behaves.

A coordinator decides which faults to cause and when, and scripts on each node carry them out. Since that tooling is tedious to build, teams often use a framework such as Jepsen, which has found serious bugs in many popular databases.

The catch is control. Faults land at roughly chosen moments, not at an exact point in each node's execution, so a bug seen once may never recur.

cards.prompt: A team has checked its replication protocol's TLA+ spec with a model checker and found no bugs. Why run fault injection tests as well?
choices: To prove the invariants hold in every state, which a model checker can't do
To replay each failing run step by step, which a model checker can't do
To measure performance, since the model checker has ruled out correctness bugs
To test the real implementation, which can have bugs the spec doesn't
cards.explanation: A model checker examines a simplified spec, while fault injection breaks the running system itself, so it finds bugs where the code strays from the spec. It proves nothing about every state; only a formal proof does that. It can't control timing finely enough to replay a run. And a clean model check says nothing about the code.

cards.title: Deterministic simulation
cards.body:
**Deterministic simulation testing** (DST) explores many situations like a model checker, but runs your real code. Network calls, disk I/O and clocks are swapped for mocks, so a simulator decides exactly when each message arrives, each timer fires and each fault strikes.

It then runs huge numbers of randomized executions, each driven by a seed. Because the simulator controls every step, a failing run can be replayed exactly, as often as you like, until the bug is found. Fault injection can't do that.

Mocked clocks bring a bonus: a simulated timeout fires instantly instead of after real seconds, so tests run faster than real time and cover more paths.

cards.prompt: A rare bug shows up once in thousands of fault injection runs, and the team can never reproduce it. Which technique would let them replay the failing run exactly?
choices: Deterministic simulation testing of the real code, with I/O and clocks mocked
Model checking, which replays the failing run step by step against the production code
Chaos engineering in production, so that the bug shows up more often
More detailed logging, which makes each run follow the same schedule
cards.explanation: A simulator that controls every message, timer and failure knows the exact order of events, so a failing run can be repeated step by step. Model checkers run a model, not the code. Injecting faults in production finds bugs but can't control their timing. Logs describe a run; they don't make the next one the same.

cards.title: Making code deterministic
cards.body:
DST needs control over every source of nondeterminism, at one of three levels. An *application* can be built for it, with a hook for a simulated network, or with all state changes in one event loop and mocked clocks. At the *runtime* level, a single-threaded runtime runs async code in a fixed order, or deterministic stand-ins replace common libraries. At the *machine* level, a custom hypervisor answers every normally unpredictable call, from clocks to disk, the same way each time.

Some nondeterminism still hides. In some languages, a hash table's iteration order can change between runs, and whether you hit a memory or stack limit varies too.

cards.prompt: Deterministic simulation needs control over every source of nondeterminism. At which levels can that control be added?
keyPoints: Application: the system is built so a simulated network, or a single event loop with mocked clocks, can be plugged in
Runtime: a single-threaded runtime or deterministic library replacements run the async code in a fixed order
Machine: a custom hypervisor makes every normally nondeterministic call, from clocks to disk, deterministic
cards.explanation: Mocked clocks also let simulated timeouts fire at once, so tests run faster than real time.

cards.prompt: A team mocks the network, disk, clock and random numbers, and runs a simulation on one thread. Two runs from the same seed still diverge. What's a likely cause?
choices: The mocked clock, which still drifts the way a quartz crystal does
TCP retransmissions, which happen underneath the mocked network
The simulator, which delivers mocked messages in a random order each time
Iterating over a hash table, whose order can differ between runs
cards.explanation: Some languages don't fix the iteration order of hash tables, a nondeterminism that survives mocking; running into memory or stack limits is another. A mocked clock is code, not quartz. With the network mocked, no real TCP is involved. The simulator's choices come from the seed, so the same seed gives the same order.

cards.title: One machine if you can
cards.body:
Everything in this chapter, lost messages, drifting clocks, frozen processes, comes from spreading work across machines. One machine handles a great deal these days, and if an embedded database on one node meets your needs, staying there spares you all of it.

But scale isn't the only reason to distribute. Surviving a machine failure takes more than one machine, and so does keeping data close to users on different continents. Done well, a distributed system can in principle run forever, since every fault and every upgrade is handled one node at a time. Even so, a bad configuration pushed to every node at once can take it all down.

cards.prompt: A workload fits easily on one machine. What can still justify making it distributed?
choices: Surviving machine failures, or serving users far apart with low latency
Easier debugging, since each node does less and fails more simply
More predictable behavior, since spreading the work evens out timing
Nothing: spreading out a system only pays off once one machine can't keep up
cards.explanation: Fault tolerance and placing data near users need several machines, however light the load. Otherwise, staying on one machine avoids a whole class of problems. Distribution makes debugging harder, not easier, and adds nondeterminism rather than removing it. Scale is only one reason to distribute.

cards.title: Eventual or strong consistency
cards.body:
Replication keeps copies of your data on several nodes, and copies can disagree. There are two broad ways to live with that.

With **eventual consistency**, the replication shows through. A read may return stale data, replicas that took writes at the same time may conflict, and your application has to cope. Multi-leader and leaderless systems usually work this way, and an app that lets people edit while offline has no other option.

With **strong consistency**, the system hides its replicas and acts like a single node. That's far simpler to program against, but it costs performance, and some faults that an eventually consistent system shrugs off cause an outage instead. It suits replicas in datacenters with fast, reliable links.

cards.prompt: A field inspection app lets inspectors edit the same records on tablets while offline for days, syncing when they're back in range. Which approach to consistency can it use?
choices: Strong consistency, provided the server sits in a nearby datacenter
Linearizability, by making each tablet the leader for its own edits
Strong consistency, as long as each sync uses quorum reads and writes
Eventual consistency, with the app expecting and resolving conflicts
cards.explanation: Edits made while disconnected can't be checked against anyone else's, so copies diverge for a while and conflicts must be handled: that's eventual consistency.
