A nearby server doesn't help a tablet that can't reach it. A leader per tablet is multi-leader replication, which isn't linearizable. Quorums at sync time come too late to stop conflicting offline edits.

cards.title: Linearizability
cards.body:
Say you refresh a ticket site, see a concert sold out, and tell a friend. They refresh a second later and are offered seats, because their request hit a lagging replica. **Linearizability** forbids that. The system acts as if there were one copy of the data, and each operation takes effect atomically at one instant between its request and its response.

A read that overlaps a write may return the old or the new value. But once the write has completed, or any read has returned the new value, every read that starts later sees that value or a newer one. So it's a **recency guarantee**: the strongest model in common use, including weaker ones like read-after-write and monotonic reads.

cards.prompt: What does linearizability promise, and why is it called a recency guarantee?
keyPoints: The system acts as if there were one copy of the data, however many replicas exist
Each operation takes effect atomically, at a single instant between its request and its response
Once a write completes, or any read returns the new value, every read that starts later sees that value or a newer one
It includes weaker guarantees such as read-after-write and monotonic reads, and is the strongest model in common use
cards.explanation: Reads that overlap a write may return the old or the new value, but never flip back to the old one after anyone has seen the new.

cards.prompt: A feature flag is off, and an admin's request to turn it on is still in progress. Client A reads 'on'; client B starts a read just after A's returns. In a linearizable system, what can B get?
choices: Either value, since B's read overlaps the admin's unfinished write
'Off', since the write hasn't been acknowledged to the admin yet
Only 'on', since A has already seen the new value
No answer until the admin's write is acknowledged
cards.explanation: Linearizability treats the write as taking effect at one instant. A's read shows that instant has passed, so any read starting afterwards must see 'on', whether or not the write has finished. Overlapping reads may return either value only until someone sees the new one. Reads never have to wait for the writer's acknowledgment.

cards.title: Not the same as serializability
cards.body:
The names sound alike, but they promise different things.

**Serializability** is about transactions over many objects. They must give the same result as if they ran one at a time in *some* order, and that order needn't match real time. So a transaction can be placed before one that really committed earlier, and read stale data.

**Linearizability** is about single objects, such as one key or one row. It never groups operations into transactions, so it can't stop write skew: two clients each check one object, then write another, and together break a rule both checked. But it is a recency guarantee, which serializability isn't. A database with both is **strictly serializable**; otherwise each can be chosen separately.

cards.prompt: Which of these can happen in a database that guarantees serializability but not linearizability?
choices: Two transactions interleave so that the result matches no serial order
A transaction that starts after another has committed doesn't see its writes
Two transactions each check a premise, then together make writes that break it
A transaction reads data that another transaction hasn't committed yet
cards.explanation: Serializability only promises some serial order, which may differ from real time, so a later transaction can be placed before an earlier one and read stale data. Non-serial interleavings, write skew and dirty reads are all things serializability rules out. A database that guarantees both is called strictly serializable.

cards.prompt: A store is linearizable per key, with no multi-key transactions. Two operators each check that the other of two backup generators is on, then switch off their own. What can happen?
choices: Both end up off: linearizability doesn't prevent write skew across keys
The second check sees the first switch-off, so one operator stops
One write is rejected, since a linearizable store aborts conflicting writes
Both end up off, but only if one check read a stale replica
cards.explanation: Linearizability covers single objects: each read and write is up to date, but nothing ties a check and a later write into one unit. Both checks can run before either write, so each sees the other generator on. The writes touch different keys, so nothing conflicts, and no stale read is needed. Preventing this takes serializable transactions.

cards.title: When you need linearizability
cards.body:
Some jobs need every node to see one up-to-date value. Electing a leader is one. Say several servers each try to grab a **lease**, a lock with a time limit, so only one runs the nightly billing. Taking it means checking it's free and claiming it in one step. If two could both succeed, you'd get split brain, so this must be linearizable; coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd exist for it.

Hard constraints are the same: a unique email address, a balance that never goes negative, a seat sold once. But if breaking the rule now and then is fine, because you can apologize and compensate, as airlines do when they overbook, a looser check will do.

cards.prompt: Nodes elect a leader by writing their name to a lease key if it's empty. The key is in a store that replicates asynchronously and serves reads from any replica. What's the danger?
choices: None, as long as the replicas eventually agree on a single holder
Taking the lease is slow, since asynchronous replication waits for every follower
Two nodes may each see the key as empty on different replicas and both become leader
None: two writes to an empty key can't conflict with each other
cards.explanation: Taking a lease is a check-then-set that must see the latest value, so it needs linearizability. With stale replicas, two nodes can both find the key free and both act as leader: split brain. Agreeing later is too late, since both have already acted. Two writes to the same empty key do conflict, and asynchronous replication doesn't wait for followers.

cards.prompt: A bakery's preorder site now and then sells one more cake than it can bake that day. When it happens, staff apologize, refund the buyer and add a voucher. Does the stock check need linearizability?
choices: Yes: any limit on stock is a hard constraint that needs a linearizable check
No: the business accepts a rare oversell and makes up for it afterwards
Yes, unless every order is handled by a single web server
No, because only uniqueness constraints ever need linearizability
cards.explanation: Linearizability matters when a constraint must never be broken, even briefly. If occasional violations are acceptable and can be put right with an apology and compensation, a looser check will do. A single web server doesn't make a replicated database linearizable. And hard limits on balances, stock or seats need it just as much as uniqueness does.

cards.title: Races between two channels
cards.body:
Linearizability also matters when information has a second path. Picture a cafe: the cashier saves your order in a replicated database, then calls out to the barista, who checks the order screen. If the screen reads a replica the order hasn't reached, the barista finds nothing, though the cashier finished first.

Machines race the same way. A service writes data to one system, then sends a message through another, such as a queue or a push notification. The message can outrun the data's replication, so the receiver reads an old version.

A linearizable data store removes the race. If you control the second channel, there are other workarounds, but they add complexity.

cards.prompt: When a user replaces a receipt scan, a web server writes the new file to a replicated file store and, once that succeeds, queues a job for an OCR worker. Sometimes the worker reads the old scan. What's the most likely cause?
choices: Messages in the queue were reordered, so an older job for that receipt ran last
The file write was acknowledged before it reached the disk
The queue isn't linearizable, and fixing that would solve it
The job arrived before the new file reached the replica the worker read
cards.explanation: Server and worker talk over two channels, and the queue can outrun the file store's internal replication, so the worker hits a lagging replica. A linearizable file store would prevent it; the stale data doesn't come from the queue. Job order doesn't matter when the worker reads whatever the store returns, and durability only matters after a crash.

cards.title: Which replication is linearizable
cards.body:
The simplest linearizable system keeps one copy of the data, but then one failed node takes it all. So which replication methods can be linearizable?

**Single-leader** can be, if every read and write goes to the leader. That assumes you truly know who leads: a node that wrongly believes it's still the leader breaks it, and asynchronous failover can lose confirmed writes. **Consensus** algorithms are likely linearizable, since they're built to prevent split brain, but reads must be confirmed with a quorum too, because a node answering alone may have been replaced. **Multi-leader** isn't: several nodes take writes at once and sync later. **Leaderless** probably isn't, even with quorums, and last write wins on time-of-day clocks almost certainly isn't.

cards.prompt: Which replication methods can be linearizable? Cover single-leader, consensus, multi-leader and leaderless.
keyPoints: Single-leader: potentially, if all reads and writes go to the leader and no node wrongly believes it's still the leader
Consensus: likely, since it prevents split brain, as long as reads are also confirmed with a quorum
Multi-leader: no, since several nodes accept writes at once and replicate them asynchronously
Leaderless: probably not, even with quorums, and almost certainly not with last write wins on time-of-day clocks
cards.explanation: Sharding doesn't change any of this, since linearizability is about one object at a time.

cards.title: Quorums can still go stale
cards.body:
Quorums (w + r > n) don't make a leaderless store linearizable. They only promise that a read overlaps a write that has *finished*. While a write is still spreading, a reader whose quorum includes an updated replica returns the new value, and a reader starting just after, whose quorum doesn't, returns the old one. Both met the quorum rule; recency still broke.

The fix costs speed. Before answering, a reader must finish read repair: it takes the newest value its quorum returned, writes it to every replica in the quorum that's behind, and waits for them to confirm. Writers must first read the latest timestamp from a quorum, so theirs is larger. Compare-and-set still needs consensus.

cards.prompt: A leaderless store uses n = 5, w = 3, r = 3. A new bid has reached one replica, which reader A's quorum includes, so A returns the new bid; reader B starts after A finishes, misses that replica and returns the old bid. Is this allowed under linearizability?
choices: Yes: w + r > n, so every read overlaps the latest successful write
Yes: the write was still in progress, so either value is acceptable for any read
No: B began after A had returned the new bid, so B can't return an older one
No: B's read didn't reach a full quorum of replicas
cards.explanation: Once any read has returned the new value, every later read must too, finished write or not. The quorum rule only guarantees overlap with completed writes, and this one is still in progress. 'Either value' holds only until someone has seen the new one. B did read three replicas, a full quorum. Synchronous read repair by A would have prevented this.

cards.prompt: To make reads from a leaderless quorum store linearizable, order the steps a reader takes.
items: Send the read to the replicas and wait for a quorum to answer
Pick the value with the newest timestamp among the answers
Write that value to any replica in the quorum that returned an older one, and wait for confirmation
Return the value to the application
cards.explanation: Finishing the repair before returning is the key step, and it costs performance. Writers must first read the newest timestamp from a quorum so their write gets a larger one. Even then, compare-and-set can't be built this way; it needs consensus.

cards.title: When the network splits
cards.body:
A **network partition** is when nodes keep running but some can no longer reach the others. Say a chain of shops runs one database, with the leader at head office and a follower in each branch, and one branch's line to head office goes down.

With single-leader replication, every write and every linearizable read must reach the leader. Staff in the cut-off branch can still read their local follower, but what they see may be stale. If the app needs up-to-date reads and writes, it's down in that branch until the line is fixed, while the other branches carry on.

Multi-leader replication behaves differently: each site keeps accepting writes and swaps them with the others once the network heals.

cards.prompt: A single-leader database has its leader in one region and a follower in another. The link between the regions fails, though clients can still reach their local region. What can clients in the follower's region still do?
choices: Read from the follower, possibly stale data; no writes or linearizable reads
Read and write as normal, with writes queued until the link returns
Nothing at all: the follower stops serving until it reaches the leader
Write to the follower, which acts as a second leader until the link comes back
cards.explanation: Writes and linearizable reads have to go through the leader, which they can't reach, so an app that needs them is down in that region. Stale reads from the local follower still work. Queuing writes per region is how multi-leader replication behaves. A follower acting as a second leader is split brain.

cards.title: The CAP theorem
cards.body:
That dilemma isn't peculiar to single-leader setups. When a fault cuts some replicas off, any linearizable system must choose: those replicas either wait or return errors, staying consistent but unavailable, or answer on their own, staying available but not linearizable. That trade-off is the **CAP theorem**.

It's often summed up as 'pick two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance', which misleads. Partitions are faults; they happen whether you choose them or not. While the network works, you get both consistency and availability, and you choose only during a partition. So read it as *consistent or available when partitioned*.

Its scope is narrow, too: only linearizability, only partitions, and an odd definition of availability, so it says little about real designs.

cards.prompt: What does the CAP theorem actually say, and why is 'pick two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance' misleading?
keyPoints: Network partitions are faults that will occur sooner or later, so they aren't something you choose
While the network works, a system can be both linearizable and available
During a partition, replicas cut off from the rest must either stop serving requests or give up linearizability
Its scope is narrow: only linearizability, only partitions, and an unusual definition of availability
cards.explanation: A better phrasing is 'consistent or available when partitioned'. PACELC adds that even without a partition, systems trade consistency against latency.

cards.title: Linearizability is slow
cards.body:
Even the RAM in a multi-core computer isn't linearizable. Each core keeps its own cache and store buffer and writes changes back to main memory later, so another core may read an old value unless the code uses a memory barrier. Cores aren't expected to survive being cut off, so fault tolerance isn't the reason: caches are just much faster.

Many distributed databases drop linearizability for the same reason, speed. Linearizable operations are slower constantly, faults or no faults. And no cleverer algorithm helps: it's proven that their response time grows at least in proportion to how uncertain network delays are. With highly variable delays they're bound to be slow, while weaker models can be much faster.

cards.prompt: A thread on one CPU core sets a flag in memory, and a thread on another core reads it a moment later but sees the old value. Why do CPUs allow this?
choices: So each core can carry on working even if it loses contact with the rest of the machine
For speed: each core works from its own cache, and writes reach main memory later
It's a hardware defect that memory barriers were invented to work around
Because RAM can't apply two operations to one address at the same time
cards.explanation: Per-core caches and store buffers make memory fast but leave several copies updated asynchronously, so memory isn't linearizable without a barrier. Cores aren't expected to survive being cut off, so fault tolerance doesn't explain it, and CAP doesn't apply. It's a deliberate design choice, not a defect. Many distributed databases drop linearizability for the same reason: speed.

cards.prompt: Why do many distributed databases choose not to be linearizable, and why can't a smarter algorithm remove the cost?
keyPoints: The main reason is performance, not tolerating network faults
Linearizable systems pay higher latency all the time, not just during a fault
It's proven that linearizable reads and writes take time at least proportional to how uncertain network delays are
On networks with highly variable delays, that makes them inevitably slow; weaker models can be much faster

cards.title: Distributed ID generators
cards.body:
One autoincrementing counter makes good IDs: 64 bits, sorted in creation order. But its node can fail, become a bottleneck, or sit a slow round trip from distant regions.

Spreading the work out costs that order. Nodes can own some bits of the ID, one handing out odd numbers and another even, or claim blocks of IDs in advance. Both keep IDs compact, but a later record may get a lower ID from another node. Random **UUIDs** need no coordination, but they're 128 bits and unordered. A wall-clock timestamp in the high bits, plus a node number or random bits, sorts roughly by time, but skew or a clock stepping back can misorder IDs, even on one node.

cards.prompt: Besides one autoincrementing counter, how can a distributed system assign IDs, and what does each option give up?
keyPoints: Shard bits in the ID, such as odd and even nodes: compact, but IDs from different nodes aren't in creation order
Preallocated blocks per node: also out of order, since a later record can get an ID from a lower block
Random UUIDs: no coordination at all, but 128 bits and in random order
A wall-clock timestamp plus unique bits: roughly ordered, but skew or a clock jumping back can misorder them, even on one node
cards.explanation: A single counter keeps creation order, but it's a single point of failure, a possible bottleneck and a long round trip for distant regions.

cards.title: Lamport clocks
cards.body:
A **logical clock** counts events rather than measuring time. Its timestamps can't tell you the hour, but they're compact, unique and comparable, and they respect causality: if one event happened before another, it gets the smaller timestamp. The distributed ID schemes above fail that test.

A **Lamport clock** is the classic one. A timestamp is a pair: a counter and the ID of the node that made it. A node adds one to its counter each time it makes a timestamp, and whenever it sees a timestamp with a larger counter, it first raises its own counter to that value. Compare timestamps by counter, then by node ID. That's a total order consistent with causality.

cards.prompt: How does a Lamport clock create, update and compare timestamps?
keyPoints: A timestamp is a pair: a counter and the ID of the node that made it
A node increments its counter each time it creates a timestamp
When a node sees a timestamp whose counter is higher than its own, it raises its counter to match
Compare counters first; equal counters are ordered by node ID
cards.explanation: This gives unique, compact, totally ordered timestamps consistent with causality, but not linearizability: nothing is promised about timestamps a node hasn't seen.

cards.prompt: Nodes fig, kiwi, lime and plum use Lamport clocks, all starting at 0, with ties broken by node name. Order these events by timestamp, smallest first.
items: Fig's first event, created before it has heard from anyone
Kiwi's first event, created before it has heard from anyone
Lime's first event, created after receiving fig's and kiwi's events
Plum's second event, created last of all; plum has never heard from anyone
Fig's second event, created after receiving lime's event
cards.explanation: The timestamps are (1, fig), (1, kiwi), (2, lime), (2, plum) and (3, fig); node names break ties. Plum's event came last in real time but sorts earlier, because plum never learned the others' counters.

cards.title: Hybrid and vector clocks
cards.body:
Lamport timestamps have two weak spots. They have no link to real time, so you can't ask for everything from Tuesday. And two nodes that rarely talk can show wildly different counters for events at the same moment.

A **hybrid logical clock** fixes both. It counts physical time but jumps ahead to any larger timestamp it receives, and it increments on every timestamp, so it never runs backwards, even if the physical clock does.

Neither kind can reliably show that two events were concurrent; they order such events arbitrarily. A **vector clock** can. It stores one counter per node with each write; if each of two writes is ahead on some node's counter, they were concurrent. The price is size.

cards.prompt: Which two limits of Lamport clocks do hybrid logical clocks fix, and how?
keyPoints: Lamport timestamps have no link to real time, so you can't find, say, all events on a given date
Counters on nodes that rarely communicate drift far apart, even for events at the same moment
A hybrid clock counts physical time units and, like a Lamport clock, jumps ahead to any larger timestamp it sees
It increments on every timestamp, so it never moves backwards even if the physical clock does
cards.explanation: The result reads almost like a time-of-day timestamp but respects happens-before, needing only roughly synchronized clocks and no special hardware.

cards.prompt: A sync service must notice when two edits were made concurrently, so it can keep both versions. Which kind of timestamp lets it tell?
choices: Lamport timestamps, since a lower counter means that edit happened first
Hybrid logical clocks, since they track physical time as well as causality
Timestamp-based IDs, provided every node keeps its clock synced with NTP
Vector clocks, which store one counter per node with each write
cards.explanation: With vector clocks, if each write is ahead of the other on some node's counter, neither came first, so they're concurrent. Lamport and hybrid clocks order concurrent events arbitrarily, so a lower counter doesn't prove one happened before the other. Wall-clock IDs are only roughly ordered. The cost: timestamps can hold one integer per node.

cards.title: Causal order isn't recency
cards.body:
A Lamport or hybrid clock only promises that a node's new timestamp beats every timestamp *it has seen*. Linearizability asks more: if one request finished before another began, the later one gets the larger ID, even if the two never shared a node or a message.

That gap bites when related writes land in different databases. Say you change a price in the catalog database, then announce a sale in the news database. If the news database never saw the price change, its clock may lag, giving the announcement the smaller timestamp. A reader whose MVCC snapshot falls between the two sees the sale at the old price. A linearizable ID generator is the simplest fix.

cards.prompt: An admin closes a poll in the polls database from a laptop, then publishes its results in the results database from a phone. Both databases stamp writes with hybrid logical clocks, and readers use MVCC snapshots. Why might a visitor see the results while the poll still looks open?
choices: The results database hadn't seen the close's timestamp, so its clock was behind
Hybrid logical clocks can step backwards when NTP adjusts the physical clock
Snapshot isolation lets readers see writes that haven't committed yet
The results were sent before the close had committed, so the two writes overlapped
cards.explanation: A logical clock only orders timestamps its node has seen. The results database never saw the close, so the later write could get a lower timestamp, and the visitor's snapshot could fall between the two. A linearizable ID generator would prevent this. Hybrid clocks never step back, snapshots exclude uncommitted writes, and the admin published only after closing.

cards.title: A linearizable ID generator
cards.body:
The simplest linearizable ID generator is one node with a counter. It atomically increments the counter per request, persists it so a restart can't issue duplicates, and replicates it to followers with single-leader replication.

To avoid a disk write and replication per ID, it reserves IDs in batches: it persists and replicates a record for the next batch, then hands those IDs out from memory. A crash or failover skips some IDs but never repeats or reorders them.

It can't easily be sharded or spread across regions, so distant clients pay a round trip. But the job is tiny, so one node serves many requests. Spanner instead waits out its clock's uncertainty, which needs tightly synced clock hardware.

cards.prompt: How do you build a linearizable ID generator that survives crashes, and what are its limits?
keyPoints: One node atomically increments a counter, persists it, and replicates it to followers using single-leader replication
To avoid a disk write per ID, it persists and replicates one record per batch; a crash skips IDs but never repeats or reorders them
It can't easily be sharded or spread across regions, so distant clients wait a round trip
Its job is so simple that a single node can handle a high request rate
cards.explanation: The alternative, used by Spanner, is to wait out the clock's uncertainty interval, which needs tightly synchronized clocks and support for computing that interval.

cards.title: Clocks can't pick a winner
cards.body:
Could a logical clock replace a lock? Say several nodes want the same resource. Each stamps its request, and the lowest timestamp wins. With a linearizable clock, no later request can get a lower timestamp than the winner, so that part works.

The trouble is knowing you've won. A node can only be sure its timestamp is the lowest after hearing back from all the other nodes that could have made a request. If one of them has crashed or is cut off, everyone waits, because its timestamp might have been lower. That isn't fault tolerant.

For locks, leases and uniqueness constraints that survive faults, timestamps aren't enough. You need consensus.

cards.prompt: To register usernames without a central lock, each node stamps claims with a linearizable clock, and the lowest timestamp for a name wins. What's the flaw?
choices: A claim made later could still get a lower timestamp than the winner, and take the name
Two nodes could get identical timestamps for the same name, leaving no winner
A node can't know it won until every other node has replied, so one down node stalls it
It only works if every node's hardware clock is synchronized to within milliseconds
cards.explanation: A linearizable clock does stop later claims from undercutting the winner, and timestamps are unique. But to be sure it's lowest, a node must hear from everyone who might hold a lower claim, so one failed or unreachable node halts the system. A single counter can be linearizable without synced clocks. Fault-tolerant locks and uniqueness need consensus.

cards.title: One problem, many faces
cards.body:
Many things in this chapter are easy on one node and hard to make fault tolerant: a leader that fails over without split brain, an ID counter that survives a crash, a compare-and-set deciding who gets a lock or a username. They're all **consensus**: getting several nodes to agree on one outcome.

It has many forms: agreeing on one value, compare-and-set, appending to a shared log in one agreed order, atomic fetch-and-add, and committing a transaction across shards all or nothing. Surprisingly, they're equivalent: a solution to any one can be turned into one for the others, though fetch-and-add works only between two nodes. With one fixed node deciding everything, each is trivial; the hard part is surviving its failure.

cards.prompt: Why can locks, uniqueness constraints, compare-and-set, shared logs and atomic commit all be called consensus?
keyPoints: Each needs several nodes to agree on one outcome, such as who holds a lock or which entry comes next
They're equivalent: a solution to any one can be turned into a solution to the others
Each is easy on one node or with one fixed decision-maker; the hard part is fault tolerance
cards.explanation: Fetch-and-add is the exception: it solves consensus only between two nodes.

cards.title: The FLP result
cards.body:
The well-known algorithms, Paxos, Raft, Zab and Viewstamped Replication, assume that nodes may crash, restart or be cut off, and that messages may be delayed or lost, but that nodes never lie. Tolerating malicious, *Byzantine* nodes is a separate field.

The **FLP result** proves that no algorithm can always reach consensus if a node may crash. That sounds fatal, but read the fine print. It's about guaranteeing that the algorithm *terminates*, and it assumes a deterministic algorithm in the asynchronous model, which has no clocks and so no timeouts. Let nodes suspect a crash after a timeout, even if they're sometimes wrong, or let them use random numbers, and consensus becomes solvable. Real systems reach it in practice.

cards.prompt: The FLP result proves that no algorithm can always reach consensus if a node may crash. Why do real systems manage it anyway?
choices: FLP applies only to Byzantine nodes, and real systems assume honest ones
FLP rules out clocks, timeouts and randomness; with any of them, it's solvable
Real systems use hardware that keeps nodes from crashing during a vote
Real systems drop agreement and let nodes decide differently for a short while
cards.explanation: FLP assumes a deterministic algorithm in the asynchronous model, with no clocks. Timeouts that sometimes wrongly suspect a crash, or random choices, are enough to get around it. FLP is about guaranteed termination, and it concerns crash faults, not Byzantine ones. Crashes can't be ruled out, and deciding differently wouldn't be consensus at all.

cards.title: Single-value consensus
cards.body:
In its classic form, one or more nodes propose values and the algorithm decides on one. Several nodes might each propose themselves as leader, or several buyers the same last ticket. To decide many things, such as every seat in a hall, run a separate instance for each.

The algorithm must guarantee four properties. **Uniform agreement**: every node that decides picks the same value. **Integrity**: once a node decides, it never changes its mind. **Validity**: the decided value was proposed by some node, which rules out cheats like always deciding null. **Termination**: every node that doesn't crash eventually decides. The first three are *safety* properties; termination is the *liveness* property, and it's where fault tolerance comes in.

cards.prompt: What four properties must a single-value consensus algorithm have?
keyPoints: Uniform agreement: no two nodes reach different decisions
Integrity: a node never changes a decision once made
Validity: whatever is decided was proposed by some node
Termination: every node that stays up eventually decides, even if others fail
cards.explanation: Termination is the liveness property that makes it fault tolerant; the other three are safety properties. Validity rules out cheats such as always deciding null.

cards.title: Termination needs a majority
cards.body:
Agreement, integrity and validity are easy without fault tolerance: let one fixed node, a dictator, make every decision. If it fails, though, nothing gets decided, like a single-leader database waiting for a person to fail over by hand. Termination forbids that: the remaining nodes must decide, even if the failed one never returns.

There's a limit. Any consensus algorithm needs a majority of its nodes working to guarantee termination, and that majority serves as a quorum. Lose more and it stalls. But good algorithms keep the safety properties however many nodes fail and however badly the network behaves, so a big outage can stop decisions without ever making them inconsistent.

cards.prompt: A single-leader database fails over only when an on-call admin promotes a follower. Judged as a consensus algorithm, which property does it lack?
choices: None: it has all four properties, as long as the admin acts correctly
Integrity, since replacing a leader means changing an earlier decision
Uniform agreement, since the followers don't vote on the new leader
Termination, since nothing gets decided until a human steps in
cards.explanation: Termination requires the algorithm to make progress on its own, even if the failed node never returns; manual failover stays stuck until someone reacts. A careful admin can keep the safety properties, but that isn't the system deciding by itself. Each leader choice is a separate decision, so replacing one doesn't break integrity. Agreement is about deciding differently, not about voting.

cards.prompt: A five-node consensus cluster loses three nodes in a power failure. What happens until enough of them return?
choices: The two survivors elect a leader and keep accepting writes
It stops making decisions, but it won't make inconsistent ones
It keeps serving linearizable reads but rejects writes
The survivors may decide conflicting values, to be reconciled later
cards.explanation: Termination needs a majority of nodes working, and two of five isn't one. Well-designed algorithms keep agreement, integrity and validity even then, so the cluster stalls rather than corrupting its decisions. Linearizable reads need a quorum too, so they stop as well.

cards.title: Compare-and-set as consensus
cards.body:
**Compare-and-set** (CAS) sets an object to a new value only if it still holds an expected one; otherwise it changes nothing and returns an error.

A fault-tolerant, linearizable CAS gives you consensus. Start with the object empty, and let each node propose by trying to change it from empty to its own value. Only the first succeeds, and whatever the object holds is the decision.

It works the other way too. When callers try CAS with the same expected value, run consensus on their new values, write the winner, and fail the rest; calls with another expected value get their own run. So the two are equivalent. Conditional writes in object stores are an everyday CAS across machines.

cards.prompt: How can a fault-tolerant compare-and-set (CAS) give you consensus, and consensus give you CAS?
keyPoints: Consensus from CAS: start a register at null and have each proposer CAS it from null to its own value
Whichever value the register ends up holding is the decision
CAS from consensus: callers with the same expected value propose their new values; the decided one is written and the others get an error
cards.explanation: CAS calls with different expected values each need their own run of consensus. Conditional writes in object stores are an everyday example of CAS across machines.

cards.title: Shared logs
cards.body:
A **shared log** is one that many nodes can append to and everyone reads in the same order. Single-leader replication has one: any client's write enters the leader's log, and every follower applies it in that order. Requested entries eventually appear, none are lost, none change or get slipped in before ones already read, and every node sees the same sequence. This is also called **total order broadcast**.

A shared log gives you consensus: everyone appends a proposal, and the first entry wins. To build a log from consensus, run a separate instance per slot. A value that loses its slot is proposed again for a later one, and a slot joins the log once all earlier slots are decided.

cards.prompt: Given a fault-tolerant single-value consensus algorithm, how can you build a shared log?
choices: Decide each slot with its own consensus run; a losing value retries in a later slot
Run consensus once to elect a writer, which then appends entries without further votes
Have each node keep its own log, and merge the logs by timestamp
Run consensus only when two nodes try to append at the same moment
cards.explanation: Each slot's value is fixed once decided, and it joins the log once all earlier slots are decided too. A single elected writer with no further votes is single-leader replication without failover, which stalls if that writer dies. Merging by timestamp needs to hear from every node before an entry is final. And a node can't reliably tell that another append is happening at once.

cards.title: Fetch-and-add
cards.body:
**Fetch-and-add** atomically adds one to a counter and returns the old value. You can build it from CAS: read the counter, CAS it to that value plus one, and retry if someone beat you.

The reverse only half works. Let nodes race on a counter starting at 0; whoever reads 0 wins. Each loser knows it lost, but not who won. If the winner crashes before announcing itself, the losers are stuck, and can't settle on someone else, since the winner may return and rightly decide its own value. With exactly two nodes that swap proposals first, it works. So fetch-and-add has *consensus number* 2, while CAS and shared logs work for any number.

cards.prompt: Nodes race on a fault-tolerant fetch-and-add counter that starts at 0, and whoever reads 0 wins. Why doesn't this solve consensus for three or more nodes?
choices: Two nodes could both read 0 if their calls arrive at the same moment
Fetch-and-add can't be made fault tolerant, so a crash loses the counter's value
Each loser reads a different number, so the nodes disagree on the result
Losers don't learn who won, and if the winner crashes first, they can't decide
cards.explanation: Atomicity ensures exactly one node reads 0, but the others learn only that they lost. If the winner crashes before telling them, they're stuck, and they can't pick someone else because the winner may return and decide its own value. The numbers read aren't decisions. With two nodes that swap proposals first, the loser knows the winner's value: fetch-and-add has consensus number 2.

cards.title: Atomic commitment
cards.body:
**Atomic commitment** makes every database or shard in a distributed transaction either commit it or abort it, together. Two-phase commit solves it, but it can stall if its lone coordinator fails.

It resembles consensus with one key difference. Consensus may decide any proposed value; atomic commit must respect every vote. Its **validity** property says a node may commit only if all participants voted commit, and if any voted abort, all must abort. A **nontriviality** property stops it from simply always aborting: if everyone votes commit and no message times out, it must commit. Agreement, integrity and termination mean much the same as in consensus.

Even so, the two problems are equivalent: each can be built from the other.

cards.prompt: How does atomic commitment differ from single-value consensus?
keyPoints: Validity: it may commit only if every participant voted commit, and must abort if any voted abort, whereas consensus may pick any proposed value
Nontriviality: if all vote commit and nothing times out, it must commit, so always aborting isn't allowed
Agreement, integrity and termination work essentially as in consensus
cards.explanation: Despite the differences, the problems are equivalent: either can be built from the other.

cards.title: Atomic commit from consensus
cards.body:
To build atomic commit on consensus, every node first sends its vote to all the others. A node that hears 'commit' from everyone, itself included, proposes 'commit' to the consensus algorithm. A node that hears an 'abort', or gives up waiting on someone, proposes 'abort'. Then every node does whatever consensus decides.

That meets the rules. 'Commit' is proposed only when every vote was commit, so only then can it win. If anyone voted abort, every proposal is 'abort'. And all nodes follow one decision, so they never split.

The reverse works too: propose a value by running a transaction on a quorum that sets a register via a local CAS; a committed value is decided.

cards.prompt: Atomic commit is built on consensus: nodes swap votes, then propose 'commit' if every vote was yes, or 'abort' otherwise or after a timeout. All voted yes, but one node timed out waiting for a vote. What happens?
choices: The transaction must abort, since any 'abort' proposal forces an abort
The transaction must commit, since every participant actually voted yes
Consensus picks one of the proposals, and every node follows it, whichever it is
The nodes that proposed 'commit' commit, and the rest abort
cards.explanation: Since everyone voted yes, either outcome is valid: nontriviality allows an abort when communication times out. What matters is that all nodes do the same thing, which consensus guarantees. One 'abort' proposal doesn't force the result here, and the votes alone don't force a commit. Nodes acting on their own proposals would break atomicity.

cards.title: What shared logs give you
cards.body:
Most consensus systems offer a shared log: Raft, Zab and Viewstamped Replication directly, and Paxos through Multi-Paxos.

If each entry is a write and every replica applies the entries in log order with deterministic code, all replicas end in the same state. That's **state machine replication**, the idea behind event sourcing. If each entry is a deterministic transaction run as a stored procedure, running them in log order makes them serializable.

Other forms of consensus fall out easily. The first entry naming a key decides that key, say one per parking space. A counter is the sum of entries so far, and numbering entries gives fencing tokens. Sharded databases often keep one log per shard, weakening cross-shard guarantees.

cards.prompt: Most consensus systems provide a shared log. What can you build on one?
keyPoints: State machine replication: every replica applies the logged writes in log order with deterministic code, so all end in the same state
Serializable transactions: run each logged transaction as a deterministic stored procedure, in log order
Single-value consensus and CAS: the first entry for a given key or object decides it
Fetch-and-add and fencing tokens: sum the entries, or number them in sequence
cards.explanation: Sharded databases often keep one log per shard, which scales but weakens guarantees that span shards.

cards.title: Leaders and epochs
cards.body:
Older single-leader databases left failover to a human: downtime, and no termination. Consensus must elect leaders automatically, which looks circular: to avoid split brain, nodes must agree on the leader, and agreeing seems to need a leader.

The way out is a weaker promise. Each period of leadership gets an **epoch number**, a term in Raft or a ballot in Paxos, with at most one leader per epoch. When a node hears nothing from the leader before a timeout, it calls an election with a higher epoch than any before, and wins if a quorum votes for it. Two leaders may briefly coexist, say if the old one was only paused, but the higher epoch wins any conflict.

cards.prompt: Consensus seems to need a single leader, yet electing one needs consensus. How do leader-based algorithms like Raft and Paxos get around this?
choices: They rely on synchronized clocks so that leader leases never overlap
An administrator picks the first leader, and each leader then names its successor
They allow several leaders at once and merge their logs afterwards
They allow at most one leader per epoch, and the higher epoch wins any conflict
cards.explanation: Each election gets a larger epoch number (a term in Raft, a ballot in Paxos), and the leader is unique only within it. Two leaders can briefly coexist, but the one with the lower epoch can't get entries accepted. Clock-based leases aren't safe on their own, named successors fail if the leader dies first, and merging logs would break agreement.

cards.title: A vote on every entry
cards.body:
Before a leader appends an entry, it asks a quorum, usually a majority, to accept it. A node says yes only if it knows of no leader with a higher epoch. The client hears of success only once the entry has reached that quorum, so losing the leader can't lose it.

This is safe because quorums overlap: any quorum accepting an entry shares a node with the quorum of the latest election. If no voter knows a newer epoch, there's no newer leader.

That's two votes: one to elect, one per entry. It resembles two-phase commit, but in consensus any node can call an election and a quorum suffices, while 2PC needs its coordinator and a yes from every participant.

cards.prompt: In a five-node cluster, N1 led epoch 6 and then froze; N2 won epoch 7 with votes from N2, N3 and N4. N1 wakes up, unaware, and asks for votes on a new entry. Why can't that entry be appended?
choices: Any majority it gathers includes a node that voted in epoch 7, which refuses
Its lease has run out, and its own local clock tells it to stop acting as leader
N5 forwards the request to the new leader, N2, which rejects it
N2 wiped N1's log entries as soon as it took over
cards.explanation: A majority is three of five, and only N1 and N5 missed the epoch 7 vote, so any three include N2, N3 or N4. They know of a higher epoch and vote no, which also tells N1 it's been replaced. Safety comes from overlapping quorums, not from clocks or forwarding, and a new leader keeps confirmed entries rather than wiping them.

cards.prompt: A consensus algorithm votes twice: once to elect a leader, then once per proposed entry. How does this differ from two-phase commit?
choices: In 2PC any participant may call a vote, and a majority of yes votes is enough for it to commit
They're the same protocol under different names, with the consensus leader playing the coordinator's part
Consensus needs a yes from every node, so unlike 2PC it blocks if one node is down
Consensus lets any node call an election and needs only a quorum; 2PC needs all participants' yes
cards.explanation: 2PC can't proceed without its coordinator or with one participant missing, which is why it blocks. Consensus tolerates a minority of failures, and if the leader dies, another node can start an election. The other choices reverse the roles, or ignore who may start a vote and how many must answer.

cards.title: Taking over as leader
cards.body:
A new leader must keep every entry its predecessor confirmed. Raft lets a node win only when its log is no less current than a majority's. Paxos lets any node win but makes it catch up before appending entries of its own. Either way, it must be up to date before serving writes or linearizable reads, or it could refill slots that already hold entries, breaking the log.

Some systems relax this to recover faster, or at all: an option lets a lagging replica become leader, and with asynchronous replication no follower is sure to be current anyway. You gain availability, but consensus theory no longer protects you, and faults can lose confirmed data.

cards.prompt: In a leader-based consensus algorithm, order how a new leader takes over and appends its first entry.
items: A follower hears nothing from the leader before its timeout expires
It starts an election with an epoch number higher than any before, and a quorum votes for it
As leader, it first catches up on any entries the old leader had confirmed
It proposes the next entry, and a quorum accepts it, none knowing of a higher epoch
It appends the entry and confirms the write to the client
cards.explanation: Raft skips the catch-up by only electing a node whose log is no less current than a majority's; Paxos lets any node win but makes it catch up first.

cards.prompt: A message broker can let a replica that's behind become leader when no up-to-date replica is available. What does turning this on trade?
choices: Faster recovery, at the risk of losing entries that were already confirmed
Lower write latency, at the cost of slower reads from followers
Stronger consistency, at the cost of longer outages
Nothing: the new leader fetches missing entries from the old leader before serving
cards.explanation: A stale leader can write new entries into slots the old leader already filled, breaking the append-only log, and consensus theory no longer protects you. What you gain is availability: the system recovers instead of waiting. It weakens consistency rather than strengthening it, and the old leader is usually gone, so there's nothing to fetch from.

cards.title: Replication done right
cards.body:
Think of consensus as single-leader replication done right. It fails over automatically when the leader dies, never loses a write once it's confirmed, and never lets two leaders both commit writes, even under the faults of the previous chapter: lost and delayed messages, long process pauses, partitions and crashes.

Many systems instead bolt automatic failover onto ordinary replication, with heartbeats and a timeout. Without a proven consensus algorithm underneath, that's likely unsafe. Delays and pauses have no upper limit, so no timeout rules them out, and they can leave a stale node in charge or two nodes both leading. A proven algorithm doesn't make your whole system correct, since bugs can hide elsewhere, but it's a good start.

cards.prompt: A database promotes a follower automatically when the leader misses heartbeats for ten seconds. It uses no consensus algorithm, and the team argues that ten seconds is far longer than any delay they've seen. What's wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Nothing: a timeout longer than any delay seen so far rules out having two leaders
Delays and pauses are unbounded, so a live leader can be ousted yet still act as leader
Ten seconds makes failover too slow to count as termination, so it isn't fault tolerant
Followers can't time missed heartbeats without synchronized clocks, so the timeout means nothing
cards.explanation: Network delays and process pauses have no upper limit, so a leader that is only slow can be declared dead and come back still believing it leads, causing split brain or lost writes. Past delays don't bound future ones. A slow failover still terminates; it just recovers later. A timeout needs only the follower's own clock, not synchronized ones.

cards.title: The cost of consensus
cards.body:
Consensus has a price. It needs a strict majority, more than half its nodes, working: three nodes survive one failure, five survive two. Every operation involves a quorum, so extra nodes add no throughput; each one makes it slower. In a partition, only the majority side makes progress.

It relies on timeouts to notice a dead leader, and those are hard to tune when delays vary, as across regions. Too long, and recovery is slow; too short, and needless elections eat the time meant for real work. There are nasty edge cases too: in Raft, one link that keeps failing while the rest of the network is fine can make leadership bounce endlessly, so nothing gets done.

cards.prompt: A team grows its consensus cluster from three nodes to four, hoping to survive two failures. How many failures can it now survive?
choices: One: a majority of four is three, so losing two halts it
Two, since two nodes are still left to form a majority between them
Two, as long as neither failed node is the leader
None, since a cluster with an even number of nodes can't elect a leader
cards.explanation: Progress needs a strict majority, and two of four isn't one, so four nodes tolerate one failure, the same as three. Surviving two takes five. Which node is leader doesn't change the count. Even-sized clusters can elect leaders; they just gain no tolerance while adding a node to every quorum.

cards.prompt: What does consensus cost, and when does it struggle?
keyPoints: It needs a strict majority working: three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two
Every operation involves a quorum, so adding nodes doesn't raise throughput; it slows things down
Timeouts are hard to tune with variable delays: too long means slow recovery, too short means endless elections
One consistently flaky link can make leadership bounce between nodes so that nothing gets done
cards.explanation: During a partition, only the side with a majority can make progress.

cards.title: Coordination services
cards.body:
**Coordination services** such as ZooKeeper and etcd look like key-value stores, but they're built to coordinate other distributed systems. They hold small, slowly changing data that fits in memory, replicated with consensus, and they aren't meant for heavy write loads.

On top of consensus they offer **locks and leases**, through a fault-tolerant CAS, so only one contender wins. They hand out **fencing tokens** from each log entry's ever-increasing ID. They do **failure detection**: a client keeps a session alive with heartbeats, and if they stop for too long, its leases and *ephemeral* entries are removed. And they send **change notifications**, so clients needn't poll. Those last two don't need consensus, but they're handy beside it.

cards.prompt: Besides holding small amounts of data, what do coordination services such as ZooKeeper and etcd offer, and which of these need consensus?
keyPoints: Locks and leases, built on a fault-tolerant CAS, so only one contender wins
Fencing tokens, taken from the monotonically increasing ID of each log entry
Failure detection: clients keep a session alive with heartbeats, and their leases and ephemeral entries go when it times out
Change notifications, so clients learn of changes without polling; this and failure detection don't need consensus
cards.explanation: They keep small, slowly changing data in memory, replicated by consensus, and aren't built for high write volumes. They can hold configuration too, though polling a file or URL also works.

cards.title: Handing out work
cards.body:
Coordination services shine at deciding who does what. One instance of a job scheduler can be made leader, with another taking over if it fails. Or a big system's shards can be assigned to nodes and moved as nodes join, leave or die. You build this from atomic operations, ephemeral entries and notifications, and the system heals itself without a person. Fencing stops a node that lost its role from doing harm: storage rejects a token older than one it has seen.

The service runs on a small fixed cluster, usually three or five nodes, however big the system, since consensus across thousands of nodes would crawl. Its data, such as shard leaders, changes over minutes or hours.

cards.prompt: A worker holds a lease on a shard through a coordination service, and the other workers watch the lease. The holder then freezes in a long pause. Order what happens.
items: The frozen worker's heartbeats to the service stop
The lease times out, and the service deletes the worker's ephemeral entry
The watchers are notified, and one of them takes the lease with a higher fencing token
The new holder writes to the shard's storage with its token
The frozen worker wakes and tries a write with its old token, which storage rejects
cards.explanation: Storage can reject the old token only once it has seen a higher one; the service derives tokens from its monotonically increasing log IDs.

cards.prompt: A storage system has 3,000 nodes and must keep track of which node leads each of its shards. Where should the consensus run?
choices: Across all 3,000 nodes, so every node takes part in each decision
Inside each shard's replicas only, with no shared view of assignments
On a coordination service of three or five nodes that the storage nodes use
Nowhere: shard leadership changes far too often for any consensus system to keep up
cards.explanation: Consensus slows down as nodes are added, so running it across thousands is very inefficient. A small, fixed coordination cluster can serve any number of clients, and assignments like 'node 12 leads shard 40' change over minutes or hours, which suits it. Without a shared view, nodes can't find or rebalance shards. Data changing thousands of times a second belongs elsewhere.

cards.title: Service discovery
cards.body:
**Service discovery** tells a client which address reaches a service. In the cloud, instances come and go, so each registers its address when it starts. A coordination service is a natural home: it already detects failures, notifies watchers, and may know which node leads.

But discovery rarely needs linearizability. It must be fast and always available, since when it stops, everything stops. So clients cache addresses, refresh them when a time-to-live (TTL) expires, and after a failed connection fetch the latest one and retry. DNS works this way, with layers of caching. ZooKeeper's *observers*, replicas that get the log but don't vote, serve possibly stale reads that stay available and add read capacity.

cards.prompt: In a microservice app, every request looks up its target's address with a linearizable read from the coordination service. What's the better design?
choices: Keep it: discovery must be linearizable, or callers will reach dead instances
Cache addresses with a TTL, and on a failed connection fetch the latest and retry
Route every lookup to the coordination service's leader, so answers are never stale
Add more voting nodes to the coordination cluster to raise read throughput
cards.explanation: Discovery rarely needs linearizability, but it must be fast and available, since everything stops without it. Caching with refresh on failure gives that; a stale entry costs a retry. Routing all lookups to the leader makes it a bottleneck. Extra voting nodes slow consensus; non-voting observers are what add read capacity, at the price of stale reads.

cards.title: Online and batch systems
cards.body:
Most systems you've met so far are **online**: a request comes in, say a page load or an API call, and the system answers as fast as it can. Their main yardstick is **response time**.

A **batch job** is different. It takes a large, fixed input, such as a year of payment records, and works through all of it in one go, often for minutes, hours or days, while nobody waits on any single result. Its yardstick is **throughput**: how much data it gets through per unit of time.

The job treats its input as read-only and builds its output from scratch on every run, so the output is *derived data*.

cards.prompt: A nightly job recomputes a risk score for each of a bank's 40 million accounts. Which measure best tells you how well the job performs?
choices: The 99th percentile time it takes to return one account's score
How many accounts' worth of data it processes per hour
How many user requests per second it can answer while it runs
How soon after it starts the first few scores appear in its output
cards.explanation: A batch job is judged by throughput, the amount of data it processes per unit of time. Response time per request is the yardstick of online systems, and nobody sends this job requests. Other jobs usually read its output only once it has finished, so how soon the first scores appear doesn't matter much.

cards.title: Human fault tolerance
cards.body:
Because a batch job never changes its input, mistakes are cheap to undo. Say a new release of a job that builds monthly listening stats for a music app has a bug. You roll back to the old code and run it again, and the stats are right once more. If you kept last month's output, you can even point readers back to it; object stores and table formats call this **time travel**.

Compare a database that a buggy release has written bad rows into: rolling back the code leaves those rows bad. Recovering from your own bugs this easily is called **human fault tolerance**, and it lets teams ship faster, since a mistake isn't permanent.

cards.prompt: A new version of a nightly batch job has a bug, and it writes wrong loyalty-point totals for every customer. What's the simplest way to recover?
choices: Restore the totals from last week's backup and replay every change made since
Write a correction job that finds each wrong total and patches it in place
Roll back to the previous code and rerun the job; its input was never changed
Nothing can be done, since the job overwrote the input files it read
cards.explanation: A batch job reads immutable input and rebuilds its output from scratch, so rerunning the fixed code gives correct totals; you could even switch back to the previous run's output if you kept it. Backups and in-place patches are what a read/write database needs, since rolling back its code leaves the bad writes behind. The job never modified its input.

cards.title: The price of batch
cards.body:
Batch processing has its costs. In most frameworks, no other job can use the output until the whole job is done. It can be wasteful, too: change one record of the input, however slightly, and the job has to work through the entire input again. And since a run takes minutes or days, batch can't serve anything that needs an answer right away.

For data that keeps arriving, the alternative is **stream processing**: the job never finishes, but keeps watching its input and handles each change shortly after it happens. That's the subject of the next chapter.

cards.prompt: What are the main downsides of batch processing?
keyPoints: Other jobs can usually use the output only once the whole job has finished
Changing even a tiny part of the input means reprocessing all of it
Jobs take minutes, hours or days, so they can't serve low-latency needs
cards.explanation: Batch jobs are judged on throughput, the amount of data processed per unit of time, rather than on response time.

cards.title: A Unix pipeline
cards.body:
Plain Unix tools make a surprisingly strong batch system. Say every line of a shop's order log starts with a customer ID, and you want the twenty customers who ordered most. You chain small commands with pipes.

`awk` pulls the ID out of each line. `sort` puts the IDs in order, so all of a customer's lines end up next to each other. `uniq -c` collapses each run of identical neighbouring lines into one line, prefixed with how many there were. `sort -r -n` then orders those lines by that number, biggest first, and `head` keeps the top twenty. Such a pipeline handles gigabytes in seconds, and changing the analysis means editing one command.

cards.prompt: With standard Unix tools, you want the ten most common error messages in an application log. Order the stages of the pipeline.
items: Extract the message field from each line
Sort the messages alphabetically
Collapse repeated lines into one line each, with a count
Sort those lines by count, largest first
Keep the first ten lines
cards.explanation: uniq only spots repeats on neighbouring lines, so the first sort is what makes the counting work, with no table of counters in memory.

cards.title: Hashing or sorting
cards.body:
You could instead write a short program that keeps a **hash table** from customer to counter. The memory it needs random access to, its **working set**, grows with the number of *distinct* customers, not of lines: a million orders from one customer still take one entry. If the distinct keys fit in memory, this works fine, even on a laptop.

If they don't, sorting wins. Sort one memory-sized chunk at a time and write each to disk as a sorted file, then merge those files into one big sorted file. Merging reads and writes sequentially, which disks handle well. Once sorted, equal keys are adjacent, so counting holds one key in memory at a time.

cards.prompt: A script counts visits per product with an in-memory hash table. The log has 3 billion lines but only 800 distinct product IDs. Will it fit in a laptop's memory?
choices: No: the table grows with every line, so 3 billion entries won't fit
Yes: the table needs one counter per distinct product, not per line
Only if the log is sorted by product ID first
No: a hash table needs random access to the whole input file
cards.explanation: The working set is the memory the job needs random access to, and here it's one key and one counter per distinct product, however often each appears. Repeats only bump an existing counter. A hash table doesn't need sorted input, and the file itself is read once, front to back.

cards.prompt: When the distinct keys don't fit in memory, why does counting by sorting still work while a hash table fails?
keyPoints: It sorts one memory-sized chunk at a time and writes each to disk as a sorted file
It then merges the sorted files into one large sorted file
Merging reads and writes sequentially, which disks handle efficiently
Once sorted, equal keys are adjacent, so counting holds only one key in memory at a time
cards.explanation: It's the same idea as merging segments in log-structured storage.

cards.title: Beyond one machine
cards.body:
The standard `sort` on Linux already does all this: when data outgrows memory it spills to disk, and it spreads the work over several CPU cores. So a pipeline built on it copes with huge files; the slowest part is usually reading the input.

The real limit is that it runs on one machine. Once the data won't fit on that machine's disks, you need a distributed batch framework, which works like an operating system spread over a cluster. A **distributed filesystem** or **object store** holds inputs and outputs. A **job orchestrator** decides which tasks run where and when, with what resources. And tasks pass data along, as pipes do, through storage or over the network.

cards.prompt: A pipeline of Unix tools built on sort processes a 200 GB log, on a machine with 32 GB of RAM and 16 cores. When would you actually need a distributed batch framework?
choices: Now, because the data is bigger than memory and sort will fail
Now, because sort uses only one core, so the other 15 sit idle
When the data no longer fits on one machine's disks
Never: a sort-based pipeline scales to any data size
cards.explanation: The standard Linux sort spills to disk when data exceeds memory and spreads its work over several cores, so one machine copes well; the bottleneck is usually reading the input. Its real limit is being one machine: once the data outgrows that machine's disks, you need a cluster.

cards.prompt: Distributed batch frameworks work like an operating system spread over many machines. What plays the part of the filesystem, the process scheduler and the pipes?
keyPoints: Filesystem: a distributed filesystem or object store that holds inputs and outputs
Scheduler: a job orchestrator that decides which tasks run where and when, and allocates resources
Pipes: tasks hand data to each other through storage or over the network

cards.title: Big blocks across machines
cards.body:
The filesystem on your laptop chops each file into small **blocks**, typically 4 KB, and keeps track of which blocks make up which file. A **distributed filesystem** (DFS) does the same, except that the blocks are spread over many machines and are far bigger: 128 MB in HDFS, a few megabytes in many others.

Big blocks pay off at scale. A petabyte in 4 KB pieces means hundreds of billions of blocks to keep track of; in 128 MB blocks it's under ten million. And every read pays a fixed cost to locate its block, which barely matters when you then read megabytes from it. A file's last block takes only the space it needs.

cards.prompt: Why do distributed filesystems use blocks of megabytes, far larger than a local filesystem's few kilobytes?
choices: Fewer, larger blocks mean less metadata and less seek overhead per read
Disks attached over a network can't write blocks smaller than a megabyte
Larger blocks make small random reads faster, which batch jobs depend on
So that each file fits into a single block, stored whole on one machine
cards.explanation: At petabyte scale, tiny blocks would mean billions of entries to track, and each seek would cost a lot next to the read that follows it. Batch jobs mostly read big files in sequence, not small random reads. Large files still span many blocks on many machines, and the block size isn't forced by the disks.

cards.title: Inside a distributed filesystem
cards.body:
Your OS builds its filesystem in layers. Drivers read and write raw blocks. A **page cache** keeps recently used blocks in memory. A filesystem layer tracks the metadata: which blocks form each file, directories, permissions. On top, the **VFS** gives programs one API, whatever filesystem sits below.

A DFS has a counterpart for each. Every machine runs a daemon, a **data node**, that keeps blocks as ordinary local files and serves them over the network. Its OS page cache keeps popular blocks in memory. A **metadata service** records which machines hold each file's blocks, plus permissions. And in place of the VFS there's a protocol, like the S3 API: any framework that speaks it can use any store that does.

cards.prompt: What plays each role in a distributed filesystem: block storage, the page cache, the metadata, and the VFS?
keyPoints: Block storage: a daemon on each machine (a data node) serves its blocks over the network, keeping them as local files
Page cache: each data node's OS keeps frequently read blocks in memory
Metadata: a metadata service tracks which machines hold each file's blocks, plus permissions
VFS: a protocol, such as the S3 API, that any storage system can implement
cards.explanation: Because the protocol is pluggable, a batch framework that speaks it can use any storage system implementing it.

cards.title: Redundancy on cheap hardware
cards.body:
Classic network storage, such as a SAN, is a central appliance with special hardware and its own network. A DFS is **shared-nothing**: ordinary servers with their own disks, joined by a normal datacenter network.

Cheap servers fail more often, so each block is stored redundantly on several machines. That can be plain copies, or **erasure coding**, which rebuilds lost data from the surviving pieces while using less extra space than full copies. It's the RAID idea, done over the network rather than across the disks of one box.

The copies help the scheduler too: a task can run on any machine that holds its input, which spreads the work more evenly.

cards.prompt: Distributed filesystems run on commodity machines rather than special storage hardware. How do they keep data safe, and what else does that give the scheduler?
keyPoints: Each block is stored redundantly across several machines, since cheap hardware fails more often
The redundancy is either full copies or erasure coding, which recovers lost data with less storage overhead
A task can run on any machine that holds its input, which spreads the load more evenly
cards.explanation: This shared-nothing design needs only an ordinary datacenter network, unlike NAS and SAN storage, which rely on a central appliance and special hardware.

cards.title: Object stores
cards.body:
Many batch jobs now use an **object store**, such as S3, instead of a DFS. Each object sits in a **bucket**, whose name is unique worldwide, under a **key** that's unique within that bucket. You read an object with *get* and write one with *put*.

Objects are **immutable**. To change one, you put a complete new version, much as in a key-value store; a few stores support appends, but most don't. There are no file handles to open, seek and write in place, and usually no links or locks. Some tools mount an object store as if it were a filesystem, but its guarantees and performance stay different underneath.

cards.prompt: How does an object in an object store differ from a file in a filesystem?
keyPoints: It's immutable: changing it means writing the whole object again with a put, since few stores allow appends
There are no file handles to open and seek within; you get or put the object
Links and locks usually aren't supported
cards.explanation: Tools can mount an object store as if it were a filesystem, but the guarantees and performance underneath stay different.

cards.title: Prefixes, not folders
cards.body:
Object keys often look like paths, such as `logs/2024/05/app.gz`, but there are no real folders: the slashes are just characters in the key. Listing a 'folder' asks for every key that starts with a prefix, and the result includes deeper keys too, like a recursive `ls -R`.

So a folder exists only while at least one key starts with it, and empty folders are impossible. To keep one around, people store a zero-byte object under its name.

Renames aren't atomic either. Renaming an object copies it to the new key and then deletes the old one. Renaming a 'folder' means doing that for each object under it, one at a time.

cards.prompt: A bucket holds objects under the key prefix reports/2025/q3/. You delete all of them, then list the prefix reports/2025/. What do you see?
choices: An empty q3 folder, until you delete the folder itself
An error, because a listed prefix must match a folder that exists
No q3, unless a zero-byte object was made to stand in for it
cards.explanation: Slashes are just characters in object keys, so a 'folder' exists only while some key starts with it. Empty folders can't exist, so teams fake them with a zero-byte object. Listing a prefix doesn't fail when nothing matches; it returns whatever keys start with it, including those in deeper paths.

cards.prompt: A job writes its results under the prefix staging/run-7/, then renames the prefix to live/ so readers see the whole run at once. What goes wrong on a typical object store?
choices: Nothing: the store moves every key under the prefix in one atomic step
Readers can see a partial set: each object is copied, then deleted, one by one
Objects under the new prefix stay locked until every reader has closed them
cards.explanation: Object stores lack atomic renames: a rename copies the object to its new key and deletes the old one, and a prefix has to be moved one object at a time, so readers can catch it halfway. Object stores also have no locks or open file handles that could hold anything back.

cards.title: Moving code to the data
cards.body:
Some DFSs, such as HDFS, let the scheduler run a task on a machine that already stores a copy of its input. The task then reads from local disk instead of pulling the file over the network.

That only saves traffic when the task's code is smaller than the data it reads. Shipping a 50 MB program to a machine holding a 20 GB file is a bargain; the reverse is not.

Object stores usually keep storage and computing on separate machines. That uses more network bandwidth, but datacenter networks are fast, and it lets you add CPU and memory without adding storage, or the other way around.

cards.prompt: On a cluster that can run tasks next to their data, a task ships with 2 GB of code and model weights, and its input file is 300 MB. Does running it on the machine holding the file save network traffic?
choices: Yes: reading local data always beats sending it over the network
Yes, as long as the file is kept in an object store, not a filesystem
No: tasks can never run on the machines that store their input
No: shipping 2 GB of code to the data costs more than fetching 300 MB
cards.explanation: Moving the computation to the data only pays off when the code is smaller than the data it reads. Filesystems like HDFS do let tasks run where a copy of the file lives. Object stores usually keep compute separate, accepting more network traffic in return for scaling CPU and memory independently of storage.

cards.title: Job orchestrators
cards.body:
On one machine, the OS kernel starts processes, hands out memory and CPU time, and keeps them apart. In a cluster, a **job orchestrator** such as Kubernetes or YARN does that.

A batch framework sends the orchestrator's **scheduler** a request: how many tasks, the CPU, memory and disk each needs, where the code lives, plus inputs, outputs and credentials. The scheduler consults the **resource manager**, which keeps a global view of every node's hardware and status, and assigns each task to a node. There, an **executor** daemon fetches the code, starts the task, isolates it from others, and watches it until it finishes or fails, then records the outcome.

cards.prompt: Order what happens when a batch framework asks an orchestrator to run a job.
items: The framework asks the scheduler to run a job, giving the task count, each task's resources and where the code is
The scheduler consults the resource manager's view of the cluster and assigns each task to a node
Each assigned node's executor fetches the job's code and launches its task
The executor monitors the task and records whether it finished or failed
cards.explanation: The resource manager is central, so its state is often kept in a coordination service to avoid a single point of failure.

cards.title: Sharing out a cluster
cards.body:
A cluster scheduler splits limited resources between competing jobs, balancing **fairness** against **efficiency**, often without knowing what will arrive next.

Take a job whose tasks must all run at once, known as **gang scheduling**. If the scheduler holds freed cores aside until there are enough, they sit idle, and if other jobs hold cores too, they can **deadlock**. If it waits without holding any, other jobs keep taking freed cores, and the big job may **starve**. If it kills, or **preempts**, running tasks to make room, their work must be redone.

Finding the best plan is NP-hard, hopelessly slow beyond tiny cases. So schedulers use heuristics: first in first out, priority queues, quotas, bin packing.

cards.prompt: A busy cluster has 96 cores, and a training job needs 64 of them at once. The scheduler waits until 64 are free, without holding cores aside as they free up. What's the risk?
choices: Deadlock: this job and others each hold some cores and wait for the rest
Idle cores: freed cores sit unused until all 64 are available together
Starvation: other jobs keep grabbing freed cores, so it may wait for ages
Wasted work: the scheduler kills running tasks to clear room for it
cards.explanation: Without reserving cores, anything freed is up for grabs, so a job that needs many at once can starve. Holding freed cores aside instead leaves them idle, and can deadlock if other jobs reserve too. Killing running tasks is preemption, a separate option that throws away their work.

cards.prompt: Why can't a cluster scheduler simply compute the best allocation of resources to jobs?
keyPoints: It must balance fairness between jobs against keeping the cluster efficiently used
It often lacks information, such as whether a larger job is about to arrive
Finding the optimal schedule is NP-hard, far too slow for anything but tiny cases
So it relies on heuristics instead, such as FIFO, priority queues, quotas or bin packing
