cards.title: Workflows of jobs
cards.body:
Like Unix commands joined by pipes, batch jobs are often chained: one job's output becomes the input of one or more others, and a job may read several jobs' outputs. This graph of jobs is a **workflow**, a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and 50 to 100 jobs in one is common.

Why split work into several jobs? One job's output may feed jobs owned by other teams, so it's written somewhere they can all read it. Data may have to pass from one tool to another, say from Spark to a SQL engine. Or one stage needs the data sharded by one key and the next by another, so the first writes its output sharded the way the second needs.

cards.prompt: Why would a pipeline be split into a workflow of several batch jobs rather than run as one?
keyPoints: One job's output may feed several jobs owned by other teams, so it goes where they can all read it
Data may need to move from one processing tool to another
A later stage may need the data sharded by a different key than an earlier one
cards.explanation: The jobs form a directed acyclic graph, and pipelines of dozens of jobs are common.

cards.title: Handing data between jobs
cards.body:
A Unix pipe passes data through a small memory buffer; when it fills, the writer waits for the reader, a form of **backpressure**. Spark and Flink can likewise feed a task's output straight into the next task, over the network if needed.

Most workflows instead have each job write its output to a DFS or object store, and the next job read it from there. That decouples the jobs, so they can run at different times. A job with several inputs runs only once every job producing them has succeeded.

Tracking that is the work of a **workflow scheduler**, such as Airflow. A cluster's own scheduler, like YARN's, handles each job alone and knows nothing of dependencies between jobs.

cards.prompt: Engines can stream one task's output straight into the next, like a Unix pipe. Why do most batch workflows instead have each job save its output to shared storage, such as an object store?
choices: Streaming between tasks only works when both run on the same machine
Writing to storage is faster than sending data over the network
Direct streaming has no backpressure, so the reader would be flooded
It decouples jobs, so the next can run later, on its own schedule
cards.explanation: Stored output lets producer and consumer run at different times, and a job with several inputs just waits until every job producing them has succeeded. Engines like Spark and Flink do pass data directly, across machines if needed, and a pipe's small buffer gives backpressure. Storage is slower, since it replicates each write.

cards.prompt: A team starts 70 interdependent batch jobs from cron at fixed times. When an upstream job runs late, the jobs after it read incomplete input. What fixes this?
choices: A workflow scheduler, which runs each job once every job feeding it has succeeded
The cluster's own job scheduler, which already tracks how jobs depend on each other
Leaving bigger gaps between the cron times so jobs have room to finish
Running all 70 jobs at once so that none of them waits on another
cards.explanation: A workflow scheduler manages the whole graph of jobs and starts each one when its inputs are ready, retrying and flagging failures along the way. A cluster scheduler, such as YARN's, handles each job on its own and knows nothing of dependencies between them. Wider gaps still break when a job runs late, and parallel jobs would read missing input.

cards.title: Failures and preemption
cards.body:
A job with thousands of tasks running for hours will probably lose one along the way, to a hardware fault or a network problem. Tasks also get **preempted**: the scheduler kills a low-priority task to make room for a more important one. Clouds sell such low-priority machines cheaply as **spot** or *preemptible* VMs.

Batch work is rarely urgent, so it suits them: it soaks up capacity that would otherwise sit idle. The catch is that preemption happens far more often than hardware faults.

Since output is rebuilt from scratch, a lost task is easy to handle: discard what it wrote and run it again on another machine. Tasks are independent, so only that task reruns.

cards.prompt: Why are batch jobs a good fit for cheap spot or preemptible VMs, and what's the catch?
choices: They're never preempted mid-task; the only catch is that prices change hourly
They're as reliable as regular VMs; the catch is less memory per core
They can wait for spare capacity; the catch is tasks get killed often
They get top priority on spot VMs; the catch is a higher price at peaks
cards.explanation: Batch work is rarely urgent, so it can soak up idle capacity at low priority, which raises the cluster's utilization. In exchange, higher-priority work can preempt it at any moment, and preemptions happen more often than hardware faults, so tasks must be cheap to retry. Spot VMs get the lowest priority, not the highest, and they're less reliable than regular ones.

cards.prompt: A job runs 2,000 tasks in parallel. Halfway through, the machine running one of them crashes. What does the framework do?
choices: Restart the whole job, since its output would otherwise be incomplete
Resume the task on another machine from the record where it stopped
Keep the failed task's partial output and have a new task append the rest
Discard that task's partial output and rerun just that task elsewhere
cards.explanation: Tasks run independently and their output is rebuilt from scratch, so retrying one task is enough: throw away whatever it wrote and run it again from the start of its input. Restarting all 2,000 would waste everyone else's work. There's no saved position to resume from, and keeping partial output risks duplicates.

cards.title: Keeping intermediate data safe
cards.body:
Retrying gets harder when one task's output is another task's input. If that data is lost, the next task has nothing to read.

MapReduce plays it safe. It writes such data to the DFS and lets readers start only after the writer has succeeded. That survives frequent preemption, but it costs a lot of replicated writes. Spark holds intermediate data in memory and spills it to local disk when it doesn't fit. It remembers how each piece was computed, so it can compute a lost piece again. Flink takes a third route: it regularly saves a **checkpoint**, a snapshot of its tasks' state, and restarts from the latest one after a failure.

cards.prompt: When one task's output is the input to another, how can a batch engine make sure a failure doesn't lose that intermediate data?
keyPoints: Write it to the distributed filesystem and let readers start only after the writer succeeds: durable, but lots of replicated writes
Keep it in memory, spilling to local disk, and record how it was computed so lost parts can be recomputed
Periodically checkpoint a snapshot of the tasks' state, and restart from that
cards.explanation: These are the approaches of MapReduce, Spark and Flink, in that order.

cards.title: The MapReduce pattern
cards.body:
**MapReduce**, published by Google in 2004, shaped most batch tools that followed, though it's now largely retired. A job has the same shape as a Unix pipeline. The framework splits the input files into records. Your **mapper** pulls a key and a value out of each record, like `awk` picking a field. The framework sorts all the pairs by key, like `sort`. Then your **reducer** gets each key with all of its values and combines them, like `uniq -c`.

A job sorts only once, between map and reduce. To sort again, say to rank the results, you write a second job that reads the first one's output and uses whatever you want to sort by as its key.

cards.prompt: A MapReduce job has counted plays per song. You now want the songs ranked by play count. How?
choices: Have the same job's reducers sort their output by count before writing it
Run a second job over the counts, using the count as the sort key
Configure the first job's shuffle to sort by value instead of by key
Have the mappers sort by count, since they see the records first
cards.explanation: MapReduce sorts only between map and reduce, and the counts don't exist until the reducers have run. So a second job reads the first one's output, makes the count its key, and lets its own sort do the ranking. Each reducer holds only its share of the songs, so it can't rank them all, and mappers run before any counting.

cards.title: Stateless mappers
cards.body:
A mapper is called once per input record and can emit zero, one or many key-value pairs. It carries nothing over from one record to the next. The framework then collects each key's values and hands the reducer an iterator over them; different keys can be reduced in parallel.

This comes from functional programming, where map and reduce work without mutable state. Since each call depends only on what the framework hands it, calls can be spread over many nodes, and when a task fails, the framework just calls it again elsewhere with the same input.

The downside: raw MapReduce is laborious. Even a join must be written by hand.

cards.prompt: Why must a mapper handle each input record without carrying any state over from the records before it?
choices: So the framework can split the input across many mappers, and rerun any that fail
Mapper output has to stay in memory, so any state it kept would crowd that out
Its input already arrives sorted by key, so earlier records are never needed again
Because each reducer reads the mapper's internal state directly when it starts
cards.explanation: Each call depends only on the record the framework passes in, the functional programming habit of avoiding mutable state. So records can be spread over many parallel mappers, and a failed one is simply called again on another node. Sorting comes after the map step, mapper output is written to local disk, and reducers see only the emitted pairs.

cards.title: Dataflow engines
cards.body:
MapReduce writes each job's output to files before the next job may start, which makes long workflows slow. **Dataflow engines** such as Spark and Flink treat a whole workflow as one job. You build it from **operators**: plain functions called per record, or higher-level ones such as join, group by, filter and aggregate. They can be wired together freely, instead of strictly alternating map and reduce.

The engine shards the input to work in parallel and copies each task's output over the network to the next task. When several operators in a row, like map and filter, leave the sharding as it is, it fuses them into one task, so records flow straight through without copying.

cards.prompt: A dataflow job parses records, drops bad ones, then reformats the rest, all without changing how the data is sharded. How does the engine run these three operators?
choices: Combined into one task per shard, so records pass straight between them
As three stages, with a shuffle after each to keep the data sorted
As three separate jobs, each writing its result to the object store
As a single task on a single machine, since no shuffle is needed between them
cards.explanation: Operators that keep the sharding, like map and filter, can be fused into a single task, which saves copying data between them. Sorting happens only where an operator such as a join needs it. Writing each step to storage is the MapReduce habit dataflow engines avoid, and the work is still spread over many shards.

cards.title: Why dataflow is faster
cards.body: Seeing the whole workflow lets a dataflow engine skip much of MapReduce's overhead. It sorts only where an operator needs sorted input, not between every stage. It keeps intermediate data in memory or on local disk instead of writing it to replicated distributed storage. An operator starts as soon as its input is ready, without waiting for the whole previous stage to end. Processes already running are reused for new operators, where MapReduce launches a fresh one per task. And since the engine knows which task consumes which data, it can place a consumer on the same machine as its producer, so the data moves through shared memory rather than the network.

cards.prompt: Dataflow engines such as Spark and Flink model a whole workflow as one job. How does that make them faster than MapReduce?
keyPoints: They sort only where an operator needs it, not between every stage
They keep intermediate data in memory or on local disk instead of replicated distributed storage
An operator can start as soon as its input is ready, without waiting for the whole previous stage
They reuse running processes for new operators instead of launching one per task
cards.explanation: Knowing the whole graph also lets the scheduler place a consumer next to its producer, so data can pass through shared memory.

cards.title: The shuffle
cards.body:
A **shuffle** sorts data too big for one machine, with both input and output split into shards. Despite the name, nothing is random: the result is sorted.

In MapReduce, one map task runs per input shard, and the job's author picks how many reduce tasks there are. Each mapper writes a separate local file for every reducer, choosing the file by a hash of the key, and keeps each file sorted. When a mapper finishes, each reducer copies its file from it. With files from every mapper, a reducer merges them in order, so equal keys sit together. Then it calls reduce once per key, with an iterator over its values, and writes one output shard.

cards.prompt: Order the steps of a MapReduce shuffle, from the map tasks to the reduce calls.
items: Each map task runs the mapper over the records of its input shard
The mapper's output goes into one local file per reducer, chosen by a hash of the key, sorted by key
Once a mapper is done, each reducer copies its own file from it
Each reducer merges the files it collected, so equal keys end up adjacent
The reduce function is called once per key, with an iterator over its values
cards.explanation: Despite the name, a shuffle produces sorted, sharded data, not a random order. Each reducer then writes one shard of the job's output.

cards.title: Sort-merge joins
cards.body:
Say a music app has a huge log of plays, each with a listener ID, and a big table of listeners with their country. To see which songs are popular where, you must **join** them, and both are sharded.

One mapper reads plays and emits each one keyed by listener ID. Another reads listeners, also keyed by listener ID, with the country as the value. The shuffle brings a listener's record and all their plays to the same reducer, and a **secondary sort** puts the listener record first. The reducer stores the country, then streams through the plays, tagging each with it. It holds one listener at a time and makes no network calls. That's a **sort-merge join**.

cards.prompt: A sort-merge join matches insurance claims with policy records on policy ID. Why does each reducer get by with very little memory?
choices: It loads the full policy table into memory once, then streams the claims past it
It looks up each claim's policy in the policy database as it goes
The mappers have already joined the records, so it just writes them out
Each policy arrives right before its claims, so it holds one policy at a time
cards.explanation: The shuffle groups records by policy ID, and a secondary sort puts the policy record first, so the reducer keeps that one record while it streams through the claims. Loading the whole table only works if it fits in memory. The join makes no network lookups, and mappers only key the records; the joining happens in the reducer.

cards.title: Grouping after a join
cards.body:
The join leaves you with plays tagged by country, but they're still grouped by listener. To count each song's plays per country, a second job shuffles them again, this time using the song ID as the key.

Now each reducer receives all the plays of one song together. It keeps a counter for each country and bumps the right one for every play, then writes out the totals. That's a **group by** with an aggregation, built from the same shuffle. Joins and groupings are what shuffles are mostly used for, in MapReduce and in its successors alike.

cards.prompt: A bike-rental firm wants ride counts per membership tier for each docking station. Rides and members are both large and sharded. Order the sort-merge join workflow.
items: Mappers read rides and members, emitting each record keyed by member ID
The shuffle brings each member's record and rides to one reducer, member record first
The reducer stores the member's tier, then tags each of their rides with it
A second job reshuffles the tagged rides using the station as the key
Its reducers count each station's rides per tier
cards.explanation: The second job is a group-by: shuffling on the station puts all of a station's rides on one reducer, which just keeps a counter per tier.

cards.title: SQL for batch jobs
cards.body:
Once engines could run jobs on clusters of thousands of machines reliably, attention turned to how jobs are written, and **SQL** won almost everywhere. Old warehouses used it, analytics and ETL tools were built around it, and developers and analysts know it. A query takes far less code than hand-written MapReduce, and you can run it interactively, so analysts and business teams can explore data themselves.

It helps the machines too. The engine turns SQL into a plan of physical operators, and a cost-based **optimizer** looks at the properties of the inputs to pick the best join algorithm, and may reorder joins to keep intermediate data small.

cards.prompt: Why did SQL become the main language for batch processing?
keyPoints: Legacy warehouses and existing analytics and ETL tools already used it, and developers and analysts know it
It needs far less code than writing MapReduce jobs by hand
It supports interactive, exploratory queries, so analysts and business teams can explore data themselves
cards.explanation: It helps the machines too: the engine can optimize a declarative query in ways a hand-written job can't.

cards.prompt: Why can a SQL query on a batch engine run faster than the same logic written by hand as MapReduce jobs?
choices: SQL engines avoid shuffling the data, which hand-written jobs always have to do
Its optimizer picks the join algorithm and join order from the data's properties
The query runs on a single large machine, so it avoids network overhead
The engine caches each query's result, so later runs are nearly instant
cards.explanation: The engine translates SQL into a syntax tree and then physical operators, which leaves room to optimize: it can pick a join algorithm suited to the inputs and reorder joins to keep intermediate state small. Joins and aggregations still need shuffles, the work is still spread over a cluster, and caching isn't where the speedup comes from.

cards.title: Warehouses and batch converge
cards.body:
Data warehouses and batch frameworks started far apart: warehouses ran SQL on special appliances, while MapReduce let you write any code over any file format. They have since met in the middle. Batch engines speak SQL and use columnar formats like Parquet; cloud warehouses borrowed scheduling, shuffles and fault tolerance, and added DataFrame APIs.

Batch frameworks still win some jobs. Iterative graph algorithms, which repeat a step until the numbers stop changing, complex ML, and images, video or audio are awkward in SQL. Row-by-row work runs poorly on columnar storage. And warehouses tend to cost more, so big jobs may be cheaper on Spark or Flink.

cards.prompt: A team runs most of its analytics in a cloud data warehouse. Which new job is the strongest case for a batch framework like Spark instead?
choices: A daily SQL report that sums sales by region from a columnar table
An ad hoc query joining two fact tables to answer a one-off question
A graph algorithm that repeats until every seller's score settles
A dashboard that groups yesterday's orders by product category
cards.explanation: Iterative graph algorithms, complex ML and processing of images or audio are hard to express in SQL, and row-by-row work runs poorly on columnar storage. Sums, joins and group-bys over tables are exactly what warehouses do well. Cost can also push large jobs toward Spark or Flink, since warehouses tend to be more expensive.

cards.title: Distributed DataFrames
cards.body:
Data scientists like the **DataFrame** from R and Pandas: a table whose columns each hold one type, transformed by calling functions to filter, join, sort or aggregate, instead of writing one big query. Classic DataFrames live in one machine's memory, so Spark and others added DataFrame APIs that run on a cluster.

They behave differently, though. A local DataFrame usually keeps an index and a fixed row order; a distributed one usually has neither, so code that relies on them can break or crawl. And Pandas runs each call at once, while Spark collects the calls into a query plan, optimizes it, and only then runs it on its dataflow engine.

cards.prompt: A data scientist moves Pandas code to a distributed DataFrame engine. Steps that relied on row order and an index now misbehave or crawl. Why?
choices: Distributed DataFrames usually aren't indexed or ordered, unlike local ones
Distributed DataFrames don't support filters, joins or aggregations
The distributed engine runs every method call immediately, one at a time
Rows are copied to every node, so each lookup scans all of them
cards.explanation: Local DataFrames keep an index and a row order; distributed ones generally don't, so code that depends on them brings surprises. They still offer relational operations. Engines like Spark don't run each call right away; they turn the calls into a query plan, optimize it, then run it on the dataflow engine. Rows are sharded, not copied everywhere.

cards.title: Where batch fits
cards.body:
Batch jobs are great at processing lots of data in bulk and poor at answering quickly. So they belong wherever the data is big and results that are hours old are fine. That covers more than you'd think: payroll, monthly utility bills, a search index rebuilt every night, pricing models refreshed weekly, and much of how banks move money between each other.

What doesn't fit is anything a person or program is waiting on right now, such as checking a password at login or choosing which ad to show as a page loads. That's work for online systems.

cards.prompt: Which of these tasks is the poorest fit for a batch job?
choices: Checking each night that a store chain's sales match its bank deposits
Forecasting next month's demand for each product a factory makes
Retraining a video site's recommendation model every week
Deciding whether to approve a card payment while the customer waits
cards.explanation: Batch jobs process lots of data in bulk but can't answer within a request, so anything a user waits on belongs in an online system. Reconciliation, demand forecasting and model training all involve large amounts of data and can live with results that are hours old.

cards.title: Batch ETL
cards.body:
Batch jobs are a natural home for **ETL** and ELT. Most transformations, like filtering rows or picking out fields, are *embarrassingly parallel*: each shard can be handled on its own.

Workflow schedulers make such pipelines easier to run and debug. When a job fails, the scheduler retries it, in case the problem was a passing glitch. If it keeps failing, it's marked as failed, so you see exactly which step broke. Then you inspect its input files. Say an upstream team switched a date column from days to timestamps. You fix the transformation, or the upstream job that wrote that input, and rerun. The input was never changed, so the rerun rebuilds a correct output.

cards.prompt: A nightly ETL job starts failing after an upstream change. Order how the problem typically gets noticed and fixed.
items: The workflow scheduler retries the job, in case the problem was transient
After repeated failures, the scheduler marks the job as failed
An engineer inspects the input files and finds that a field the transformation uses is missing
The transformation logic, or the upstream job, is fixed
The job is rerun, rebuilding its output from the unchanged input
cards.explanation: Because input is read-only and output is regenerated, a fixed job can simply be rerun; nothing has to be patched by hand.

cards.title: Batch analytics
cards.body:
Analysts can query data right where batch jobs keep it: a SQL engine reads files on a DFS or object store, while a table format and a catalog record which files form each table. That setup is a **data lakehouse**.

Queries come in two styles. **Pre-aggregation** runs on a schedule, managed by a workflow scheduler: it rolls data up into cubes or *data marts*, which are then queried in the warehouse or loaded into a real-time OLAP store. **Ad hoc** queries answer one-off questions, such as why an outage happened; each answer prompts the next query, so fast execution matters. Spreadsheets and BI tools reach these engines through SQL.

cards.prompt: An executive dashboard shows each region's daily revenue and is refreshed every morning. Meanwhile, an analyst is chasing an unexplained dip in sign-ups. How do the two workloads differ?
choices: Dashboard: pre-aggregated on a schedule; analyst: ad hoc queries where speed matters
Both are ad hoc, since each one asks something new every time it runs
Dashboard: ad hoc queries each morning; analyst: a data cube built ahead on a schedule
Neither suits batch processing, since both need a real-time OLAP store
cards.explanation: A fixed, repeated question like daily revenue by region is rolled up into cubes or data marts by a scheduled job, then served from the warehouse or a real-time OLAP store. The analyst's work is ad hoc: each answer prompts the next query, so fast execution matters. Batch engines with SQL handle both.

cards.title: Batch jobs in ML
cards.body:
Machine learning leans heavily on batch jobs. **Feature engineering** turns raw data into something a model can learn from; models usually need numbers, so text and categories must be converted. **Training** is a batch job whose input is the training data and whose output is the model's weights. **Batch inference** uses a trained model to make many predictions at once when nobody needs them in real time, including scoring it on a test set.

Large language models are trained the same way: batch jobs extract plain text from web pages, drop low-quality and duplicate documents, and split the rest into tokens.

cards.prompt: How is batch processing used to build and use ML models?
keyPoints: Feature engineering: turning raw data, such as text or categories, into numeric data a model can train on
Training: the training data is the job's input, and the model's weights are its output
Batch inference: making predictions in bulk when they aren't needed in real time, including scoring a test set
cards.explanation: LLM training leans on batch jobs too, to extract text from web pages, drop low-quality and duplicate documents, and tokenize what's left.

cards.title: Writing straight to production
cards.body:
Batch jobs often produce data users will see, like recommendations, which must reach the database serving live traffic. Normally a job's output is all or nothing: if the job succeeds, every task's work counts exactly once, even after retries; if it fails, there's no output.

The tempting shortcut is for each task to write its records straight into the database, one by one. A network round trip for each record makes that orders of magnitude slower than a batch task's normal pace. Many parallel tasks writing at once can swamp the database and slow its live queries. And the guarantee is gone: others see a half-done job's writes, and a retried task can write records twice.

cards.prompt: Why is it a bad idea for a batch job to write its results straight into a production database, one record at a time?
keyPoints: One network round trip per record is far slower than the throughput a batch task normally reaches
Many parallel tasks writing at once can overwhelm the database and slow its live queries
Writes to an outside system are visible at once, so others can see a half-finished job's output
A retried task may write the same records twice

cards.title: Publishing through a stream
cards.body:
A better route is to publish the output to a stream, such as a Kafka topic, which many databases and search engines can ingest. Streams are built for sequential writes, which suits bulk output. The stream is a buffer, so the database reads at its own pace and keeps room for live traffic. Several systems can consume the same output. And the stream can sit in its own network zone, a **DMZ**, as a security boundary between batch and production.

A stream alone isn't all or nothing, though. The job must announce when it's done, and consumers keep what they receive hidden from queries until then, like uncommitted data under read committed.

cards.prompt: What do you gain by having a batch job push its output through a stream topic rather than writing it into the database directly?
keyPoints: Streaming systems are built for sequential writes, which suits a batch job's bulk output
The stream acts as a buffer, so the database can read at a pace that leaves room for live traffic
Several downstream systems can consume the same job's output
It can sit in its own network zone (a DMZ), as a security boundary between batch and production

cards.prompt: A batch job streams fresh product recommendations into a serving store through a topic. The job fails halfway and is restarted. How can the store avoid serving a mix of old and new recommendations?
choices: The topic guarantees all-or-nothing delivery, so nothing reaches the store until the job ends
The store keeps incoming data hidden from queries until the job announces it has finished
The store serves records as they arrive, then deletes them if the job later fails
Each task writes straight to the store, skipping the topic, so a failure undoes its writes
cards.explanation: A stream doesn't make output all-or-nothing by itself, so the job must notify consumers when it completes, and the store must keep what it has received invisible to queries until then, like uncommitted data under read committed. Serving first and deleting later exposes partial output, and direct writes are visible at once, with nothing to undo them.

cards.title: Bulk loading
cards.body:
Another approach, common when filling a database for the first time, is to have the batch job build the database itself. It writes complete database files, such as RocksDB's sorted SST files, to a DFS or object store, and the serving system imports them in one go while it keeps serving the old data.

This is very fast, and the switch from the old dataset to the new one can be atomic. The weakness is small changes: building a whole new database is a poor way to update a few rows. So some stores support both, accepting row-by-row updates as well as full dataset swaps.

cards.prompt: Order how a batch job replaces a key-value store's entire dataset by bulk loading.
items: The batch job builds a complete set of database files from its input
The files are written to object storage or a distributed filesystem
The serving store imports the files in bulk while still serving the old version
Reads switch atomically from the old version to the new one
cards.explanation: This is fast and makes version switches atomic, but small incremental updates are awkward, so some systems combine full swaps with row-level updates.

cards.title: From batches to streams
cards.body:
A batch job reads a fixed input and knows when it's finished. But most data never stops arriving. So batch systems slice it into hourly or daily chunks, and results trail reality by that much. **Stream processing** handles each event soon after it happens.

An **event** is a small, immutable record of something that happened, usually with a timestamp: a song played, a thermometer reading. A **producer** creates it once, any number of **consumers** may process it, and related events are grouped into a **topic**.

Consumers could check a shared table for new rows. But polling faster mostly finds nothing new, so the cost per event climbs. It's better to notify them.

cards.prompt: Producers and consumers share a database table, and to cut latency the consumers now poll it every 50 ms. What's the main drawback?
choices: Rows inserted between two polls are skipped, since each poll sees only a snapshot
The more often they poll, the more polls come back empty, so overhead climbs
Polling reorders events, because the table returns rows in arbitrary order
Each poll locks the table, so producers can't insert while consumers read
cards.explanation: As polling gets more frequent, a growing share of requests find nothing new, so the cost per event rises; notifying consumers works better. A consumer that tracks where it left off misses nothing between polls, rows can be read in insert order, and ordinary reads don't block inserts.

cards.title: When consumers fall behind
cards.body:
A messaging system must answer two questions. First, what if producers send faster than consumers can keep up? It can **drop** messages, and they're lost. It can **buffer** them in a queue, and then you must ask what happens once the queue outgrows memory, or the disk fills. Or it can apply **backpressure**: block the producer until the consumer catches up, as Unix pipes and TCP do with a small fixed buffer.

Second, what if a node crashes? Durability costs disk writes or replication, and so speed. Losing the odd message is fine for a reading that's resent every few seconds, though mass losses can go unnoticed. When you count events, every lost one makes the total wrong.

cards.prompt: A producer sends messages faster than its consumers can handle them. What are the three broad options, and what does each cost?
keyPoints: Drop them: whatever is dropped is lost
Buffer them in a queue, which then has to cope with outgrowing memory or filling the disk
Apply backpressure: block the producer until consumers catch up, as Unix pipes and TCP do
cards.explanation: Traditional brokers usually queue without limit; a log-based broker is a buffer that's large but fixed in size.

cards.prompt: A fleet of e-scooters reports battery level every 30 seconds, and a second stream reports each finished ride for billing. Where is losing the odd message acceptable?
choices: In the ride stream, since billing can be rebuilt from the battery readings
In neither: any lost message makes a stream's results worthless
In both, as long as fewer than one in a hundred messages is lost
In the battery stream, since a fresh reading arrives shortly anyway
cards.explanation: A missed periodic reading is soon replaced by the next, but every lost ride is a charge that never happens, so that stream must be delivered reliably. Accepting some loss buys throughput and latency. No loss rate is fine for counting, and heavy drops in a metrics stream can go unnoticed.

cards.title: Message brokers
cards.body:
Producers can send straight to consumers: UDP multicast, brokerless libraries, or **webhooks**, where a service calls a URL you registered whenever something happens. These assume both sides stay online. A consumer that's down misses whatever was sent meanwhile, and a producer that crashes loses its buffer of messages to retry.

A **message broker** is a server in between. Producers write to it, and it delivers to consumers. Clients can come, go and crash, because the messages live on the broker, which now owns durability. Brokers usually let queues grow rather than drop or block. So consumers are **asynchronous**: a producer waits only for the broker to accept a message, not for anyone to process it.

cards.prompt: A shop calls its warehouse service's webhook for every new order. The warehouse service is down for an hour during a migration. What changes if the shop sends orders through a message broker instead?
choices: The shop's requests now wait until the warehouse has processed each order
Little: a broker also needs the consumer to be online when a message is sent
Orders wait on the broker until the warehouse reconnects, and the shop carries on
The broker drops orders while no consumer is connected, to keep its queue short
cards.explanation: A broker holds messages while a consumer is away, and a producer only waits for the broker to accept each one, so the outage just delays processing. Waiting for processing would make delivery synchronous, which brokers avoid. Needing both sides online is the weakness of direct messaging such as webhooks, and brokers usually queue rather than drop.

cards.title: Brokers versus databases
cards.body:
A broker is a kind of database for messages; some can even take part in two-phase commit. But it differs in four ways.

A database keeps data until you delete it, while many brokers delete a message once it's delivered, so they're no place for long-term storage. Because of that, brokers expect short queues: if consumers lag and the backlog spills to disk, each message takes longer and throughput can drop. A database lets you pick data with indexes and queries; a broker lets you subscribe to topics matching a pattern. And a query answers from a snapshot and never tells you it went stale, while a broker notifies you as new messages arrive.

cards.prompt: A traditional message broker is a kind of database for messages. How does it differ from a regular database?
keyPoints: It usually deletes a message once it's delivered, so it's no place for long-term storage
It assumes short queues; a big backlog slows each message and can cut throughput
Clients pick data by subscribing to topics that match a pattern, not with indexes and a query language
Instead of answering queries from a snapshot, it tells clients when new data arrives

cards.title: Load balancing and fan-out
cards.body:
When several consumers read one topic, there are two basic patterns. With **load balancing**, each message goes to just one of them, so they share the work. That helps when messages are slow to process: add consumers to go faster. With **fan-out**, every message goes to every consumer, so independent consumers each get the full stream without disturbing each other, like several batch jobs reading the same file.

**Consumer groups** combine the two. Each group that subscribes to a topic gets every message, which is fan-out between groups. Inside a group, each message goes to only one member, which is load balancing.

cards.prompt: An orders topic in a log-based broker is read by two consumer groups: 'billing' with three instances and 'analytics' with two. How many times is each order processed?
choices: Twice: once by one instance in each group
Five times: every instance in both groups gets it
Once: by whichever instance in either group claims it first
cards.explanation: Within a group, messages are shared out for load balancing; across groups, each group gets every message, which is fan-out. Delivering to every instance would make billing charge three times. Treating both groups as one pool would leave analytics without the orders billing took.

cards.title: Acknowledgments and redelivery
cards.body:
A consumer can crash after receiving a message but before finishing with it. So brokers use **acknowledgments**: the consumer says when it's done, and only then is the message removed. If the connection drops or times out with no acknowledgment, the broker assumes the work wasn't done and delivers the message again, perhaps to another consumer. Sometimes the work was done and only the acknowledgment got lost, so it happens twice.

Combined with load balancing, redelivery reorders messages. A worker crashes on message 7 while another handles message 8; message 7 comes back later, after 8. That's harmless for independent messages, not for ones that depend on each other. Giving each consumer its own queue avoids it.

cards.prompt: A queue shares one bank account's events among four consumers. 'Account opened' is sent before 'deposit', but the consumer handling 'account opened' crashes before acknowledging it. What can happen?
choices: The broker holds back the deposit until the opening is acknowledged, keeping them in order
The opening is lost, since the crashed consumer had already received it
The deposit is handled first, and the opening later, once it's redelivered
Both events are redelivered together, which restores their order
cards.explanation: The broker redelivers the unacknowledged message, but by then another consumer may already have handled the deposit. Even brokers that try to keep order reorder messages when load balancing meets redelivery. Acknowledgments exist so a received message isn't lost in a crash, and nothing resends the deposit. A separate queue per consumer avoids this.

cards.title: Dead letter queues
cards.body:
Redelivery has a nasty failure mode. Say a message is malformed, with a price written as text where a number belongs, and handling it crashes the consumer. With no acknowledgment, the broker sends it again, the next consumer crashes too, and so on forever. If the broker keeps strict order, the queue is stuck behind it; if not, it moves on but keeps wasting work on a hopeless message.

A **dead letter queue** (DLQ) breaks the loop: instead of endless retries, the message is moved to a separate queue. Anything landing there is an error, so it's monitored. An operator then drops the message, fixes and resends it, or changes the consumer to cope.

cards.prompt: A malformed message keeps crashing consumers until a dead letter queue steps in. Order what happens.
items: A producer publishes a message with a date field in the wrong format
A consumer crashes while handling it, before acknowledging it
The broker redelivers it, and the next consumer crashes as well
Rather than retry it forever, the broker moves it to a dead letter queue
An alert fires, and an operator drops it, repairs and resends it, or fixes the consumer
cards.explanation: Without the dead letter queue, a broker that enforces strict ordering would be stuck on that message for good; one that allows reordering keeps going but wastes work retrying it.

cards.title: Reading without deleting
cards.body:
Traditional brokers, in the AMQP and JMS style, treat messages as passing traffic. Acknowledging one deletes it, so reading is destructive: you can't run a consumer again and get the same result, and a consumer added today sees only what's sent from now on. A database is the opposite: a new client can read data written long ago.

A **log-based broker** combines the two. Producers append messages to a **log** on disk, and consumers read it in order, getting notified when they reach the end. Reading changes nothing; only the consumer's position in the log, its **offset**, moves. And the consumer can move it back: run new code over yesterday's messages, write the output elsewhere, and repeat.

cards.prompt: Why can't you rerun a consumer over old messages from an AMQP/JMS-style broker, and how does a log-based broker make it possible?
keyPoints: Acknowledging a message deletes it from the broker, so reading is destructive
A consumer that subscribes later only sees messages sent after it joined
In a log-based broker, reading leaves the log unchanged; only the consumer's offset moves
So you can start a consumer at an older offset, send its output somewhere new, and repeat
cards.explanation: That makes a log behave like batch input: read-only data turned into derived output by a repeatable process.

cards.title: Partitions
cards.body:
One disk can take only so many writes, so a log-based broker splits a topic into **partitions** (shards) on different machines, each read and written independently. Within a partition, every message gets the next offset, so its messages have a total order. Across partitions, order isn't guaranteed.

So events that must be seen in order have to share a partition. Choose the partition from a key: in a chat app, hash the conversation ID, and every conversation's messages stay in the order they were sent, while different conversations spread over all the partitions.

cards.prompt: A parcel tracker writes scan events to a 12-partition topic, picking partitions round-robin. A consumer sometimes sees 'delivered' before 'out for delivery' for the same parcel. What's the fix?
choices: Add partitions, so each one carries less traffic and lags less
Make the consumer acknowledge each event before the broker sends the next
Switch the topic to fan-out, so every consumer sees every event in order
Partition by parcel ID, so each parcel's scans land in one partition
cards.explanation: A log-based broker orders messages within a partition but not across partitions, so events that must stay in order have to land in the same one. More partitions spread one parcel's scans even wider. Acknowledging doesn't order events in different partitions, and fan-out decides who receives messages, not their order.

cards.title: Sharing a log
cards.body:
Fan-out is free with a log: each consumer reads at its own pace, and nothing gets deleted. Load balancing works differently. The broker hands each member of a consumer group whole partitions, and the member reads each one in order, on a single thread.

A group can't have more busy members than the topic has partitions; any extra ones wait, so to scale out you add partitions. And one slow message holds up everything behind it in its partition: **head-of-line blocking**.

So pick a traditional queue when each message is expensive, you want to spread them one by one over workers, and order doesn't matter. Pick a log for huge volumes of quick messages where order matters.

cards.prompt: A log-based broker assigns whole partitions to the consumers in a group. A topic has 8 partitions, and its group can't keep up, so the team grows it from 8 instances to 20. What happens?
choices: Throughput rises about 2.5 times, since the broker spreads messages over all 20
Eight instances get partitions to read, and the other twelve sit idle
The broker splits each partition by offset among several instances
Several instances get each message, so the work is duplicated
cards.explanation: Each partition is read by a single member of the group, so the number of busy consumers can't exceed the number of partitions; to scale further, add partitions. Splitting a partition by even and odd offsets is possible, but you'd have to build it yourself, and members of one group don't each get the same message.

cards.prompt: Which workload suits an AMQP/JMS-style broker better than a log-based one?
choices: Generating PDF invoices, where each takes seconds and order doesn't matter
Applying a database's changes to a search index in commit order
Taking in millions of small click events per second for several analytics teams
Feeding a service that must rebuild its state from last month's events
cards.explanation: Assigning individual messages lets many workers share slow, independent jobs, and one slow job doesn't hold up the rest. A log-based broker suits the others: it keeps order within a partition, handles huge volumes of cheap messages, serves many consumers independently, and keeps old messages for replay.

cards.title: Consumer offsets
cards.body:
Since each partition is read in order by a single consumer, its progress through that partition is one number: its offset. Everything before it has been processed, nothing after. So the broker needn't track an acknowledgment per message; it just records each consumer's offsets now and then. Less bookkeeping, plus room to batch and pipeline, is a big reason logs are fast.

It's how a database follower resumes from its position in the leader's log after a disconnection. If a consumer fails, another member of its group takes over its partitions, starting from the last recorded offset. Any messages handled after that offset was saved are handled a second time.

cards.prompt: How does a log-based broker keep track of what a consumer has processed, and why can a consumer failure lead to duplicates?
keyPoints: It records one offset per partition; every message before it counts as processed
That works because each partition is read in order by a single consumer
Storing only offsets means little bookkeeping and allows batching, which helps throughput
After a crash, reading resumes from the last recorded offset, so messages handled since then are processed again
cards.explanation: The offset plays the role of a replication log sequence number: the broker acts like a leader and the consumer like a follower.

cards.title: A huge ring buffer
cards.body:
An append-only log would fill the disk eventually, so it's split into **segments**, and the oldest are deleted or archived. A consumer whose offset points into a deleted segment misses those messages. The log is a fixed-size buffer that discards its oldest entries, a *ring buffer*, but on disk it's huge: a big drive written flat out takes most of a day to fill, and real traffic leaves room for days or weeks.

Only the lagging consumer suffers; producers and other consumers carry on. You can alert when one falls far behind. A stopped consumer leaves nothing behind but its offset, while a traditional broker keeps filling an abandoned queue until someone deletes it.

cards.prompt: A log-based broker keeps three days of messages. One consumer is switched off for five days while the others keep running. What happens when it comes back?
choices: The broker kept its unread messages, as it does for unacknowledged ones
Producers were blocked once that consumer fell three days behind
It missed two days of messages; the other consumers were unaffected
Every consumer lost two days of messages, since they all share one buffer
cards.explanation: The log is a large but fixed-size buffer on disk; once old segments are deleted, a consumer whose offset points into them can't read them. Deletion doesn't wait for slow readers, and producers aren't blocked. Each consumer holds only its own offset, so the laggard hurts no one else. Alerting on consumer lag leaves time to step in.

cards.title: Dual writes
cards.body:
Real applications combine a database, a cache, a search index and a warehouse. Each holds its own copy of the data, so every change must reach them all. Copying full dumps with batch ETL is slow. The tempting shortcut is **dual writes**: the application writes each change to every system itself.

That breaks in two ways. Two clients updating the same record can interleave, so one system applies their writes in one order and another in the reverse order. No error is raised, yet the copies now disagree for good, and nobody notices. And one write can succeed while the other fails: the atomic commit problem. Underneath, no single leader orders the writes for both.

cards.prompt: Ana sets a product's price to 9 and Ben sets it to 12, each writing to the database and then to the search index. The database ends at 12 and the index at 9. Order the four writes.
items: Ana writes 9 to the database
Ben writes 12 to the database
Ben writes 12 to the search index
Ana writes 9 to the search index
cards.explanation: No error occurred, yet the two systems now disagree for good: each kept the last write it saw, and nothing orders writes across both. The other way dual writes go wrong is one write failing while the other succeeds.

cards.title: Change data capture
cards.body:
A database's replication log is already a stream of all its writes. Followers apply it in the same order and end up identical, as long as applying an event is deterministic.

**Change data capture** (CDC) extracts every change committed to a database as a stream that other systems consume. The application writes only to the database, which alone decides the order of writes. A search index or warehouse applies the changes in that order and ends up matching it. In effect the database is the leader and the rest are followers, and a log-based broker carries the changes because it keeps them in order. CDC is usually asynchronous, so followers lag behind.

cards.prompt: How does change data capture (CDC) avoid the problems of dual writes, and what's its main drawback?
keyPoints: The application writes only to the database, so there's no second write to fail on its own
The database alone decides the order of writes and records it in its log
Derived systems apply the changes in log order, so they end up matching the database
It's asynchronous, so derived systems lag behind, with the usual replication lag problems
cards.explanation: In effect, CDC makes the database the leader and each derived system a follower; a log-based broker carries the changes because it keeps them in order.

cards.title: Snapshots and log compaction
cards.body:
A new search index needs every row, not just recent changes, and change logs are usually truncated. So you begin with a consistent **snapshot** of the whole database, tied to a known position in the log, and apply changes from there.

**Log compaction** saves redoing that. The broker keeps only the newest message for each key and drops older ones; a null value, a *tombstone*, deletes the key. If each CDC event carries a primary key and the row's full new value, a compacted topic holds the latest value of every key, maybe some older ones too. A new consumer reads it from offset 0 to get a full copy.

cards.prompt: A CDC topic is log-compacted, and each event carries a primary key and the row's full new value. A new search index is built by reading the topic from offset 0. What does it get?
choices: Only the changes made since compaction last ran
The latest value of every current key, and perhaps some older ones
Every change ever made to every row
Only rows changed in the retention period; the rest need a snapshot
cards.explanation: Compaction keeps at least the newest event for each key and discards overwritten ones, so the topic holds a full copy of the database. If the log were simply truncated by age instead, rows untouched lately would be missing, and you'd need a consistent snapshot tied to a known offset every time you added a consumer.

cards.title: CDC versus event sourcing
cards.body:
**Event sourcing** also records changes as a log, but at a different level. With CDC, the application uses an ordinary mutable database, updating and deleting rows as it likes, and changes are pulled from the database's log at a low level. Each event says what happened to a row.

With event sourcing, the application itself is built on immutable events that it appends to an event store; nobody updates or deletes them. Each event records something that happened in the app, such as 'order cancelled', not the row changes it caused.

You can bolt CDC onto a database already in use, often without the application even knowing. Adopting event sourcing means redesigning the application.

cards.prompt: CDC and event sourcing both record changes as a log. How do they differ?
keyPoints: CDC: the app updates and deletes rows in a mutable database, and changes are pulled from its log at a low level
Event sourcing: the app is built on immutable events it appends itself, and events aren't updated or deleted
CDC events describe low-level state changes; event-sourced events describe what happened at the application level
CDC can be bolted onto a database that already exists, often without the app knowing; event sourcing is a major redesign

cards.title: Schemas become APIs
cards.body:
In microservices, only one service touches its database; others use its API, so the team can change tables freely. CDC undoes that. Consumers see the tables as they are, so the schema becomes a public API: drop a column and you break whoever reads it. If the reader is a production service, not a warehouse job, that can mean an outage; *data contracts* help prevent it.

The **outbox pattern** separates the two. The service also writes to an outbox table with its own stable schema, and only that table is exposed to CDC. It is a dual write, but both writes go to one database in one transaction. The costs: maintaining the mapping, and extra write load.

cards.prompt: A service drops a column from an internal table, which breaks another team's production service that reads the table through CDC. What lets the first team change its tables freely from now on?
choices: Let consumers query the service's tables directly instead of using CDC
Have the app write each change to the database and then publish it to a topic itself
Replay the CDC log from the beginning so every consumer picks up the new schema
Expose only an outbox table with a stable schema, filled in the same transaction
cards.explanation: CDC exposes the upstream schema, turning internal tables into a public API. An outbox decouples them; it is a dual write, but both writes commit in one database transaction. Direct queries couple consumers even more tightly, a separate write to a topic can fail on its own, and replaying doesn't help consumers that need the column. The cost: maintaining the mapping, and extra writes.

cards.title: Compacting an event log
cards.body:
Replaying either kind of log rebuilds the current state, but compaction suits only one. A CDC update event carries the whole new version of a row, so the latest event for a key says everything, and earlier ones can go.

An event-sourced event records what a user did, such as 'added two tickets to the basket', not the state that resulted. Later events don't replace earlier ones; the state depends on all of them, so you can't compact by key. Such systems often save snapshots of the derived state, so they needn't replay the whole log each time. But snapshots only speed up reads and crash recovery: the plan is still to keep every raw event forever.

cards.prompt: Why can a CDC log be compacted by key, while an event-sourced log usually can't?
choices: Event-sourced systems keep snapshots of state, which already make compaction unnecessary
Compaction would reorder the surviving events, which event sourcing forbids
A CDC event holds the full new row; an action event doesn't override earlier ones
cards.explanation: In CDC the latest event for a key fully determines its value, so earlier ones can go. Event-sourced events record user actions, and the state depends on the whole history. Snapshots there only speed up reads and recovery; the raw events are still meant to be kept. Compaction drops events but never reorders the ones it keeps.

cards.title: State and its changelog
cards.body:
Every piece of changing state comes from the events that changed it. A shop's stock count is every delivery minus every sale; a leaderboard is every score posted. Even when something is undone, the fact that it happened stays true.

So a mutable database and a log of immutable events you only append to aren't rivals: they're two views of one thing. In calculus terms, state is the event stream *integrated* over time, and the stream of changes is the state *differentiated* by time. Keep the log durably and the state can always be rebuilt. The log then holds all the information; storing the current state too is only a way to read it fast.

cards.prompt: How does a database's current state relate to an append-only log of its changes?
keyPoints: The current state is the result of applying every event so far, like integrating the stream over time
The change stream is what you get by recording each change to the state, like differentiating it
Kept durably, the log holds all the information; storing the current state too is only a way to read it faster
cards.explanation: Log compaction sits between the two: it keeps only the newest version of each record.

cards.title: Why keep events immutable
cards.body:
Accountants have kept immutable records for centuries. Each transaction goes into an append-only ledger, and the balances are derived by adding it up. A mistake is never erased: a new entry that cancels it is added, so the trail stays complete for auditors.

Software gains the same way. If buggy code overwrites rows in place, the old values are gone and recovery is hard. With an append-only log, you can see what went wrong and rebuild the state.

Events also hold more than the current state. A listener adds a song to a playlist and removes it a minute later. The playlist ends up unchanged, but the log still shows the hesitation, which may interest your analysts.

cards.prompt: A ticketing app keeps all its data in an append-only event log. A glitch recorded one customer's purchase twice. What's the right way to fix it?
choices: Delete the duplicate purchase event, then rebuild the state from the log
Append a refund event for the duplicate, leaving both purchases in the log
Rewrite the duplicate event in place as a 'cancelled' event
Correct the derived ticket count directly and leave the log alone
cards.explanation: Like an accountant's ledger, an immutable log is corrected by appending a compensating event, so the record of what happened stays for auditing and diagnosis. Deleting or rewriting an event destroys that history. Patching only the derived state leaves it out of step with the log, so the next rebuild brings the error back.

cards.title: Many views from one log
cards.body:
Once the log is the record and everything else is derived, you can build as many read-optimized **views** from it as you like, each just another consumer. CDC streams work as well as event sourcing.

It makes change easier. For a new feature, build a new view from the log and run it beside the old ones, without touching them. Once readers have moved over, shut the old one down. That's often simpler than migrating a schema in place.

It also defuses the normalization debate, which assumes data is written in the shape it's read. Write once to the log, and let each view denormalize as its queries need: the process deriving the views keeps the duplicates consistent.

cards.prompt: Why do arguments over normalized versus denormalized schemas matter less when read views are derived from an event log?
keyPoints: Writes go to the log in one form, and each view can take whatever shape suits its queries
Duplicated data in a view stays consistent, because the process deriving it from the log keeps it updated
A new view can be built from the log beside the old one, instead of migrating a schema in place

cards.title: Concurrency with an event log
cards.body:
Deriving views from a log has a catch: views are updated asynchronously, so users may not see their own write straight away. Updating them synchronously would take a distributed transaction or waiting, which is rarely practical.

But a log also removes a lot of concurrency trouble. Many multi-object transactions exist because one user action changes data in several places. Design one event to describe the whole action, like 'move 20 from savings to checking', and the action is a single append, which is easy to make atomic. And if the log and the state are sharded the same way, one single-threaded consumer per shard applies events one at a time, in the log's order, so writes need no locks.

cards.prompt: How can deriving state from an event log reduce the need for multi-object transactions and locks?
keyPoints: An event can describe a whole user action, so the action is a single append, which is easy to make atomic
If the log and the state are sharded the same way, a single-threaded consumer per shard needs no concurrency control for writes
The log fixes one serial order of events within each shard, so there's no nondeterministic interleaving
cards.explanation: The cost is on the read side: views are usually updated asynchronously, so a user may not see their own write straight away.

cards.title: Limits of immutability
cards.body:
Keeping every change forever isn't always practical. Datasets that mostly grow are easy. But a small dataset with many updates and deletes can pile up a history far bigger than itself, and then fragmentation, compaction and garbage collection decide whether the system stays healthy.

Sometimes data must really go: privacy law requires erasing personal data on request, or leaked sensitive data must be contained. Appending a 'deleted' event isn't enough; you need history rewritten as if the data had never existed.

That's hard. Storage engines, filesystems and SSDs write new data elsewhere rather than overwriting, so old copies linger, and backups are kept immutable on purpose. In practice, deleting makes data harder to find, not impossible.

cards.prompt: When does keeping an immutable history of every change stop being practical?
keyPoints: When a small dataset sees many updates and deletes: history grows huge, and compaction and garbage collection become critical
When data must go for legal or administrative reasons, such as privacy law or a leak; appending a 'deleted' event isn't enough
Truly deleting is hard anyway: storage engines, filesystems and SSDs write to new places, and backups are deliberately immutable
cards.explanation: In practice, deletion makes data harder to retrieve rather than impossible.

cards.title: Crypto-shredding
cards.body:
**Crypto-shredding** makes immutable data deletable. You encrypt any data you might need to delete, and to delete it you destroy the key. The ciphertext stays where it is, in logs and backups, but nobody can read it.

This moves the problem more than it solves it: the data stays immutable, but now the key store must be mutable. And you must decide up front which data shares a key, because destroying a key wipes everything it protects, never just part. Encrypt a year of records under one key, and you can only shred the whole year. A key per item, on the other hand, makes the key store as large as the data.

cards.prompt: A health app encrypts each clinic's patient records with one key per clinic, planning to crypto-shred data on request. One patient asks to be erased. What's the problem?
choices: Forgetting the clinic's key would erase every patient of that clinic
Nothing: forgetting the clinic's key erases only that patient's records
The key store is immutable too, so no key can ever be forgotten
Crypto-shredding only works on data that has never been backed up
cards.explanation: A key can only be shredded for all the data under it, so which data shares a key must be decided up front. One key per record would make the key store as big as the data itself. The key store has to be mutable; that's where the problem moves. Backed-up ciphertext is harmless once its key is gone.

cards.title: Processing a stream
cards.body:
Once you have a stream, you can do three things with it. Write it into a database, cache or search index for others to query. Push it to people, as alerts, notifications or a live dashboard. Or turn it into new streams, perhaps via several steps. Code that does that is an **operator**, or *job*.

Operators look a lot like batch jobs: they read input without changing it, append output elsewhere, and shard, map and filter the same way. The crucial difference is that a stream never ends. Sorting needs the whole input, so sort-merge joins are out. And a job running for years can't simply start over after a crash, so fault tolerance has to work differently.

cards.prompt: Stream operators work much like batch jobs. What's the crucial difference, and what does it change?
keyPoints: A stream never ends
Sorting an unbounded input is impossible, so sort-merge joins are out
A job that has run for years can't just restart from the beginning after a crash, so fault tolerance must work differently
cards.explanation: Sharding, parallelism, and simple mapping and filtering carry over from batch processing unchanged.

cards.title: Complex event processing
cards.body:
Stream processing grew up in monitoring: a bank flagging a card used in two countries within an hour, or a greenhouse alarm when the heating fails. That calls for matching patterns across events.

**Complex event processing** (CEP) lets you describe a sequence of events to look for, much as a regular expression describes a sequence of characters. You write the rule in an SQL-like language or a GUI. The engine keeps a state machine of partial matches and emits a *complex event* when the whole pattern appears.

This flips the usual roles. A database stores data and forgets each query once answered. A CEP engine stores the queries long term, and checks each arriving event against them.

cards.prompt: An intensive care unit wants an alert when a patient's heart rate rises over three readings in a row and their oxygen level then drops within ten minutes. Which approach fits best?
choices: Store the readings and have a dashboard query the last ten minutes every few seconds
A nightly batch job that scans the day's readings for the sequence
A stream job computing each patient's hourly average heart rate
A standing pattern query that every new reading is matched against as it arrives
cards.explanation: This is complex event processing: the pattern is registered once and kept, and the engine tracks partial matches as events flow past, reversing the usual roles of stored data and passing queries. Polling repeats work and adds delay, a nightly job is far too late, and an average can't detect a sequence.

cards.title: Stream analytics
cards.body:
**Stream analytics** cares less about exact sequences and more about statistics over many events: how often something happens per minute, a rolling average, or this hour compared with the same hour last week. These are computed over a time interval called a **window**, such as the last five minutes, which smooths out noise while still showing changes quickly.

To save memory, jobs sometimes use probabilistic algorithms: Bloom filters to test membership, HyperLogLog to estimate how many distinct items there are, sketches to estimate percentiles. Their answers are approximate, which has led to a myth that stream processing is inherently inexact. It isn't: approximation is an optimization a job may choose, and streams can be processed exactly.

cards.prompt: A stream job counts distinct listeners per song with HyperLogLog. A colleague concludes that stream processing always gives approximate answers. Are they right?
choices: Yes: a stream never ends, so every answer can only be an estimate
Yes: stream processors can't keep enough state to be exact
No: approximation is an optional way to save memory
No, but exact answers need a microbatching engine
cards.explanation: Probabilistic algorithms like HyperLogLog save a lot of memory at the cost of exactness; that's an optimization the job chose. Stream processors can count exactly, and many keep large state. An unbounded input means results keep updating, not that they're estimates, and exactness doesn't depend on the engine's design.

cards.title: Incremental view maintenance
cards.body:
Keeping a cache, index or warehouse in step with a change stream is **maintaining a materialized view**, and so is building event-sourced state. Unlike analytics, it needs every event since the beginning, not a recent window, which suits some window-oriented stream frameworks poorly.

Databases offer materialized views, but they usually refresh them by rerunning the whole query, on a schedule or on request. That wastes work, since most of the data hasn't changed, and the view is stale until the next refresh.

**Incremental view maintenance** (IVM) fixes both. It turns a query into operators that compute incrementally, updating only the results each change affects. That's cheap enough to run constantly, so the view stays fresh.

cards.prompt: Why is refreshing a materialized view by rerunning its query a poor fit for streams, and what does incremental view maintenance (IVM) do instead?
keyPoints: A rerun reprocesses all the data, though most of it hasn't changed
Changes only show up at the next scheduled refresh, so the view goes stale
IVM turns the query into operators that update only what changed, so it can run often and stay fresh
cards.explanation: Maintaining such a view needs events from all time, not just a recent window, which suits some analytics-oriented stream frameworks poorly.

cards.title: Searching a stream
cards.body:
Sometimes you want to know when a single event matches complex criteria, such as a full-text search. A scientist might ask for an alert whenever a new paper mentions a certain protein.

A normal search engine indexes the documents first, then runs each query against the index. Searching a stream turns that around: the queries are stored, and each new document is checked against them, as in CEP. Testing every document against every query works, but it slows down as the queries multiply. So you index the queries too, and check each document only against the queries that could match it.

cards.prompt: A job board lets millions of users save searches and get an alert when a matching job is posted. What keeps the matching fast as saved searches pile up?
choices: Index the saved searches, so each posting is checked only against likely matches
Index the postings, and rerun every saved search against the index each hour
Test each new posting against every saved search, spreading the work over more machines
Collect postings in a queue and match them all in a nightly batch
cards.explanation: Searching a stream flips normal search: the queries are stored and documents flow past them, so indexing the queries narrows the candidates for each document. Rerunning searches hourly or nightly delays the alerts. Testing every pair works at small scale, but its cost grows with the number of saved queries.

cards.title: Actors and stream processors
cards.body:
Services can also talk by passing messages, as in the actor model. That's message-based too, but it isn't stream processing.

Actor frameworks serve mainly as a way to manage concurrency and spread code across machines; stream processing is a way to manage data. Messages between actors are often short-lived and go to one recipient, while an event log is durable and read by many subscribers. Actors can talk in any pattern, including request and reply in cycles, while stream jobs form acyclic pipelines in which one job derives each stream from known inputs.

You can process streams with actors, but many frameworks lose messages in a crash unless you add retries.

cards.prompt: Actor frameworks and stream processors both pass messages. What mainly sets them apart?
choices: Actors are a data management technique, while stream processing manages concurrency
Actor messages are often transient and one-to-one; logs are durable and shared
Actors form acyclic pipelines, while stream jobs can exchange requests in cycles
Actor frameworks guarantee delivery after crashes, while stream processors don't
cards.explanation: Actors are a way to manage concurrency and distributed execution; stream processing manages data, with each stream derived from known inputs in an acyclic pipeline. The other choices swap the roles: actors can talk in cycles, and many actor frameworks lose messages in a crash unless you add retries.

cards.title: Event time and processing time
cards.body:
Analytics often groups events by time, but which time? A batch job uses the timestamp inside each event, since the hour it runs has nothing to do with when things happened. That also makes it deterministic: the same input always gives the same result.

Many stream frameworks instead use the clock of the machine doing the work, **processing time**. That's simple, and fine while events arrive almost instantly. But processing gets delayed by queues, network faults, restarts, or reprocessing after a bug fix, and delays can reorder events too. Then each event is counted when it was handled, not when it happened, so the results mirror the job's own hiccups. Grouping by **event time** avoids that.

cards.prompt: A job counts game logins per minute by its own machine's clock. During a deploy it stops for ten minutes, then works through the backlog. What does its chart show?
choices: A steady line, since every login is still counted exactly once
A gap for ten minutes, then normal values from then on
A spike during the outage, as unprocessed logins pile up
Ten minutes at zero, then a spike that never really happened
cards.explanation: Windowing by processing time puts each login in the minute it was handled, not the minute it happened. Counting by the timestamps inside the events would show the true, steady rate. Batch jobs window by event timestamps for the same reason, which also makes reruns give the same result.

cards.title: Straggler events
cards.body:
With event time, you can never be sure a window is complete. Say you count orders per minute. Most new events now belong to 10:42, but one from 10:40 may still be stuck on a phone with no signal. At some point, perhaps after a quiet spell, you close the 10:40 window and emit its count.

An event that turns up after its window has closed is a **straggler**. You can ignore it, while tracking how many you drop and alerting if that grows. Or you can publish a corrected value for the window, possibly retracting the old one. Producers can also send a marker saying nothing older is coming, but then consumers must track each producer separately.

cards.prompt: A job counts toll-gate passes in one-minute windows by event time. A pass from 08:14 arrives at 08:21, after the 08:14 count was published. What are the sensible options?
choices: Count it in the 08:21 window, since that's when it was processed
Keep every window open indefinitely, so nothing can arrive late
Drop it and count the drops, or publish a corrected 08:14 count
Reject it and have the gate resend it with a newer timestamp
cards.explanation: You can never be sure a window has all its events, so stragglers are either ignored, with a metric to alert if too many are, or folded into a correction that may retract the old value. Moving or restamping the event corrupts both counts, and open-ended windows never produce output. Producers can also announce that no earlier timestamps will follow, but then each producer must be tracked.

cards.title: Whose clock?
cards.body:
Events can be held up on the way. A fitness watch records runs offline and syncs hours later. The time that matters is when the run happened, by the watch's clock, but a user's device clock may be set wrong. The server's clock is trustworthy, but it only knows when the data arrived.

The fix is to log three timestamps: when the event happened, by the device clock; when the device sent it, by the device clock; and when the server received it, by the server clock. Receive time minus send time estimates how far off the device clock is, if network delay is small. Apply that offset to the event time, assuming the clock didn't drift meanwhile.

cards.prompt: A warehouse scanner buffers events while offline and uploads them hours later, and its clock may be wrong. Which three timestamps let you correct for its clock, and how?
keyPoints: When the event happened, by the scanner's clock
When the scanner sent it, by the scanner's clock
When the server received it, by the server's clock
Receive time minus send time estimates the clock offset, which is then applied to the event time
cards.explanation: This assumes network delay is small and the scanner's clock offset didn't change between the event and the upload.

cards.title: Kinds of window
cards.body:
With a **tumbling** window, time is cut into equal back-to-back slots, and each event falls in exactly one: round its timestamp down to the hour, say.
