A **hopping** window is fixed in length too but overlaps the next, like a one-hour window moving forward every 15 minutes, built by combining 15-minute tumbling windows. A **sliding** window groups events that lie within some interval of each other, with no fixed boundaries; you keep a time-sorted buffer and drop events as they age out. A **session** window has no fixed length: it groups one user's burst of activity and closes after a stretch of inactivity.

A count needs one number, however big the window; a sliding window buffers its events.

cards.prompt: A ride-hailing dashboard updates every minute with the number of ride requests in the previous ten minutes. Which kind of window is that?
choices: Hopping: ten minutes long, advancing a minute at a time
Tumbling: fixed ten-minute blocks that follow each other without overlap
Sliding: any requests within ten minutes of each other
Session: closing after ten minutes with no requests
cards.explanation: A hopping window has a fixed length but overlaps the next one, which smooths the numbers; it can be built by adding up one-minute tumbling windows. Tumbling windows would update only every ten minutes. A sliding window has no fixed boundaries, and a session window has no fixed length.

cards.title: Stream-stream joins
cards.body:
Streams need joins too, but events keep coming. In a **stream-stream join**, both inputs are activity events. Say an app logs 'notification sent' and 'notification opened', both carrying the notification's ID, and you want open rates. An open may never come, may come days later, or may even arrive first. So you pick a window: join the two if they're at most a day apart.

The job keeps recent events from both streams, indexed by ID. Each new event is stored and checked against the other side; a match emits a result, and a send that expires unopened emits a 'not opened'. Copying send details into the open event isn't a join: it only covers notifications that were opened.

cards.prompt: An insurance site logs a 'quote shown' event and, if the visitor buys, a 'policy bought' event with the same session ID. To measure conversion, a developer copies the quote details into the purchase event and skips the join. What's lost?
choices: Nothing: the purchase events now hold all the data needed
The quotes that never led to a purchase
The event order, since purchases can arrive before quotes
The ability to shard both streams by session ID
cards.explanation: Conversion compares purchases with quotes, and the quotes nobody acted on exist only in the quote stream. A window join keeps recent quotes in state by session ID, matches purchases against them, and can emit a 'not converted' event when a quote expires unmatched. Arrival order and sharding are separate concerns.

cards.title: Stream-table joins
cards.body:
A **stream-table join** *enriches* events with data from a database, say, adding each customer's loyalty tier to their orders. Querying the database for every event is slow and can overload it. Instead the job keeps a local copy of the table: a hash table in memory, or an index on local disk.

A batch job can use a snapshot, because it finishes. A stream job runs for months while the table keeps changing, so its copy has to stay current. It subscribes to the table's changelog through CDC and updates the copy as rows change. So it's really a join of two streams, where the table side's window stretches back to the very first change, newer versions replacing older ones.

cards.prompt: A stream job adds each warehouse's address to shipment events by querying the warehouse database for every event, and the database is struggling. What's the usual fix?
choices: Cache each lookup indefinitely, since warehouse rows rarely change
Load the warehouse table once at startup, as a batch job would
Keep a local copy of the table in the job, updated from its change stream
Buffer shipments and query the database once an hour in bulk
cards.explanation: A local copy answers lookups without a network round trip, and subscribing to the table's CDC stream keeps it current. A batch job can use a one-off snapshot because it ends; a long-running stream job's copy would drift out of date, as would a cache that never expires. Hourly bulk queries delay every event.

cards.title: Table-table joins
cards.body:
In a **table-table join**, both inputs are changelogs. A music app might keep, for each listener, a list of new releases by the artists they follow, built from a releases changelog and a follows changelog.

Every change to either input meets the other input's current state. A new release meets its artist's current followers and lands in each of their lists. A new follow meets that artist's existing releases; an unfollow removes them. What comes out is a stream of changes to a materialized view of the join, a cache of the query's result.

If a stream is a table's derivative, this is the product rule: (uv)' = u'v + uv'.

cards.prompt: A view holds each warehouse's stock value, the sum of quantity times price, built from a stock-level changelog and a price changelog. A product's price changes. What must the job do?
choices: Wait until that product's stock next changes, then apply the new price
Recompute every warehouse's total from both full tables
Update only warehouses that receive the product after the change
Join the new price with current stock in each warehouse and adjust its total
cards.explanation: In a table-table join, every change to either input meets the current contents of the other: a price change meets current stock levels, and a stock change meets current prices. Waiting, or touching only later arrivals, leaves totals wrong. Recomputing everything throws away the point of maintaining the view incrementally.

cards.title: Joins that depend on time
cards.body:
All three joins build state from one input and consult it when a record arrives on the other, so the order of events matters. A log keeps order within a partition, but not across streams.

Say orders in foreign currencies are joined with a changelog of exchange rates. Orders processed just before a rate change get the old rate, those just after get the new one. Rerun the job and the streams may interleave differently, so the result changes: the join is **nondeterministic**. Data warehouses call this a *slowly changing dimension*. One fix: give each rate version an ID and record it in the order, but then compaction can't drop old versions. Or copy the rate into each order.

cards.prompt: A job joins sales with a changelog of each salesperson's commission rate. Rerunning it over last year's sales gives different totals from the first run. What makes the join deterministic?
choices: Give every rate version its own ID, and record that ID in each sale
Turn on log compaction for the rates, so reruns see one consistent table
Join each sale with the rates as they stand today
Use more partitions, so both streams are processed in step
cards.explanation: Order across streams isn't guaranteed, so a sale may meet the old or the new rate depending on how the inputs interleave. Pinning the version in the sale fixes that, at the cost of keeping every version, which rules out compaction; copying the rate into each sale also works. Today's rates are wrong for old sales, and partitions don't order streams relative to each other.

cards.prompt: Compare the three kinds of join in stream processing: what are the inputs of each, and what state does the job keep?
keyPoints: Stream-stream: two streams of activity events; it keeps recent events from both, within a time window
Stream-table: activity events plus a table's changelog; it keeps a local copy of the table, a window reaching back to the start
Table-table: two changelogs; each change is joined with the other side's latest state, giving a stream of changes to the joined view
cards.explanation: All three build state from one input and query it when records from the other arrive, so the order of events matters.

cards.title: Microbatching
cards.body:
Batch jobs hide failures: a failed task reruns, its partial output is thrown away, and the result looks as if each record was processed once. That's called **exactly-once** semantics, though *effectively-once* would be more accurate. A stream job can't hold back its output until it's done, because it's never done.

**Microbatching** cuts the stream into small blocks, typically about a second long, and runs each as a tiny batch job. The size is a trade-off: smaller blocks bring more scheduling and coordination overhead, larger ones mean waiting longer for results. Each block also acts as a tumbling window by processing time, so longer windows need state carried from one block to the next.

cards.prompt: A microbatching stream job runs one-second batches. The team considers cutting them to 10 ms. What's the main cost?
choices: Results become visible later than before
More scheduling and coordination overhead for the same data
Exactly-once guarantees no longer hold within the job
Event-time windows can no longer be computed
cards.explanation: Each batch has fixed scheduling and coordination costs, so tiny batches spend more on overhead; bigger batches cost latency instead, which is why about a second is typical. Batch size doesn't change exactly-once within the framework. Each batch acts as a processing-time tumbling window, so longer or event-time windows just need state carried between batches.

cards.title: Checkpointing
cards.body:
Another approach takes rolling **checkpoints**. Markers called *barriers* are injected into the input and flow through the job along with the messages. When a barrier reaches an operator, the operator writes its state to durable storage, and the checkpoint records how far into each input the job had read. If an operator later crashes, the job reloads the last checkpoint, discards any output produced since, and resumes reading from the recorded positions. Unlike microbatches, barriers don't impose a window size.

Inside the framework, both approaches give effectively-once results. But output that has left it, such as writes to an outside system, messages to an external broker or emails, can't be taken back. A restart repeats it.

cards.prompt: Order how a stream processor that uses checkpointing recovers from a crash.
items: Barriers flow through the stream along with ordinary messages
As a barrier passes, each operator saves its state to durable storage
An operator crashes some time later
The job restores the state from the latest checkpoint and discards output produced since
It resumes reading input from the positions recorded in that checkpoint
cards.explanation: Unlike microbatching, the barriers don't impose a window size on the job.

cards.prompt: A stream job uses checkpointing for exactly-once processing. After a crash and a restart from the last checkpoint, which of its outputs may contain duplicates?
choices: Its own operator state, such as running counts
Messages it passed between operators inside the job
Rows it wrote to an external database
cards.explanation: Inside the framework, output since the checkpoint is discarded and recomputed, so the visible effect is as if each record were processed once: effectively once. Writes that have left the framework can't be discarded, so a restart repeats them unless they're idempotent or committed atomically with everything else.

cards.title: Atomic commit for streams
cards.body:
To look exactly-once despite faults, everything that processing an event causes must happen if and only if the processing succeeds. That means messages sent downstream or to outside systems, emails included, any database writes, changes to the operator's own state, and acknowledging the input, such as moving the consumer offset forward. Either all of it commits, or none of it does.

That's a distributed transaction, and XA-style ones that span different technologies are known to be painful. But in a restricted setting it can be done efficiently. Some frameworks keep the transaction internal, managing both state and messaging themselves, and spread its overhead by covering many input messages in one transaction.

cards.prompt: For a stream processor to appear to handle each event exactly once, what must commit atomically, and how do frameworks keep this affordable?
keyPoints: Every output: messages to downstream operators or external systems, and database writes
Changes to the operator's state
Acknowledging the input, such as moving the consumer offset forward
The transaction stays inside the framework rather than spanning different technologies as XA does, and covers many messages at once

cards.title: Idempotence
cards.body:
Instead of transactions, you can make writes **idempotent**: doing one twice has the same effect as doing it once. Setting a user's email address is idempotent; adding 10 points to a score is not, since a retry adds 20.

Other writes can usually gain that property with a little metadata. Messages in a log-based broker have increasing offsets, so store with each value the offset of the message that last updated it. On a replay, a message whose offset isn't newer was already applied, so skip it.

This assumes a restart replays the same messages in order, processing is deterministic, and no other node writes the same value; during failover, fencing keeps out a node wrongly presumed dead.

cards.prompt: A consumer reads sales from a topic partitioned by store and adds each one to that store's total in an external database. After restarts, some sales are counted twice. Which change makes the update safe to repeat?
choices: Retry each increment until the database confirms it was written
Commit the consumer offset before applying each sale's increment
Process the partition with a pool of threads so it finishes faster
Save the offset of the last applied sale with the total, and skip any not newer
cards.explanation: With the offset stored beside the value, a replayed sale is recognized and ignored, so the increment becomes idempotent. This relies on a replay delivering identical messages in identical order, deterministic processing, and no other writer, with fencing during failover. Retrying adds duplicates, committing the offset first loses sales in a crash, and threads complicate offsets.

cards.title: Recovering state
cards.body:
Windowed counts and the tables behind joins are state, and they must survive a failure. There are three broad ways.

Keep the state in a remote, replicated datastore, though a network query for every message is slow. Or keep it local to the job and replicate it now and then: write periodic snapshots to durable storage, or send each change to a log-compacted topic, much like CDC. Or don't replicate it at all and rebuild it from the input: replay the events of a short window, or reread a compacted changelog to restore a local table copy.

Which works best depends on the hardware. On some networks, a remote read is faster than a local disk.

cards.prompt: A stream job keeps state, such as window counts or a table for joins. What are the ways to recover that state after a failure?
keyPoints: Keep it in a remote, replicated datastore, though querying it for every message is slow
Keep it local and replicate it periodically, as snapshots to durable storage or as changes to a compacted topic
Rebuild it from the input: replay a short window, or reread a compacted change stream
cards.explanation: Which is best depends on the hardware: in some systems a network round trip is quicker than a local disk access.

cards.title: No tool does everything
cards.body:
Ask how to store data and find it again, and you'll hear many good answers, each right in different circumstances. A product has to pick one. Making even one code path fast and robust is hard, so software that chases every use case ends up doing each one worse than a specialized tool. Even databases sold as general-purpose are designed with some workload in mind.

Meanwhile, one application uses its data in many ways. A job board needs a durable database for its listings, a search engine for free-text keywords, a cache and analytics. No single tool serves all of that well, so you end up **combining several**, each holding its own copy of the data.

cards.prompt: Why do most applications end up combining several data systems instead of using just one?
keyPoints: Every tool, even a 'general-purpose' database, is designed around a particular usage pattern
A product that tries to cover too many use cases tends to do each one worse than a specialized tool
One application uses its data in several ways, such as keyword search, analytics and caching, and no single tool serves them all well
cards.explanation: The hard part then becomes getting the data into every one of those systems, in the right form.

cards.title: One order for every write
cards.body:
With data copied into several systems, be clear where each write lands first and which copies derive from which.

Say a shop writes every product change to its database, then uses change data capture to apply those changes, in the same order, to a search index. The database is the only way in, so the index can't drift. If the app wrote to both directly instead, two concurrent edits could reach them in opposite orders, and the copies would disagree forever.

So funnel all input through one system that picks a **total order** for writes, and derive everything else in that order. Updates applied from such a log can be deterministic and idempotent, so recovering from a fault means replaying.

cards.prompt: When the same data is copied into several systems, what makes keeping the copies consistent much easier?
keyPoints: All input goes into one system first, which decides a single order for every write
Every other representation is derived by applying the writes in that same order
Updates derived from an ordered log can be made deterministic and idempotent, so recovering from a fault is a matter of replaying
cards.explanation: This is state machine replication again; whether the ordered log comes from CDC or event sourcing matters less than having one total order.

cards.title: Derived data or transactions
cards.body:
The classic way to keep several systems in step is a **distributed transaction**. It applies changes atomically through an atomic commit protocol. Log-based derived data reaches the same goal through deterministic retries and idempotence, so every change eventually lands everywhere.

The biggest practical difference is freshness. A transaction usually lets you read your own write straight away. Derived systems are typically updated asynchronously, so a read may lag behind.

But XA, the standard for transactions across products, is slow and copes badly with faults, and nothing better is likely to be widely adopted soon. So logs are the most promising way to connect different systems, ideally with stronger read guarantees added on top.

cards.prompt: Log-based derived data and distributed transactions both keep several systems consistent. What's the biggest practical difference?
choices: Transactions recover from faults by idempotent retries, while logs depend on an atomic commit protocol
Derived data can't promise that every change will eventually reach every system that needs it
Transactions usually let you read a value right after writing it; derived data may lag behind
Derived data only works between systems built by the same vendor, so it suits fewer setups
cards.explanation: Transactions typically give you read-your-writes; asynchronously updated derived systems don't by default. The mechanisms are the other way around: transactions use atomic commit, logs use deterministic retry and idempotence. Retries make sure every change does arrive, and logs are the easier way to link systems from different vendors.

cards.title: Where total order breaks
cards.body:
A totally ordered log usually needs one leader that orders all events, as in any single-leader database. That's fine while small, but growth breaks it in four ways.

With more events than one machine can handle, you shard the log, and events in different shards have no defined order. Across regions, each usually gets its own leader, since coordinating between them is slow. Microservices each keep their own durable state, so events from two services aren't ordered either. And apps that apply changes locally at once, or work offline, see events in a different order from the server.

Formally this is **total order broadcast**, equivalent to consensus, and most consensus algorithms assume one node can order the whole stream.

cards.prompt: Why does a single totally ordered event log stop being practical as systems grow? Name four situations.
keyPoints: More events than one leader can handle forces you to shard the log, and the order across shards is undefined
Spanning several regions usually means a leader per region, so events from different regions have no defined order
Microservices each keep their own durable state, so events from different services aren't ordered
Clients that apply changes locally right away, or work offline, see events in a different order from the servers
cards.explanation: Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, and most consensus algorithms can't split the work of ordering across several nodes.

cards.title: Capturing causality
cards.body:
Events with no causal link can go in any order, and updates to one object can share a log shard. The trouble is a dependency that crosses systems. A customer changes their address in the profile service, then orders in the order service. The label printer joins the two streams; if it sees the order first, the parcel goes to the old address.

There's no simple fix. **Logical timestamps** order events without coordination, but recipients must still handle late arrivals and extra metadata. Another option: log an event recording what the user saw before acting, and have later events cite its ID. **Conflict resolution** repairs state afterwards, but can't take back an external side effect like a printed label.

cards.prompt: A file-sharing app keeps folder permissions in one service and uploads in another, and a notifier joins the two to email new-file alerts. An owner removes a colleague from a folder, then uploads a pay review into it, yet the colleague gets the alert. Which approach does most to prevent this?
choices: Make the notifier process every event exactly once, so no event can ever take effect twice
Merge the two services' states with an automatic conflict resolution algorithm
Sort the events by the time-of-day clock reading each service stamped on them
Have the upload event cite the ID of an event recording the permissions the owner saw
cards.explanation: The notifier handled the upload before the permission change because the causal link between them was never recorded; pointing to an event that captures what the owner saw records it. Duplicates aren't the problem. Conflict resolution can repair state but can't recall an email already sent. Clocks on different machines drift, and recipients would still get events out of order.

cards.title: Derived data, asynchronously
cards.body:
Batch and stream processors are the machinery of data integration: they turn inputs into search indexes, materialized views, recommendations and metrics. Batch inputs are finite and streams are unbounded, but both favor **deterministic, pure functions**: output depends only on input, inputs are never modified, outputs are only appended. That helps with faults and makes dataflows easy to reason about.

A relational database updates secondary indexes in the same transaction as the table; derived systems could work that way too. But **asynchrony** is what makes log-based systems robust. A failed consumer just falls behind and catches up later, while a distributed transaction aborts if any participant fails, spreading one fault everywhere. Indexes that span shards also work best updated asynchronously.

cards.prompt: A relational database updates its secondary indexes in the same transaction as the table. Why do log-based systems update derived data asynchronously instead?
choices: A fault in one consumer stays local, whereas a distributed transaction aborts if any participant fails
Asynchronous updates mean anyone reading derived data always sees the very latest writes
Synchronous updates can't apply writes to derived systems in the same order as the source
Asynchronous consumers needn't be idempotent, because a log delivers every message to each consumer exactly once
cards.explanation: Asynchrony is what makes log-based systems robust: a slow or failed consumer falls behind and later catches up, while a distributed transaction spreads one participant's failure to all the others. Asynchronous updates give up freshness rather than gaining it. Ordering isn't what's wrong with synchronous updates. Consumers do need idempotence, since messages can be redelivered after a fault.

cards.title: Reprocessing to evolve
cards.body:
Stream processing carries each new change into derived views within moments. Batch processing does something else: it can run over all the history you've accumulated and derive a brand new view from it.

That makes reprocessing a powerful way to evolve a system. Without it, a schema can only change in small ways, like gaining an optional field or a new kind of record, because existing data stays as it was. With it, you can rebuild the dataset in a completely different model that suits new requirements: write the new derivation code, run it over the whole input, and the new view appears. If the code turns out to be wrong, fix it and reprocess again.

cards.prompt: A team's pipeline keeps a product catalog view current from a stream of changes. Now they want each product split into one document per variant, a completely different shape. What lets them do this?
choices: Add optional fields to each document, since that's the only change derived data allows
Deploy the new code and let incoming changes reshape the view over time
Run the new derivation code over the whole history of inputs to build the new view
Have the stream processor rewrite the stored input events into the new shape
cards.explanation: Reprocessing all the accumulated input with new code can restructure a dataset into an entirely new model. Optional fields are the limit only when you can't reprocess. Waiting for new changes leaves products that never change in the old shape. The input events stay as they are; it's the derived view that gets rebuilt.

cards.title: Migrating gradually
cards.body:
Reprocessing also means you never have to switch models overnight. Keep the old schema and the new one side by side, as two views derived independently from the same underlying data, both kept up to date.

Then move a small share of users to the new view to test its speed and shake out its bugs, while everyone else stays on the old one. Raise the share bit by bit, then drop the old view. It's like building a new bridge beside the old one and moving traffic across lane by lane.

Every step can be undone, since a working system is always there to fall back on. Less risk of lasting damage lets you move faster.

cards.prompt: A recipe app is restructuring its meal-plan data: it derives a view in the new model from the same underlying data, next to the old view, and moves 5% of users onto it. Then a bug turns up in the new view. What's the best response?
choices: Restore the old view from a backup, since it stopped being updated once the migration began
Move those users back to the old view, which is still kept up to date, and fix the bug
Roll the underlying data back to its state from before the migration started
Move every user to the new view quickly, so there's only one view left to fix
cards.explanation: Both views are derived from the same data and both stay current, so every stage of a gradual migration can be undone: there's always a working system to fall back on. The old view never stopped updating and the underlying data wasn't touched, so there's nothing to restore or roll back. Rushing everyone onto a buggy view throws that safety net away.

cards.title: Unifying batch and stream
cards.body:
An early attempt to combine batch and stream processing, the **lambda architecture**, ran the two side by side and had enough problems that it has fallen out of use. Newer systems do both in one engine, an approach sometimes called the **kappa architecture**.

That takes three things. The engine must be able to run old events through the same code that handles new ones, for example by rereading a log-based broker or files in object storage. It needs **exactly-once semantics**: output as if no faults had happened, which means throwing away the partial output of failed tasks. And it must window by **event time**, because when you replay last year's events, the moment they're processed tells you nothing.

cards.prompt: What does a single system need in order to handle both reprocessing of history and processing of live events?
keyPoints: It can replay historical events through the same engine that handles new ones
It gives exactly-once semantics: the output is as if no faults happened, with failed tasks' partial output thrown away
It windows by event time, since processing time means nothing when replaying old events
cards.explanation: This style is sometimes called the kappa architecture; the earlier lambda architecture had many problems and has fallen out of use.

cards.title: Unix and relational databases
cards.body:
Databases, stream processors and operating systems all store and process data. Unix and relational databases, both from the early 1970s, did so with opposite philosophies.

Unix gives programmers a logical but low-level view of the hardware: files and pipes are just sequences of bytes. Relational databases give them a high-level abstraction that hides disk layout, concurrency and crash recovery behind SQL and transactions.

Each is *simpler* in its own way. Unix is a thin wrapper over hardware resources. In a database, a short declarative query leans on an optimizer, indexes, join algorithms and replication without its author knowing how they work. The tension is still alive: NoSQL can be read as the Unix approach applied to distributed OLTP.

cards.prompt: Unix and relational databases both manage information, with opposite philosophies. In what sense is each one 'simpler'?
choices: Unix hides concurrency and crash recovery from programmers; databases hand them raw sequences of bytes
Unix is a thin layer over the hardware; a short SQL query draws on machinery its author needn't know
Both are simple because they share one abstraction: files and pipes that carry bytes
Databases are simpler to implement, while Unix is simpler to write queries against
cards.explanation: Unix gives programmers low-level abstractions, files and pipes of bytes; relational databases hide disk layout, concurrency and recovery behind SQL and transactions. The first choice swaps the two. They don't share an abstraction, and a database with an optimizer, indexes and replication is hard to build. NoSQL can be read as a Unix-style approach applied to distributed OLTP.

cards.title: Building views from live data
cards.body:
Many database features mirror what people build with stream processors: indexes, materialized views, replication logs.

Say you want a new search index over a database that keeps taking writes. You copy a consistent snapshot, pick out the words in each record, sort them and write the index out. Then you apply every change made since the snapshot, and from then on follow the stream of changes. Adding a follower replica works the same way, and so does starting change data capture.

CREATE INDEX does the same inside one database, on a single table: it's reprocessing existing data into a new view.

cards.prompt: A relational database runs CREATE INDEX on a table that stays open for writes. Order what it does.
items: Scan a consistent snapshot of the table
Pick out the values being indexed and sort them
Write out the index
Apply the writes made since the snapshot was taken
From then on, update the index with every write to the table
cards.explanation: It's the same pattern as setting up a new follower or bootstrapping CDC: derive a new view from a snapshot, catch up on the backlog, then follow the changes.

cards.title: The organization as a database
cards.body:
Zoom out, and an organization's whole dataflow looks like a single giant database. Each batch, stream or ETL job that carries data from one place and shape to another is doing what a database does internally when it keeps an index or a materialized view up to date.

In this picture, batch and stream processors are elaborate versions of triggers, stored procedures and view maintenance. The derived systems they feed are like index types: where one database offers several kinds of index, the organization has a search engine, a warehouse and a cache. The difference is that each one is separate software, running on its own machines, often run by its own team.

cards.prompt: In what sense does an organization's dataflow look like one huge database?
keyPoints: Batch, stream and ETL jobs that move data between systems act like the database code that keeps indexes and materialized views current
Stream and batch processors play the role of triggers, stored procedures and view maintenance
Each derived data system is like an index type, but it runs as separate software, on separate machines, run by separate teams
cards.explanation: Unbundling the database means providing its features this way, rather than inside one integrated product.

cards.title: Federation and unbundling
cards.body:
If no storage format suits every access pattern, there are two ways to make many tools act as one.

A **federated database**, or *polystore*, unifies reads: one query interface over many storage engines. Users can combine data from several stores in one query, while each application still talks to its own store directly. It's in the relational tradition: a high-level language and clean semantics over a complicated implementation.

An **unbundled database** unifies writes. It takes the index maintenance a database does internally and spreads it across technologies, using change capture and event logs so every change reaches every store despite faults. It's in the Unix spirit: single-purpose tools, connected through a uniform low-level interface. Syncing writes is the harder problem.

cards.prompt: Analysts want to join data from a document store, a graph database and a warehouse in one SQL query, while each application keeps using its own store directly. Which approach fits?
choices: An unbundled setup that streams every store's writes through a shared event log
Distributed transactions that span all three stores whenever a query runs
Migrating all the data into one integrated database that every team shares
A federated query engine that offers one interface over all three stores
cards.explanation: Federation unifies reads: one high-level query interface over many stores, while applications still use each store natively. Unbundling unifies writes, keeping several stores in sync, which isn't what's needed here. Distributed transactions are about making writes atomic, not about querying. One shared database would take away the specialized stores the applications depend on.

cards.title: Logs between technologies
cards.body:
Transactions work well inside one system; some stream processors even use them internally for exactly-once output. Across technologies built by different groups, though, there's no standard transaction protocol they all speak. An ordered log read by **idempotent consumers** is a far simpler contract that any system can implement: the order keeps the copies consistent, and idempotence absorbs redelivered messages.

The big win is **loose coupling**, at two levels. In the system, if a consumer slows or crashes, the log buffers its messages while the producer and other consumers carry on; once fixed, it catches up, missing nothing. Among people, teams build, improve and run their pieces independently, with the log as a well-defined interface between them.

cards.prompt: A stream processor writes its output to a key-value store and a search index, each built by a different team. Why use an ordered log with idempotent consumers rather than a distributed transaction?
choices: Distributed transactions can't give exactly-once semantics, not even inside a single stream processing system
No standard protocol spans systems built by different groups, but a log is easy for any of them to use
The log updates both stores synchronously, so readers always see the same state in each
Idempotent consumers make the order of events irrelevant, so no coordination is needed at all
cards.explanation: Within one system, transactions can work well; some stream processors use them internally for exactly-once semantics. Across technologies written by different groups there's no shared protocol, so a log is the practical interface. Log consumers are asynchronous, not synchronous. And order still matters: idempotence copes with duplicates, not with reordering.

cards.prompt: Log-based integration gives loose coupling. How does that show at the system level and at the human level?
keyPoints: System: if a consumer is slow or fails, the log buffers its messages; the producer and other consumers carry on, and the consumer catches up later without missing anything
Human: teams build, improve and run their components independently, with the event log as a well-defined interface between them
cards.explanation: Synchronous distributed transactions do the opposite: they tend to turn one local fault into a widespread failure.

cards.title: When one database is enough
cards.body:
Unbundling doesn't replace databases. Stream processors still need them to hold state, and the output of batch and stream jobs still needs them to serve queries.

Composing tools has a price. Each extra piece brings its own learning curve, configuration and operational quirks, so run as few as you can. An integrated product often performs better and more predictably on the workload it was built for than tools glued together with your code. And building for scale you don't have is premature optimization that can lock you into a rigid design.

Unbundling is about breadth, not depth: covering more kinds of workload than any one product can. If a single tool already does everything you need, use it.

cards.prompt: A small company needs storage, secondary indexes and simple keyword search, and the one database it already runs handles all three well. An engineer proposes adding an event log, a stream processor, a search engine and a cache. What's the best advice?
choices: Stick with the single database; composing tools pays off only when no one product meets your needs
Adopt the composed design now, since a set of composed systems beats any single product on every workload
Adopt it, because a database that serves searches can't also act as a system of record
Compose the tools, but have the application write to each store directly and skip the log
cards.explanation: Unbundling is about breadth: covering workloads no single product handles. When one tool does everything you need, extra moving parts only add learning and operational work, and building for scale you don't need is premature optimization. An integrated product is often faster on its own target workload. Writing to several stores directly brings back the ordering problems a log solves.

cards.title: Code apart from the database
cards.body:
Every derived dataset is some function of its inputs. A secondary index's function is standard, so databases build it in. A full-text index often needs language processing tuned to your domain, a machine learning model needs features specific to your app, and a cache must know what your screens display. That takes custom code.

Databases can run code in triggers and stored procedures, but those were an afterthought, and they handle dependencies, version control, rolling upgrades, monitoring and calls to other services poorly. Deployment tools such as Kubernetes do only that job, and do it far better. So the norm is to deploy application code on its own, stateless, with its state in databases.

cards.prompt: A team needs a cache of personalized homepage cards, built by custom code that uses a machine learning library and calls a pricing service. Where should that code run?
choices: As stored procedures, so the code sits right next to the data it reads
Nowhere special: the database builds this kind of dataset in, as it does indexes
Inside a trigger, since triggers fire on every write and keep the cache fresh
As its own service, deployed with standard tools and fed by the database's changes
cards.explanation: Custom derivation code needs dependency management, versioning, rolling upgrades, monitoring and network calls, which deployment tools handle well and databases handle poorly. Stored procedures and triggers both run code inside the database, where it was an afterthought. Only standard functions like secondary indexes come built in; app-specific ones don't.

cards.title: From variable to dataflow
cards.body:
In a typical web app, the database acts like a mutable variable shared over the network: code reads and writes it, and the database keeps it durable. As with most variables, you usually can't subscribe to it; to notice a change, you poll, repeating the query.

A spreadsheet works differently: change a cell and every formula that uses it recalculates. **Dataflow** brings that to data systems. Code reacts to a state change in one place by making state changes somewhere else, with stream operators chained like Unix pipes.

This needs two things that log-based brokers provide: changes processed in a stable order, and fault-tolerant delivery. Lose a single message, and a derived view is out of sync for good.

cards.prompt: How does dataflow thinking change the relationship between application code and the database?
keyPoints: Usually the database is a passive shared variable: the application reads and writes it, and has to poll to notice changes
In dataflow, a change in one place's state triggers code that updates state elsewhere
Derived data needs stable ordering and reliable delivery: a single lost message leaves a view out of sync for good
cards.explanation: Databases also make poor hosts for application code (no package management, versioning or rolling upgrades), so that code runs separately, for example as stream operators.

cards.title: Subscribe instead of asking
cards.body:
Microservices usually call each other with synchronous requests. Dataflow systems share their main benefit, teams working independently, but talk through one-way asynchronous streams.

Say a shipping service needs each country's current tax rate. With requests, it asks a tax service for every shipment. With dataflow, it subscribes in advance to a stream of rate changes, keeps the latest rates in a **local** database, and queries that. Skipping the network request is both faster and sturdier: shipments keep flowing while the tax service is down.

This is a stream join, and it depends on time. Reprocess old shipments later and they'll pick up today's rates, unless you look up the rate that applied at the time.

cards.prompt: A food delivery app's order service needs each restaurant's current delivery fee, which the restaurants service owns. How does a dataflow design get the fee?
choices: It calls the restaurants service for each order, so the fee is always current and the coupling stays low
It reads the restaurants service's database directly, which saves a hop through its API
It follows a stream of fee changes into a local store and queries that, with no network call per order
It sends each order to the restaurants service, which adds the fee and passes the order along
cards.explanation: Subscribing ahead of time replaces a request to another service with a local query: faster, and it keeps working while the restaurants service is down. Calling per order adds latency and a runtime dependency. Reading another service's database ties you to its internals. Routing every order through the other service makes each order depend on it being up.

cards.prompt: An order processor joins each order with a local table of delivery fees, kept current from a stream of fee changes. Months later, the team runs old orders through the same code again to rebuild a report. What's the risk?
choices: Old orders get today's fees, unless the join looks up the fee in effect when each order was placed
Each order is counted twice, since replayed orders look like brand new events to the stream processor
The join fails, because the fee table can't be read while a replay is in progress
None: using a local table makes the join's output identical whenever it runs
cards.explanation: The join depends on time: the fee table now holds current fees, not the ones that applied back then. Reproducing the original output needs the historical fee at each order's time. Rebuilding a report from scratch doesn't double-count, and nothing blocks reads during a replay. A local table doesn't remove the time dependence; querying a service wouldn't either.

cards.title: Write path and read path
cards.body:
Data travels from where it's written to where it's read. The **write path** is the part done eagerly: as soon as data arrives, jobs update every derived dataset, whether or not anyone will look. The **read path** runs only when a request comes in: read a derived dataset, maybe process further, answer. Think eager versus lazy evaluation.

The two meet at the derived dataset. A search index is the classic case: each new document updates the entries for every word in it, and each query looks up its words and combines the matches. Without an index, every query would scan all the documents. Where they meet decides how much work happens at write time and how much at read time.

cards.prompt: What do the write path and read path each cover, and where do they meet?
keyPoints: Write path: work done eagerly as soon as data arrives, whether or not anyone has asked for it
Read path: work done only when a request comes in
They meet at a derived dataset, which sets how much work happens at write time versus read time
cards.explanation: The write path is like eager evaluation and the read path like lazy evaluation; indexes, caches and materialized views move the meeting point toward writes.

cards.title: Moving the boundary
cards.body:
Caches, indexes and materialized views all do one thing: they move work from the read path to the write path, precomputing results so that reads get cheaper.

Take a shop's sales dashboard. With nothing derived, every page view sums all the raw orders: cheap writes, costly reads. Keep running totals per day, and each order does a little extra work so reads are quick. Also store finished results for the few reports people open most, and writes do more again, since each order must refresh those too. Precomputing every report anyone could ever ask for would make reads trivial, but the possible requests are endless, so it can't be done.

cards.prompt: For keyword search over a growing set of product manuals, order these designs from the least work on the write path to the most.
items: Scan every manual for the keywords at query time
Keep an inverted index updated as manuals are added
Keep the index, plus stored results for the most popular searches
Store the results of every possible search
cards.explanation: Each step moves work from reads to writes. Stored popular results are a materialized view that new manuals must be added to; storing every possible search is infeasible, since the possible searches are effectively endless.

cards.title: Clients that follow the stream
cards.body:
Web and mobile apps now keep lots of state on the device and work offline. That state is a **cache** of the server's: the screen is a materialized view of the app's model objects, which are a local replica of server data.

A classic web page reads its data once, then goes stale until you reload. With **WebSockets** or **server-sent events**, the server can push changes over an open connection, extending the write path right to the user's screen. A new client uses the read path once to load its starting state, then follows the stream. After time offline, it resumes from the last event it saw, as a log consumer resumes from its offset.

cards.prompt: How does the write/read path picture change when clients keep state on the device and the server pushes changes to them?
keyPoints: Device state acts as a cache of the server's state, and the screen is a materialized view of the client's model objects
Pushing changes, for example over WebSockets or server-sent events, carries the write path right through to the user's device
A new client still uses the read path once to load its initial state, then follows a stream of changes
A device that was offline catches up from the last event it saw, like a log consumer resuming from its offset
cards.explanation: Few apps work this way yet, because most databases, frameworks and protocols assume stateless clients and one response per request.

cards.title: Reads are events too
cards.body:
Usually writes go through a log, while reads are one-off requests sent straight to the nodes holding the data. You could instead send reads through the stream processor as events, and have it emit each answer to an output stream.

Serving a read is then a **stream-table join**: each read event is routed to the shard holding its data and joined with it.

Logging reads durably shows what a user saw before deciding, such as the hotel price shown before a booking, which helps trace causality and provenance, at the cost of extra storage and I/O. Queries spanning many shards can also reuse the processor's routing and joining.

cards.prompt: What does sending read requests through a stream processor as events give you, and what does it cost?
keyPoints: Each read is routed to the shard holding its data and joined with that state, like a stream-table join
A durable log of reads records what a user saw before acting, which helps trace causality and provenance
Logging reads costs extra storage and I/O
Queries spanning many shards can reuse the stream processor's routing and joining
cards.explanation: A one-off read leaves the join once answered; a subscription is a join that stays open for future changes.

cards.title: Correctness beyond transactions
cards.body:
Fix a bug in a stateless service, restart it, and all is well. Databases remember for years, so a bug's damage can last as long.

For decades, transactions' atomicity, isolation and durability were the main tools for correctness, but they're shakier than they look. Isolation levels confuse people, some products break their promises under faults, and serializability with atomic commit usually works only within one datacenter and limits scale.

Even perfect transactions don't make an app safe. If a buggy release writes garbage or deletes records, the database faithfully commits it, whatever its isolation level or commit protocol. That's a strong case for **immutable, append-only** data: when faulty code can't overwrite good data, you can recover from its mistakes.

cards.prompt: A team's database runs every transaction at serializable isolation. A bug in a new release overwrites some customers' delivery addresses with blanks. What would have made this easiest to recover from?
choices: Nothing more: serializable isolation already stops committed data from being lost
Running every transaction at strict serializability instead of plain serializability
Keeping data immutable and append-only, so the earlier addresses still exist
Committing each write with two-phase commit across all of the database's replicas
cards.explanation: Isolation protects against races between transactions, not against code that writes the wrong thing: the database faithfully commits the bug's output. If old values are never overwritten, faulty code can't destroy good data. Strict serializability adds recency and 2PC adds atomicity across nodes; neither stops a buggy write.

cards.title: Exactly once
cards.body:
When processing a message fails, you can drop it and lose data, or retry. But maybe the first attempt worked and only its confirmation got lost, so a retry processes it twice. That's corruption too: a customer billed twice, loyalty points granted twice.

**Exactly once** means the final effect is as if no fault happened, even though the work ran more than once. One of the most effective ways is to make the operation **idempotent**, so running it again changes nothing. Setting a value is naturally idempotent; adding to one isn't. For those you have to keep extra metadata, such as the IDs of operations already applied to each value, and use fencing so a replaced node can't keep writing.

cards.prompt: A stream consumer adds one to a page-view counter for each event. After a crash, it reprocesses some events it had already applied. What gives an exactly-once effect?
choices: Skip any event whose processing status is unclear after a crash
Store the IDs of events already applied next to the counter, and ignore repeats
Process events faster, so the window in which a crash can strike is smaller
Retry each event until a confirmation arrives, however many attempts it takes
cards.explanation: Adding to a counter isn't naturally idempotent, so record which event IDs have taken effect and skip them: the result then matches a run with no faults. Skipping uncertain events loses data instead. A smaller window makes duplicates rarer, not impossible. Retrying until confirmed is exactly how duplicates arise.

cards.title: Duplicates that slip through
cards.body:
TCP drops duplicate packets, but only within one connection. Many databases tie a transaction to its connection, so if the link dies after the client sends COMMIT, the client can't tell whether it took effect. A retry on a new connection is beyond TCP's reach, so a non-idempotent transfer may happen twice.

Two-phase commit lets a coordinator reconnect and settle an in-doubt transaction, covering the hop between app server and database. It doesn't cover the hop before. A request from a browser reaches the server, but the page times out before the response gets back. The user sees an error and submits again. To the web server that's a new request, and to the database a new transaction.

cards.prompt: A shop's app server uses two-phase commit with its database, so in-doubt transactions are resolved after network faults. Shoppers on weak mobile signal still get charged twice now and then. Why?
choices: On recovery, the 2PC coordinator replays in-doubt transactions it already committed, so some commit twice
The phones' TCP stacks resend packets, and the server applies the repeated data again
The database's isolation level is too weak to notice two identical transactions
A shopper's retry after a lost response is a new request and a new transaction, out of 2PC's reach
cards.explanation: When the response to a POST is lost, the shopper submits again, and to the server and database that's an unrelated request. 2PC only covers the link between coordinator and database, and TCP only drops duplicates within one connection. No isolation level treats two separate transactions as duplicates; each is valid on its own.

cards.title: Request IDs from the client
cards.body:
To make a request idempotent across several network hops, think about its whole journey, not one database's transactions. Give each request a unique ID before it leaves the client: a UUID embedded in the form, say, or a hash of the form's fields. A resubmission then carries the same ID.

Pass that ID all the way to the database and record it in a table with a **unique constraint**. A second insert with the same ID fails, aborting its transaction. Relational databases generally enforce uniqueness correctly even at weak isolation levels, unlike a check-then-insert in application code.

That table of requests is also an event log. Balance updates could be derived from it downstream, deduplicated by the same ID.

cards.prompt: To stop a resubmitted payment form from charging twice, where should its request ID come from?
choices: From the client, such as a hidden form field, so a resubmission carries the same ID
From the web server, which tags each incoming POST with a fresh ID as soon as it arrives
From the database, as an autoincrementing key on the new payments row
From the sequence numbers of the TCP connection that carried the request
cards.explanation: The ID has to be fixed before the first attempt leaves the client, then passed all the way to the database, where a unique constraint rejects the second insert. An ID made by the server or the database is new on every retry. TCP sequence numbers belong to one connection, and a retry usually opens a new one.

cards.title: The end-to-end argument
cards.body:
Request IDs are one case of the **end-to-end argument** (Saltzer, Reed and Clark, 1984): some functions can be done fully and correctly only with help from the application at each end. TCP, database transactions and stream processors each suppress duplicates in their own scope, but none alone can stop a user's retry.

Integrity works the same way. Ethernet, TCP and TLS checksums catch packets damaged in transit, but not bugs in the software at either end or corruption on disk; only checksums made and checked by the endpoints catch it all. Wi-Fi passwords and TLS likewise each guard one stretch; only end-to-end encryption guards it all.

Low-level features still help, as a performance gain: they make problems rarer.

cards.prompt: What does the end-to-end argument say, and why keep low-level reliability features anyway?
keyPoints: A function like duplicate suppression can be done completely and correctly only with help from the application at the endpoints
So the layers in between, such as TCP, database transactions or stream processors, can't fully provide it on their own
Low-level versions still help: they make problems rarer, which is worth having for performance
cards.explanation: The same goes for checksums and encryption: only an end-to-end check or end-to-end encryption covers every hop.

cards.prompt: A photo backup service relies on TCP and TLS checksums to protect files on their way to storage. Some customers still restore corrupted photos. Which fix follows the end-to-end argument?
choices: Use a stronger TLS configuration so that no packet can be altered while in transit
Have the app checksum each photo before upload and verify it after restore
Add Ethernet checksums on the links inside the storage cluster as well
Store three replicas of each photo so one bad disk can't destroy it
cards.explanation: Network checksums only cover their own hop; they miss bugs in the software at either end and corruption on disk. A checksum made and checked by the app covers the whole path. More network-level checks leave the same gap, and replicas faithfully copy a photo that a bug already corrupted.

cards.title: Uniqueness needs consensus
cards.body:
Many features need **uniqueness**: one account per email address, one ticket per concert seat.

In a distributed system, enforcing it takes consensus. When concurrent requests want the same value, something must pick one winner and reject the rest. Usually a single leader decides, with an algorithm like Raft electing a new one if it fails. You can scale this out by sharding on the value that must be unique, say by a hash of the email address, so every claim to one address reaches the same leader.

Asynchronous multi-leader setups can't do it, because two leaders could each accept the same value at once. If violations must be rejected immediately, synchronous coordination can't be avoided.

cards.prompt: A global gaming platform needs unique player tags and wants a taken tag rejected immediately. Which setup works?
choices: Multi-leader replication, with a leader per region accepting tags and syncing asynchronously
Shard players by region, with each region's leader checking tags within its own shard
Shard by a hash of the tag, with one leader deciding the claims in each shard
Let any replica check its local copy for the tag, then accept the write
cards.explanation: Uniqueness needs consensus: all claims for one tag must reach one decision-maker. Sharding by the tag spreads the load while keeping that true. Asynchronous multi-leader replication lets two leaders accept the same tag at once. Sharding by region sends claims for one tag to different leaders. A replica's local copy may be stale.

cards.title: Uniqueness through a log
cards.body:
A log-based system can enforce uniqueness too. A shared log shows every consumer the same order, which is equivalent to consensus, and a stream processor reads each log shard in sequence on a single thread.

Say a sign-up service wants unique email addresses. Each sign-up becomes a message, appended to the shard chosen by hashing the address. That shard's processor works through its messages in order, tracking taken addresses in a local database. If the address is free, it records it and emits an acceptance to an output stream; if not, a rejection. The client watches that stream for the answer to its own request.

The first claim in the log wins, and more shards means more throughput.

cards.prompt: A link shortener lets users claim custom names like /spring-sale, and keeps them unique with a sharded log and stream processors. Order how a claim is decided.
items: The claim is appended to the log shard picked by hashing the name
That shard's processor reads the claims one at a time, in log order
It marks the name taken in its local table if it's free, or rejects the claim if not
It writes an accept or reject message to an output stream
The client that made the claim picks up its result from that output stream
cards.explanation: Claims that could conflict land on the same shard and are handled in sequence, so the first in the log wins. It's consensus built on a shared log, and it scales by adding shards.

cards.title: Route conflicts together
cards.body:
The same trick enforces far more than uniqueness. The rule: send any writes that could conflict to the same shard, and process them one at a time. The processor can then apply whatever check it likes, because it sees every competing request in a fixed order.

What counts as a conflict depends on the application, and that decides the shard key. To keep an account from going below zero, shard by account, since all spending from one account competes for the same money. To avoid selling more of a product than the warehouse holds, shard by product. The right key is whatever two clashing requests always have in common.

cards.prompt: A coworking space uses a sharded log and stream processors to stop overlapping desk bookings. How should booking requests be sharded?
choices: By member ID, so each member's bookings are processed in order
By desk ID, so all bookings that could clash pass through one processor in turn
By the hour being booked, so bookings for the same time share a shard
Randomly, with each processor checking the other shards' tables before accepting
cards.explanation: The rule is that writes which might conflict go to the same shard and are handled one after another. Bookings clash only on the same desk, so shard by desk. Sharding by member splits one desk's bookings across processors. An hourly split breaks bookings that span hours, and checking other shards brings back the cross-shard coordination the design avoids.

cards.title: Transfers without atomic commit
cards.body:
A payment touches several shards: payer, payee, maybe a fees account. Atomic commit across them would couple those shards and hurt throughput. Sharded logs can do it instead.

Say a carpool rider pays a driver, and the app takes a cut. The rider's client gives the request a unique ID, and it's appended to the shard for the rider's account. That shard's processor, its local state derived entirely from the log, sees a new ID, checks the balance and reserves the amount. It emits an outgoing payment event to its own shard and incoming ones to the driver's and the app's shards, all carrying the request ID. When the outgoing event comes back around, it carries out the reserved payment.

cards.prompt: A player buys an item from another player for 100 gold, and the marketplace takes a 5-gold cut. The game handles this with stream processors over logs sharded by account. Order the steps.
items: The buyer's client gives the request a unique ID, and it's appended to the buyer's account shard
The buyer's processor sees a new ID, checks the balance in its local state and reserves 100 gold
It emits a debit event to its own shard and credit events to the seller's and marketplace's shards, all carrying the request ID
Later, when the debit event comes back around on its own shard, the buyer's processor carries out the reserved debit
cards.explanation: The seller's and marketplace's processors apply their credits independently, ignoring any request ID they've already seen. Only the first append has to be atomic; everything else follows from it.

cards.title: Atomicity from one append
cards.body:
The driver's and the app's processors apply their incoming events on their own, ignoring any request ID they've already seen. The design needs only three things: each account's events handled strictly in log order, **at-least-once** delivery, and deterministic processors.

Say the rider's processor crashes partway, after emitting some of its events. On restart it reads the same request again, reaches the same decision because it's deterministic, and emits the same events with the same ID. Downstream processors drop the duplicates.

So atomicity doesn't come from a transaction. It comes from appending the one request event to the first log, which is atomic. Once that's there, every later event will be written eventually, perhaps after crashes and with duplicates.

cards.prompt: A transfer is handled by stream processors over logs sharded by account. The paying account's processor crashes after emitting the payee's credit event but before emitting its own debit event. What happens after it restarts?
choices: A coordinator steps in and aborts the credit already emitted, as in 2PC
The request is lost, because only some of its output events were written
The client has to resubmit under a new request ID, since the original one has already been used up
It redoes the request, decides the same way and re-emits all events; duplicates are dropped by ID
cards.explanation: With at-least-once delivery the request is read again, and a deterministic processor reaches the same decision, so it emits the same events with the same ID. The payee's processor recognizes the ID and ignores the second credit. No coordinator is involved, nothing is lost, and a new ID would risk a double transfer.

cards.prompt: A transfer is split into stages run by stream processors over logs sharded by account, with no atomic commit protocol. Where does its atomicity come from?
choices: Appending the one request event to the first log is atomic; every later event follows from it
Each processor wraps the events it emits in a local serializable transaction
The client waits on the output stream until every stage has confirmed its part
Each consumer compares its state with all the other consumers' state before it applies an event
cards.explanation: Once the request is logged, every downstream event will eventually be written, perhaps after crashes and with duplicates that request IDs absorb. That needs strict log order per account, at-least-once delivery and deterministic processors. Local transactions don't span shards, waiting only informs the client, and cross-checking consumers would be the coordination the design avoids.

cards.title: Timeliness and integrity
cards.body:
The word *consistency* mixes up two requirements. **Timeliness** means what users see reflects the latest state. Reading a stale replica breaks it, but only for a while: wait, read again, and it's fixed. Linearizability is a strong form; read-after-write is a weaker one.

**Integrity** means no corruption: nothing lost, nothing contradictory or false, and every derived dataset correctly reflecting its source. An index missing rows breaks it. Waiting won't help; it stays broken until someone explicitly checks and repairs it. The C in ACID is really about integrity.

In most apps integrity matters far more. A parcel tracker that shows a scan a few hours late is annoying; one that loses a parcel's history is a disaster.

cards.prompt: 'Consistency' mixes up two requirements, timeliness and integrity. What does each mean, and what happens when it's violated?
keyPoints: Timeliness: what users observe reflects the latest state
A timeliness violation is temporary: waiting and reading again fixes it
Integrity: no corruption, meaning no lost, contradictory or false data, and derived data correctly reflects its source
An integrity violation is permanent: it needs explicit checking and repair
cards.explanation: Linearizability is a strong form of timeliness; in ACID, 'consistency' usually means an application-specific kind of integrity.

cards.prompt: A loyalty app shows the points from a purchase only the next morning. Separately, a bug credited some purchases to the wrong member. How do these problems differ?
choices: Both are timeliness problems: given enough time, the points will all end up in the right place
The delay is an integrity problem, and the misdirected credits are a timeliness problem
The delay is timeliness and fixes itself; the wrong credits break integrity and need repair
Both are integrity problems, since in each case a member sees the wrong balance
cards.explanation: A lag goes away by waiting: that's timeliness, which eventual consistency allows to slip. Credits on the wrong account stay wrong until someone finds and fixes them, a permanent integrity violation. Waiting won't undo a bug's output, and a balance that's behind isn't corrupt. In most applications integrity matters far more than timeliness.

cards.title: Dataflow splits them apart
cards.body:
ACID transactions give you timeliness and integrity together; asynchronous dataflow pulls them apart. There's no timeliness unless a client chooses to wait: the payer's app can watch its account's shard for the outgoing or declined event. That wait only tells the user the outcome. The balance check is just as correct whether anyone waits.

Integrity is central to streaming, and it holds without distributed transactions. The write is captured as a single message, appended atomically, as in event sourcing. All other state is derived from it by deterministic functions. A request ID generated by the client travels through every stage, deduplicating end to end. And messages are immutable, so derived data can be reprocessed to recover from bugs.

cards.prompt: In a log-based payment system, the app waits for an 'approved' or 'declined' event on the output stream before showing a result. A user closes the app before the event arrives. What happens to the balance check?
choices: It's skipped, because no client is waiting for the outcome anymore
It runs as usual; the waiting only exists to tell the user the outcome
The payment is rolled back, because the client never saw it confirmed in time
It runs, but the payment may take effect twice once the app reopens
cards.explanation: The check's correctness doesn't depend on anyone waiting; waiting just gives the user a synchronous answer. ACID transactions bundle timeliness and integrity, but dataflow systems separate them: integrity comes from the log and request IDs, timeliness only if a client chooses to wait. Nothing rolls back, and the request ID prevents a double effect.

cards.prompt: Reliable stream processing can keep integrity without distributed transactions. Which mechanisms make that work?
keyPoints: The write is captured as a single message, which can be appended atomically
All other state updates are derived from that message by deterministic functions
A request ID generated by the client travels through every stage, for end-to-end deduplication
Messages are immutable, and derived data can be reprocessed to recover from bugs
cards.explanation: The first point fits naturally with event sourcing.

cards.title: Constraints you can bend
cards.body:
Strict uniqueness needs consensus, but many businesses bend such rules on purpose. A shop that oversells orders more stock, apologizes and offers a discount, just as it must when stock gets damaged. Airlines overbook deliberately, and need compensation processes anyway for flights canceled by storms. Banks allow overdrafts but cap daily withdrawals.

Fixing a violation afterwards is a **compensating transaction**, and its cost in money or reputation is often low: a refund, a correction email. Whether it's acceptable is a business call. If it is, write optimistically and check the constraint afterwards, but still validate first where recovery is costly, like shipping goods you can't recall. Integrity is still required; timely enforcement isn't.

cards.prompt: A wallet app records spending optimistically and checks spending limits afterwards, apologizing and reversing charges when a limit is broken. Which step should still be checked before it happens?
choices: Appending the spending event to the log, so that no bad event ever gets stored
Updating the balance view that's derived from the spending log
Sending money out to an external bank, where it can't easily be clawed back
Showing the user their updated balance after each purchase they make
cards.explanation: Checking after the fact works when a mistake can be put right cheaply with a compensating transaction, and whether that cost is acceptable is a business call. Actions that are hard to undo, like money leaving the system, should still be validated first. Writing the event and updating views can safely come before the check, since both can be corrected later.

cards.title: Avoiding coordination
cards.body:
Dataflow systems keep integrity with no atomic commit, no linearizability and no synchronous coordination between shards, and many apps accept loose constraints as long as integrity holds. So many apps can run **coordination-avoiding** systems, faster and more fault tolerant.

Such a system could replicate asynchronously between regions with multiple leaders, each region running on its own. Its timeliness is weak, since linearizability needs coordination, but its integrity is strong. Serializable transactions still help in small scopes, and synchronous coordination goes only where it's needed, such as before an action you can't undo.

Coordination cuts apologies for inconsistencies but costs performance and availability, which can mean more apologies for outages. You can't get apologies to zero; aim for the best balance.

cards.prompt: A service runs in three regions with asynchronous multi-leader replication. All state is derived by deterministic stream processors with end-to-end request IDs, and constraints are checked after the fact. What can it guarantee?
choices: Linearizable reads, since every region derives exactly the same state
Strong integrity but weak timeliness: each region runs alone, but reads may be stale
Neither, because asynchronous multi-leader replication always ends up corrupting the data
Strict uniqueness constraints, with no coordination between the regions
cards.explanation: Integrity comes from the dataflow mechanisms, not from coordination, so it survives without cross-region agreement. Timeliness is what's given up: linearizability would need coordination. Strict uniqueness also needs consensus, so it can't be had without coordinating. Asynchrony delays updates, but with deterministic derivation and request IDs it needn't corrupt them.

cards.prompt: Strict constraints and coordination change how often a business has to apologize. How?
keyPoints: Fewer apologies for inconsistencies, such as an oversold item
Possibly more apologies for outages, since coordination costs performance and availability
Apologies can't reach zero, so coordinate only where needed, such as before actions you can't recover from
Many businesses need apology and compensation processes anyway, for things like cancellations or damaged stock

cards.title: Rare faults, real bugs
cards.body:
Every correctness argument rests on a **system model**: some faults can happen, like crashes and lost messages, and others are assumed never to, like losing data after fsync, memory corrupting itself or the CPU miscalculating. Really these are probabilities, and at a large enough scale even very unlikely events happen.

Software is no safer. Mature, heavily tested databases have shipped bugs, such as uniqueness constraints that failed, or write skew under serializable isolation. Application code gets far less testing, and often misuses integrity features, say by running at a weak isolation level where it isn't safe. ACID consistency assumes each transaction takes the data from one valid state to another, which holds only if the transaction itself is bug-free.

cards.prompt: Why should you expect corrupted data sooner or later, even on a well-tested database?
keyPoints: Fault assumptions are really probabilities, and at a big enough scale, even very rare faults do occur
Mature databases have shipped bugs, such as broken uniqueness checks or write skew under serializable isolation
Application code gets far less testing and often misuses integrity features, for example by using a weak isolation level unsafely
ACID consistency assumes every transaction is bug-free; when that fails, integrity isn't guaranteed
cards.explanation: So you need a way to find corruption, called auditing, and not just trust in the guarantees.

cards.title: Trust, but verify
cards.body:
Since corruption will happen sooner or later, you need a way to find it, fix it and track down its cause. Checking the integrity of data is called **auditing**. Finance does it routinely, because everyone knows mistakes happen.

Mature storage systems don't fully trust their disks: big distributed filesystems and object stores run background jobs that keep reading files back, comparing them with other replicas and moving them to other disks. The only way to know data is still there is to read it and check, and you want to find out early, not when you need it. That holds for every copy you'd rely on in an emergency.

Few systems audit themselves this way yet.

cards.prompt: A team takes nightly backups and has never tried restoring one. What does 'trust, but verify' suggest?
choices: Take backups more often, so less recent data is at risk
Keep extra copies of each backup on several different disks
Nothing more: a backup job that reports success each night is all the proof needed
Restore from them regularly and check the result, before a real failure does
cards.explanation: The only way to know data is still there is to read it back and check. An untested backup may be broken, and you'd find out only after losing data. More frequent or extra copies of a broken backup don't help. Large storage systems apply the same idea by continually reading back files and comparing them with other replicas.

cards.title: Designing for auditability
cards.body:
When a transaction changes several rows in place, it's hard to tell later why. The transaction log shows which rows changed, but the code that chose those changes ran once and is gone.
