Event sourcing does better. Each user input is a single **immutable event**, and all state is derived from it by deterministic code, so replaying the same events with the same code version gives the same state. That makes integrity checks practical: hash the event log to detect corruption, and rerun the derivation, or run a second one alongside, to check derived state. You can also replay the exact circumstances behind a strange result, a kind of time-travel debugging.

cards.prompt: Why is an event-sourced system easier to audit than one where transactions update rows in place?
choices: Each input is one immutable event, and state comes from deterministic code you can rerun and compare
Its events can be edited to fix mistakes, so the log never holds any bad data
Transaction logs already show why each change was made, so both kinds of system are equally easy to audit
Its events can't be corrupted, so it needs no integrity checks of its own
cards.explanation: In-place updates don't record the decision behind them, and the logic that made it is gone. With events, you can hash the log to detect corruption, rerun the derivation (or a redundant one) to check derived state, and replay to debug. Events are immutable, not edited. They can still be corrupted, which is why the hashes are worth having.

cards.title: Checking end to end
cards.body:
If you can't trust every disk and every line of code, check your data now and then. Otherwise corruption shows up only after it has done damage downstream, when it's far harder and costlier to trace.

The end-to-end argument applies here too. The more of the system one check spans, the fewer places corruption can hide. Verify a whole derived data pipeline from input to output, and every disk, network link, service and algorithm along the way is covered without checking each one separately.

Continuous checks work like automated tests: they catch bugs early, so changing the system or adopting a new storage technology is less risky. When you aren't afraid of change, you can evolve the app faster.

cards.prompt: Why is it worth checking integrity end to end, across a whole derived data pipeline?
keyPoints: A check over the whole pipeline implicitly covers every disk, network, service and algorithm along it
Without checks, corruption surfaces late, after it has done damage downstream and is harder to trace
Like automated tests, continuous checks catch bugs early, so changes and new storage technology are less risky
cards.explanation: Less fear of breaking things means you can evolve the system faster.

cards.title: Blockchains and Merkle trees
cards.body:
Few systems make auditing a priority. Some keep a separate audit table, but proving it matches the data is hard. Signing a log with a hardware security module makes tampering detectable, yet can't prove the right entries went in.

Blockchains are shared append-only logs guarded by cryptographic checks: their transactions are events, and smart contracts are essentially stream processors. Their consensus orders events like the protocols inside one company, except that it's **Byzantine fault-tolerant**: it keeps working when some nodes hold corrupted data, because replicas keep checking one another. That costs too much for most apps, but lighter tools from the same kit help elsewhere, such as **Merkle trees**, trees of hashes that prove a record is in a dataset.

cards.prompt: How do blockchains differ from the consensus protocols used inside a single organization's systems?
choices: They don't require nodes to agree on the order of events, only on each event's content
Their logs are mutable, so participants can agree to edit mistakes out of past entries
They have lower overhead than other consensus protocols, so they suit most applications
They're Byzantine fault-tolerant: they keep working even if some nodes hold corrupted data
cards.explanation: A blockchain is an append-only log shared between parties and protected by cryptographic checks; consensus orders the events, and smart contracts act like stream processors. Unlike Raft-style protocols, they keep working when some nodes are corrupted. Their overhead is too high for most applications, but lighter tools from the same kit, like Merkle trees, are used elsewhere, for example in certificate transparency.

cards.title: Ethics is part of engineering
cards.body:
Every system has a purpose, and its effects reach further, some intended and some not. Many datasets are about people. A technology isn't good or bad in itself: a group chat app can organize a street cleanup or a harassment campaign. What counts is how it's used and whom it affects, so its builders can't look only at the technology and leave the consequences to others.

Ethics is also less precise than most of computing. Words like 'good' and 'harm' need interpretation, and people disagree. So it can't be settled by ticking off a list once. It's a process you keep repeating: reflecting with the people your system affects, and answering for what it does.

cards.prompt: A team builds a tool that estimates people's income from their shopping receipts. One engineer says how clients use the estimates isn't an engineering concern. How does the chapter see this?
choices: A tool is neither good nor bad in itself, so its effects are the clients' concern alone
Engineers answer only for bugs in the tool; misuse is a legal matter for the clients
Testing the tool's accuracy thoroughly is how engineers meet their responsibility
A tool's effects depend on how it's used, and its builders must weigh them too
cards.explanation: The chapter agrees that technology isn't good or bad in itself, but draws the opposite conclusion: because harm depends on use and on who is affected, engineers can't attend to the technology alone and leave its effects to others. Handing the question to clients or lawyers is the same dodge. An accurate tool can still be put to harmful use.

cards.prompt: A team has completed every item on its company's ethics checklist and considers the product's ethics settled. What does the chapter say this misses?
choices: Nothing: completing a checklist is exactly how a team shows its product is ethical
A technical review, since technology that's built well can't be used to cause harm
Ongoing reflection, in dialogue with those affected, and accountability for results
A legal review, since ethical duties come down to whatever the law requires
cards.explanation: The chapter treats ethics as a participatory process that repeats: reflecting together with the people involved and answering for the outcome, not confirming compliance once. A technology isn't good or bad in itself; harm depends on how it's used and whom it affects. And ethical ideas need interpretation and judgment, so they can't be reduced to legal rules.

cards.title: Algorithmic prison
cards.body:
Predicting how many umbrellas a shop will sell harms nobody. Predicting whether a person will repay a loan, reoffend or make costly insurance claims shapes that person's life.

The organizations deciding face lopsided costs. Turning away a good customer loses a little business; letting in a bad one can cost a lot. So when in doubt, they say no.

Now suppose many of them use similar scores. Someone flagged as risky, rightly or not, is refused by employers, landlords, insurers, banks and airlines alike. That badly limits their freedom, and has been called **algorithmic prison**. A court must presume you innocent until proven guilty; these systems need no proof, and rarely allow an appeal.

cards.prompt: Why do organizations that use predictive models for loans, rentals or hiring tend to reject applicants when the model is unsure?
choices: Regulators require them to reject anyone the model can't classify with confidence
Turning away a good applicant costs them little; a bad loan or bad hire costs a lot
Rejected applicants can appeal, so a wrong no is cheaper to correct than a wrong yes
Models are more reliable at predicting failures than at predicting successes
cards.explanation: From the organization's side the costs are lopsided: a missed opportunity is cheap, while a default or a problem employee is expensive, so caution wins. No rule forces the rejection. Appeals are usually hard to get, which is part of the harm to the person. The cost asymmetry, not model reliability, drives the habit of saying no.

cards.prompt: What is 'algorithmic prison', and why is it so harmful?
keyPoints: Someone the algorithms label as risky, rightly or not, gets turned down again and again by many organizations
Being shut out of jobs, housing, travel, insurance and banking together badly limits their freedom
Unlike a court, the system needs no proof of guilt and doesn't presume innocence
There's usually little chance to appeal

cards.title: Rules learned from data
cards.body:
A person picking who gets a job interview has biases, even when trying not to, and institutions can discriminate out of habit. Some hope deciding from data will be fairer to people who are often overlooked.

But a machine learning system doesn't apply rules someone wrote; it infers its own from past data. Those patterns are opaque: a feature may predict the outcome without anyone knowing why. And a model can only extrapolate from the past. If the data carries a systematic bias, the model learns it and usually amplifies it. A fairer future takes **moral imagination**, which only people can supply. Models should serve us, not rule us.

cards.prompt: How does a decision system trained with machine learning differ from software that encodes a person's decision rules?
choices: Its rules are inferred from data, so even its builders may not know why it decides as it does
Its rules are learned from data, so it can't pick up the biases of the people who made that data
Its rules can be read off the trained model, so it's easier to explain than hand-written rules
Its rules are fixed by experts in advance, so it applies one person's judgment consistently
cards.explanation: Instead of someone writing down when to say yes or no, the rules are inferred from data, and the learned patterns are opaque: a correlation may show up without any known cause. That opacity makes decisions harder to explain, not easier. Learning from data is exactly how bias gets in, since a biased input tends to be learned and amplified. Fixed expert rules describe the older approach.

cards.title: Proxies and laundered bias
cards.body:
Anti-discrimination laws forbid treating people differently because of **protected traits** such as age, gender, ethnicity, disability, religion or sexual orientation. Deleting those columns from the data doesn't solve it. Other features can act as **proxies**: a first name can hint at gender and ethnic background, and the clubs listed on a CV can hint at class. A model can rediscover the hidden trait from them.

Yet people sometimes talk as if an algorithm could take biased data and turn it into fair, impartial decisions. Critics mock this as machine learning being *money laundering for bias*: prejudice goes in, and comes out looking neutral and objective because a computer produced it.

cards.prompt: A hiring model is never shown candidates' ages, but it does see the year they graduated. Can it still discriminate by age?
choices: No: a model can't base decisions on a trait that isn't in its input
Only if some candidates' ages leaked into the training data by mistake
No, as long as it's retrained regularly on recent hiring decisions
Yes: graduation year closely tracks age, so the model can learn age from it
cards.explanation: Features that correlate with a protected trait act as proxies for it, so leaving the trait out doesn't stop the model from using it. No leak is needed; the correlation is enough. Retraining on new decisions that carry the same bias just relearns it. Expecting fair output from biased input is wishful thinking.

cards.prompt: Why has machine learning been called 'money laundering for bias', and why can't a model remove that bias by itself?
keyPoints: Biased data goes in, and the output looks neutral because an algorithm produced it
Models extrapolate from the past, so past discrimination gets codified and often amplified
Making the future fairer than the past takes moral imagination, which only people can supply
cards.explanation: Data and models should serve as tools, not make the decisions for us.

cards.title: Who answers for a decision
cards.body:
When a clerk wrongly refuses your benefit claim, someone is responsible, and you can appeal to a person who can put it right. When an algorithm makes the same mistake, it's unclear who answers for it: the developer, the company that deployed it, whoever picked the training data?

Say a scoring system keeps turning down people of one nationality. Is there any route to redress? If a court reviews one of its decisions, can anyone explain to the judge how it was reached? With an opaque model, often not. Algorithms get things wrong just as people do, and blaming the algorithm shouldn't let the people behind it escape responsibility.

cards.prompt: Why does automated decision making raise a problem of accountability?
keyPoints: When a person makes a bad decision, they can be held responsible and the decision can be appealed
When an algorithm makes one, it's unclear who is responsible or how to get redress
An opaque model is hard to explain, for example to a judge reviewing one of its decisions
Blaming the algorithm must not let people avoid their responsibility

cards.title: Judged by people like you
cards.body:
A traditional credit score looks at your own record: the loans you took and whether you repaid them. It rests on relevant facts, and errors can be corrected, though rarely easily. Machine learning scores take in far more inputs and are far more opaque, so it's hard to see how a decision came about or whether it was fair.

They also ask a different question. Not 'how did you behave?' but 'how did people like you behave?' That's stereotyping, by your postcode, your school or your friends. If you land in the wrong group, or the data about you is wrong, there's almost no way to get it fixed.

cards.prompt: A lender has no loan history for an applicant who recently moved to the country, so it scores her by how people with similar jobs, phones and shopping habits repaid their loans. What's the main ethical problem?
choices: It stereotypes her: she's judged by what people like her did, not by what she did
None, provided the model is accurate on average across all applicants
Its only real flaw is that shopping data is a noisier signal than income
None: since she has no history of her own, similarity to others is the fairest basis
cards.explanation: A traditional credit score asks how you behaved; this asks how people like you behaved, which is stereotyping, and anyone put in the wrong bucket has little recourse. Being right on average doesn't make it right for her. Noise isn't the core issue. Having no history makes judging her by others convenient, not fair, and such wide, opaque inputs make unfair treatment hard to detect.

cards.title: Right overall, wrong for you
cards.body:
Much data is statistical. A distribution can be right for a population and still wrong about many individuals in it. If a train line runs on time 90% of the time, that tells you little about whether your train tomorrow will be late.

Predictions work the same way. A model's output is a probability, and it may well be wrong for any one person. Trusting data blindly to decide about people isn't just naive; it's dangerous. Data-driven decisions need ways to avoid reinforcing old biases, to make algorithms transparent and hold them to account, and to fix the mistakes they will inevitably make.

cards.prompt: A model predicts that 20% of the students in a group will drop out, and exactly 20% do. What does this tell you about one particular student in that group?
choices: That the model is accurate for her too, since it's accurate for the whole group
That she'll stay, since most of the group stays
Little: the prediction can be right for the group and still wrong for her
That she'll drop out if she has the group's most typical traits
cards.explanation: Statistical data can be correct as a distribution while individual cases are wrong, so a group rate says little about any one person. Accuracy for the group doesn't carry over to each member. Predicting that she'll stay or leave from the group's majority or its typical traits is the same mistake: a prediction is a probability and can be wrong for individuals.

cards.title: Help or exploitation
cards.body:
Analytics can reveal a lot about people's finances and social lives: who is in debt, who just lost a job, who lives alone. That knowledge cuts both ways.

Say a supermarket's data shows which households struggle to afford food. A city could use that to send support where it's needed most. A predatory business could use the same finding to target exactly those people with loans at crushing interest, or with gambling offers. One use helps the vulnerable; the other exploits them. Building such systems means working out how to get the good uses while preventing the harmful ones.

cards.prompt: A city's data team finds it can identify isolated elderly residents from their phone and shopping data. How does the chapter view an insight like this?
choices: It could steer help to them or let predatory firms target them, so its uses must be guarded
It's harmless, since accurate knowledge of people's circumstances can only be used to help them
It should never be computed, since any inference about a person's circumstances is a harm
It matters only if individual residents can be named from the data
cards.explanation: Analytics that reveal people's financial and social situation can focus aid on those who need it most, or help predatory businesses find vulnerable people to sell risky products. The chapter asks for realizing the good without enabling the harm. Accuracy doesn't prevent exploitation, refusing all analysis throws away the benefit, and targeting a group works without names.

cards.title: Predictions that feed themselves
cards.body:
Even predictions with milder stakes can do harm. A video app that's very good at guessing what you'll enjoy may keep showing you views you already hold. In such **echo chambers**, stereotypes, misinformation and polarization grow, and they've visibly affected election campaigns.

When predictions shape people's lives, watch for **self-reinforcing feedback loops**: a system's output changes the world that it later learns from. Say a lender charges more interest to people its model rates as risky. The higher payments make them more likely to fall behind, which seems to prove the model right, so their rate rises again. The math looks rigorous, but it's a downward spiral built on a bad assumption.

cards.prompt: A recommendation system makes no decisions about anyone's loans or jobs. Why can it still cause harm by predicting well what users want to see?
choices: Users soon grow tired of accurate suggestions, so they spend less time on the service
It can't: harm arises only when predictions decide access to jobs or loans
Accurate predictions need so much tracking data that the service slows down
It may show only views people already hold, breeding echo chambers and polarization
cards.explanation: A system that's good at predicting what people want may feed them only opinions they agree with, so stereotypes, misinformation and polarization spread, with visible effects on election campaigns. The chapter says even these milder predictive systems raise hard issues, so harm isn't limited to decisions about access. Boredom and speed aren't the concern.

cards.prompt: A city sends food inspectors mostly to the neighbourhoods its model rates highest for violations, then retrains the model each month on what the inspectors find. What's the risk?
choices: Inspected areas log more violations, drawing more inspections, whatever the true rates
Retraining on fresh findings corrects any early mistakes, so the risk is small
The model drifts toward equal ratings everywhere, because retraining averages out the gaps
cards.explanation: The prediction shapes the data it's retrained on: places inspected more record more violations, which confirms the model and sends even more inspectors there. That's a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Fresh data doesn't help, since it comes from the skewed inspections. Nothing pulls the ratings toward equality; the gaps grow.

cards.title: Systems thinking
cards.body:
Not every feedback loop can be foreseen; loops can even form between algorithms, as when pricing software at rival shops learns to push prices up together. But many consequences can be predicted if you look at the whole system: not just the software, but also the people who use it and are affected by it. That's **systems thinking**.

In practice, you ask how the system reacts to different behaviors, structures and kinds of people. Does it widen the gaps that already exist, making the rich richer and the poor poorer? Or does it push against injustice? Good intentions don't rule out harmful side effects, so these questions belong before launch.

cards.prompt: How can systems thinking help a team spot harmful feedback loops before they happen?
keyPoints: It considers the whole system, including the people who interact with it, not only the software
It asks how the system responds to different behaviors and characteristics of people
It checks whether the system widens existing gaps between people or works against injustice
cards.explanation: Not every loop can be foreseen, and loops can even form between algorithms, as when pricing systems learned to collude and raise prices.

cards.title: Who the customer is
cards.body:
If a calendar app stores only the appointments you type in, so it can remind you, it's doing a job for you. You're the customer.

Logging what you do as a side effect is murkier. Some of it helps you: noticing which songs you skip improves a music app's suggestions. But if ads pay for the service, the advertisers are its real customers, and your interests come second. The tracking gets more detailed, the data is kept longer, and it's built into marketing profiles. The service now has interests of its own, which can clash with yours.

cards.prompt: A note-taking app used to store only the notes people typed, to sync them. Now it also logs which notes each person opens and when, to sell audience segments to advertisers. What has changed?
choices: Nothing: logging activity is just another way of storing what users give it
The app now has interests of its own: advertisers are its real customers
Users now get more from the app, since extra tracking improves its features
It becomes surveillance only once raw notes are handed to advertisers
cards.explanation: Storing what users deliberately enter is a service to them; logging their activity as a side effect lets the service develop interests that may clash with theirs. Some tracking does improve features, but this tracking serves advertisers, so users' interests come second. Tracking that mainly serves the advertisers funding a service already fits the word surveillance, whether or not raw data leaves the company.

cards.title: Calling it surveillance
cards.body:
In an ad-funded service, you get the product free and are nudged to use it as much as possible, while the tracking mainly serves the advertisers. There's a harsher word for that: **surveillance**.

Try a test. Take a line from a pitch deck, like 'our recommendations are powered by user data', and swap in the other word: 'powered by user surveillance'. It sounds different. Not all data collection is surveillance, but seeing it that way clarifies your relationship with the collector. The industry has built the largest surveillance network in history, with microphones in phones, speakers, TVs and even toys, many poorly secured.

cards.prompt: The chapter suggests rereading phrases like 'data-driven organization' with 'surveillance' in place of 'data'. What is the exercise meant to show?
choices: That every kind of data collection is illegal surveillance and should be stopped
That much data collection works like surveillance, changing how we see the collector
That only governments carry out real surveillance, while companies merely collect data
That the industry's marketing language describes its data pipelines inaccurately
cards.explanation: Not all collection is surveillance, but viewing it that way clarifies our relationship with the collector and who benefits. The chapter says outright that some collection doesn't qualify, so 'every kind' is wrong. Its point is that companies, not only governments, now run the largest surveillance infrastructure ever built. The exercise is about power, not technical accuracy.

cards.title: Why people accept it
cards.body:
Past dictatorships could only have wished for a microphone in every room and a tracker in every pocket. Today people carry them willingly, because digital services bring big benefits. The difference is that companies collect the data to provide services, not a state seeking control.

Two other reasons come up. One is 'I have nothing to hide'. That holds only if you fit in with those in power, belong to no marginalized group and have no reason to fear persecution; many aren't so lucky. The other is that the purpose looks harmless, like better ads. But the same data can feed decisions that matter, like your insurance premium or a job application.

cards.prompt: Why do people accept surveillance by companies, and why are those reasons weaker than they seem?
keyPoints: Digital services bring big benefits, so people take on the tracking voluntarily
'Nothing to hide' holds only for people who fit existing power structures and don't fear persecution
The purpose looks harmless, like recommendations and ads, but the same data can feed decisions on insurance or jobs
cards.explanation: A surveillance organization may even spot someone's illness or money troubles before that person does.

cards.title: What data gives away
cards.body:
Data often reveals far more than it seems to contain. Records of where you go, whom you talk to, what you buy and how healthy you are now pile up almost unavoidably. Combined and analyzed, they can tell an organization things about you that you don't know yet, such as an illness or money trouble on the way.

Even raw sensor readings can be intrusive. A phone's location pings show where you sleep, pray and see a doctor. A heart rate log can hint at stress or illness. And both sensors and analysis keep getting more accurate, so data that looks harmless today may say much more tomorrow.

cards.prompt: A power company reads households' smart meters every few seconds, only to bill them accurately. Why might this data still be sensitive?
choices: Analysis can infer intimate details such as daily routines, and keeps getting better
It isn't: meter readings contain no names, messages or other personal content
It's sensitive only if the company passes it on to other businesses
It's sensitive only while fresh, since old readings say nothing about people's habits
cards.explanation: Innocent-looking sensor data can reveal surprisingly intrusive things, such as when people are home or asleep, and both sensors and analysis keep getting more accurate. Missing names don't help, since the readings belong to a household. Data held in-house can still be leaked, stolen or used for decisions about people, and old routines still reveal a lot.

cards.title: Meaningful consent
cards.body:
Services say you agreed: you accepted the terms and the privacy policy. That's weaker than it sounds.

Most people have little idea what data they hand over or how it's kept and processed, and privacy policies tend to hide more than they explain. Without understanding, consent isn't meaningful. The derived datasets built from everyone's data, tracking and outside sources are exactly what no user can grasp. Your data also describes others: upload your address book, and people who never signed up are in the database.

And there's no negotiation. You can't trade less data for less service. The service sets the terms; the deal runs one way.

cards.prompt: Why does agreeing to a service's privacy policy rarely amount to meaningful consent?
keyPoints: Most users don't know what data they hand over or how it's kept and processed, and privacy policies obscure more than they explain
Derived datasets combine data from all users with tracking and outside sources, in ways users can't understand
One user's data often reveals things about people who never agreed to anything
The deal is one-sided: the service sets the terms, and users can't negotiate

cards.title: Consent under the GDPR
cards.body:
In the EU, the **GDPR** sets a high bar for consent. It has to be given freely, and be specific, informed and unambiguous. Freely means you can say no, or change your mind later, without being worse off for it. The request has to be easy to find and written in clear, plain language. Silence, inactivity and pre-ticked boxes don't count.

Consent isn't the only lawful basis for processing personal data, though it's the one internet services use most. Others include obeying another law, protecting someone's life, and a **legitimate interest**, such as stopping fraud, which fraudsters would never agree to.

cards.prompt: A recipe app's sign-up form has a pre-ticked box agreeing to share cooking habits with partners, with details in a long legal policy. Does this count as consent under the GDPR?
choices: No, since the GDPR forbids sharing personal data with any partner company
Yes, since anyone who objects can untick the box before signing up
Yes, since the long policy discloses exactly what is shared and with whom
No: pre-ticked boxes aren't consent, and the request must be in plain language
cards.explanation: The GDPR requires consent that is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, requested in clear, plain language, and it says silence, inactivity and pre-ticked boxes don't count. Leaving a box ticked is inactivity, so the untick option doesn't save it, and burying details in legal text isn't plain language. Sharing isn't banned outright; it needs a lawful basis.

cards.prompt: Under the GDPR, which of these can justify processing someone's personal data without their consent?
choices: Any processing the user hasn't actively objected to
Any processing described in the service's privacy policy
Detecting fraud, under the legitimate interest basis
Any processing that stays inside the company and isn't sold
cards.explanation: Consent is the most common basis for internet services, but not the only one: others include complying with other laws, protecting someone's life, and legitimate interests such as fraud prevention, which fraudsters would hardly agree to. Not objecting is silence, which isn't consent. A mention in a policy, or keeping data in-house, doesn't create a lawful basis.

cards.title: Opting out isn't free
cards.body:
If you dislike the tracking, why not stop using the service? Because that choice often isn't free. When most people treat a service as essential for social life, opting out isn't realistic; using it is effectively mandatory. Network effects make it worse: the more people rely on it, the more you lose by leaving, as with a professional network where recruiters look for candidates.

Platforms are also built to keep you hooked, with tricks from games and gambling. Walking away takes time and knowledge to understand the policy, and the means to miss social and work opportunities. That's a privilege. For many people, the surveillance is inescapable.

cards.prompt: Every parent at a school coordinates through one messaging app that tracks its users heavily. When a parent objects, a colleague says she can simply stop using it. Why does the chapter reject that answer?
choices: It doesn't: as long as the tracking is disclosed in the terms, leaving is a free choice
Leaving would cut her off from the other parents, so using it isn't really optional
It doesn't, as long as a rival app without tracking is available to her
Leaving is hard only because the app won't let her export her messages
cards.explanation: When most people rely on a service to take part socially, especially with network effects, opting out has a social cost, so using it is effectively mandatory. Disclosure in the terms doesn't make the choice free. A rival app doesn't help if the other parents aren't on it. And declining at all takes time, knowledge and privilege that many people don't have.

cards.title: Privacy as a decision right
cards.body:
Some say privacy is dead, since so many people post personal things online. That misreads the word.

Privacy doesn't mean keeping everything secret. It means choosing what to reveal, to whom, and what to keep to yourself. It's a **decision right**: in each situation, you pick your own spot between full secrecy and full openness. You might share your running routes with a club and your salary with no one, and tell your friends about a new relationship long before your boss. That freedom to choose is part of your autonomy, and sharing one thing doesn't give up your say over the rest.

cards.prompt: Someone argues that privacy is dead, since millions of people post intimate details of their lives online. What's wrong with the argument?
choices: Nothing: anyone who shares their life willingly has given up their right to privacy
It's wrong only because most posts are carefully curated and reveal little that's genuine
Privacy only concerns data held by governments, not what people choose to post
Privacy means deciding what to share and with whom; posting is using it, not losing it
cards.explanation: Privacy isn't keeping everything secret; it's a decision right to place yourself where you choose between secrecy and openness, situation by situation. Someone who posts publicly is exercising that choice, and sharing some things doesn't forfeit control over the rest. Whether posts are curated is beside the point, and the concern covers companies as much as governments.

cards.title: Rights moved to the company
cards.body:
When data is taken through surveillance, privacy rights aren't so much lost as transferred. The company in effect says 'trust us with it', and from then on it decides what is revealed and what stays secret.

It keeps most of what it learns hidden, because showing it would look creepy and hurt a business built on knowing more about people than rivals do. Intimate facts come out only indirectly, for example through ad tools that let a brand reach people who are deep in debt. Nobody in that group may be identifiable, yet they've lost their say over the disclosure. The company exercises their privacy right, to maximize its profit.

cards.prompt: An ad platform lets advertisers target 'people going through a divorce'. Advertisers never learn who is in the group. Has anyone lost privacy?
choices: Yes: the company, not the users, chose to make that intimate fact usable for profit
No, since nobody in the group can be personally identified
Only if an advertiser combines the group with outside data to unmask particular people
No, since users accepted targeted advertising in the terms of service
cards.explanation: Surveillance moves the decision about what to reveal from each person to the collecting company, which exposes intimate facts indirectly through targeting tools. Even if nobody can be reidentified, users have lost agency over that disclosure. Unmasking would make it worse but isn't needed for the loss. Accepting terms isn't meaningful consent when users can't see what's inferred about them.

cards.title: Plan for hurtful data
cards.body:
Many companies worry less about how intrusive their data collection is than about whether it seems creepy, so they manage that impression. Often badly. A fact can be accurate and still hurt: a shopping app that keeps suggesting baby clothes to someone who lost a pregnancy is right about the data and wrong about the person.

Assume any data may be wrong, unwelcome or inappropriate, and build ways to handle those failures. Deciding what's inappropriate takes human judgment; an algorithm knows nothing of it unless you explicitly program it to respect people's needs. So the people building these systems need humility: expect such failures and plan for them.

cards.prompt: A photo app automatically builds 'on this day' slideshows. Some users are shown photos of a relative who has since died. What does the chapter suggest the engineers should do?
choices: Nothing: the photos are all accurate, so the feature is doing exactly what it should
Drop the feature entirely, since any use of people's past data will upset someone
Build ways to handle such failures, since software can't judge what's painful
Ask users to accept the feature in the privacy policy, so complaints can be dismissed
cards.explanation: Data can be accurate yet hurtful, so systems should expect it to be wrong, undesirable or inappropriate and include ways to deal with that. Judging what's inappropriate is a human call that algorithms don't make unless built to. Accuracy isn't the bar, and consent clauses don't undo the hurt. The chapter asks for humility and planning for failure, not abandoning the data.

cards.title: An unprecedented shift
cards.body:
Privacy settings hand back a little control: you choose what other users can see. But the service itself keeps full access, and its policy usually lets it analyze your data internally far beyond what you see.

Moving privacy rights from people to companies on this scale is new in history. Surveillance always existed, but it was costly and manual; now it's automated and scales cheaply. People have long confided in others, like a patient in a doctor, but strict ethical, legal and regulatory rules limited how that information was used. Internet services gather sensitive data in bulk without meaningful consent, and users can't see what's done with it.

cards.prompt: Why does the chapter call the shift of privacy rights from individuals to internet companies historically unprecedented?
keyPoints: Surveillance used to be costly and manual; now it's cheap, automated and scalable
Older relationships of trust, like patient and doctor, came with strict ethical, legal and regulatory limits on using data
Internet services gather sensitive data at huge scale without meaningful consent, and users can't see how it's used
cards.explanation: Privacy settings help only a little: they control what other users see, while the service itself keeps broad access to analyze everything.

cards.title: Data exhaust or labor
cards.body:
Behavioral data is a byproduct of using a service, so it's sometimes called **data exhaust**, as if it were waste. Analyzing it then sounds like recycling.

It makes more sense the other way round. If targeted ads pay for the service, the activity that generates the data is a kind of **labor**. Some go further: the app is bait, there to get people to feed in ever more personal information. And the data is valuable. **Data brokers** quietly buy, merge, analyze and resell personal data, mostly for marketing, and startups are valued by user counts, that is, by how much they can watch.

cards.prompt: Behavioral data is sometimes called 'data exhaust'. Why does the chapter reject the term?
choices: It implies worthless waste, but if ads fund the service, producing it is a kind of labor
It implies a byproduct, but most behavioral data is entered on purpose by users
It overstates its value, since behavioral data is mostly worthless to companies
It's jargon that conveniently hides from users the fact that their data is being collected
cards.explanation: Calling it exhaust frames analytics as recycling waste. Economically, if targeted ads pay for the service, the activity that produces the data is a form of labor, and the app can even be seen as a lure for more data. Behavioral data is a byproduct of using a service, not typed in, and it's valuable: data brokers trade it and startups are judged by how many users they have.

cards.title: A toxic asset
cards.body:
Valuable data attracts people who want it. Governments may get it through secret deals, pressure, court orders or plain theft. Criminals and hostile spy agencies break in, and insiders leak. If the company goes bust, the data is sold with its other assets; if it changes hands, new management may not share your values.

So critics call personal data a **toxic asset** or **hazardous material**. Each time you collect it, weigh the benefit against the risk of it reaching the wrong hands. Think beyond today's government too: a future one may ignore civil liberties and force you to hand the data over. Building tools that could someday serve a police state is poor *civic hygiene*.

cards.prompt: Why do critics call stored personal data a 'toxic asset' or 'hazardous material'?
keyPoints: Governments may obtain it through secret deals, coercion, legal orders or theft
Criminals or hostile intelligence services may break in, or insiders may leak it
If the company goes bankrupt, the data is sold off with its other assets
New management may not share the values of the people who collected it
cards.explanation: So each collection decision weighs the benefit against the risk of misuse; data that's been purged can't be leaked, stolen or demanded.

cards.prompt: A startup stores detailed movement histories of a city's residents. The founders trust today's government to respect civil liberties. Why isn't that enough?
choices: It is enough, as long as today's laws strictly limit who may access the data
It is enough, as long as the data is encrypted wherever it's stored
Future governments may not respect rights, and could force it to hand the data over
It only matters if the startup also stores data about people in other countries
cards.explanation: Data collected now can outlive today's politics, so collectors must consider every possible future government; installing technology that could someday serve a police state is poor civic hygiene. Laws can change along with the government. Encryption doesn't help when the company holding the keys is compelled. The risk applies at home, not just abroad.

cards.title: Knowledge is power
cards.body:
Knowing a lot about people gives you power over them. Being able to watch others while staying hidden from them yourself is one of the strongest kinds of power there is. That's why totalitarian governments want surveillance: it lets them control the population.

Tech companies aren't openly after political power. But much of their data was gathered quietly, out of public view and beyond any oversight, and it gives them a great deal of power over people's lives anyway.

cards.prompt: How does accumulating data about people turn into power over them?
keyPoints: Knowledge about people gives power over them, which is why totalitarian governments want surveillance
Watching others while staying hidden from scrutiny yourself is an especially strong form of power
Tech companies gather much of their data out of public view, so they gain power over people's lives even without seeking political power

cards.title: Lessons from industry
cards.body:
The information age is reshaping economies and daily life about as deeply as the Industrial Revolution did. That revolution brought lasting growth and, in time, better living standards. It also brought foul air and rivers, cramped slums, brutal working hours and children toiling in mines.

Safeguards came only slowly: environmental rules, workplace safety, bans on child labor, food inspections. They made doing business more expensive, and society gained enormously; hardly anyone would go back. Data is this era's pollution, and protecting privacy is its environmental challenge. Future generations will judge how we handled it, as we judge those who ignored the smoke.

cards.prompt: What lesson does the chapter draw from the Industrial Revolution for the information age?
choices: Harms like pollution faded as economies grew, so data's harms will fade too
Safeguards raised business costs but helped society enormously; data needs the same
Its safeguards held back growth, which is a warning against regulating data
Rules should wait until a technology's harms are fully understood, as they did then
cards.explanation: Industrialization brought growth along with pollution and exploitation, and safeguards such as environmental and child labor laws came slowly, raised costs and benefited society hugely. Data is the information age's pollution, and protecting privacy is its environmental challenge. The harms didn't fade without rules, and the chapter urges confronting data's problems now rather than repeating that delay.

cards.title: Purpose limits and big data
cards.body:
The GDPR says personal data must be gathered for purposes that are specified, explicit and legitimate, and not used later in ways that don't fit them. What you collect must also be limited to what those purposes need. That's **data minimization**.

Big data runs the other way: collect as much as you can, combine it with other datasets, and explore to find new insights. Exploring means using data for purposes nobody had in mind when it was collected, which is exactly what the law rules out. The GDPR has changed online advertising somewhat, but it's weakly enforced, and the wider tech industry's culture has barely moved.

cards.prompt: Why does the GDPR's rule that data be collected for specified, explicit purposes clash with the big data approach?
choices: The GDPR limits only how long data is kept, so the clash is about storage costs
The GDPR bans combining datasets from different sources under any circumstances
There's no real clash, since the GDPR has transformed practice across the industry
Big data hunts for uses nobody foresaw, the opposite of purposes fixed up front
cards.explanation: Big data aims to collect as much as possible, combine datasets and explore for new insights, which means using data for unforeseen purposes; the GDPR wants purposes stated at collection. It doesn't ban combining data as such, and it's about purpose, not only retention. It has been weakly enforced and hasn't changed much industry culture.

cards.title: Weighing regulation
cards.body:
Companies that collect lots of personal data mostly oppose regulation, calling it a burden that slows innovation. They have a point. Think of health records: sharing them puts privacy at risk, but analyzing them together could lead to better diagnoses and treatments, and save lives. Rules that are too strict could block such breakthroughs.

So the question isn't simply more regulation or less. The opportunities have to be weighed against the risks, and striking that balance is hard.

cards.prompt: Why is it hard to decide how strictly to regulate the use of personal data?
keyPoints: Companies argue regulation burdens innovation, and that is partly justified
Sharing data such as medical records risks privacy but could lead to better diagnoses and treatments that save lives
Too much regulation could block such breakthroughs, so the opportunities must be weighed against the risks

cards.title: A change of culture
cards.body:
Laws alone won't fix this; the tech industry's attitude to personal data needs to change. Users are not metrics to push up. They're people who deserve respect, dignity and agency.

That means companies limiting their own collection and processing of data, to earn and keep the trust of the people who rely on their software. It means telling users plainly what happens to their data instead of leaving them guessing. And it means leaving each person in control of their own data, which is what privacy is, instead of taking that control away through surveillance.

cards.prompt: How does the chapter want the tech industry to change its attitude toward personal data?
keyPoints: See users as people owed respect, dignity and agency, not as metrics to optimize
Regulate its own collection and processing of data to earn and keep users' trust
Explain to users how their data is used instead of keeping them in the dark
Leave people in control of their own data instead of taking it through surveillance

cards.title: Privacy as a commons
cards.body:
Your control over your own data is like a national park. If nobody deliberately protects it, it gets ruined: a **tragedy of the commons** that leaves everyone worse off. Ubiquitous surveillance isn't inevitable, though; it can still be stopped.

A practical first step is to keep less. Collect only what you need, and delete data as soon as it's no longer needed instead of keeping it forever. Data you don't hold can't be leaked, stolen, or demanded by a government. In the end, thinking about the social impact of your work is part of doing the job.

cards.prompt: The chapter compares each person's control over their own data to a national park. What is the comparison meant to show?
choices: Like a park, personal data should be open for anyone to visit and use
Like a shared environment, it will be ruined unless it's deliberately protected
Like a park, it's already protected well enough by the laws in place
Like a force of nature, ubiquitous surveillance can't be held back
cards.explanation: Control over our own data is like a commons: if nobody explicitly protects it, it gets destroyed and everyone is worse off. It isn't something to open up for anyone's use, and the GDPR's weak enforcement shows existing laws aren't enough. The chapter insists that ubiquitous surveillance isn't inevitable and can still be stopped.

cards.prompt: A fitness app keeps every user's full GPS history forever, in case it proves useful for some future feature. What first step does the chapter recommend?
choices: Encrypt the history, so that keeping it forever carries no risk
Strip the names from the history, so nothing personal can leak
Keep only what a feature needs, and delete it once it's no longer needed
Ask users to renew their consent every year, then keep it all
cards.explanation: The chapter's first step is to minimize what you collect and purge data once it's no longer needed, since data you don't have can't be leaked, stolen or handed to a government. Encryption doesn't help when the company itself is compelled or breached with its keys. Location traces reveal a person even without a name. Renewed consent doesn't remove the risk of holding it.
